Section 12 · interview

Retired Engineering Director: Netflix Culture, Hiring, Meta Leadership, and Work-Life Balance

A retired engineering director who worked at Netflix and Facebook recounts how Netflix culture scaled, how he hired engineers, what he learned leading at Meta, and why a 2004 illness changed his view of work.

David's view: judgment, trust, and balance matter more than heroics and long hours

The host introduces David as a retired engineering director who worked at both Netflix and Facebook, and the conversation follows his 36-year career. In David's view, strong engineering organizations depend on three things: colleagues who are good to work with, a fair and objective way to record who did what, and a pace that leaves people a life outside work. He argues that engineering judgment matters more than LeetCode speed, that a new leader must earn trust before changing a team that already works, and that a serious illness in 2004 turned him against 24/7 work culture. Everything below is David's opinion or recollection from an auto-generated transcript, and several names and figures are unverified.

Source: 00:40–1:17:19 ↗

QHow did Netflix differ from the other companies David had worked at?

David

David says every earlier employer, from IBM through several smaller companies, tolerated prima donnas: very smart people who were hard to work with, who yelled at colleagues and customers, and who could not admit mistakes. He describes one 1990s engineer treated as indispensable, with a cubicle packed with junk, who avoided other people and fixed problems overnight while managers did not understand his work. When he quit, the company survived, and the rest of the team came to understand the area he had guarded.

At Netflix, David says, nobody was like that. The culture deck said the company did not hire brilliant jerks and would let go anyone difficult or unapproachable, however smart. David calls this revolutionary in the early 2000s and notes that the large tech companies he knows now work the same way.

His interview with Patty McCord, then chief people officer, who approved every hire at that small company, surprised him. David says she told him Netflix did not value 24/7 work and that he should impress the company with what he could do in an eight-hour day. David later watched a manager say he could not keep working around the clock. McCord thanked the manager, then told him not to do it again and to set up his team so that he did not have to. David calls that unthinkable in 2008 or 2009 and says he learned more about leading and collaborating from McCord than, he thinks, even from Reed Hastings.

David gives his own example. During early, unstable attempts at continuous deployment, a strong engineer remarked that David must enjoy having weekends off, because the systems would fail if the team stopped working. David told him in a one-on-one to take a vacation and said he did not care if things broke. The engineer took a week off, others rested too, and David says the team then stabilised the system quickly with its own approach.

David ends with Hastings. According to David, Hastings saw DVDs by mail as a stepping stone to streaming, which is why the company is not called DVDsbymail.com. Hastings was not a video expert but built a team of strong leaders and engineers to solve the problem.

Source: 00:40–07:59 ↗

QHow did the Netflix culture change as the company grew?

David

David first says the culture memo is aspirational. When people asked whether Netflix really worked that way, he answered that it described what the company aspired to be.

He then describes what failed to scale. Netflix credited the team, not individuals. When the company shipped on the PlayStation 3, David says, Sony's DVD division asked Netflix to stop because it had not designed the console for this, and Netflix carried on. Afterwards nobody named the foundational engineers; the credit went to Netflix. That worked when the company was small. As it took on many products, individual contributions got lost, and if engineers are not credited, he says, leaders collect the credit.

Netflix also had no engineering levels. Everyone was an engineer or a senior software engineer, and a business card could carry any title except manager, director, VP or chief. That suited an all-senior team. As it hired more juniors, David argues, teams contain strong, good and weak engineers, and without an objective way to tell them apart and reward wins, the best people leave. By the late 2010s he was arguing for levels. He assumes they have since been added, but he has been away for six years.

David adds that McCord interviewed almost every early hire and Hastings met a few new hires at a time, which could not continue as the company grew. When he left, he felt the memo suited a very small, aggressive, engineering-focused company.

What is the culture memo?
David

David describes a deck of roughly 15 slides, released around 2007 or 2008 by his recollection. Its ideas included no brilliant jerks, very smart people, inspiring people to sail the seas rather than telling them how to build a ship, top-of-market pay, and a "keeper test" under which the company fires aggressively. David calls it revolutionary at the time. In his reading it was about freedom and responsibility: hire excellent people, explain why the work matters, give context, and trust them to execute without micromanagement.

He adds that the talent was not limited to engineers. His HR partners challenged his hire and no-hire decisions, and he says he learned how to build a team from them.

Source: 08:28–10:17 ↗
If everyone was at the same level, how did Netflix pay people differently?
David

David says Netflix generally did not hire new graduates, though he found ways around that. Pay followed a concept of personal top of market, and the memo encouraged people to interview elsewhere. His own starting salary in 2007 was $175,000, which he calls solid for then. If Google had offered him $200,000 a year later, he says, his manager would have had to match it or let him go. Leaders therefore had to track offers and market rates.

David says this became unsustainable. An engineer matched to a double-pay offer could, three years later, earn three times as much as a peer doing similar work, with no performance review or context to explain the gap. In another case, five candidates Netflix had made offers to each received Facebook offers about 1.2 times higher, the memo said to match, and without leveling nobody could justify it. He argued with his leadership using year-over-year spreadsheets and believes Netflix fixed this after he left, since a large company needs pay ranges.

Source: 14:32–18:53 ↗
Source: 08:01–14:31 ↗

QHow does David identify really strong software engineers in hiring?

David

David says his hiring succeeded all the way up to Meta. Large companies such as Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft need structure and consistent standards, so they use a formal interview system. At smaller companies, when he made the hire or no-hire decision himself, he, three team members and HR interviewed each candidate.

He tells of a late-1990s candidate who had built driverless-train software. David was the last interviewer, and his 45-minute slot ran to 90 minutes, with two whiteboards covered in state transitions. He says her grasp of a complex system of interacting parts was among the best he had seen. Others gave her coding questions and she did fine, but the panel was lukewarm and his boss pushed back. David argued that the team was struggling to integrate disparate systems and needed her. They hired her, and he says she excelled. He claims his hiring record at small companies was close to perfect.

David knows his next view is controversial: he does not love LeetCode. He says it shows how fast someone can write code for a problem practiced many times. He accepts that at the volume Meta and Google hire, they have little alternative.

His alternative is an engineering foundation: understanding complex systems, strong technical intuition, and sound decisions without enough data. He has seen engineers from other fields do very well in software. He has also seen people who aced LeetCode and rehearsed system-design questions such as Google type-ahead get hired and then produce poor engineering, which he saw in their review packets. He believes this foundation is largely innate, like musical talent, and says he can help someone improve their software but cannot teach them to make good decisions.

His second story is about a project partner in graduate classes at San Jose State, taken in his 50s just before he joined Meta. She was finishing a master's in civil engineering, worked in wastewater treatment, and wanted to move into software. David was impressed by her analytical mind and command of statistics and wanted Netflix to hire her. Her take-home video-software task took three weeks and had rookie mistakes, so to help close the deal David suggested she teach the team something. She spent two hours at a whiteboard on wastewater treatment, and halfway through David realized he was watching a very complex state machine. A manager asked what sewage had to do with software but hired her, and later told David at a Meta event that she was doing very well. David says that when you see a brilliant engineering mind, LeetCode speed or building a scalable type-ahead does not matter, because those can be learned quickly.

David accepts that this approach does not scale at Meta or Google, where legal and policy problems would break it, so they set a bar and a level. His level advice is to take a lower offer: someone who was a 6 elsewhere and is offered a 5 at Meta should accept it and execute at the higher level, because bonuses, multipliers and refresh stock follow. An over-leveled hire who struggles has no clean fix. His rule is that when in doubt, go low and earn the quick promotion.

How do you spot that fundamental engineering skill? Is there a question you ask?
David

David says to interview the person, not the process. The wastewater candidate showed mastery of a hard engineering problem and explained it to engineers who knew nothing about it, until those who understood saw a finite state machine. He argues that many engineering systems, such as engines and other mechanical systems, reduce to states and transitions, though structural engineering differs.

Netflix would have hired her at a junior level, such as data analyst. As a full software engineer against the usual expectations she would have failed. A smaller company, he says, is flexible enough to hire and build up such a person.

Source: 29:16–30:51 ↗
Source: 18:55–29:15 ↗

QWho was the strongest engineer David worked with, and what made that person strong?

David

David names Giannis, though he usually avoids names. The captions garble the surname, so it is omitted here. They met in 2000 at InterVideo. Giannis had left the industry to teach signal processing in Greece, and in summer 2010 David brought him in during a break to help with ideas about parallel encoding. David says that work led to content-based encoding, which the whole industry now uses, and to an early patent.

Giannis later joined Netflix and, David says, took the idea further, in what the captions render as "convex all encoding", probably convex hull. David says it delivers the highest quality for a given bandwidth and is now the model at both Netflix and Meta. Giannis also built a cost-benefit model for codec evaluation. David sees his strength as forcing academic rigor into practice: decisions rest on tests across 10,000, a million or a billion videos, not on what two compressed videos suggest in theory.

Source: 30:52–32:59 ↗

QHow did David come to be recruited to Meta?

David

David says the early Netflix culture deck advised interviewing often to learn your market value. When Facebook contacted him in late 2017, as he recalls, he had not interviewed in about ten years. He went in, in his own words, a bit full of himself, citing how Netflix had built the highest-scale encoding platform. One interviewer told him Facebook could not solve its video scale problem with CPUs. David was floored, later thanked him, and realized he had understood video too narrowly. He got an offer and turned it down because he was not ready.

Soon after, Giannis told David about a Facebook offer and the custom chip (ASIC) work he would do. David saw a passion in him that he had not seen for a while. He thinks Netflix's culture, not built around individual contributions, may not have rewarded Giannis, and that the problems may not have seemed big enough to him. David says he did not try to talk Giannis out of it: as his boss he did not want to lose him, but as his friend he could not argue against it. David had been interviewing mainly to exercise his interview skills, but in the end he came to see Facebook's video work as a very hard problem. His team was solid and a successor was ready, so in 2019 he left Netflix, and Facebook offered him a job quickly.

At Netflix his encoding team had grown from one person to about 55, and trust grew with it. At Meta he took over a video processing team of 55 to 60 who did not know him. In an early meeting he talked about what needed work. A team member told him in a one-on-one that he had been there two weeks and was already telling the team what to do. David concluded he needed to stop talking and build trust, a skill he had never had to develop.

His lesson is that leadership is about relationships. If a team is broken, the leader's job is to fix it. If it is already executing well, the job is first not to break it and second to help it move forward, and he had jumped to the second step. David calls the saddest thing about Meta that it was his last job. He believes he would now be a much better organizational and engineering leader but no longer wants that responsibility, and he says he learned the most about engineering leadership there.

Concretely, what does building trust look like for a senior leader joining an existing team?
David

David says it meant slowing down and spending a lot of time in one-on-ones, asking questions, taking notes, and learning the system, the roles and the people. In a technical role, he says, a leader must understand why the team does what it does.

His first decision came when the team needed a manager. Many told him to promote an existing manager, but he did not know them and refused to decide just because it looked politically right. After taking time with them, he concluded an existing manager was the right choice. That manager had felt the role was his, so the relationship was difficult at first. David told him he was sorry for the delay but had needed to understand first, and that he was now confident in him. By the time the manager left Meta, David says, he no longer assumed the worst.

Looking back, David thinks his investment was still too small. He would tell his boss that for the first six months he was in school and that critical decisions would be made together.

Source: 41:30–45:24 ↗
Source: 33:02–41:28 ↗

QWhat was David's favorite work or project at Meta?

David

David first names bringing Netflix-level quality to Meta's scale, which he says succeeded. He then turns to COVID. He joined in late July 2019, and by March 2020 everyone was working from home. Meta planned for New Year's Eve from the summer because video traffic spiked for 24 hours. By April 2020, David says, every day looked like New Year's Eve in uploads, streams and live video. Systems that had never run at that sustained load were slowly bleeding out, with race conditions among the problems. He says the prime minister of India was addressing the country on Facebook Live, and he was terrified by the weight of it. The team worked from home, found the problems and resolved the race conditions. After about a month the systems and metrics held, and David says he was proud of that.

He also describes how his view of the company's value changed. He had first seen Facebook through a US-centric lens as a social app. He came to see what 3.5 billion customers means. By David's rough comparison, Netflix's roughly 300 million subscribers are the wealthiest 5 percent of the world by income, while Meta reaches the wealthiest 50 percent. He calls wealthy a loaded term, since at the bottom people live on about $68 a day. He says Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook are a lifeblood for small shops across India, and an Uber driver from Somalia in Seattle told him WhatsApp kept his scattered family in touch.

David says US debate about social media focuses on harms such as fake news and overlooks how much the products improve lives elsewhere. He believes the company changed lives by giving people a business, a platform to share and earn from video, and a way to stay close to family, and that it feels good to be part of that in a small way.

Source: 45:26–50:51 ↗

QHow did work-life balance change across David's career?

David

David says that in the late 1990s he worked hard for a visionary executive because the team was trying to catch up, not because anyone demanded it. At InterVideo, a startup, the expectation was 24/7. He arrived around 10:30 in the morning and left around 10 at night, sometimes at 2 or 3 in the morning, often seven days a week, chasing deals to lift the stock price after the IPO.

In January 2004 he fell ill on a Sunday and kept getting worse. On the Friday his wife took him to the emergency room, where, he says, a doctor said it was colon cancer, with a blockage that could kill quickly. He was in hospital for about three weeks with two surgeries and chemotherapy. It was stage three with lymph node spread, and he puts his five-year survival prognosis at about 25 percent. His children were two, four and seven, and he says the youngest barely knew him.

In hospital he decided that his way of working was wrong. He told his boss he still wanted the job but could not work that way, and he says that if a company threatens to fire you for not being there late, the best thing you can do is leave. He believes InterVideo used hours to cover for poor leadership. He calls work-life balance something thrust upon him, and he was determined never to be a leader who expects people to kill themselves for a job. Hearing at Netflix that the company did not value 24/7 work was a shock.

His advice is not to wait for cancer or a heart attack. Bake balance in early, take vacation, and leave the company alone for a week. If it cannot survive seven days without you, David says, that is its problem.

David says high-performance companies such as Meta and Netflix are often misunderstood. He recalls a Meta poster of a rocking horse that read, in effect, do not mistake motion for progress. He suggests agreeing with your boss on the most important work and telling the boss which tasks you will not do; if one matters, someone else must do it or priorities must change. Crunch time will come at big tech companies, but it should be the exception, planned in advance, such as a push in May and June followed by a vacation. He says balance is achievable even at Netflix or Meta, if the manager gives clear context.

Source: 50:52–59:03 ↗

QWhich job taught David the most, and why?

David

David says his last four jobs each contributed. The first turned him into a high-performance software engineer, performing by problems solved, not hours worked. The second gave him a video foundation. Netflix, he says, was zero to one, and there he learned leadership, hiring and firing, context setting and cross-functional work, which he brought to Meta.

What he lacked on arrival at Meta was an objective process for planning, reviews and performance. He calls the PSC performance cycle both his most dreaded and his favorite time of year. In his account, everyone writes a self-review, the manager builds a packet with feedback tied to goals, and managers then defend their engineers in calibration meetings. Each manager thinks their team is the best, David says, so the aim is to persuade with data about who deserves what level and who did what on a project. He valued getting each engineer's impact on paper. He says departing employees keep every performance package they were ever given.

David had heard horror stories about the performance cycle but found it mattered once inside. His greatest joy, he says, was giving a direct report a top rating, and he also valued helping people who were below expectations recover. He adds that he used to think he understood scale from books on sharding and microservices, but in his view those authors do not know scale at Meta's level. The most valuable thing he would bring to a new job is a system for objective planning, review and performance.

Source: 59:04–1:04:07 ↗

QIs there a top book that influenced David's career?

David

David chooses a late-1990s book he names as 12 Secrets to Microsoft Success; the title comes from auto-generated captions and was not checked. He says it described radical thinking at Microsoft. One idea was betting the company, which he says he saw at Netflix, Amazon and Meta when a big opportunity is worth risking the company on without going all-in. Another was good failure: in a healthy company, projects and people will fail, and what counts is how you fail, what you learn and whether the bet was reasonable and managed early.

As he recalls the book, Microsoft was the first company to say publicly that it aimed to hire the top 5 percent of software engineers, and it coined the term dogfooding. When the NT server was failing badly in the mid-1990s, he says, Bill Gates made the whole company move to it, which put the bugs in front of everyone and got them fixed. After rapid growth Gates also imposed a company-wide hiring freeze because people were working on things that did not matter, such as Microsoft Bob. Executives were forced to kill projects, and David says the bottom 20 percent were cut, which he thinks should have happened anyway.

David says Microsoft set early models for modern engineering leadership, and others borrowed from it. Before the 2022 crash he thought the hiring rate did not add up. During COVID everyone accelerated hiring and nobody slowed. He believes that had big-tech leaders read the book, they would have seen in late 2021 that hiring was out of control.

Source: 1:04:09–1:09:49 ↗

QIs there anything David regrets that others could learn from?

David

David says his first six years out of school were wasted at very large failing companies. He names Hughes, spun off from General Motors, and an IBM division sold to Siemens, both of which failed. He had a good salary and an easy job, thought only about the moment, and did not think about growth. He does not mean being ambitious about a vice-president title in ten years, just thinking about growth.

For software engineers in particular, he says, everything learned will be obsolete in about five years. When he joined Meta, the bootcamp and the whole development environment had been replaced; he had been proficient as a director, but when he later went to an individual-contributor role he found everything had changed. His way of staying successful, David says, is to keep pushing toward the edge and keep learning new engineering skills.

Source: 1:09:52–1:11:37 ↗

QWhat advice would David give himself at the start of his career?

David

First, work on hard problems. David says that if the job is not difficult, you are not growing. Once a role flatlines, he says, an engineer at a company like Meta, where moving internally is easy, should find another hard problem. Hard problems are what move engineers forward.

Second, company size does not matter, but everyone should work at a small company or startup at some point, ideally while young. He cautions against being too taken with the technology and says to work for visionary leaders who can also execute, since vision without execution goes nowhere. He cites Zuckerberg and Hastings as visionary, and says Hastings was one in 1999, when Netflix had four people. Leaders should make you dream of sailing the seas, not just cut lumber for a ship.

Third, plan for work-life balance deliberately from the first job. Work and life are in tension, he says, but the best engineering comes from people who love the work and also enjoy time off.

Fourth, start financial planning on day one, because as technical people succeed they earn more and, without a plan, will not know where it goes. David recommends a deliberate plan for spending and for short- and long-term savings, small regular contributions in your 20s, and no extended credit or debt. He says that by the early 40s this will not usually allow retirement unless you were lucky, as with an early job at Facebook or Netflix, but it can give financial independence, so you could take a lower-paying job. In his view a 401(k) alone and Social Security will not be enough for those who start late. He knows many engineers in their 50s who earned well but have no plan, and says a good engineer employed for 30 to 35 years has no reason not to retire comfortably. He says elsewhere that he is not a financial planner, so this is one person's opinion.

Source: 1:11:39–1:17:19 ↗

Section 13 · companion

Escalation, corroboration, and credible alternatives

Ethan Evans explains why leaders can resist evidence of a weak manager and how careful, truthful framing can make a difficult career conversation easier to hear.

QHave reports escalated problems with their managers to you, and why might a skip-level leader resist acting?

Ethan Evans

Ethan Evans says such escalations were common. He describes an uncomfortable incentive: accepting one report’s account can create three problems for the skip-level leader—deciding what to do about the manager, replacing and training someone if necessary, and covering the work in between. Dismissing the report as oversensitive instead makes the problem easier to delegate back to the manager. Evans presents this as a possible subconscious bias, not a defense of ignoring a valid concern.

He recounts discovering a leader’s poor treatment of women only after several reports accumulated and he spoke with affected colleagues. A lone earlier report might not have moved him, a failure he describes candidly. Multiple independently supported accounts changed his understanding. He therefore recommends corroboration when colleagues are willing to provide it; the speaker’s “mutiny” metaphor concerns workplace escalation and should not obscure the seriousness of the example.

Should a high-performing IC compare observations with colleagues before escalating?
Ethan Evans

If possible, yes. It first checks whether the problem is a broader pattern or a working-style mismatch. A colleague who works well with the manager may offer a useful adjustment; colleagues seeing the same problem may corroborate it. Shared dissatisfaction is not enough unless they are also willing to speak.

Evans proposes telling the skip-level leader that named colleagues are willing to share similar examples and asking the leader to speak with them. He thinks many leaders will do that, while explicitly refusing to guarantee it. The host flags the difference between casual complaints and formal escalation, including the possibility of retaliation or being wrong.

Source: 03:04–05:21 ↗
Source: 00:00–03:03 ↗

QCould you seek a move for business reasons instead of organizing an escalation?

Ethan Evans

Evans separates two approaches. If there is a genuinely plausible case that another role would make the engineer equally or more valuable to the organization, lead with that case and do not introduce the manager complaint. If the real need is incompatible working relationships, explain that blame-free and think several moves ahead about the choices the leader actually has.

He describes his own move at Amazon. His leader wanted to keep him in the current role, but Evans had another available role outside that leader’s organization as well as a preferred role inside it. Explaining that remaining where he was had ceased to be an available choice changed the decision from “keep him here or move him internally” to “keep him in the organization or lose him.” After weeks of resistance, the internal move happened quickly. The story depends on having real alternatives, not on inventing an outside offer.

Source: 04:35–08:06 ↗

QHow did you communicate those alternatives without sounding threatening?

Ethan Evans

He framed the situation in terms the leader would recognize. Both were vice presidents, and the alternative offer came from a senior vice president. Evans explained that he needed to answer and that once he gave his word, he would have to honor it—as the leader himself would. That let the leader understand the constraint without a blunt demand.

Evans recommends preparing the key phrase before a predictable conversation rather than improvising under pressure. The facts and commitment should remain true; careful framing changes how the other person receives them. Delivery matters too. The same statement about needing to consider one’s career can sound hostile or calm and understandable depending on tone and body language.

He acknowledges that some engineers dislike workplace politics. His argument is that leaders still have emotions, stress, and defensiveness, so understanding the human interaction helps a person communicate an honest need more effectively. He does not claim he has fully figured out how to teach the skill.

Were there three different roles involved?
Ethan Evans

Yes: the current role, the role he wanted inside the same organization, and another available role elsewhere. The host characterizes the alternative as leverage. Evans agrees with the underlying structure while emphasizing that he did not explicitly issue a threat; he stated the true consequence of accepting another offer and giving his word.

Source: 09:35–10:24 ↗
Source: 08:07–12:34 ↗

Section 14 · interview

Managing managers changes the consequences of small actions

A Meta senior manager explains why wider organizational scope requires new interaction habits.

QWhat skill gaps appear when a first-line manager steps into a manager-of-managers role?

Meta senior manager

The guest emphasizes learning how to add value to the managers who report to you. A more senior role changes which interventions help and which undermine the organization. He illustrates this with a skip-level meeting in which a newly promoted leader asks leading questions about an employee’s manager. The employee may start relying on the senior leader instead, while the manager feels bypassed and weakened.

The important failure is not simply having the meeting. It is overlooking how questions and judgments propagate through a management chain. Small actions become magnified across multiple relationships. The guest says these subtleties are often learned through observation and practice, not only from reading about management.

He expects some mistakes during the transition, just as new managers make mistakes when moving from individual contribution. A promotion decision should therefore consider the support around the person: whether their own leader can help them recognize and repair problems. Strategy and organizational design also matter, but early interaction errors can cause damage before those longer-term responsibilities become the main issue.

Source: 00:00–03:10 ↗

QHow do individual-contributor and management growth compare, and are they meritocratic?

Meta senior manager

He says that evaluation becomes more opaque at high levels in either path. In calibration discussions, a person may be associated with a valuable initiative without having been instrumental in its success. The same attribution problem applies to managers. A short review period can make it difficult to separate a persuasive account from a clearly demonstrated contribution.

Longer observation can clarify the picture: a leader who repeatedly produces good outcomes over several years is easier to assess than someone in one half-year cycle. He thinks some senior IC and first-line-management work is more visible to an outside observer, while higher-level work often requires access to the internal details and leadership chain.

He does not offer a simple verdict that one ladder is fair and the other unfair. His concern is insufficient evidence and accountability when the relevant impact is hard to trace. The resulting frustration is real for employees with limited visibility, and a desire for fairness does not automatically create the data needed to judge it.

Source: 03:12–05:49 ↗

Section 15 · interview

Make growth explicit, adapt your coaching, and remove friction

Laurent connects candid career alignment, fair evaluation, sustainable team leadership, and whole-problem ownership across Airbnb, Instagram, and Stripe.

QWhy did you choose to join Airbnb?

Laurent

Laurent had worked at Apple and Meta and decided developer productivity was the area he cared about: making engineers more effective at writing software. Moving to San Francisco turned his existing commute into roughly ninety minutes each way, which prompted a search. Airbnb combined people he liked, an office he could walk to, and a developer-infrastructure organization early enough to offer substantial work to shape.

He joined as one of two test-infrastructure engineers just as the broader effort was becoming multiple teams. The choice combined everyday quality of life with a technical opportunity; it was not a purely title-driven move.

Source: 00:44–02:43 ↗

QWhy transition from test-infrastructure IC work into management?

Laurent

One manager was responsible for several teams and more than fifteen people, leaving limited time for development and support. Laurent had already begun doing some of that work as tech lead. As his team grew toward six to eight engineers, many early in their careers, he thought a dedicated manager could support them better and improve delivery of the large project.

He pitched the need to his manager and offered to try the role with help. He began with two reports and later managed the whole team. His rationale was an organizational problem he could help solve, rather than management as the automatic reward for technical seniority.

Did managing former peers create uncomfortable power dynamics?
Laurent

Yes, so they addressed them openly. A colleague used the first one-to-one to test his judgment: recruiting had said an employee missed an assigned interview, so what would the new manager do? Laurent said he would first ask what had happened and establish the facts. The colleague considered that a pass; immediately punishing the employee would ignore possibilities such as a mistaken name or inaccurate email.

The anecdote illustrates hearing all sides before acting. Formal authority does not eliminate the need to investigate or earn trust with people who were previously peers.

Source: 03:55–05:38 ↗
How many managers would fail that test?
Laurent

He does not supply a percentage. Instead he criticizes treating management as one fixed style—tough, hands-off, or micromanaging. A directive approach may help a team of beginners and fail with experienced engineers. Good management requires adapting to the people and situation.

Source: 05:38–06:33 ↗
Source: 02:13–04:37 ↗

QHow did management change your experience of boredom at work?

Laurent

He treats boredom as a signal to examine what is wrong rather than simply tolerate it. Becoming a manager initially supplied intense learning: hiring levels, reviews, promotions, then building relationships and planning reports’ growth. Later he used his optimization instincts to improve the team’s working conditions.

He built a calendar tool to reduce fragmentation across his own and reports’ schedules. He also surveyed every team process in detail—meetings, planning, code review, and ways of working—to improve team health. The survey showed that everyone thought the long stand-up was useful for someone else, while no one actually benefited much from it. Changing that and other processes improved engagement and enabled more work with less time.

After a three-week wedding trip, he returned to find the team had planned the next quarter and assignments using the process they had established. That successful independence also left him bored. The next possible step was managing managers, but he did not feel ready and missed coding, shipping, and seeing the effect in production. He returned to IC work. The story frames a well-functioning team as success even when its manager then wants a different challenge.

Source: 06:33–11:51 ↗

QDid learning management make you a better IC afterward?

Laurent

Yes. Understanding reviews, career framing, progression, and promotion helped him navigate his own work, while coaching and difficult-conversation skills improved his leadership of others. He continued developing those abilities after returning to IC work. The benefit was a new set of skills rather than merely privileged knowledge of a committee.

Source: 11:36–12:57 ↗

QIs pitching the organizational value a good way to move into management?

Laurent

He broadens the lesson to alignment with a manager. People often hesitate to say they want promotion, expertise, or another kind of growth, then present a year’s activity at review time and hope for the desired result. He prefers an ongoing conversation that gives both employee and manager the chance to shape the work.

As a manager he used a “surprise factor” exercise: before delivering the review, each person wrote the expected rating and promotion result, and they compared that with his own written assessment. Agreement was the desired outcome. He got close to full agreement without reaching it. The purpose was reducing uncertainty and demonstrating whether communication during the year had been effective.

Can a positive review surprise also reveal a problem?
Laurent

Yes. Someone doing excellent work without knowing it may be unnecessarily cautious. A manager should have coached that person toward greater confidence and productive risk-taking earlier rather than leave them anxious until an unexpected promotion. Positive surprises, like negative ones, can reveal missed communication.

Source: 15:04–15:53 ↗
Source: 12:37–15:01 ↗

QWhen should ICs try management, and what are the tradeoffs?

Laurent

Laurent found the experience invaluable and encourages people who are considering it to try. It is a different job, so direct experience can reveal both useful skills and whether the role fits. Even a poor outcome can teach something about one’s preferences and limitations.

He recommends starting with an intern while warning that one intern is a highly biased sample. Interns often need more direction and inspire strong personal attachment, unlike a group of experienced ICs. He recalls emotionally difficult intern calibrations because mentors strongly wanted their own intern to succeed and confused a return offer with proof of good management. A manager can do a good job even when the correct decision is no return offer. He helped run calibration sessions to make that distinction clearer and the process less frightening.

Source: 15:31–18:53 ↗

QWere your own promotions and reviews free of surprises?

Laurent

He first says he was often surprised, then clarifies that the surprises were ratings rather than promotions. He sees that as evidence he had not understood the system and its values well enough. In one transition, he expected his technical leadership to support a staff promotion but switched into management near the end of the cycle.

The rating came back as meets expectations because he had spent too little time in the new role. He found that frustrating and redirected his effort toward reaching the next management level. He now thinks he should have explicitly asked beforehand how the timing of a role change would affect review and promotion.

Did the role change reset your progression?
Laurent

He does not give a universal reset rule. Companies, organizations, and even local teams can develop informal calibration rules about tenure, role transitions, or unusually fast promotions. Some later become codified and communicated; others remain unstated until someone asks.

As a manager he challenged rules he found demotivating or inconsistent with the intended values and tried to explain calibration transparently to ICs. His bar was that an employee unexpectedly observing the meeting should be proud of the work, not feel that unfair decisions were being plotted. Because he sees management as representing company interests, strong value alignment was necessary for him to defend the decisions sincerely.

Source: 21:17–23:46 ↗
Source: 18:38–21:38 ↗

QHow can a manager or IC successfully challenge an established rule?

Laurent

He starts by examining the biases a process may introduce and what makes employee evaluation fair. Gather evidence, understand the reason behind the rule, and make a case. The history may reveal a useful constraint you did not see—or an old precedent that no longer fits.

He generally prefers initial one-to-one conversations to a public confrontation in calibration. In front of a group, people can interpret disagreement as a threat to reputation and become defensive. Understanding those human dynamics improves the chance of changing the process rather than just winning an argument.

What if a senior leader proposes penalizing people for a low count of code changes?
Laurent

He would first clarify what the penalty and metric actually mean. Different contributions make lines of code or pull-request counts a poor general measure of engineering output. At Stripe, concerns about that kind of measurement motivated a more useful inquiry into the journey of a code change: thinking, writing, CI, review, iteration, and merge.

Time spent in different stages can reveal organizational friction. If one area takes twice as long to land changes, investigate why—perhaps a poor codebase or inefficient process. He explicitly rejects equating fast shipping with high productivity or slow shipping with low value. The metric is a diagnostic signal that helps remove obstacles, while a manager must assess the complete contribution, including noncoding work.

Source: 26:29–30:00 ↗
Source: 23:50–26:42 ↗

QWhat stood out about Airbnb’s engineering culture?

Laurent

He found it harder to explain why low-level infrastructure mattered in a designer-led company, but that different professional perspective also produced useful ideas. During a period of reliability problems, the company drew on people with emergency-response backgrounds to improve crisis management.

He admired the rigor and practices that resulted and took some to later jobs. His positive example is the willingness to ask which other field already handles a similar kind of problem well, rather than assuming all incident-management expertise must originate inside software engineering.

Source: 29:51–31:48 ↗

QWhy return from Airbnb to Meta?

Laurent

After four years, the original stock grant’s vesting cliff affected earning potential, which was one reason to consider a move. He also thought he wanted to be an infrastructure generalist after working across testing, compute, databases, and other areas. He later decided that self-description was wrong, but it led him to Instagram at the time.

A disruptive July Fourth on-call experience prompted him to pursue reliability improvements. He knew Facebook already had tools addressing patterns Instagram still suffered from. He pitched adopting and partnering around that infrastructure to his skip-level manager and joined the resulting cross-organization project.

How did you find the right Facebook partners and gain buy-in?
Laurent

He was paired with a Facebook-side IC whom he regards as an exceptional technical leader. She brought the right people into discussions and secured the Facebook-side alignment. He credits her role rather than suggesting he independently knew and persuaded every partner.

Source: 33:44–34:42 ↗
Source: 31:29–34:42 ↗

QHow did you choose a mentor, and what makes coaching useful?

Laurent

He sought people who were thoughtful, direct, able to challenge him, and capable of changing his mind in a way he could engage with. Those traits need not belong only to engineers; he sees them in his current coach too.

The Facebook-side collaborator had those qualities and helped him examine where his problem framing was wrong. A useful measure of coaching is whether the person actually changes how they think and act afterward, rather than repeating the same behavior. Although the host asks about his explicit mentorship pitch, the answer mainly explains selection and value; it does not provide a detailed script for making that request.

Source: 34:42–36:24 ↗

QWhat were your first impressions of Stripe?

Laurent

He encountered strong engineers, as he had in other jobs, and especially valued the emphasis on collecting and analyzing data before deciding. He considered its metrics-and-experimentation culture even stronger than the Meta culture he knew. That judgment is his personal comparison. It suited his own enjoyment of measuring progress and success.

Source: 35:57–37:31 ↗

QHow did your technical-lead role grow across a much larger developer-infrastructure organization?

Laurent

He joined to lead build, test, and tooling across roughly thirty-five engineers, in areas he knew well. His first task was gaining credibility with people who already understood the local systems. He deliberately avoided citing his previous employer as automatic proof that a design should be copied or rejected.

Instead, he embedded with teams for about a month on concrete work, learned their rhythm, and asked questions that helped people reconsider decisions themselves. He made an exception for urgent incident response, where direct instructions could be necessary. Over a year he worked across most parts of the group and met the people repeatedly.

Leading a larger organization also meant accepting that each specialist knew more about their own domain than he did. He could guide with a broad developer-productivity perspective without pretending to be the local expert everywhere. Later he took two-to-eight-week assignments with different people or teams to bootstrap work and make it sustainable. Documentation and automation should allow the work to continue without requiring his constant presence or interrupting vacations. Being the sole keeper of secrets was the opposite of success.

Source: 37:31–43:24 ↗

QHow did you scale yourself across so many engineers?

Laurent

Set realistic expectations: no leader of seventy people can know every current project in detail. Maintain contacts who can supply information, and be willing to say that you do not know yet and will return with an answer by a stated date. He believes confident misinformation damages trust much more than candid uncertainty; his emphatic career warning expresses that concern rather than a literal rule applying to every mistake.

He used office hours instead of attempting weekly meetings with everyone, providing enough capacity that people could get time within the week. Because about half the group was in Europe, he shifted his schedule to begin around five-thirty in the morning and create overlap with both European and American colleagues. Scaling still required direct communication and accessible help, just through a different structure.

Source: 43:03–45:52 ↗

QWhat do coaches commonly get wrong?

Laurent

They identify with a single style—hands-off, highly directive, or hint-based—and apply it to everyone. Laurent instead uses the person’s mastery, confidence, motivation, and immediate situation to choose the help. In his early Facebook onboarding work, three of four mentees progressed normally while one stalled; learning a situational-leadership model helped him adjust and unlock that person’s performance.

He describes moving from direction for a beginner, to encouragement and shared decision-making, to support, and finally delegation as skill develops. The assessment is specific to a skill and situation. A technically capable person can still need explicit help with something unfamiliar. A tired parent calling at four in the morning about an iPhone problem needs clear steps, not generic praise or a lecture on systems. Choosing only the supportive stage leaves many other needs unmet.

What specifically went wrong with the stalled boot-camp mentee?
Laurent

Laurent assumed every newcomer belonged in the same low-skill, high-motivation starting stage. This person had already studied the documentation extensively, knew more than the others in some areas, but had lost confidence and motivation. Repeated direction interrupted rather than supported learning.

After listening to what the mentee had done, he offered less prescriptive advice and more support. Performance improved sharply. The correction came from assessing the individual’s actual state, not applying more of the same technique with greater intensity.

Source: 51:18–53:03 ↗
Source: 45:52–51:16 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 47:48–51:16 ↗

QWhy can the senior-to-staff transition feel harder than the next transition?

Laurent

He sees a mindset change at staff: independently find the problem, choose and pitch it, solve it end to end, explain the result, and document it. Senior engineers can be strong designers and implementers while still working on problems identified by someone else.

In his model, later levels continue that complete cycle with larger scope rather than introduce the same fundamental autonomy shift again. This is his account of the distinction, not an assertion that later promotions are easy or mechanically determined.

Source: 53:03–54:45 ↗

QHow can someone stuck at senior begin finding staff-level problems?

Laurent

Laurent channels frustration with real workflows. In developer productivity, each awkward command, window, delay, or repeated manual task can expose an opportunity. Stripe’s friction logs institutionalized that observation: work through a flow, record the steps with images, and ask why each action or loading screen exists.

He could identify dozens of possible improvements during a code change, then group related problems, rank them, and address the valuable ones. The goal is not merely collect annoyances. Look for families whose removal improves the overall experience. He also imagines a tired user: where would that person get confused, stuck, or drop off?

He applies the same habit beyond software. Repeated business travel can be an opportunity to refine the process each time until the twentieth trip is smoother than the first. The staff habit is continually learning from use, identifying friction, and deliberately improving it.

Source: 54:33–57:20 ↗

QWhich book most influenced your career?

Laurent

He names Kim Scott’s Radical Candor, which helped him handle difficult conversations while building trust, motivating, and coaching reports. He appreciated its explanation of the manager-employee relationship and ideas he thinks many experienced managers still miss. This is his personal recommendation grounded in his transition, not an external review of the book.

Source: 57:24–59:19 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning of your career?

Laurent

The field changes even faster than it appears. Laurent contrasts interview practices he encountered early—such as estimation puzzles—with much more technical and monitored interviews he observes in the interview’s 2025 context. The examples illustrate change rather than establish a universal hiring policy.

He recommends staying curious and regularly reading technical news and discussions. He follows highly ranked weekly Hacker News items and has used that habit throughout his career. He expects the skills and experience of software engineering to keep changing substantially and would encourage his younger self to remain attentive rather than assume the original model of the job will persist.

Source: 58:49–1:00:17 ↗

Section 16 · interview

Support people, stay close to the product, and make tradeoffs explicit

Fiona Fung reflects on management, mentorship, product feedback, and the choices that took her from Microsoft to Meta and Anthropic.

Fiona Fung’s account connects three habits: make the partnership with people explicit, experience the product yourself, and treat culture as something people enact. The examples span developer tools, Marketplace, VR, and her early experience with Claude Code. Her comparisons describe those teams at the times she worked on them; they are observations from a career, rather than permanent descriptions of entire companies.

Source: 00:03–00:18 ↗

QHow do you balance an important project against team health?

Fiona Fung

First establish whether the situation really warrants an exceptional push. Fung remembers Marketplace lockdowns or war rooms that concentrated people on an urgent objective. That focus could be valuable, but it had a real cost to morale. Leadership should discuss the tradeoff deliberately with the team, rather than allowing the cost to remain implicit.

One war room had a growth target as its exit condition. The team initially imagined that a few fixes might achieve it, but the effort continued much longer than expected. In hindsight, she would have assessed the likely duration more realistically, discussed the effect on team health, and explained the journey and expected length up front. A measurable target alone did not make the sustained intensity manageable.

How long did that war room last?

It felt like at least two months. There were physical rooms in Menlo Park and Seattle, and at one point the team launched 75 experiments at once. The contrast with a week-long launch push is central to the lesson: the team did not understand the duration when it entered the arrangement.

Source: 02:25–03:04 ↗
Source: 00:34–02:24 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 00:49–03:04 ↗

QWhat changes when you become a manager of managers?

Fiona Fung

The relationship becomes a partnership between people who each bring management skills as well as technical skills. When she first supported managers, including a TypeScript manager she considered an exceptional compiler engineer, she asked what each person did well and how they could divide responsibility. Supporting another manager creates more opportunities to complement strengths.

Delegation also needs a balance of trust and verification. If delegation removes too much contact with the project, the supporting leader can lose touch. She asks managers for fast feedback and transparency about both successes and problems. The useful conversation is the one that exposes where help is needed; a reassuring report that everything is fine can conceal the very issue the partnership should solve.

Source: 03:05–05:30 ↗

QHow can a mentor make the relationship useful?

Fiona Fung

Begin by asking the mentee what they want from the relationship and what success would look like after three or six months. An explicit goal gives both people a way to use their time effectively.

Also distinguish mentoring from coaching. In her description, mentoring combines listening with advice drawn from experience. Coaching acts more like a mirror, helping the other person discover answers within themselves. Clarifying which mode the person wants can change how the conversation should work.

Should the mentee or mentor drive the relationship?

The most effective relationships she has seen start with goals set by the mentee. The mentor contributes experience, advice, and resources, but the person seeking mentorship should state what they hope to gain.

Source: 06:23–06:54 ↗
Source: 05:32–06:21 ↗
Two modes of helping someone grow
ModeWhat the helper contributesUseful starting question
MentoringListening, experience, advice, and resources.What do you want to gain over the next few months?
CoachingA mirror that helps the person find their own answers.What do you need to understand or discover for yourself?
Source: 05:40–06:54 ↗

QWhat should an individual contributor do with one-on-one time?

Fiona Fung

Put routine status reporting into an asynchronous channel. Fung uses messages or a shared, living one-on-one document where either person can add updates.

Use the live conversation for topics that benefit from interaction: something the person wants to learn, a deeper discussion of their work, or a product question worth exploring together. The point is to reserve the scarce meeting time for conversation, while making the operational updates available separately.

Source: 06:55–07:41 ↗

QWhy did you leave Microsoft for Facebook?

Fiona Fung

She had friends enjoying Facebook, but repeatedly wanted to finish the work in front of her at Microsoft. Her final project there involved JavaScript and TypeScript, and she cared about helping the team deliver TypeScript 1.0. A former Visual Studio colleague, who became her first Facebook manager, contacted her in late 2014 about building a product around buying and selling in groups. She joined in 2015.

The commerce mission mattered for three reasons. Used goods could make a meaningful affordability difference for people with tighter budgets. Reuse could give existing goods a second, third, or fourth life. A selling platform could help a local business begin without first needing a physical store. Marketplace also represented a new kind of connection for her: meeting new people, rather than only reconnecting with people she already knew.

After eleven and a half years at Microsoft, she also wanted to test and broaden her engineering ability outside an ecosystem in which she had become comfortable. The move combined a mission she cared about with a chance to learn beyond familiar tools and practices.

Source: 07:41–10:58 ↗

QWhat stood out about the difference between Microsoft and Facebook?

Fiona Fung

Both offered talented colleagues who cared about their work. The clearest difference in her example was speed: early Marketplace shipped weekly updates, while the Visual Studio work she remembered used roughly four-week sprints. Even those four-week sprints had once felt short compared with earlier development cycles.

Facebook also felt much smaller at the time. She appreciated the expectation that a problem was everyone’s responsibility, regardless of role. Her example is a willingness to lean in and help, rather than to treat an issue as belonging exclusively to someone else.

Source: 10:59–12:12 ↗

QWhy is using your own product so valuable?

Fiona Fung

Her first job involved using Visual Studio to build Visual Studio, so daily product use was built into the work. It gave her empathy for users and a feel for the product’s condition. She carried that habit into Marketplace, keeping items to sell so that she could experience the workflow herself. Meeting users also made the effect of the work tangible and motivating.

On VR and related device teams, she used Quest devices and early Ray-Ban products. For a manager who rarely gets to write code, using the product can be a way to experience what the team is building and to contribute directly. She describes reproducing a difficult floor-height bug at home and collecting logs as a small piece of maker time.

Peterman adds that a leader’s report can bring attention to a bug that was already known but had lost urgency. Fung emphasizes another effect: team members notice when a leader uses and cares about their product, and that can build rapport.

Source: 12:14–15:34 ↗

QHow do you make frequent product use sustainable?

Fiona Fung

Integrate the product into something you enjoy. She used VR for exercise, watching movies, and knitting while watching. Enjoyable everyday use creates repeated exposure without making the activity feel like a chore.

At the time of the interview, building Claude Code with Claude Code made that feedback loop part of her day job and let her ship production software again. She also mentions continuing to submit Meta product feedback after leaving.

Leaders can add structured product sessions. On her last VR team, she and her product and design partners tried nearly ready features together on Fridays and gave fast feedback. That complements daily use with a regular opportunity to inspect what is approaching release.

Source: 15:37–17:26 ↗

QHow can an engineering leader work well with product management?

Fiona Fung

Start with the shared objective of the leadership group and the strengths each person brings. Because there will be more work than people, agree explicitly on who owns which pieces and divide the work accordingly.

Using the product also improved her partnership with product managers. Their one-on-ones could become substantive product conversations grounded in something they had actually experienced. The discussion links partnership and product knowledge: an engineering leader has more to contribute when they stay close to what customers use.

Source: 17:28–18:31 ↗

QWhat does kindness contribute to an engineering organization?

Fiona Fung

She connects the principle to the pandemic, when device teams were trying to ship Quest 2 and develop Ray-Ban products without normal access to offices, labs, and colocated specialists. People were doing difficult work while also coping with pressures at home.

A personal example made the principle vivid. Her grandmother was in a Canadian care facility that she could not visit. Staff could arrange only limited FaceTime calls, and a rare available slot conflicted with a one-on-one she had promised to attend. The person she supported readily accepted a last-minute cancellation. What may have felt like a small accommodation to him had a large effect on her.

The lesson is that a colleague’s private circumstances are often invisible. Kindness is a practical way to work with people whose full situation you do not know, while the team is trying to accomplish difficult things together.

Source: 18:32–21:25 ↗

QWhy did you choose Anthropic?

Fiona Fung

She was happy working on VR and Horizon OS at Meta and was not conducting a broad search for a new job. The choice she describes was essentially joining Anthropic or staying in a role she already enjoyed.

Using an internal AI tool to build useful work tools showed her that AI was already changing her own workflow. Conversations with Anthropic employees then drew her to their mission orientation, emphasis on safety, and sense of shared responsibility. She likens that attraction to the mission that had drawn her to Marketplace. These are her reasons for the move and impressions of the organization at that time.

Source: 21:26–23:12 ↗

QDid Facebook’s culture change as it grew?

Fiona Fung

Yes. She treats culture as a living thing expressed through actions, rather than a statement on a wall. Growth changed the company, although she still saw strong commitment to the mission within teams such as VR.

When new employees asked which team would give them the most impact, she also asked what they were passionate about. That question restored a dimension that could disappear in a comparison focused only on career impact.

How should someone choose between greater impact and work they care more about?

Have an honest conversation with yourself about what motivates you. Impact, learning, and working with good people can matter in different proportions to different people; she does not prescribe one universal winner.

Share those priorities with your manager. When supporting someone new, she asks what they want from the partnership, what has worked or failed before, and what is important to them. An explicit discussion is more useful than either person guessing the other’s priorities.

Source: 24:36–25:43 ↗
Source: 23:13–24:35 ↗

QWhat stood out during your first two months at Anthropic?

Fiona Fung

She saw the mission and responsibility toward society expressed in onboarding, which made it feel more substantial than an interview slogan.

The speed of the Claude Code team also stood out, even compared with the Marketplace period she remembered as fast. Broad internal use supplied a rapid cycle: build an idea, launch internally, get feedback from employees, release publicly, and keep learning. Her concern as the team grew was preserving that agility and speed.

Source: 25:45–27:21 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 25:55–27:21 ↗

QWhat feedback most changed your career?

Fiona Fung

It was feedback on how she received feedback. Her instinct as an engineer was to debug the situation immediately: ask questions, replay what happened, and determine how to improve. Someone pointed out that giving constructive feedback was already uncomfortable, and her questions could make the person feel they had to justify it.

She changed the first conversation to listening and learning. Questions could wait until another day, after she had reflected. The distinction is about timing and the experience of the person raising the issue: a sincere wish to understand can still feel like a demand to defend the feedback if it arrives too quickly.

Source: 27:23–28:43 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning of your career?

Fiona Fung

Enjoy the experience while it is happening. Work and life move quickly, and the moments that later feel like the good old days are also the moments you are living now.

Source: 28:44–29:08 ↗

Section 17 · interview

Rebuild trust and align expectations when joining a team

Selected passages on senior onboarding, rebuilding relationships/trust, concrete peer expectations, feedback, and role-fit conversations.

QWhy did you ask for a demotion at Meta?

Igor

Igor joined at senior staff and felt he had to acquire deep technical context, relationships, and trust quickly enough to perform alongside experienced peers. He describes a much longer ramp than the title alone suggests: an external hire can initially know less about the environment than an intern who has already spent a few weeks there. The higher the expected scope, the more layers of competence and context there are to rebuild.

After about a year and two months, his own assessment was that he had reached something closer to staff-level effectiveness. Performance pressure made that gap feel risky. His description of the company’s performance environment is his experience at the time, rather than a statement of current policy.

He also discovered a preference for the work in the E5–E6 range: coding, debugging, designing, and mentoring. The senior staff role involved more leadership, meetings, and design documents, with less direct coding. He asked whether he could drop a level, understanding that existing stock and compensation made this awkward. He was told that staying in the same job category while reducing the level was not supported by the process available to him.

What made you think you were below the expected level?

Much of it was his own comparison with other senior staff engineers, although he later confirms that he also received feedback. He stresses that capability is continuous and multidimensional, rather than a set of perfectly discrete levels. His desire for a change was also about enjoying the work, not simply judging himself incapable.

Source: 03:56–06:34 ↗
Did you try to escalate the request?

He asked and received a negative answer; he acknowledges that more escalation might have produced an exception. He instead chose to explore returning to Google, where he had spent fourteen and a half years before joining Cruise and then Meta. That was a familiar environment and an available alternative.

Source: 06:37–07:31 ↗
Source: 00:37–06:34 ↗

QWhy had the senior role worked at Google and Cruise?

Igor

At Google he joined as a junior engineer and grew through repeated promotions, including attempts that initially failed. The senior staff promotion followed a substantial project on a team where he had already spent years. Expertise, familiarity, and credibility had accumulated together.

Cruise also required a difficult first-year ramp. Over time he found a role that combined coding, mentoring, and broader technical guidance. He was happy there before the accident and subsequent company disruption he describes led him to leave.

What made the Cruise and Meta ramps different?

Cruise was smaller, with less infrastructure to learn and more unclaimed work that needed an owner. In his Meta organization, the space for senior people felt crowded, so finding suitable scope was harder. He explicitly limits that observation to the organization he experienced.

Source: 09:35–10:37 ↗
Source: 07:32–09:34 ↗

QWhat would you change about your onboarding?

Igor

He spent too much time trying to build foundational knowledge by reading documents before doing enough actual work. In retrospect, he would learn and build in parallel: take a task, get his hands dirty, and acquire the relevant context while making progress.

He had not changed companies often, so this form of onboarding was new to him. He also felt the management team had limited experience ramping senior external hires because many senior employees had grown inside the company and already understood its basic machinery.

What could the manager have done to help?

A concrete example of how another senior external hire had recently ramped would have helped. He does not present the problem as management neglect: they tried to support him, but neither side had an established recipe.

Source: 12:13–12:52 ↗
Source: 10:39–12:12 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 01:03–12:52 ↗

QDoes moving companies become harder for senior individual contributors?

Igor

He has seen Google colleagues leave and return after a move did not work out. Such stories are harder to hear because people tend to share successes more readily than failures. He also suspects repeated moves could build the skill of ramping in a new environment; his own limited experience should not be treated as proof that every senior move will fail.

Source: 12:53–14:18 ↗

QDid anyone give you feedback about the level gap?

Igor

Yes, although he does not share the private details. He gives a project example: work he expected to take two weeks became much more complicated. Even if he completed it successfully, he did not think its scope would justify E7. Underestimating complexity and selecting insufficiently broad work were different problems that combined in the same project.

Source: 14:18–15:24 ↗

QWould returning to Google also restore your old team context?

Igor

No. The people and infrastructure would be new. The advantage was familiarity with the company’s operating patterns and culture, rather than retaining all of the specific knowledge and relationships from his previous role.

What cultural difference affected you?

In the Meta organization he observed, aggressive deadlines could be imposed repeatedly, missed, and then extended. He thought the resulting pressure could lose credibility: people learn to discount urgency when the deadline repeatedly appears artificial.

He contrasts this with the Google environment he remembered from much earlier, where exceptional pressure more often accompanied a concrete reason. He explicitly does not know whether that comparison still describes Google, and says he did not personally feel much pressure at Meta. The concern is about the pattern he observed around him, not a universal company ranking.

Source: 16:04–19:06 ↗
Source: 15:24–16:04 ↗

QWas returning at L6 instead of your former L7 straightforward?

Igor

It required work from the recruiter because the usual return process supported the same level or a higher one. A request for a lower level could raise questions about why the person wanted it and whether they would accept the lower compensation.

He explicitly reassured the recruiter that he understood and would accept a significant compensation reduction. They made the arrangement possible in his case. He does not claim to know how his hiring manager interpreted the request.

What concerns might a hiring manager have?

He speculates that a manager could wonder whether there were undisclosed problems behind the move. These are possible questions he imagines, rather than accusations or information about what actually happened in the hiring discussion.

Source: 20:33–21:24 ↗
Source: 19:09–21:24 ↗

QHow did the return hiring process work?

Igor

The recruiter sent openings, he spoke with several hiring managers, and he pursued the team that seemed to fit best. He then spoke with engineers and the manager’s manager.

Despite having been away for about three and a half years, he did not have to repeat the normal interview process. There was a discussion of whether returning at L6 would require a coding interview because a more senior role might have involved less coding, but he received an exception.

He does not know whether that was a general return policy or a special arrangement for him. The process described is one person’s experience.

Source: 21:25–23:14 ↗

QWhy are you willing to discuss this publicly?

Igor

He is generally open about positive and negative experiences, but also emphasizes the security that makes his openness possible. He does not depend on an employer for a work visa, has access to health insurance through his spouse, has grown children and no mortgage, and can afford time without work.

Those conditions reduce the consequences of losing a job after speaking publicly. He would not automatically advise someone with different constraints to disclose their workplace challenges. His willingness to share comes with a clear acknowledgment of privilege.

Source: 23:17–25:08 ↗

QWhat changed between pursuing promotions and pursuing a lower level?

Igor

Earlier in a career, it can be difficult to imagine what a role several levels above actually feels like. Experiencing the progression clarified his preference: his happiest work involved a relatively small team, substantial coding and debugging, design, and mentoring. A higher title was less valuable to him once its daily work became concrete.

Source: 25:12–26:20 ↗

QWhat did strong senior peers do that you felt you lacked?

Igor

He warns against combining everyone else’s strengths into one imaginary competitor. One colleague may be strong at presentations, another at communication, and another at leadership. Comparing yourself with the whole group can create an impossible standard.

He thinks that with enough time he could have become fully productive at E7. He simply was not enjoying the process and did not have to continue it. Friends and family questioned leaving before being forced out, or declining to seek the same level elsewhere. His response separates an ability to do something from a desire to spend his life doing it.

Source: 28:49–30:41 ↗

QIs there a mentorship story you particularly remember?

Igor

An intern he hosted when he was around L4 later joined full time and eventually became the manager of that team. Igor had moved to another project by then, so he did not report to his former intern. His lesson is straightforward: do not underestimate an intern’s potential.

Source: 42:27–43:11 ↗

QWhat advice would you give your earlier self?

Igor

Ask whether the work matters to the company and who needs it. He remembers working on projects whose purpose was unclear to him and that leadership later shut down. Choosing useful work is a more concrete guide than remaining on a project only because it has been assigned.

What can a junior engineer do if the project seems unhelpful?

Talk to other managers and look for a better project where internal movement is practical. He found movement easier at Google than at an earlier employer, and cautions that the advice depends on the company. He explicitly distinguishes his own experience from reputations he has only heard about.

Source: 47:39–49:00 ↗
Source: 46:49–47:37 ↗

Section 18 · interview

Barbara Liskov: Make Foundational Contributions Visible

Selected passages on presentations/writing as sources of recognition and why foundational work can become invisible.

QWhy do some names and ideas become better known than similar work?

Barbara Liskov

Asked why Paxos became more familiar than Viewstamped Replication, Liskov recalls Lamport’s explanation that he gave the talks while she implemented the work. She acknowledges his presentations and papers as a source of visibility. When the host wonders whether the catchier name also helped, she agrees that it is a appealing name without treating naming as a proven causal explanation.

Source: 18:32–20:38 ↗

QWhy did some people question the significance of your Turing Award work?

Barbara Liskov

Liskov first challenges the host’s assumption that only she faced negative comments. Her husband happened to read those comments online; she thinks other recipients may have encountered similar treatment if they looked.

Her more interesting interpretation is that some of the work had become so fundamental that people could no longer imagine the previous world. Even her graduate students had not fully grasped that abstract data types and the modular-programming mindset had to be invented. A specific protocol is easy to identify as an invention; a way of thinking that permeates ordinary practice can become part of the unnoticed background.

She therefore viewed the dismissive comments, despite their intent, as a kind of compliment to the broader research community that created those foundations. The impact had become difficult to see precisely because the ideas were taken for granted.

Source: 30:39–33:43 ↗
