Section 19 · interview

Werner Vogels: Learning Culture, Mentorship, and Communication

Selected passages on problem discovery, postmortem culture, mentoring, writing as leverage, recognition, and communication.

QHow do you find the problems that matter most?

Marc Brooker

Brooker recommends looking broadly rather than optimizing only the volume of one’s own code. Customers reveal work they find difficult, investments they are making, and operational chores they wish did not distract from their businesses. Technical trends supply another input: faster networks, storage, compute, multicore systems, and GPUs can make previously impractical designs possible. Changes in the wider world create openings too.

Source: 01:02–05:31 ↗

QWhat makes a good postmortem?

Marc Brooker

Begin by understanding what actually happened, rather than fitting the event to an existing bias. If that is impossible, the difficulty itself identifies missing observability, logging, metrics, or simulation capability. Then examine causes at several levels: the code defect, why testing missed it, why the testing approach or assumptions were inadequate, and which team or organizational decisions shaped those conditions.

Source: 11:33–16:56 ↗

QWhy should a team with weak postmortem habits invest in them?

Marc Brooker

The choice is where to spend engineering time: improving the product or fighting the same fire repeatedly. A weak culture may lack a sufficiently clear focus on outcomes and customer experience. Standards need not be identical everywhere; durability-critical systems deserve especially high standards, while another product may deliberately accept more defects to optimize other goals. The important distinction is an intentional tradeoff.

Another failure mode is normalizing operational heroics. A team that stays up all night, tolerates constant pages, and fixes every emergency may feel admirable from inside, yet spend its strongest ownership and expertise on an expensive repeating break-fix cycle. The corrective move is to redirect that energy into understanding and removing causes. Preventing recurrence creates time for deeper product improvements.

Source: 18:56–23:45 ↗

QWhat would you say to a new engineer frightened by those higher expectations?

Marc Brooker

He does not expect a new graduate to know everything immediately. Employers and early-career engineers both benefit from people succeeding, so organizations must build a supported learning path. First customer conversations can be scary; mentorship, feedback, guardrails, and progressively larger experiences make them learnable.

He compares this with other professions where much practical learning occurs on the job. What changes is the emphasis of the learning, not the fact that graduates need it. Leaders must rethink the career ladder rather than simply hire beginners and demand expert performance. He acknowledges uncertainty while remaining optimistic about the scale of opportunity.

Source: 40:35–44:21 ↗

QWhy write so much as an engineer?

Marc Brooker

Writing lets expertise travel across both people and time. A product, individual mentorship, and talks all spread knowledge, but an old written explanation can still help a reader a decade later. He values writing as a multiplier rather than merely as a visibility activity.

It also sharpens the writer’s thought. Putting an idea into prose forces a depth and clarity that speech or slides may not. Brooker sometimes writes with no intention of publishing. He appreciates Leslie Lamport’s stronger case for formal mathematics while seeing prose as an accessible starting point. Sharing ideas, preserving them, and understanding them better are separate but compatible motives.

Source: 50:12–53:51 ↗

QWhat do you say to engineers who see documentation as busy work?

Marc Brooker

Ask what the writing is for and whether it operates at the right level of the problem. Brooker does not find every design notation useful; he criticizes UML as focusing on a semantic level that did not help his own work. A document can be valuable because it preserves a decision for future readers or helps reason through a difficult, hard-to-reverse design or API choice. Routine, reversible choices do not all warrant the same process.

For important designs, recording the rationale also distinguishes careful decisions from temporary guesses made without data. Future engineers can reconsider arbitrary choices with new evidence while taking more care to understand the reasoning behind deliberate ones. The amount of prior thought matters alongside the result. Writing for that purpose is a skill worth developing even if the activity is not naturally enjoyable.

Source: 53:52–57:54 ↗

QHow do you balance doing the work with discussing it?

Marc Brooker

He sees both extremes as failure modes. A deeply capable person who never communicates could have more impact by sharing and could miss important problems by staying inside an IDE. Someone who only talks could make their advice more relevant by returning to practice.

Brooker personally spends roughly seventy-five to eighty percent of his effort practicing and the remainder teaching or communicating. Strong colleagues vary from approximately ninety-ten to fifty-fifty; he offers these as observations rather than an optimal allocation formula. Dedicated communicators can have a different job, provided they remain curious and honest about what they do and do not know. During fast change, he would lean somewhat more toward practice without severing contact with the outside world.

Source: 57:57–1:02:34 ↗

QIs it better to be overrated or underrated?

Marc Brooker

For the long term, he would choose underrated. Being overrated may feel good but is difficult to sustain. Sports and crafts expose the gap between appearance and capability quickly; engineering can leave room for qualitative perceptions longer. The careers he admires are built on honesty about actual knowledge and skill, not on maintaining an inflated image. This complements his recommendation to communicate useful expertise rather than hide it.

Source: 1:02:36–1:04:30 ↗

QWhich AWS engineers do you admire, and why?

Marc Brooker

He highlights retired colleague Al Vermeulen, whose work included major contributions to S3 and database design. Brooker remembers debating fine points of Paxos with him around 2010 while also seeing him discuss executive-level cloud strategy and explain what the business should build. He admired the ability to move across those levels without losing depth.

More generally, he respects colleagues motivated by useful work and customer impact rather than celebrity. Breadth, detail, and purpose together form the example he wants to follow.

Source: 1:04:33–1:07:20 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself when first joining AWS?

Marc Brooker

Be a little bolder about moving when learning and impact begin to taper. He loved his early teams in EC2 and EBS and was more hesitant to leave than he now thinks ideal. He made about four substantial organizational changes and suspects a few more might have been better, rather than recommending constant movement.

He would repeatedly ask what he is learning, whom he is learning from, and whether another environment would help him learn more quickly. Following curiosity has been both useful and enjoyable in his own career.

Source: 1:08:41–1:10:32 ↗

Section 20 · interview

Charlie Marsh: Honest Communication and Building a Team

Selected passages on honest communication, user trust, founder/team fit, and choosing trustworthy partners.

QHow do you balance a provocative headline with honesty?

He opposes misleading clickbait. The aim is communicating the most interesting true parts effectively. Lying can attract attention but destroys the basis for a useful relationship with users.

Source: 11:58–12:42 ↗

QWhat about charts with a truncated axis?

He rejects deceptive chart presentation and then emphasizes the real benchmark difficulty: caches, project selection, and unrelated native builds can change the observed result. No single graph captures every situation. That does not remove the obligation to give users an honest sense of performance; he admits his own team may sometimes get the balance wrong.

Source: 12:44–14:34 ↗

QDid willingness to walk away give negotiating leverage?

He agrees that he had a strong position while declining to portray himself as an expert negotiator. He emphasizes aligned, supportive investors and little pressure beyond suggestions to grow more aggressively. That positive experience was fortunate; he recognizes other founders can have different relationships.

Source: 1:08:53–1:09:56 ↗

QWhat surprised you as an engineer becoming a first-time founder?

He distrusts universal startup advice because successful founders can give contradictory instructions and survivorship bias hides alternatives. Choose principles suited to the team and the life you want. Remote work let him hire a team he could not have assembled in one location, despite real benefits of meeting in person. Fundraising optimized for trustworthy partners, reasonable terms, and getting back to work. He did not force a cofounder relationship merely because it was recommended, though he later felt the absence of a peer sharing the burden.

How did you compensate for founding alone?

He leaned on his wife, consulted the early team, and built relationships with other founders. Each source of support has limits, including how much to place on family or employees. He also chose to work extensively himself without requiring everyone to do so: he wanted people to succeed during normal hours and be rewarded for useful performance. His advice is to make the actual culture honest and deliberate, rather than imitate a fashionable schedule.

Source: 1:14:50–1:17:54 ↗
Source: 1:13:48–1:14:50 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself after graduation?

Trust decisions made for sound personal reasons, while remaining aware that hindsight can make a lucky path look inevitable. He worried that choosing Khan Academy cost him big-company experience and compensation; he now values the experience he actually wanted. He would not pretend to know how the alternative would have gone.

Could the broader ecosystem exposure have been essential?

He agrees and adds his earlier startup experience. That company did not achieve all its ambitious drug-discovery goals, which briefly made him question the years invested. Being an early employee taught him both how a company develops and technical lessons later used at Astral. In retrospect the experiences connected to building tools he loves. He recognizes that this reassuring account comes from a path that worked well, rather than proving every disappointment will produce the same payoff.

Source: 1:20:34–1:21:55 ↗
Source: 1:18:56–1:20:34 ↗

Section 21 · interview

Thariq Shihipar: Manager Updates and Professional Visibility

Selected passages on preparing manager updates, honest communication, intentional writing, and public professional visibility.

QHow much glue writing, such as launch posts, updates and design docs, is now written by LLMs at Anthropic?

Thariq

Thariq's rule of thumb is that if you would be happy to show someone the prompt, you can send them the output. Often the prompt just collects context. Before each one-on-one, Thariq has Claude read Slack messages, GitHub messages and PRs and compile a report of what Thariq did. The manager lacks that context, and Thariq is comfortable with them knowing the prompt.

For data readouts, Thariq suggests showing you have read the result, for example with small edits or a sanity check of the numbers. For a pitch or new concept, people want to know you believe in it. Even if Claude's idea is excellent, Thariq would say that Claude generated it and that Thariq thinks it is great. What people dislike is feeling misled.

Some writing depends on individual words. Anthropic's internal essays arguing for a direction are generally human-written, and Thariq says having Claude write your essay is looked down on, because every word should be intentional.

So routine writing is AI-written but human-reviewed, and novel thinking stays human?
Thariq

Thariq agrees and adds that writing is a way of thinking, so if you need to think more about a readout, summarize it yourself. Gathering context is different: no one will hold it against you, and acknowledging the shortcut is good.

Source: 42:48–43:46 ↗
Source: 39:00–42:47 ↗

QShould software engineers post on Twitter or X to build visibility?

Thariq

Thariq says to share your work externally as much as you can, though some employers do not allow it; side projects are an option. Before joining Anthropic, Thariq worked with different companies, built things, and wrote and talked about them. Thariq says this increased their "surface area of luck", and that the bar is much lower than people think.

Thariq says they give this advice to many people and almost none follow it, while everyone who did is in a job they are excited about or running their own company. The recipe: ignore your resume, choose an interesting project, work hard and lock in, then ship it and write about it. There will be reasons not to, but if the first attempt fails, do it again.

Twitter may not be the right place; Reddit or Hacker News might fit better. The goal is to find people who like what you do. People want high-quality content, which is a lot of work, and Thariq says there is no shortcut such as asking Claude to run your Twitter account. Engage authentically. Thariq compares it with going to the gym daily: simple, disciplined and easy to quit, and Thariq says they have not seen anyone who kept trying fail.

Can you give an example of expanding your luck surface area?
Thariq

Thariq describes how they got the job at Anthropic. Thariq did a fellowship at Good Fire, an interpretability AI company, doing applied research on using interpretability to make better products, and agreed up front that the goal was to share what Thariq built.

Thariq built an interpretability visualization and posted it. It got about 500 likes, which was big at the time. Several people saw it, some sent direct messages, and Thariq got an intro into a role at Anthropic. The project took about a month, and Thariq was paid for it.

Thariq says there is no shortcut: do interesting, novel work, work hard and be proud of it.

Source: 58:52–1:00:55 ↗

Section 22 · companion

Ambition, impact, and the limits of promotion checklists

A host and CTO debate how to make valuable work visible without reducing career growth to a transactional promotion checklist.

QShould an engineer organize a career around promotion or around developing useful behaviors and impact?

Guest

The guest strongly favors impact over title. In evaluating advancement, he wants to see important outcomes rather than an attempt to negotiate a checklist whose completion mechanically triggers promotion. A person can technically satisfy a stated activity while performing it in a way that adds little value; that leaves the underlying reason for advancement unmet.

He also acknowledges a personal reaction: repeated attempts to pin leadership down on rewards can feel transactional and annoying to him. That is his perspective as a leader, not a guarantee that all managers respond alike. His substantive argument is that genuine impact remains what should be recognized.

Source: 00:00–02:34 ↗

QHow should quieter engineers balance impact with making their work visible?

Guest

The host challenges a pure impact-first account: good engineers can be weak at communicating their results and may lose out when promotion decisions depend on people noticing. He distinguishes useful visibility from cynical self-promotion.

The guest agrees that visibility matters. Engineers need contact with people who understand important challenges, coordination with collaborators, and recognition of their capabilities so others can entrust them with bigger work. His distinction is the purpose and framing of the communication: making work understandable and coordinating it can lead to different behavior than trying to brag about oneself.

Updates should also recognize collaborators and thank the team. That makes the contribution legible without implying only the sender mattered, helps others feel valued, and supports the trust required for leadership. The host observes that two motives can produce superficially similar updates; the guest emphasizes how much the message centers the individual versus the work and other people.

Source: 02:34–06:34 ↗

QDoes the loud high performer often get promoted sooner than an equally strong quiet colleague?

Guest

The host argues that persistent lobbying can win extra attention even when both people have real impact. The guest says outcomes depend on organizational culture and that his own culture tries not to reward that behavior. He admits there are edge cases where lobbying earns consideration simply by keeping someone top of mind.

He does not advise abandoning ambition. He wants ambition expressed as a desire for greater impact: ask whether you are working on the most important problem, what you could learn, and where you could contribute more. A hardworking engineer can otherwise spend extraordinary effort on a low-priority task and still miss the outcome they sought.

Making those aspirations known and asking for opportunities are valuable conversations. What he opposes is reducing the relationship to contractual boxes followed by a demand for promotion. The debate therefore retains a real tension: the host worries about unequal recognition, while the guest prefers impact-centered visibility and managerial judgment to promotion bargaining. Neither establishes that recognition will always perfectly match contribution.

Source: 06:34–09:28 ↗

Section 23 · interview

Michael Novati: Reputation, Feedback, and Cross-Team Influence

Selected passages on internal newsletter visibility, cross-team reputation, managerial feedback, leadership relationships, and broad influence.

Build motivation through user relationships

Michael Novati

Socially, Facebook was a product everyone had heard of and had opinions on. Novati could get plenty of feedback about what people liked and disliked, and found it motivating to build something people cared about. Novati adds that the company went through ups and downs, even during the tenure.

Source: 02:49–04:15 ↗

QWhat does Novati think of "move fast and break things," now that the culture has changed?

Michael Novati

Novati describes having been "the move fast and break things person" at the time and still likes the framing. In Novati's reading, the "break things" half was partly an outside perception, and Facebook did not want to tell the public that people were recklessly breaking everything. The original spirit was breaking norms: first-principles thinking, trying things from scratch, not following trends for their own sake. It was not meant as causing havoc.

Novati still thinks it would be a fine motto today. At a larger, more mature company, though, even the smallest bug can cost millions or tens of millions of dollars, so Novati can see why the company dropped it.

Source: 05:52–08:28 ↗

QDid the culture change over the years, given that Novati started when there were about 200 engineers?

Michael Novati

Novati describes an extremely engineer-driven culture. Designers and product managers had to win engineers over, because work an engineer would not build did not get built. Nearly all internal tools were written in-house and used by employees, which set an engineering-first tone that Novati loved.

Novati sees the 2012 IPO as a turning point. The stock fell afterward because people asked how Facebook would make money, a question that had barely come up in the first three years. As the company grew, Novati developed a more mature view: ad optimization, cost savings, and efficient infrastructure became more important. Early on, senior engineers argued out designs head-to-head, largely independent of management. By the end, VPs of two teams more often negotiated and the result percolated down.

Source: 07:39–10:23 ↗

QWhat was the internal newsletter that made Novati well known, and why start it?

Michael Novati

It was called "the weekly Novati", a weekly post on the Notes product, Facebook's blogging feature. Notes had no owner when Novati joined in 2009, so Novati improved it at hackathons, adding rich text to what had been plain text. The change was an 11,000-line diff, so large that Novati had to organize an in-person meeting to review it. Novati also used the product constantly, as part of Facebook's dogfooding habit.

A few slightly controversial posts about product building drew traction, so Novati posted more regularly, often off the cuff. Facebook was adamant about staying on the Menlo Park campus, while startups such as Stripe and Uber in San Francisco were drawing employees away. Novati wrote repeatedly about it, including a post proposing a South San Francisco office, and that office later opened.

Would Novati recommend an internal newsletter like that today?
Michael Novati

Overall, Novati says, no. There was no strategic reason to write it. It came from Facebook's value of being open and transparent: Novati wanted to strip away pleasantries and look at products honestly, for example admitting when a product grew through luck and not substance. Novati contrasts this with startups and boot camps that treat a little traction as proof they built something great. The posts had nothing to do with performance reviews or influence.

The cost was friction. Novati once openly called out that engineers with titles such as network engineer or data engineer could not move between teams as easily as software engineers. Novati did not realize it was a sore point behind the scenes, and executives said the post did not help and that they now had damage control to do. Novati's lesson is that an off-the-cuff style has consequences, though Novati still tries to be direct and open on Reddit and LinkedIn.

Source: 18:56–22:11 ↗
Did HR ever ask Novati to take posts down?
Michael Novati

Nothing took the form of a takedown order, Novati says, but HR did give feedback. One post covered which companies were poaching Facebook engineers, and Uber was then offering very large stock grants. HR pointed out it might unintentionally encourage people to explore other jobs. Novati had not thought of that and says such off-the-cuff posts may not have been worth the friction.

Concerned, Novati messaged Zuckerberg directly. Zuckerberg was fine with it and encouraged Novati to keep posting.

Source: 22:13–23:34 ↗
Could Novati really message Zuckerberg directly and get a reply?
Michael Novati

Yes. Facebook was small when Novati joined, and Novati dealt regularly with the executives. When leaving, Novati messaged each executive one-on-one, including Chris Cox, and says they replied with thanks. Novati felt a relationship with all of them, formed from interacting genuinely while the company was small, and got to know Zuckerberg best, partly outside work. Novati has not spoken with many of them in the past couple of years as Facebook has grown.

Source: 23:35–24:26 ↗
Source: 16:01–18:55 ↗

QWhich engineers impressed Novati most, and why?

Michael Novati

The product infrastructure team, which built PHP abstractions that evolved into today's React framework. Novati watched the framework go up brick by brick and saw those engineers as a different type, a specialty that was not Novati's. The person most like Novati was Evan Priestley, who Novati says was the top committer before Novati. Priestley wrote the internal code-review suite essentially alone, and it was later forked and open sourced (the captions render its name unclearly).

Would Novati choose Priestley or four regular senior engineers for a new product team?
Michael Novati

Priestley. Novati then qualifies it as context-dependent. Being called a coding machine is not magic: it comes from hard work, from holding a lot of code in memory, and from attention to the littlest details. Novati says that on Oculus firmware, productivity would be slow at first. In a comfortable codebase where everyone has ramped up, Novati would pick the coding machine. For something truly new, a more diverse group may bring more flexibility and creativity. A coding machine, Novati says, makes things happen that people thought impossible.

Source: 31:45–33:26 ↗
Can Novati give an example a team of seven senior engineers would not have finished?
Michael Novati

Novati's canonical example is a framework called Preparables. A component had a data-fetching function and a rendering function, so all data could be fetched in parallel before rendering. It was later replaced by async/await and more modern approaches. Thousands of classes used it, and Novati manually and relentlessly refactored every one away, roughly three to six thousand by Novati's estimate, until the parent class was gone. It took several months and was a solo effort.

A second project removed every direct PHP endpoint hit on the server in favor of the routing framework. Neither was the company's top priority, Novati says, and without personal drive they would have consumed resources better spent on new products. One person doing them made all engineers' lives easier by removing legacy frameworks.

Source: 33:28–36:19 ↗
Source: 29:50–31:42 ↗

QWhat impressed Novati about the React-framework engineers, whose archetype differed from Novati's?

Michael Novati

Novati files them under the specialist archetype: people very good at one stack. Another example is an engineer who was one of perhaps ten people in the world who deeply understood email protocols, including the practical side of spam and routing. Novati likes a sports-team analogy: on a baseball team every player can play most positions reasonably, yet you want distinct roles and mutual respect for each player's place. Novati respects those engineers and sees the team as exceptional when it has different kinds of players.

Was it that they solved problems others could not?
Michael Novati

Yes, Novati says, and their abstractions were especially impactful because every engineer used them daily. Novati's own cleanup work also eased everyone's life, so there was some similarity. Their frameworks cut the mental overhead of tasks such as fetching data. Novati notes that an elegant, fast, easy-to-use API is very hard to design, and that making things simpler can be more work than writing a lot of code.

Source: 46:30–47:27 ↗
Source: 45:06–46:29 ↗

QNovati has said about 30 percent of time went to the team and 70 percent to self-directed projects. How does that work?

Michael Novati

Novati frames it as being a senior engineer on a team of about ten while spending more than half the time on codebase-wide initiatives: cleanups, refactors, a new framework, one-off help, and emergencies. The 30 percent was a share of mental focus, not a slice of the eight-hour day. Novati was on the team all day, reviewing code, bouncing ideas off junior engineers, mentoring them toward promotion, and writing features the team had queued. Novati also joined product meetings and assessed feasibility of what product managers proposed. The volume of code from team work was that of a senior engineer.

How did Novati manage the relationship with the manager, given that most bandwidth went elsewhere?
Michael Novati

Novati often, though not always, reported to more junior managers and acted almost as a peer who helped them manage the team. The skip-level manager usually did the performance reviews, and Novati effectively reported to that skip unofficially. Novati met a VP monthly for the whole org and the skip every two weeks. On the org chart Novati reported to a frontline manager, but in practice Novati was a dotted-line resource for senior people, "a weapon of the org" that went wherever needed.

Source: 49:40–50:59 ↗
Source: 47:30–49:38 ↗

QHow did Novati transition into IC7, solving the hardest problems for the whole org?

Michael Novati

Novati says output was already at coding-machine level from day one. What improved was taste and judgment. As an example, there were two forks of the task tool on the same data source, one fast and streamlined, one bloated with features and slow. In a week or less, Novati merged them into one with the speed of the first and the features of the second. Novati told no one, posted to the whole company that the tools were merged, and says this could not be done now.

Everyone congratulated Novati, but the lesson was that surprising hundreds of users with changed URLs was not the best way. Novati had not understood the consequences for teams. Over many large changes, some too fast and some buggy, Novati kept the same speed while improving judgment: how much to change at once, what other people will feel, and which spots are sensitive. That accumulation of judgment and taste is what crosses the line into IC7, Novati says. Advice on building it depends on context: talk to a manager, then a skip-level manager, then a very senior engineer in a similar org.

So high productivity and initiative let Novati take on extra work and become known for it?
Michael Novati

Yes, Novati says, but judgment and taste matter more than the code. They extend to the push process. Facebook had no continuous integration then. If something broke in production, the pushing team had to ship a fix, and an engineer who broke too much lost its trust, which would hurt a coding machine. Novati built that relationship, and more than once said a change needed to land and that if it broke the site Novati would resign. Novati had burned credibility before, so had to be very sure of the fix. An engineer who simply writes a lot of code, without years of built-up trust, could not get away with it.

Source: 54:31–56:28 ↗
Would Novati have resigned if it had broken again?
Michael Novati

Novati thinks so. The statement puts so much pressure on Novati, perhaps a personality trait, that Novati triple-checks every line and thinks through every odd case.

Source: 56:30–56:54 ↗
Source: 51:00–54:30 ↗

QWhat do taste and judgment mean for a software engineer?

Michael Novati

Novati likens taste to the patina on a cast-iron pan, built up in layers of history. Some people have stronger instincts early, perhaps from upbringing or from experience outside code such as dancing or sports. In general it takes experience. Novati's second image is a speed skater: you cannot read a book, put on skates, and be fastest. It takes years of feeling the ice at different temperatures and the difference between a skate used once and twice.

Novati sees too many people early in their careers trying to jump ahead, like entering the Olympics before building that feel. That is okay, Novati says, and nothing is wrong with them. The advice is to put in practice and reps, get feedback, iterate, and have the grit to keep going; without feedback, practice does not improve skill.

Is taste about how to design software, or about which problems are worth solving?
Michael Novati

Both, for different people, Novati says. A product manager's taste is mostly about what to build, built by shipping many things and watching some fail. Novati says the exceptional ones have shipped mostly things that failed or were mediocre, and learned at each step (a loose, unmeasured claim). For an engineer, Novati says, taste applies to the code itself and to strategies for moving fast.

Source: 59:16–1:01:04 ↗
Source: 56:55–59:14 ↗

QNovati was touching everyone's code. Did other teams give feedback, and how was it handled?

Michael Novati

Yes. In one case Novati refactored an old framework in the live version of a team's tool while that team was building a newer tool and carefully maintaining backward compatibility. They had many diffs in flight, and the refactor caused merge conflicts. They wanted it reverted. Novati had not paid attention to that, and the lesson is to be careful where teams are mid-migration on complex, longer-term work.

Did anyone object that Novati added something without owning its maintenance?
Michael Novati

That never came up, Novati says. The philosophy then, which Novati reports Kent Beck also described recently, was that every line you write you are responsible for. If you are willing to be woken at 3 a.m. to fix your code, you can skip tests. If you want to work nine to five, write more tests so the code is stable while you are away.

Novati did not refactor and forget. Sometimes two years later an automatic bug would be assigned because Novati had touched the code last, and Novati fixed it as now Novati's. Novati had no territorial conflicts and did not step on people's product judgment. Novati compares it to surgery, learned the hard way through early over-aggressiveness: finding the line between disrupting people's day-to-day work and still getting the cleanup done.

Source: 1:01:47–1:04:18 ↗
Source: 1:00:06–1:01:46 ↗

QAs engineers get more senior they are pulled into more meetings. How did Novati protect focus time?

Michael Novati

Novati minimized meetings. When calendar invites arrived without context, Novati asked what they were for and pushed back on many. Novati skipped standups unless relevant, for example during a crunch to ship within a month, and did not attend ones that were social chitchat. Novati was strict about time and chose teams deliberately, valuing managers who understood that their job is to help reports perform exceptionally. Novati's managers protected Novati from unnecessary meetings so impact could be highest.

Novati admits being too arrogant at times. Novati recalls walking out of a meeting or two after deciding it was no longer useful, and now regrets it, feeling bad for whoever ran the meeting.

Did HR ever ask Novati to be nicer?
Michael Novati

No, Novati says, because it was not a table-flipping situation. Novati had good relationships with the product managers, who liked that Novati built and fixed things fast, including bugs that were not Novati's. Meta's product managers want things moving fast and watch every pixel. They would often give Novati permission to leave when a meeting no longer needed Novati. Novati describes the attitude as cutthroat about not spending time in meetings when Novati could be coding.

Source: 1:06:39–1:07:55 ↗
Source: 1:03:27–1:06:35 ↗

QHow did Novati develop the skill of picking problems that mattered, so the code was more impactful?

Michael Novati

Novati says first that Novati is not great at it and is still poor at prioritizing. Novati tended to pick things where Novati could already see the answer, so the only question was how fast the code could be typed. That is also why LLMs help Novati so much: the idea is in Novati's head and the tool gets it out faster.

Novati calls this one of the things that probably held back the career. When a manager asked for task A, and Novati could not see the answer, Novati did B through H instead. That earns a passing grade and is appreciated, but if A really mattered, the company's overall impact would likely have been higher had Novati done it. Novati frames it as a weakness, limited by what Novati can figure out how to do.

So the priority list was whatever Novati could crank out instantly, not full business value?
Michael Novati

Novati agrees and adds that if you crank out enough, it adds up and can have huge impact, but it is a different way of thinking about work.

Source: 1:10:08–1:10:19 ↗
Source: 1:07:57–1:10:08 ↗

QWhat did the IC7-plus engineers have in common?

Michael Novati

Novati says there was a common bar regardless of archetype, whether coding machine, specialist, or fixer. Everyone showed extremely strong diligence and conscientiousness, and was sharp. Novati cites a straight-A school record and a sense of being fairly smart, yet acknowledges that many in the group are probably smarter. In a room, a newly proposed protocol would not get an hour-long presentation; people would ask sharp follow-up questions at once. Attention to detail was very high.

For Novati these are personality traits, such as using obsessive tendencies productively on every detail of the product. Others reached them through 25 years of experience. In conversations with junior colleagues, Novati says, context is often missing, follow-ups are less sharp and take longer, and projects are usually smaller in scope.

Source: 1:10:20–1:12:55 ↗

QAt the highest levels of performance, how much is talent and how much is hard work and growth?

Michael Novati

Talent exists, Novati says, shaped by biology, upbringing, and opportunity, and some of it is undiscovered. Someone who feels untalented may simply not have found it yet, or may be talented at something that is not their day job. Novati says this is the mission behind the current work of helping people find the most impactful work they can do, since not everyone had the chance to explore. Novati believes everyone is better than most at something, and finding it is a big piece of high performance.

Hard work, in contrast, is within your control. A friend of Novati's makes the point that talent and luck are outside your control and effort is not. If you are good at your job and like it, Novati says, you can outwork similar people and will probably be recognized for it.

Source: 1:20:43–1:23:00 ↗

QWhat percent of Novati's career growth is luck?

Michael Novati

Novati says 50/50. Coming from Canada, Novati's first day at Facebook was a surprise: Novati took a laptop and left onboarding, and was called back because Novati had not collected a phone. Facebook handed over a phone and accessories as if rolling out a red carpet, and Novati wondered what it all was. Staying in Canada would probably have gone well, Novati says, but without the same acceleration.

The luck was landing at Facebook when Novati did: a perfect fit for Novati's personality then, aligned values, and code that matched what Novati could handle. Novati has seen people without the same drive who got the luck and are doing well, and says either factor can work out. Novati says both applied here.

Source: 1:23:01–1:24:26 ↗

QWhat advice would Novati give to a just-graduated self?

Michael Novati

Novati sees many people, including those preparing for interviews, seeking approval: a green check mark, a perfect grade. Novati was that person, wanting an A+ without really knowing what was being learned. Because of that, Novati treated feedback as a grade to judge by and not as input for improving, and pressured toward 100 percent next time instead of toward improvement.

The advice to ambitious people who want perfect scores is to reflect on feedback and push past the comfort zone, instead of treating feedback as judgment.

Source: 1:24:27–1:25:39 ↗

Section 24 · interview

Bobby Holly: Visibility, Team Credit, and Distinguished-Level Impact

Selected passages on impact-centered visibility, giving team credit, senior role models, and distinguished-level leadership.

QWhere were you in your career at that point, and how did it grow as you worked on these projects?

Bobby Holly

Holly says early Mozilla had a choose-your-own-title culture, and Holly chose 'negative entropy' for the complex codebase. By Firefox Quantum, Mozilla had a more standard ladder. Holly had reached senior staff during Quantum CSS, and after launch Holly and the engineer who led the other half of Quantum were promoted to principal engineer, a level held by probably fewer than five people at the time by Holly's estimate.

Holly's long-term dream was to be like Boris Sabarski, one of Mozilla's three distinguished engineers, and the route was to be prolific across as many parts of the code as possible: WebRender, mobile, multiprocess, layout. Holly's manager, who ran engineering, asked Holly to spend one day a week not opening a terminal and to think about impact more broadly than direct code. Holly was shocked and says it was not a natural way to work.

Do you have a way of thinking about which contributions are more impactful than others?
Bobby Holly

Holly says it was a guided search for the biggest problem on offer, which changed over time: DOM bindings and security, then media playback to solve the YouTube problem, multiprocess, the Rust-based CSS engine, WebRender, and then mobile. Holly's model was to jump into the most pressing area, learn its code and work with its leaders, not always typing the code but reviewing, setting direction and setting priorities. The host summarizes this as prolific but aimed at the organization's biggest problems, and Holly agrees.

Source: 46:39–47:52 ↗
Source: 43:50–46:26 ↗

QIn the industry I hear two approaches to growth: focus on the promotion first, or build skills and behaviors and let the promotion follow. Which is better?

Bobby Holly

Holly has strong opinions and says to focus on impact, not title. That is what Holly looks for when deciding whom to advance. Someone having that level of impact does not need to sell themselves the way promo hacking implies, which means pinning down a management chain on exactly what must be done to earn a promotion.

Speaking frankly, Holly finds that annoying, comparing it to a child asking for a reward in exchange for doing what was asked. Holly also sees a substantive problem. A person focused on impact will achieve things, whereas a person focused on boxes someone else presented may technically satisfy a stated condition in a box-checking way that misses the point. Impact is what should be recognized and rewarded.

Softer-spoken engineers often do great work but market it poorly. Brag documents and sharing wins seem a reasonable balance. How do you weigh the two framings?
Bobby Holly

Holly says similar activities can be framed several ways, and the framing shapes how they are carried out and what they achieve. Visibility is a basic fact of impact: you need to be connected to people who understand the biggest challenges, coordinate with them, and make sure they know what you can do so they can put you in a position to do more. But Holly says trying to brag and trying to communicate, coordinate and create visibility for important work lead to very different outcomes.

Source: 50:27–53:02 ↗
The wording of an update can be subtle, and the same post can come from different incentives. Can people tell?
Bobby Holly

Holly says much depends on how much the update is about you versus the work, the team and other people. Everyone knows the sender likely had a significant hand in the work, so an important part of any update is giving visibility to others and thanking the team. Holly sees that as part of leadership: being a humble leader who creates recognition for other people's contributions.

Source: 53:03–54:51 ↗
Doesn't the squeaky wheel get the grease? A loud high performer who lobbies for promotion is often rewarded before a quiet, solid one.
Bobby Holly

Holly says it depends on the organization and its technical culture, and Mozilla tries hard not to reward that. The message is not to avoid ambition but to frame it as the impact you want, not the status you want. Holly allows that in edge cases people lobbying for themselves get a little more consideration because they are top of mind.

The conversations Holly likes best are about how to grow and have more impact, such as whether you are working on the most important thing. Holly calls it the saddest outcome when someone works very hard on something not important enough to give the impact they want. Pinning leaders down on which boxes to check is, Holly says, extremely annoying, and you do not want leadership to find you annoying.

Source: 55:17–57:13 ↗
Source: 48:34–50:26 ↗

QYou were focused on impact and had distinguished engineers as role models. What did the growth look like next?

Bobby Holly

Holly kept working on the hardest challenge in the browser and moving from team to team, assuming that Boris Sabarski's level of impact would eventually mean becoming a distinguished engineer. Then the CTO at the time sat Holly down. The existing distinguished engineers had held the title since about 2010 and no new ones had been made since. The CTO said Mozilla would make new ones for the first time in almost a decade and that Holly would not be among them.

Holly was a little surprised, since Holly thought anyone would say that, though perhaps not at Boris's level, Holly knew the Firefox code better than almost anyone. The CTO explained that this was the traditional Mozilla model and that he now wanted something oriented around industry impact.

The definition of impact shifted while you were working toward distinguished engineer. What was your thinking about the new criteria?
Bobby Holly

Holly found it inspiring, though some people worried Holly would be upset. Holly compares it to doing a new Pilates move and discovering a muscle you did not know you had and that is extremely weak. What defines a distinguished engineer, Holly says, depends on what matters to the organization. Early on, Mozilla's make-or-break problem was managing a sprawling codebase with few people, which called for a prolific contributor and enabler. At some companies the title means building a billion-dollar business, but Mozilla is about changing the world, so its criteria focus there.

Holly says Holly probably still has not reached the industry impact of some of Mozilla's other distinguished engineers, and that the eventual promotion was a hybrid of the old and new definitions. But understanding that model of impact was profound and shaped where Holly directed effort.

Source: 59:04–1:00:54 ↗
Source: 57:14–58:56 ↗

QWhat does distinguished-engineer-level impact look like? Can you describe some people who have done impressive work?

Bobby Holly

Holly describes three engineers promoted at the time as archetypes of world-changing impact for an individual contributor at Mozilla.

The first is Martin Thompson, still at Mozilla, whom Holly calls an international standards extraordinaire. His name is in the author line of protocols such as HTTP/2, QUIC and web push, and Holly says he was heavily involved in WebRTC and geolocation, adding that Holly is not familiar with every credit. This was core design work, not editorial formatting. By designing new protocols that were faster, giving the industry a business reason to adopt them, while leaking less metadata and having fewer security issues, he increased the privacy and security of the internet.

The second is Luke Wagner, whom Holly considers the person most single-handedly responsible for WebAssembly. Running non-JavaScript code such as AutoCAD in browsers had relied on plugins, which Holly calls awful for security and user experience. A side project from another engineer compiled C++ to naive JavaScript, which worked but was very slow. Wagner, then a lead engineer on the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine, wanted it viable, and the idea became having the tool emit a restricted subset of JavaScript the engine could detect, verify and run more natively. That started a flywheel of compiled native experiences in browsers and then momentum for a real bytecode format, WebAssembly, which is native-speed, sandboxed and portable. Google was pushing a plugin-like alternative, Native Client, so Wagner handled the technical and political pieces to forge a browser consensus.

The third is Tim Terbury, the codec lead. Native video playback was blocked because the dominant format, H.264, was heavily patent-encumbered, which an open-source browser could not ship. Mozilla spent years developing royalty-free codecs. Terbury's team built the Opus audio codec and then a video codec called Daala, which was incorporated into AV1, now an industry standard from the Alliance for Open Media. Holly says that powers video today and that the vision for truly unencumbered codecs came from Terbury.

The value these engineers created is huge, with WebAssembly making a company like Figma possible, but the value is captured elsewhere. Does that bother people at Mozilla?
Bobby Holly

Holly says Mozilla has no shareholders and is not trying to make gobs of money. Its mission is an internet that is open and accessible to all. Holly grants it is convenient for big tech companies to have a royalty-free codec, but notes they could pay. Mozilla's angle is to build formats that empower everybody and create economic value, even though some capture more than others.

Holly adds that Mozilla wants to keep existing, which means thinking about revenue, and a lot of its revenue comes from Google, one of the dominant advertising players. Mozilla would like to change that, but it is hard and not where its heart is, so Holly describes a real tension about how much to focus on business versus impact.

Source: 1:08:31–1:11:02 ↗
Source: 1:00:56–1:08:29 ↗

QWhat advice would you give someone who wants to become a distinguished engineer?

Bobby Holly

Holly's answer is writing, which anyone can work on at any level. Holly says Mozilla, including Holly personally, did not have much developed capability here, and that writing is one of the most powerful skills. Holly points to an internal memo, now public, called 'writing things down', which argues that writing matters both for the artifact, which helps coordination, wide review and feedback, and for the process, since writing is thinking, refining and articulating ideas. Holly calls clarity of thinking one of the most important things and says you only get it by forcing yourself to write your ideas down.

As timely advice, Holly says not to use an LLM to produce text you put your name on. It is fairly easy to tell, and more importantly you lose the thinking that writing forces.

Do you have tips on how to write well?
Bobby Holly

Holly says a document should be no longer than what you have to say. When you run out of things to say, you either refine your ideas or you are done, because fluff is never useful and padded documents are among Holly's least favorite things. Focus on substance over rhetoric. Holly rejects the idea that non-native English speakers cannot write as well as others: there is a baseline of articulation to work on, but good writing is not flowery words. It is clarity of thought, which is relatively easy to express once you have it, if you practice.

Source: 1:12:53–1:14:16 ↗
Source: 1:11:04–1:12:49 ↗

QIf you could give yourself advice when you had just entered the industry, what would it be?

Bobby Holly

Holly's answer is to be humble. Holly says the younger attitude was not strictly about self but about engineering, that engineers were the center of the universe. Over time Holly realized that many other things matter, and that when you start at an organization you do not understand why certain processes and functions exist, such as a legal team. Moving into leadership, Holly developed appreciation and empathy for the different players in the organization and industry, recognizing that everyone has a point of view and a place they are coming from, and that working to understand where people are coming from is how to make progress.

Source: 1:32:09–1:33:27 ↗

Section 25 · panel

Ryan and Ricky: Visibility, Self-Advocacy, and Promotion

Selected passages on promotion conversations, visible work, self-advocacy, impact measurement, and communication.

QWhat do the engineering levels mean, from junior to staff?

Ricky

Ricky explains that junior engineers write and ship code with a fair amount of help. Mid-level engineers work more independently but still need help at times. Senior is often a stopping point, with few people expected to go further. Staff engineers set a team's direction and lead engineers at other levels. Ricky estimates that moving from junior to mid-level takes about two to four years, and mid-level to senior a similar time.

Ricky says some companies use an up-or-out policy, where people who do not reach the next level leave, and that Google is less aggressive about this. Ricky estimates, without exact data, that 90 percent or more of people reach these levels. The speakers say the levels site is fairly accurate, except that equity pay moves with the stock price.

Source: 01:41–05:45 ↗

QHow do interns succeed, and how are they judged?

The speakers say interns are judged on three things. The first is productivity: how much of the assigned project they finish, ideally in half the internship. The second is quality, shown by fewer rounds of code review by the end. The third is communication, including proposing improvements or a new project after finishing the first one. A strong intern does all three.

What was Ricky's own internship like?
Ricky

Ricky's junior-year internship at Google produced only about 800 lines of code, which felt low. Halfway through, Ricky had about 300 lines, while a UCLA friend on the same program had about 11,000. Ricky spent much of the time learning the codebase and wrote a detailed design doc comparing several approaches. That work showed productivity, and Ricky received a return offer.

Source: 07:29–09:47 ↗
Source: 05:47–07:27 ↗

QHow did you get promoted so quickly to staff engineer in your 20s?

Ricky

Ricky says each level expects a different kind of work. Many projects at the current level do not earn the next promotion. One project at the next level, which clearly shows readiness, counts for more. Managers often describe these expectations as behaviors. Ricky and Ryan focused on projects that would move them up, not on busy work that would not.

Ricky also says that, after each promotion, Ricky asked the manager what the next level required and then took on that kind of work. The manager explained which skills to build, and Ricky credits this for the fast promotions.

Source: 09:50–11:20 ↗

QIs career success mostly luck?

Ryan

Ryan says luck is a big part of it, but people can raise their own luck through initiative. After about eight months at Amazon, Ryan felt stuck and could not see the path to the next level. Ryan applied to many companies and received offers from every company interviewed with except one. That led to Meta.

Source: 11:22–12:24 ↗

QWhat one piece of advice would the speakers give?

Ricky

Ricky says the main advice is to ask a lot of questions, at work and during an internship. Ricky once told a mentee to keep asking, and at the end of the internship the mentee said Ricky had not really meant it. Ricky says the biggest difference between people who succeed quickly and those who do not is how fast they start asking questions, learning, and unblocking themselves. Fear of looking foolish holds many people back.

What separates strong interns from weak ones?
Ryan

Ryan has had five interns at Meta. The strong ones had the nerve to propose improvements and ask questions, even though Ryan was the senior person. Some suggestions were wrong, but many were right. The weaker interns were quieter, and Ryan could not tell how they were progressing. Time passed with little progress, and such interns often did not get return offers.

Source: 15:24–16:11 ↗
Source: 13:09–15:22 ↗

QAre the best engineers the smartest students in the class?

The speakers say no. Strong engineers need solid technical skill and soft skills, such as persuading and influencing others. Work is a large group project, and disagreements are common. Telling a colleague that their idea is bad does not win them over. Naming the other person's frustration, acknowledging their view, and proposing a middle ground makes it more likely that the work ships. The speakers say these skills matter about as much as coding.

Source: 16:13–17:49 ↗

QHow much of the job is actually code?

One speaker says code is a smaller part of the job than new graduates expect. Writing is a large part of it. A design doc comes before the code, a change needs a written description, and a finished project needs a write-up of its results. The speaker says this writing is how a person influences others, so people skills often decide how far an engineer goes.

Source: 17:52–19:30 ↗

QDo experienced engineers still get imposter syndrome?

Ricky

Ricky says imposter syndrome is very common, and that most people feel it. Ricky felt it on joining Google, after passing the interviews and the internship, and found the other engineers very strong. Even after promotions, Ricky wondered whether the company had made a mistake. Ricky copes by learning as much as possible and doing the best job possible, on the view that even being fired would leave something learned. Ricky says the feeling still returns in waves.

Did praise at work reduce the stress?
Ricky

Ricky describes being an anxious person who was always stressed about work. A manager once told Ricky to calm down. Ricky was not sure whether the praise meant a passing grade or a strong one. Talking through expectations with the manager helped, and the stress eased somewhat.

Source: 21:02–21:48 ↗
Source: 19:32–21:01 ↗

QHow do you advocate for yourself at work?

Ryan

Ryan says good work is required but not enough, because people decide promotions and they must know about the work. The last few percent of effort is to tell people about it. That can mean writing about a result, presenting it in a meeting, or telling a manager that a milestone is done early and the next task is ready. Ryan says a clear post about strong results makes a return offer hard to refuse. Ryan says this step is often skipped, especially by introverted people.

Is visibility a separate skill from doing the work?
Ricky

Ricky says visibility can come from a manager, a product manager, or teammates, as well as from the person's own writing. Ricky compares unseen work to a tree falling in a forest that nobody sees, and says people cannot promote work they do not know about.

Source: 23:41–24:21 ↗
Source: 21:50–23:10 ↗

QHow do managers measure impact?

The speakers define impact as the concrete, measurable results of the work, such as revenue, cost, speed, or user growth. The measure depends on the team. On an ads team it may be money. On infrastructure it may be the cost or latency of a database. On a growth team it may be daily active users or sign-ups at key steps. Engineers should learn the measure from their team and manager, because that is how their work is rewarded.

The speakers also say one small change that improves a key number can matter more than ten thousand lines of typo fixes. Their example is a one-line change that gives a 20 percent gain on something that matters.

Source: 30:40–32:25 ↗

QDo you need an MBA for engineering management?

Ryan says no, and Ryan is a manager without one. Ryan describes a graph from a company that gathers LinkedIn data, covering a few thousand directors and above. Pay with and without an MBA looked comparable, and pay without one was slightly lower. Ryan describes this as research done with a company, not a published study.

Did family expectations about an MBA affect Ricky?
Ricky

Ricky's mother believed Ricky would not succeed without an MBA, and pushed for a top school. She has become more relaxed since Ricky reached staff engineer, and now reads about careers and thinks the path is good.

Source: 33:20–34:12 ↗
Source: 32:27–33:18 ↗

QWhat are your goals now, and did you push for promotion?

Ricky

Ricky says Ricky was not very career-driven at first. Ricky and Ryan were roommates and still are. Ryan would ask whether they could aim for promotion faster than the usual timeline. Ricky had seen data on how long each level took, and Ryan's push made Ricky test whether a faster path was possible.

Ricky says Ricky put in the effort, was promoted faster than average, and did not give up other interests to do it.

Source: 40:18–41:49 ↗

QShould people change jobs every two or three years for pay or promotion?

Ricky says the answer depends on the case. Ricky has stayed on the same team under the same manager at Google, while still looking at other teams. Ricky notes survivorship bias, because people who left may have had a worse time. Ricky suggests asking every six months whether you still want to be there, whether the opportunities still fit, and whether the team and manager support you.

Ryan says the common advice to job hop for promotion is more nuanced. Early in a career, job hopping can be the fastest route, because momentum matters less than reaching the next level. At senior levels it can backfire. Ryan says companies usually do not hire outside candidates straight into E7 or L7, and promotion there depends on credibility and a track record that frequent moves do not build. Ryan's advice is to job hop aggressively early and to be more deliberate later.

Can leaving a company help someone come back at a higher level?
Ryan

Ryan says this is rare. Ryan has seen a person leave a company, join a startup, and come back to Meta at a higher level. Ryan says a person who leaves a clear ladder is harder to place, so a return can leave room for a higher offer, but few cases work this way.

Source: 45:15–46:05 ↗

Section 26 · interview

Austin McDonald: Behavioral Interviews, Downleveling, and How Hiring Committees Decide

Austin McDonald, a former Meta hiring committee member, explains how leveling and hiring decisions are made and why scope-focused behavioral stories decide outcomes for senior engineers.

Senior hiring turns on scope shown in behavioral stories (Austin McDonald's view)

Austin McDonald, introduced by the host as a former Meta hiring committee member who led mobile hiring across the company, argues that for senior engineers the behavioral interview, and even the first recruiter conversation, is where level is decided. A candidate who wants to avoid being downleveled should know the company's rubric, choose the highest-scope stories that still fit the question, show technical, organizational and business depth, and treat every contact (recruiter, hiring manager, closing questions) as evaluative. The second half moves to interviewer dynamics, story structure, and Austin's own reflections on regret, scope and fear. Everything about Meta's process is Austin's account of their own time there and may differ at other companies or today.

Source: 00:49–1:41:33 ↗

QWhat actually happens in a hiring committee, and who touches a candidate between first contact and the final decision?

Austin McDonald

Austin says that when a senior packet reached the committee, the first thing Austin read was the behavioral interview. Austin wanted to see the scope the engineer had operated at, their level of influence, insight and communication, and the size of the organization they had worked in. Committees are made up of engineers and influential engineering managers, recruited by a chair such as Austin, and work with recruiting on two decisions: hire or not, and level. Austin describes a company-wide committee that mostly does a gut check against a cross-company bar, and says that at Meta a final committee of engineering directors makes the hiring and leveling call.

The path starts with a sourcer, an entry-level recruiting job whose task is to find candidates or process referrals. The sourcer looks at the job description, years of experience and past companies. The phone screen that follows is often a coding interview, and sometimes a multiple-choice technical quiz used as a pre-filter. A clearly strong phone screen goes straight to on-site scheduling. A borderline one comes to the hiring committee for the first time, which decides whether to add a follow-up, move the person on, or pass for now.

The committee is also consulted for specialized candidates, for example a low-level C++ mobile engineer who needs a fitting system design interview, and for the choice between senior and staff. That choice changes the loop. At Meta, Austin says, staff candidates get two system design interviews, so no one could be hired at staff without them, and principal and distinguished loops add further behavioral interviews. After the on-site, the committee decides hire, level and follow-ups. Behavioral interviews generate most follow-ups, because Austin considers them among the hardest to give and to read. Committee members sometimes go with the recruiter to the directors to argue for taking a chance on someone whose packet is weak in one area but strong in a trait the company needs.

How is a candidate's starting level first decided?
Austin McDonald

Austin says the early call rests on years of experience and previous title: a staff engineer at Google will likely be brought in as staff at Meta. Many companies, Meta included, do not publish levels, so a LinkedIn profile rarely shows level, which is why years of experience carry so much weight.

Source: 06:45–07:34 ↗
What happens to a high-titled candidate from outside big tech?
Austin McDonald

Austin says sourcers and recruiters know that titles inflate in parts of the industry. A manager of 50 or 75 people at a business-oriented company might be downleveled to a team of eight or ten engineers at Meta, and individual contributors are treated the same way. Calling oneself a principal engineer on LinkedIn does not draw principal-level outreach, because different companies attach different expectations to the same level. Austin adds that a consistent industry-wide scale would be nice, but it does not exist.

Source: 07:36–08:53 ↗
Could someone get through by inflating a title on a resume?
Austin McDonald

The host posed this as a hypothetical about an unethical candidate. Austin says the first phone screen at staff and above is also a scope check: some coding, some system design, and a walk through a large shipped project. Lying convincingly is hard, because interviewers sense whether the story is true and follow-up questions expose gaps. Austin says coaching clients who recite AI-generated stories start giving vague, inconsistent answers once asked about the technology.

Austin concedes that anyone can be fooled by a good enough liar, but the on-site interviewers for staff and principal candidates are very senior and highly calibrated, so a liar would have to lie repeatedly and convincingly. Austin jokes that someone able to do that might be good enough for the job, and says that in a career of hiring thousands of people, Austin has not heard of a hire later found to have invented their background.

Source: 08:54–12:17 ↗
Source: 01:45–06:43 ↗

QThe host said engineers often assume the behavioral round can be improvised. What should a candidate do to be placed at staff?

Austin McDonald

Austin says the most important task, in any behavioral story and in the first chat with a recruiter, is to establish scope: what size of business problem was solved with technology, how much ambiguity was handled, and what kind of organization the candidate operated in. The recruiter call is effectively a behavioral interview, so the opening “tell me about yourself” should be the greatest hits of the resume, with metrics, and with depth and complexity.

Austin contrasts “I improved performance in the Facebook app” with an account of organizing about 100 engineers across a twelve-month performance project that hit hard technical problems, needed several staff engineers, and ended in three core principles. A candidate should convey technical depth, organizational depth and business impact, because every interviewer in the loop is listening for the same things. Crisp practice on that opening is the first place to land in the right leveling bucket.

Responding to the host's point that staff promotions also require cross-organization work, Austin agrees and says preparing for behavioral interviews makes someone a better engineer. Most of Austin's coaching clients undersell rather than exaggerate. They need to show how hard the problem was and what impact it had on the team, code quality and the organization over time. Telling the whole story takes preparation, but it is the same skill used in weekly one-on-ones and executive updates.

Is the first recruiter call already an evaluation?
Austin McDonald

The host noted that recruiters pitch the first call as a casual chat. Austin answers “always be closing”: the call is evaluative, though softer, since the recruiter wants to find a candidate who gets through. Recruiters at big companies are paid by the hires they deliver. They advocate for candidates but are not friends, and compensation is a topic to handle carefully.

Austin advises against showing up unprepared or disconnected. If not ready, reschedule and spend time preparing what to say, since that is the best route to a higher-level offer.

Source: 17:16–19:23 ↗
Does the final chat with the hiring manager also carry signal?
Austin McDonald

Austin says yes. The pressure is lower, and at companies such as Meta or Google a team-matching phase brings conversations with several managers. These chats are more social than interviews, where a long self-introduction cuts into the interviewer's time for collecting signal. The manager is asking whether they like the candidate, whether they will fit the team, and whether the candidate can solve problems like the manager's own.

So Austin recommends asking the recruiter and sourcer in advance what the manager values and what the team is working on, then telling stories that show the candidate can solve those problems.

Source: 19:25–21:12 ↗
Source: 13:18–17:14 ↗

QWhat is the most common mistake candidates make in compensation conversations with recruiters?

Austin McDonald

Austin says they are not a negotiation expert and recommends getting advice from people who are. Their own view is that early anchoring is dangerous: when asked early about compensation expectations, a candidate should be careful, because whatever is said anchors the rest of the conversation.

Austin tells candidates to learn the local laws and says that in California and New York recruiters are required to share salary and total-comp bands, which a candidate can use to see where they sit (this legal claim is Austin's and was not checked). Austin thinks the biggest mistake is not having multiple offers. Without them, a candidate negotiates from weakness, so Austin urges candidates to time offers to land at about the same moment, even though that is more stressful and more work.

Source: 21:14–22:52 ↗

QIf a candidate who wants only staff roles sees they are being funneled into the wrong loop, can that be corrected mid-process?

Austin McDonald

Austin says that depends on the company and process, but it is a good conversation to have with the recruiter. Companies uplevel candidates as well as downlevel them, and recruiters will usually try to keep someone in the process. Austin suggests pushing to complete as much of the evaluation as possible for the desired level up front, so that follow-up interviews and late changes are not needed. If a team offers only a lower level, it depends on the job and total compensation, but Austin would aim to excel and then ask for consideration at the higher level.

Austin names two methods. The first is to anchor every conversation at the higher level, starting with “tell me about yourself” and then in the behavioral and system design interviews, so that interviewers see large-scope projects and impact and reset what they expect from the rest of the interview. The second is story choice. Behind every behavioral question is a question the interviewer actually cares about: is the candidate operating at the expected level? Interviewers forget the details quickly.

Austin says their book gives four considerations for choosing a story, and scope comes first. The candidate's job is to leave having told the most important stories of their career, and since the interviewer drives, to steer the conversation toward the signal that best represents them.

Source: 22:54–26:51 ↗

QWhat do senior, staff and principal scope look like, and how should a candidate express them?

Austin McDonald

Austin first says to research the specific company's level expectations, then offers a simple rubric for big-tech-style companies, shown in the table below. Levels are really about how much ambiguity a person can handle. Austin notes that the ambiguity facing an intern differs from the ambiguity facing a chief executive, and says that difference is what separates both levels and pay.

Staff versus senior comes down to breadth of impact: a whole team or several teams rather than a small project. Stories involve working across a large organization. For that reason Austin thinks startup engineers struggle to reach staff unless they were founders, because a few engineers and one stakeholder limit how much organizational leadership they can show.

Austin adds two more things to quantify or mention. For technical complexity, a candidate should give a sense of the time involved, the risk, how many people were consulted, and how hard it would have been to back out of a decision. For leadership, which engineers often forget because they love to talk about technology, a candidate should describe influence, getting concessions from other teams, aligning roadmaps, and mentoring people to make the team and organization better. Austin recommends reflecting on one's own career to identify what differentiates it, and talking about those things.

How should a specialist who solves problems no one else can describe their scope?
Austin McDonald

The host asked about people who push the industry forward on their own. Austin says to start with business impact, which technology-focused engineers find hard. There was a reason the technology was needed and a context around it, and Austin encourages people to ask what Steve Jobs would say about the advance and why the project was critical to the company.

Source: 32:27–33:22 ↗
Is it too much to say that a team of staff engineers failed before the candidate succeeded?
Austin McDonald

The host said that framing works when a manager says it in a promotion committee, but that a candidate saying it about themselves may sound like too much. Austin disagrees outright. In Austin's view behavioral interviewers are pattern matchers, and having solved problems others could not is one of the patterns for a higher level.

Austin finds it fine to say a candidate was the third owner of a project and where earlier owners failed, as long as the point is not to boast but to show insight into why those efforts failed, whether a product-market fit that did not work or a technical approach that did not work. Austin sees that judgment and reflection as a mark of seniority, and says many candidates simply tell a problem-solved story with no lesson, which Austin treats as a sign of someone below the level.

Source: 33:23–35:27 ↗
Is it unfair that candidates who sell themselves well do better?
Austin McDonald

The host noted that commenters complain about people who manage optics, and that promotion content draws the same objection. Austin replies that this is how people work, in careers and in personal relationships alike: saying “can't you feel that I love you” does not work, and behaviors must be shown and communicated.

Austin calls self-advocacy an unpleasant but worthwhile tax on progress that candidates can skip only by giving up staff-level promotion or hiring. Austin tells people that a principal engineering job is about a million dollars a year in compensation, so they should be fully ready for the process.

Source: 35:29–37:24 ↗
Source: 27:35–32:19 ↗
Austin McDonald's rubric of scope by level
LevelWhat the person ownsWhat that looks like
New gradTasksTakes a task from the manager or ticket system, completes it, and comes back for the next.
Mid-levelA feature (many tasks, a couple of weeks)Delivers a feature end to end.
SeniorA project (many features)Leads and delegates, often through mid-level or junior engineers, with communication and organization.
Staff (level 6 at Meta)A goal such as an engagement or revenue goalCoordinates several projects, working across teams and a large organization, with influence and mentoring.

Next level upA business or industry (many organizations)Responsibility for an entire business containing many organizations.
Source: 27:35–29:44 ↗

QWho actually makes the hiring decision?

Austin McDonald

Austin lists the decision points. The sourcer, who decides from a LinkedIn profile whether to contact someone, is distinct from the recruiter, who takes over after the phone screen, runs the negotiation, organizes the loop and advocates before the committee. The phone screener is another decision point, whether a sourcer's multiple-choice question or an engineer's coding screen.

The hiring committee then decides, usually by consensus and sometimes by vote, whether to hire at a level, add a follow-up, or drop the candidate. Two or three engineering directors above the committee make the final call, again mostly by consensus and sometimes by vote.

Source: 37:26–39:08 ↗

QDid Austin ever see bias in a hiring committee, such as nepotism, and how much do referrals matter?

Austin McDonald

Austin has never seen overt nepotism or bribery, but has seen referrals play a huge role, especially when the referrer is senior or shows up in the committee room to advocate. The referrer's seniority matters: a VP or director risks personal reputation, while a note that someone knew a candidate at school carries little weight. Content matters as well. A referral saying the person worked directly with the candidate and listing specific strengths helps much more, so Austin tells candidates to write the referral for the referrer.

Austin says referrals matter most for candidates on the bubble. Austin's own phone screens went poorly, and Austin believes a follow-up interview was granted because a former schoolmate who had worked with them directly had referred them.

Could a very strong referral rescue a lukewarm interview performance?
Austin McDonald

The host described a candidate with a lukewarm result and the strongest possible VP referral. Austin says referrals help on the bubble, usually by winning a follow-up, and Austin has never seen a general consensus not to hire overturned for an engineer. It may happen more in leadership hiring, which Austin calls a different matter. At senior manager and director level, Austin thinks who you know sometimes matters more than raw performance, because the number of decision makers shrinks and they are easier to influence.

Austin adds that a good hiring process is not like that: it identifies what makes people successful and evaluates for it without bias.
