QHow well does interview performance predict performance on the job?

Austin McDonald

Austin says the committee did not track how many interviews someone passed. It looked at the interviewer's stated confidence in a hire-and-level decision, and that confidence correlated with later performance. Austin reads this as evidence that calibrated interviewers who have run hundreds of interviews sense what good looks like even when it is hard to define, and that a rubric reduces bias without removing the gut feel.

Austin also notes that some candidates excel in interviews and then do poorly, and others look rocky and then do well. Interviewing is a skill separate from the job, and Austin says candidates need to spend time getting good at it.

Source: 43:49–45:26 ↗

QWhat does the behavioral rubric look like, and how should a candidate use it?

Austin McDonald

Austin says it varies by company. Well-run large companies often employ industrial-psychology PhDs, called selection scientists, who study what makes engineers successful and codify it into signal areas. At Meta, according to Austin, there are five: driving results, embracing ambiguity, resolving conflicts, growing continuously and communicating effectively. These are not Meta's company values. Candidates should ask the recruiter for the rubric in advance or search for it.

Austin groups the typical five to eight items into eight broader signal areas, described in their book, and tells candidates to categorize their stories by those areas. Inside the interview the core loop is decode, select, deliver: work out why the question is being asked and which area it probes, select a story that supplies that signal, and tell it engagingly. At smaller companies a formal rubric may not exist. There Austin suggests relying on company values and asking recruiters or team members what makes engineers successful and what the hiring process looks for.

How can one story serve different questions, and what does the interviewer need from the candidate?
Austin McDonald

The host says that as an interviewer of hundreds of candidates, including engineering managers, the host often asked a targeted question and watched candidates talk past it into a rehearsed spiel, leaving a blank in the rubric. The host sees the interview as a mutual exercise in filling out that rubric.

Austin agrees and offers a movie-trailer image, credited to PM behavioral coach Robert Hamilton. One story may contain action, romance, ambiguity, communication and conflict, and the candidate can re-cut it into a trailer that fits the question. That has to happen early, in the opening context. Austin says candidates should treat themselves as partners helping the interviewer reach the signal sought.

Source: 47:57–50:12 ↗
Source: 45:39–47:54 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 46:23–50:12 ↗

QHow should candidates tailor behavioral stories for OpenAI and Anthropic?

Austin McDonald

Austin starts by mapping stories onto the eight general signal areas, because most company values reduce to them, and then adds whatever the company's own values contribute. For OpenAI, Austin reads “act with humility” as growth: taking feedback and improving yourself and those around you. “Feel the AGI” is outside the eight areas. Austin reads it as being optimistic about what AI could do for the world.

For Anthropic, the caption renders a value as “hold light and shade”, which Austin takes to mean understanding both the positive and negative implications of AI. A story about using AI at Anthropic should mention the potential harms the candidate thought about and how they assessed and mitigated them. Without that, Austin says, the interviewers will not feel comfortable hiring. At OpenAI a candidate who is not AI-forward or excited about new domains for AI will interest them less. These are Austin's readings of the values, not official definitions.

Source: 50:14–52:20 ↗

QWhat are the most common behavioral interview mistakes for senior engineers?

Austin McDonald

Austin lists several. First, the wrong stories, meaning stories that do not match the target scope. Second, too much context: senior people are good communicators and tend to talk, but only the context needed to understand the behaviors is useful. If about thirty seconds pass without an action in the story, Austin suggests the candidate is giving too much backstory or technical detail. Work stories are not exciting, Austin admits, so the action must keep moving.

Third, inviting uncharitable readings. Interviewers hiring a senior leader are risk-averse, so a candidate should think defensively. Saying the codebase had heavy technical debt may sound like a good story, but a senior engineer in the room invites the question of how it got that way. Austin recommends adding the judgment behind the situation, for example that the team was a startup that had to close its next funding round and so accepted the debt, then chose to prioritize paying it down.

Fourth, too little on non-technical work: mentoring, organizing, delegating, influencing the roadmap, resolving conflicts, working across teams and managing up. Fifth, long, multi-year stories need an organized shape. Austin suggests opening with a short table of contents (the business context, then perhaps five parts such as proposing the idea, aligning stakeholders, solving hard problems and a long rollout), so the candidate can return to the key parts after interruptions.

How should a candidate choose which story to tell?
Austin McDonald

Austin gives four criteria in order. Scope comes first, which Austin says surprises people who assume relevance is first: how can a big-scope story fit the question? Relevance is second, since a story about an unambiguous project cannot answer a question on ambiguity. Recency is third: stories from the last two to three years are fine, beyond three or four years needs a strong reason, and the limit stretches with seniority, so a principal with a 30-year career may use a ten-year-old story. Uniqueness is fourth: across several behavioral rounds a candidate should avoid repeating the same story, for example keeping the project deep dive separate from the general ambiguity answer.

Source: 57:10–58:35 ↗
Is it acceptable to answer like a politician and steer toward a stronger story?
Austin McDonald

The host compared this to a politician delivering a rehearsed answer that fills in the rubric rather than the question asked. Austin says, unfortunately, yes. The aim is to leave having shown the most business value and problem solving, and strictly answering the narrow question can leave a bigger story untold.

Austin's example is a question about a conflict with a product manager. A candidate can say they had one and outline it, then offer that a longer conflict with a director of engineering, involving data collection and many meetings, might be more interesting, and ask whether to tell that instead. The interviewer may constrain the candidate back to the smaller story, but the interviewer may also only be gathering conflict-resolution signal.

Source: 58:37–1:00:39 ↗
How can a candidate tell whether they are talking too long?
Austin McDonald

Austin says interviewers differ. Some, like Austin, listen and take in what the candidate finds interesting. Others interrupt, turn a detail over, ask many follow-ups or move quickly between questions. Candidates should be emotionally prepared for the second type, who can make a candidate feel they are failing when the interviewer is just bouncing around.

Austin advises reading cues such as eye contact and note-taking, and if engagement drops, pausing to ask whether this is what the interviewer wants. A calibrated interviewer will interrupt even if rude in order to collect signal, but weaker ones need the candidate to make stopping easy. Austin recommends talking for no more than two to four minutes at a time, since a monologue longer than four or five minutes has to be very good.

Source: 1:00:04–1:02:29 ↗
Source: 52:22–57:07 ↗

QHow should a candidate split preparation time across coding, system design and behavioral rounds?

Austin McDonald

Austin says most people spend too much time on coding and too little on system design and behavioral, which are murkier to prepare for. For juniors, the technical signal matters most, and the behavioral focus should be on thinking, motivations and ideas tried, as signals of future impact, since juniors have fewer accomplishments.

For mid-level engineers, Austin says the old approach of focusing only on technical work and not flubbing the behavioral no longer works. Austin gives two reasons: layoffs have produced many candidates, so one must shine across all interview types, and more technical work is being done with agentic coding, so employers want mid-level engineers who own problems end to end and keep learning as engineering changes quickly. Austin says that ownership and growth show up in the behavioral interview. Coding practice should come early because coding assessments come first, but some weeks before the on-site a candidate should choose core stories, study values and the rubric, and make sure each key area has a story.

From senior up, Austin says it mostly comes down to behavioral. For a staff packet Austin went straight to the behavioral interview, since there are only so many ways to design a web crawler or solve two-sum, and the behavioral shows organizational impact, influence, conflict handling, scope and business impact. At staff-plus levels, extra rounds may include a cross-functional partner such as a PM or a project deep dive. Austin sees the technical rounds there as checkmarks to pass and the behavioral ones as what gets someone hired.

Austin thinks most people underinvest in behavioral preparation, which takes at least a few weeks. Staff candidates and above should start when they start LeetCode, work on positioning stories, get feedback, and do mocks with a friend or professional. For in-demand companies such as Meta, OpenAI or Anthropic, Austin recommends a mock interviewer calibrated to that company who can give a feel for its culture.

Can a packet with a modest technical result and a strong behavioral result still go through?
Austin McDonald

Austin says yes at the highest levels. At staff, principal and manager levels, where less day-to-day coding is expected, the committee would discount a weak coding performance. That is much harder for junior candidates.

Austin tells of a candidate whose accomplishments were limited and technical performance only okay. Austin kept seeing ideas the candidate had tried to push even though a manager disagreed or the organization blocked them. Austin pushed for the hire and says the person later became a staff engineer. Austin's reading is that the behavioral interview assesses a slope of growth, even for juniors.

Source: 1:07:10–1:08:33 ↗
Source: 1:02:31–1:07:09 ↗

QHow much does subjective likeability matter, and how does presence affect the outcome?

Austin McDonald

Austin says it scales with level. At big companies, behavioral interviews for juniors are structured, with forms, to reduce the “beer test” effect. For seniors the interviewer expects the person to influence others on the job, so how they come across counts. Austin describes a Silicon Valley quality of “casual excellence”: looking calm yet sharply competent. A disheveled or nervous candidate who cannot be present is giving signal about how they will show up in meetings and before a CEO.

Austin adds that cultural norms differ by country and company. The conversation here is about a Silicon Valley or Seattle style that opens with playful banter and then turns to hard-hitting questions, and candidates should learn the expectations of the place they are applying to.

How can a staff engineer who is not a people person come across strongly?
Austin McDonald

Austin starts from the idea that the inside shows on the outside, so the work begins with belief rather than a mask. Austin cites a recent podcast by the author of a book on Silicon Valley etiquette, named in the captions as Sam Lesson (spelling unverified), who stressed lowering heart rate before the conversation. Austin points out that a company that will be around has other chances, so a candidate can give themselves permission to make mistakes and appear calmer.

The second belief is empathy: the interviewer wants to find a great engineer, is not an enemy, and is a human who would be glad to work with the candidate. On the outside, Austin suggests dressing one notch up, checking the video background, and showing care in the first minutes rather than waiting passively. A candidate who is not extroverted can still let their regard for people show through a warm greeting and stated enthusiasm. Austin recommends practicing that opening in mock interviews, noting that the interviewer may be nervous too and that a hiring manager or leader shapes the candidate's view of the team.

Source: 1:11:20–1:15:16 ↗
Does a curt, concise candidate or a warm, bubbly one score better?
Austin McDonald

The host posed this contrast. Austin says it depends on who conducts the interview, and that Austin would favor the warmer person because Austin likes to engage. But rapport does not mean bubbliness, it means connecting with the other person. A candidate should start positive and energetic, then read the interviewer. Someone who skips the introduction and goes straight to “tell me about a time” wants efficiency, so the candidate should be efficient. Someone who opens with several minutes of weather and sports is a different type, and the candidate should match that energy.

Source: 1:15:18–1:17:29 ↗
Source: 1:09:03–1:11:19 ↗

QWhich counts more, the first impression or the last impression?

Austin McDonald

Austin says that if forced to choose, the beginning. Austin often decides within the first ten or fifteen minutes whether to hire, since Austin opens with the biggest-scope questions (favorite project, most ambiguous project, something proud of). If Austin would like to see that performance replicated in the organization, the rest of the interview is a check on other areas such as conflict resolution and growth.

The ending still matters, mainly through the candidate's questions. Austin says candidates often prepare stories but then ask something generic like a day in the life of an engineer, which is similar everywhere. Questions drawn from real thought about the team, organization, product and company, and that help the candidate decide whether to join, leave the impression of an engaged candidate.

What share of the outcome is already set early in the interview?
Austin McDonald

Austin says no social science has been applied directly to tech interviews, and one cannot simply transfer research from a fast-food company. Austin recalls research saying roughly 40 percent of decisions are made in the first 15 percent, about the first ten minutes (Austin's recollection, not verified). In Austin's own experience it is rare to decide against someone early and then be won back at minute 38. More common is feeling unsure, then writing notes against the rubric, which is meant to move the decision from a gut reaction to something more deliberate.

If Austin decided early, it was hard for the candidate to overcome, usually because of poor story choice, work below the expected level, or weak storytelling. The host adds from experience that interviewers seem to zone out halfway once they have already decided, which makes the first half important, and that the closing questions are also evaluative.

Source: 1:19:11–1:21:43 ↗
What makes a good question to ask at the end?
Austin McDonald

Austin says everything is evaluative, from the recruiter call to the closing questions. A candidate should start from what matters to them: worry about the company's long-term product prospects, or, for career growth and a supportive manager, a request such as asking the manager to describe helping someone grow from one level to the next. Technology-stack questions seem more junior to Austin, though in an AI context a question about model construction or evaluation could be strong. One of Austin's favorites is what makes someone in this role successful, which signals interest in succeeding.

Austin would not try to impress with a deep question, but would let a genuine concern read as depth. Questions about the conversation for the role, or about free food, may matter to the candidate but do not belong with a behavioral interviewer.

Source: 1:21:45–1:24:03 ↗
Source: 1:17:40–1:19:09 ↗

QWhat are the best ways to tell a behavioral story with the least effort?

Austin McDonald

Austin says a story needs an arc, with a beginning, middle and end, and must deliver the signal area the interviewer is after: past behavior that can be repeated in the new organization. STAR (situation, task, action, result) is the best-known shortcut. Austin does not love it but says that anyone with prepared STAR stories the night before should use them, since they give an arc, context for the actions, and results.

Austin prefers CALR: context, actions, results, learnings. The difference between situation and task is not useful in a long project, which has many tasks, so context followed by actions is simpler. For senior engineers STAR leaves no room for reflection, judgment or learning, and Austin looks for whether the candidate can see what made them successful or not and apply it forward.

How should a candidate adapt the length of an answer to the question?
Austin McDonald

Austin says senior candidates manage time. A “trunk” question such as a project that was really ambiguous invites a longer story. A “branch” question, such as whom the candidate spoke to for a piece of information, seeks a communication signal and deserves something shorter than a full STAR or CALR story. A “leaf” question, such as which framework was used, only needs the answer before moving on. Austin says detecting how long the interviewer wants to listen is both a mark of seniority and a way to manage the interview.

Source: 1:26:37–1:27:59 ↗
What matters more, what the candidate says or how they say it?
Austin McDonald

Austin says mostly what, because engineering interviews are structured and engineers value substance. A candidate who sounds confident and positive but shows no structured approach to ambiguity or conflict will not win support. Form follows function.

Austin adds that delivery matters more at senior levels, because senior people must tell engaging status stories, for example when a VP asks how a project is going. Details belong only when they serve a purpose, such as technical depth or, in a cross-team story, how another tech lead's hostile look showed the candidate pushing through resistance. Most candidates, Austin thinks, need more work on basic story structure and on naming the repeatable actions they took.

Source: 1:28:01–1:30:24 ↗
Source: 1:24:30–1:26:34 ↗

QThe host asked Austin to explain, in terms of scope, why Austin was promoted to M2 at Meta.

Austin McDonald

Austin says getting to M2 meant solving hard problems in recruiting, with the most important being diversity. Austin left a team building products for teenagers, which Austin calls a hard time for Facebook, to lead teams in the internal recruiting products organization that supports candidates, recruiters and sourcers. What drew Austin was a team working to hire more diverse engineers, and Austin was motivated by opening technology, which Austin calls the largest wealth opportunity, to more people.

Austin says a product team cannot decide school curricula or all hiring decisions, but could move the needle by improving interview preparation, and credits that with helping diversity hiring at Meta. Austin also supported other teams in building high-quality candidate data in Facebook's applicant tracking system. The host heard multiple teams, an ambiguous problem and strong self-motivation. Austin agrees and adds company-wide impact from leading the iOS and Android recruiting pipelines, which scaled Austin beyond the teams directly managed. These are Austin's own account of their record.

Source: 1:30:27–1:33:41 ↗

QLooking back on big tech, does Austin regret anything?

Austin McDonald

Austin does not regret leaving and says they enjoyed working with wonderful people. The regret is the anxiety brought into teams and into their own life. Austin points out that no one at the end of life wishes they had gotten a few more percent of an engagement number, and says people value relationships and connection.

Austin says they made conscious choices to favor life experience over career but were not always honest with themselves about the trade-offs in pay, progression and status. Since leaving big tech to support a spouse's business, income has dropped. Before leaving, Austin decided to accept lower cash flow in exchange for more time with their kids and more community volunteering, and has returned to that choice when money was tight. Austin wishes to have made that kind of values-driven decision earlier.

What did being dishonest with oneself look like?
Austin McDonald

Austin describes frustration and at times bitterness when others were promoted or got jobs. Austin says the honest answer was that those people moved teams faster and worked harder, while Austin prioritized family and community. Austin does not think people can have everything: some may be able to be a level-seven IC and leave at 5:00, depending on talent and skills built, but for most people accomplishing something extraordinary takes extraordinary steps.

Austin says that deciding what mattered, including what their children would remember about them in ten or fifteen years, was clarifying.

Source: 1:35:58–1:37:30 ↗
Did that clarity remove the feelings of envy?
Austin McDonald

Austin says the feelings return on a semi-regular basis, especially in Silicon Valley where people stack wealth quickly. Each time Austin asks whether that is what they want. Being aligned with one's own values, with a mission statement or vision for life, is what Austin finds satisfying.

Source: 1:37:32–1:38:10 ↗
Source: 1:33:42–1:35:56 ↗

QWhat is the best career advice Austin ever received?

Austin McDonald

Austin says it was the importance of creating scope. Many people wait for someone to give them the opportunity, but a manager once told Austin that to get an M2 role, Austin had to create an M2-scope team and solve problems of that size. Advancing does not mean doing the same thing better. It means doing something different, which is creating more scope and room for the organization to succeed.

Austin adds a test: what is the VP saying about your project, and if the VP is not telling peers or their manager, is it the right work? Candidates already work backwards from the signal area they want to show in an interview and from the packet they want in a promotion. Austin suggests working backwards in the same way from what leadership should say about the accomplishment, then finding a way to achieve it. QWhat advice would Austin give a younger self just after college?

Austin McDonald

Austin says imposter syndrome held them back. After completing a computer science PhD, Austin spent summers doing university research while peers took industry internships at places like Google or Facebook, because Austin did not want to go through interviews and risk rejection. Austin loves their career and would not change much, but says that fear slowed their understanding of how big organizations and large codebases work, coming from academia.

Austin's summary advice is simple: do not give in to fear.

Section 27 · interview

Vlad Feinberg: Visible Contributions and Supportive Collaboration

Selected passages on internal-transfer visibility, proof of contribution, kindness, and being a colleague others want to support.

Make useful contributions visible

Vlad Feinberg

Feinberg says the strongest signal is evidence of building something that others use. Useful contributions to an existing project give a candidate concrete proof of impact and make their capabilities visible to the people who might work with them.

Source: 30:49–32:42 ↗

QDoes the advice change for an internal transfer, such as an infrastructure engineer moving into a frontier team?

Vlad Feinberg

Feinberg says the advice so far assumed an external hire. Many large organizations do not build frontier models, but still use them. Feinberg gives the example of a colleague from the search side who moved onto Feinberg's team. That colleague's approach was to help the product area adopt the technology as well as possible. Feinberg says there is a large gap in applying and serving LLMs effectively inside such an organization.

Feinberg says becoming the person who closes that gap creates business value and raises the standing of the organization. It also makes that person the natural partner for the research side, so models work well inside that org. Feinberg says transferring is then optional. The work is already cutting edge, because it puts new technology into a product people use.

Source: 32:43–35:11 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself just after college, what would you say?

Vlad Feinberg

Feinberg's first advice is to chase the problems people face today. Feinberg says a person should not avoid a smaller or less glamorous part of a big problem, even if it is not fancy research math. Working on what matters shows what moves the frontier. Feinberg calls for humility in how to approach problems.

Feinberg's second piece of advice is professional: be the co-worker others want to see succeed. Feinberg contrasts this with workplace leaders who squeeze people for short-term results. Feinberg says the most effective people are kind, and cites a mentor who first introduced Feinberg to computer science as one example.

Feinberg says a generous approach can look naive when viewed as workplace game theory, but it builds collaboration and a willingness to help. That trust matters for large projects that need several people and skill sets to finish. Feinberg's summary is to be the kind of person other people want to see succeed.

Source: 58:59–1:02:50 ↗

Section 28 · interview

Make your work and leadership easy to discover

Selected passages on choosing collaborators, leading groups, presenting work clearly, and making a professional brand discoverable.

QHow do you choose good teammates?

Jia Chen

Look at demonstrated skills and projects rather than titles alone. She checks GitHub work, activity, and experience relevant to the proposed project. She also values enthusiasm, effort, resourcefulness, and a willingness to attempt the unfamiliar. The best credential is useful evidence that the person can contribute to this particular build.

Source: 04:43–05:13 ↗

QWhat is the social part of a hackathon?

Jia Chen

It includes both the team and the judges. Inside the team, motivation matters over the whole event: one person giving up can affect a small group disproportionately. An enthusiastic teammate can lift the group, and she has seen the strongest results when everyone is fully engaged.

Source: 07:03–08:02 ↗

QHow do you present a project to judges?

Jia Chen

Keep the pitch short: state the idea, explain what it does, and spend most of the time demonstrating it. Watch whether the judges understand and let them interact with the result. In her experience, many judges were not deeply technical, so a list of frameworks was less persuasive than a product whose value they could see.

This does not rule out technical ambition. A complex project can feel clear and simple when it works well and the presentation makes its purpose obvious. The mistake is assuming that complexity alone is the reason it should win.

Source: 08:02–09:44 ↗

QDid hackathons strengthen your initiative?

Jia Chen

She already had some willingness to try unusual things, but thinks the events helped. School sometimes felt repetitive, and building offered a more stimulating outlet. Coming from an environment where few people were seriously pursuing startups made that experimentation feel different from the usual path.

Source: 15:21–16:26 ↗

QWhat can a student at a less recognizable school do to stand out?

Jia Chen

Develop initiative and responsibility: lead a club, help decide the direction of a substantial project, or make useful work visible. Her point is to become someone who makes decisions and carries them through, rather than relying exclusively on the school’s name.

Source: 19:27–20:18 ↗

QWhat does a personal brand do for a student?

Jia Chen

It makes subsequent work easier to discover. A project shown to a small group reaches only that group; a visible body of work can reach many more recruiters or potential collaborators at once. She sees it as increasing the chances that useful opportunities find her.

How did you overcome fear of putting yourself out there?

She discussed ideas with a few close friends. Knowing that a small group would support her helped make negative reactions from strangers less important. She acted while still feeling nervous, with a grounding support network.

Source: 25:01–26:00 ↗
What is one concrete step for someone who does not want to become a frequent creator?

Move the project beyond localhost. Publish a working version, make the repository available where appropriate, and give people a usable link. Visibility can begin with sharing the work itself rather than posting constantly.

Source: 26:00–26:26 ↗
Source: 24:29–25:01 ↗

Section 29 · interview

Sash: Collaboration, Visible Work, and Career Reputation

Selected passages on cross-functional collaboration, prototype visibility, reputation, performance recognition, and mentor feedback.

QHow did you choose your first team at Meta?

Sash

An initial London-based option lost its appeal when code review across locations took days. Sash then met someone who saw his mix of design and engineering experience as a fit for a team that would turn designers’ unused prototypes into shipped experiences.

That News Feed delight team prioritized animations, playful interactions and other small moments of enjoyment without a clear metrics requirement at the outset. He loved it, but the team lasted only about half a year. Looking back, he recognizes that an enjoyable proposition without a durable impact story was unlikely to survive scrutiny in that organization.

Source: 00:49–02:49 ↗

QHow could a design-oriented team prove its work was successful?

Sash

Sash retrospectively sees the need for an executive sponsor with a credible theory of value. He recalls a survey measure asking whether people felt Facebook cared about them, which supplied a possible connection for delight work. The measure was subjective and open to interpretation.

He thinks it is harder to defend such teams when the company is intensely focused on efficiency. This explains a tension in his choices: he sought work he found compelling even when its measurable payoff was uncertain.

Source: 02:49–03:50 ↗

QWhat were you optimizing for when choosing teams?

Sash

Initially, fun. He followed people, intuition and opportunities that seemed interesting, then made sense of the resulting path afterward. Over time he became somewhat more deliberate but still preferred risky zero-to-one work.

He noticed that many strong engineers wanted a clear product definition, diagram or design before beginning. His comfort working without those gave him a useful niche. Breadth accumulated tools, relationships and knowledge that could become valuable on later projects, although that does not guarantee a successful outcome for every move.

Source: 03:52–05:38 ↗

QWhat makes a designer especially good to work with?

Sash

A willingness to collaborate continuously. An initial design need not anticipate every engineering constraint, but the team eventually has to resolve missing data, network failure and other real-world conditions. Engineering can also introduce possibilities the designer may not have considered, such as sensors affecting an interaction.

He values short feedback loops. On an unreleased hardware project, he worked on a makeshift pipeline that showed Figma designs on the device quickly so designers could change them and immediately see the result. Both sides listening and adjusting produces a stronger product than handing off a supposedly finished idea.

Is the key both rapid iteration and two-way communication?

Yes. He likes beginning with an ambitious picture rather than rejecting it immediately through constraints, then jointly adapting it to processing power, heat or other limits. The constraints still matter; delaying premature dismissal gives the collaboration more room to discover a good solution.

Source: 07:29–08:23 ↗
Source: 05:38–07:27 ↗

QHow was your performance judged when you committed so little code?

Sash

The early team’s expectations centered on reducing uncertainty, not simply landing production code. It was staffed with senior people who understood that a risky project needed that kind of work. Sash describes this as one way a large company can encourage exploration without promising a promotion.

He also sees a tension in review cadence: frequent feedback is useful, but a short cycle can discourage bets whose outcome takes multiple cycles. He does not claim there is a review process that perfectly serves everyone. The important point in his example is that expected contribution was aligned with the project’s exploratory stage.

Source: 12:07–13:37 ↗

QWhat made the senior back-end engineer on that project so effective?

Sash

Deep familiarity with the existing system. The colleague knew how to create a feed, make a post work without an image and understand consequences elsewhere in the application. Their conversations rapidly became working front-end/back-end changes that Sash could test.

Large, mature primitives also helped. A high-level operation could provide defaults and integrations without each engineer rebuilding lower layers. The knowledgeable partner knew how to use those facilities appropriately. Sash’s playful comparison with a copilot emphasizes accurate context and judgment, rather than a literal substitute for the person.

Source: 29:03–30:54 ↗

QDid sharing prototypes build the reputation that led to new opportunities?

Sash

He cannot know exactly what others thought, but believes repeated internal demonstrations made people associate him with fast, exploratory work. Prototypes using company technology could not be shared publicly, so internal posts were an important venue even when immediate engagement was modest.

Responding to an ambiguous inquiry with something working also showed initiative. Early projects benefit from people who can move without a fully assigned checklist. He thinks that behavior stands out amid the meetings and alignment work common in a large company.

Source: 30:55–33:15 ↗

QWhy does a prototype communicate better than a written proposal?

Sash

A written description depends on everyone constructing the same mental model. An image narrows that ambiguity; a video narrows it further. An interactive prototype lets people experience the behavior directly and talk about a specific interaction.

Sash has seen meetings progress for some time before participants discover they imagined different products. A prototype can expose that disagreement early and shorten the ambiguous part of a project. Its fidelity helps alignment, not merely publicity.

Source: 35:20–36:46 ↗

QHow do you assess your growth from IC4 to IC6 despite frequent team switches?

Sash

Staying in one space usually makes leveling easier: expertise, goodwill and relationships compound around a known problem. He saw that in a colleague who remained on the original team for years. He often found that kind of continuity less interesting for himself.

His choices favored enjoyable projects and breadth over maximizing promotion speed. They accumulated connections and knowledge, with some wrong turns along the way. Because he worked long hours, enjoyment mattered to sustaining the effort.

He explicitly resists turning his path into universal advice. The right strategy depends on the career and life a person wants. His eventual promotion does not prove that repeated switching is the fastest route, only that the route can develop a useful niche for someone with his preferences.

Source: 36:47–39:53 ↗

QHow did your path compare with people from your original bootcamp group?

Sash

He remembers peers becoming managers or remaining in the same application or domain, generally doing well. They preferred vertical growth more than his broad exploration. The comparison is a small anecdotal sample, not evidence that one strategy wins.

When leaving, he found it difficult to identify a replacement for a role centered almost entirely on prototyping. He thinks large-company incentives naturally direct most people toward predictable impact. Yet a company also needs some people prepared to test uncertain directions. That balance may help it discover options beyond its established work.

Source: 39:54–42:13 ↗

QWhat are the limits of optimizing only for a metric?

Sash

Sash invokes the familiar problem that a measure can become less informative once it becomes a target: people learn to game it. He also thinks important parts of product quality are difficult to measure and require taste.

A relentlessly increasing local measure can obscure opportunities that require a temporary setback or a different direction. He recognizes the difficulty of translating that insight into a scalable framework, because large organizations also need repeatable processes. His preference for experimentation is a response to that tension, not a fully specified replacement for metrics.

Source: 42:14–42:57 ↗

QDo you regret any of the ten team switches?

Sash

Some paid off less than he hoped, but he learned from them and built relationships. Trying to be a good teammate made those connections useful in both directions: someone could invite him to a later project, or he could bring them along.

The size of that network became particularly visible after he left Meta, when people offered introductions or expressed interest in what he might build next. He values the adventure and people as outcomes, rather than evaluating every move only by title progression.

Source: 42:59–44:39 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself at the beginning of your career?

Sash

Address weaknesses enough that they do not obstruct the work, then invest in the strengths that make the contribution distinctive. A manager helped him see that fixing every shortcoming was not necessarily the highest-value development plan.

For Sash, that means choosing a setting where his comfort with ambiguity, design collaboration and rapid prototyping can be useful. The advice asks a person to understand their own strengths and fit, rather than copy his specific team choices.

Source: 46:43–47:36 ↗

Section 31 · interview

Anders Hejlsberg: Broad Impact Without Losing the Work You Enjoy

Selected passages on delegation, staying engaged while guiding architecture, broad IC impact, and choosing a motivating role.

QHow did you learn to let go of implementation work?

Anders Hejlsberg

Hejlsberg offers a counterexample to the assumption that letting go is always progress. On C#, his central role became language design and specification, with less direct compiler implementation. He gradually found that too detached from the difficult coding problems he enjoyed.

Participating directly in TypeScript’s compiler restored that enjoyment. He likes design work, but writing code is also what makes him eager to begin the day. The lesson was to delegate without accidentally removing the activity that motivates him.

Source: 43:03–44:48 ↗

QHow can a very senior engineer continue coding while meeting expectations for broad impact?

Anders Hejlsberg

His impact comes from architectural guidance as part of a group, while he remains involved in a portion of the implementation. That involvement lets him notice awkward code, emerging refactoring needs and practical issues that a specification alone would not reveal.

He distinguishes the impact of any single line he writes from the judgment supported by staying close to the codebase. Combining guidance with direct work allows him to understand the thing people use, not only describe its syntax.

Should every high-level engineer therefore be hands-on?

He does not make that universal claim. He consciously chose an individual-contributor path instead of management because it suits how he does his best work. Other people should identify what motivates them enough to sustain a lifetime of work. The example is a personal choice about contribution and satisfaction.

Source: 46:10–47:09 ↗
Source: 44:50–46:09 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself at the start of your career?

Anders Hejlsberg

Learn to work with other people earlier. Also, do not automatically accept another person’s declaration that a technical goal cannot be achieved: their limit may reflect their experience rather than a fundamental impossibility.

This advice invites investigation and persistence, rather than proving that every ambitious idea will work.

Was there a project where you encountered that skepticism?

He recalls people dismissing what the early Turbo Pascal product could do, even when the team described an implementation it had already built. Not knowing that others considered it impossible helped him attempt the work.

Source: 1:04:38–1:04:55 ↗
Source: 1:03:58–1:04:55 ↗

Section 32 · interview

Build tooling around real pain, then earn adoption

The Bento story links a staff-level technical vision with onboarding, legacy support, team creation, and explicitly agreed exploration.

QWhat was the work behind your senior-staff-equivalent promotion?

Guest

The guest began on a project estimating usage of a Facebook property around 2015. Moving between separate data-pipeline and machine-learning systems was cumbersome, so he built helper scripts that let pipeline work live within the orchestration environment. Sensible defaults removed repeated boilerplate, with an escape hatch for advanced configuration. He estimates that a task needing roughly 300 lines in the older system could need about 20 in his library.

That experience redirected his interest from a single analysis to helping analysts and machine-learning engineers work faster. Notebook setup was another repeated pain: people used outdated wikis to install Jupyter or RStudio manually. With his manager’s agreement, he spent an initial two or three months exploring an automated setup, then recruited others. The earliest Bento was just a setup script; the larger vision was a browser-accessible environment integrated with internal libraries and eventually other languages.

Over roughly a year, the team built the platform and on-demand instances that users could request and release without maintaining their own server. He also assembled a team of six to eight people by inviting engineers who already loved building tools on the side to do it full time. He moved into a tech-lead-manager role and says his TLM2 promotion depended largely on his individual technical work and the Bento vision. The host explains that level as senior-manager or senior-staff equivalent.

Source: 00:00–05:35 ↗

QHow did you turn a useful internal tool into something widely adopted?

Guest

Bento did not initially require converting everybody’s existing workflow. The team targeted onboarding programs, where new data users had no attachment to legacy setup. In a fast-growing company, that supplied many users; existing employees then saw more colleagues on the new system.

For people who remained on legacy notebooks, the team provided maintenance and support in previously underserved channels. That created trust before a migration request. When someone needed an awkward setup, the team could offer either a long manual recipe or the simpler supported Bento path.

The team also spoke with analytics leaders about concrete pain in their groups. Those conversations revealed a larger backlog of data-tooling needs. Because no dedicated team served that area, the guest moved from core data science into developer infrastructure to create one. Adoption was therefore a mix of a convenient entry point, service to existing users, leadership relationships, and a fitting organizational home.

Source: 05:33–08:49 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 00:05–08:49 ↗

QHow do you take a promising risk when short-term performance expectations are strict?

Guest

The guest thinks underperformance has greater consequences than it did a decade earlier, but the key practice is the same: agree on expectations before departing from normal work. He was assigned to data consulting, while the proposed work was infrastructure, so he asked his manager and skip to make a bounded exploration part of his job.

If the tool succeeded, the team benefited; if it failed, completing an agreed exploration was still the expectation. He sees that as much safer than disappearing for three months and returning with work nobody knew had displaced his normal obligations.

Over-communicate and be prepared to hear no. He credits a manager who supported this experiment and remembers later proposals that leadership rejected. The story does not promise that every risk can be negotiated away or that an exploratory project guarantees a promotion.

Source: 08:51–11:20 ↗

Build agency, confidence, and organizational judgment

Selected passages on agency, confidence, useful strengths, collaboration, speaking up, and reading organizational context.

QWhat did imposter syndrome delay?

Guest 3

A third guest would trust his judgment sooner. Successful projects, good collaboration, and feedback eventually built confidence, but earlier anxiety kept him from trying some ideas because he feared rocking the boat. Several of those disruptive projects later worked well. He wishes he had tested them earlier and spent less time worrying, while grounding the eventual confidence in experience rather than claiming every first idea was right.

Source: 06:28–07:19 ↗

QHow can a combination of ordinary strengths become distinctive?

Guest 5

A guest who admired specialists in design and engineering worried that being only moderately strong across several areas would not work. His actual advantage was negotiating across those areas. He would focus less on being the best at a single discipline and more on the unusual combination he could bring.

He would also be braver about sharing ideas. His fear of public speaking at school contrasted sharply with his comfort pitching a product he cared about. Explaining material as a test of knowledge made him anxious; advocating for a change he wanted to create gave him a different purpose. Passion did not magically remove every challenge, but it changed what speaking meant to him.

Source: 08:46–10:49 ↗

QWhat matters beyond being the person who writes requested code?

Dwayne

Addressing his younger self as Dwayne, this guest would ask how anyone knows that a requested implementation is the right thing to build. He would seek participation in those decisions, instead of defining his value only by what he can type. That wider role would have helped counter his early imposter syndrome and clarify that ideas and judgment can matter more than raw output.

Source: 12:24–13:15 ↗

QHow would you become more courageous without pretending embarrassment disappears?

Brian

Addressing himself as Brian, the next guest would be more courageous and less embarrassed by failure. He immediately qualifies the short advice as the beginning of a larger conversation about understanding feelings, not a command that makes them vanish. He thinks being more in touch with emotion, possibly through therapy, can help both the person and their relationships.

Is that easier said than done when embarrassment is something you simply feel?

Yes. He agrees and says the two-sentence advice would need deeper discussion of the feelings and how to understand them. He does not supply a complete technique for eliminating embarrassment.

Source: 13:24–13:56 ↗
Source: 13:15–13:56 ↗

QHow do you choose an environment that values your strengths?

Guest 9

Another guest says a strong front-end engineer can struggle on a back-end team, or a person who loves improving frameworks can receive poor results on a team focused on product delivery. Activity alone is insufficient: even hundreds of changes may not serve the team’s priorities. Recognize a persistent mismatch and seek a team and management chain that need what you are good at. The principle is fit between strengths and valued work, rather than simply doing more of a strength in any environment.

Source: 13:56–14:41 ↗

QWhat should guide you when an organization’s inherited practices seem strange?

Guest 11

The final guest recommends common sense. Large companies can have misaligned incentives and processes retained mainly because they have always existed. Startups also need judgment about what markets and users actually want. He would trust and develop that practical judgment rather than assume organizational convention has already answered the problem.

Section 34 · companion

Senior scope grows in depth, breadth, and time horizon

Philip Su explains why the highest engineering levels require qualitative judgment and illustrates that scope through building Meta’s London engineering site.

QWhat distinguishes the work at E7, E8, and E9?

Philip Su

Philip Su begins with scope of influence: how large, valuable, or long-running an effort can someone reliably bring to completion? He offers approximate historical expectations, such as influencing roughly ten to fifteen people at senior/staff-adjacent levels and perhaps fifty at E7. He explicitly warns that his leveling information may be stale. These are illustrations from his experience, not a promotion standard for any company today.

Higher levels also differ qualitatively. An unusually deep specialist may solve problems that several less-senior engineers cannot substitute for. A broad generalist may integrate many kinds of work for a small or new team more effectively than separate hires. Headcount alone misses that distinction.

He recalls E9 being created after his initial E8 promotion and early decisions involving only a few very different candidates. Such a small and varied group makes a universal checklist implausible. At the top, informed judgment from peers and more-senior leaders matters: do they recognize work of that level, and why? He compares it to the qualitative recognition involved in academic seniority. The point is not that all evaluation is arbitrary, but that a list of tasks cannot fully represent exceptional and varied contributions.

Source: 00:00–05:37 ↗

QWhat if a strong E7 has no E8 or E9 nearby to learn from or assess them?

Philip Su

Su recognizes the problem both in small companies and in weaker teams inside huge organizations. Being the strongest local person can distort self-calibration or remove opportunities to observe better judgment. He recommends an environment where there is room to grow alongside strong colleagues, rather than treating being locally best as the only goal.

At very high levels, merely copying another senior person may not work because their archetype and strengths can differ from yours. He favors access to a coach who participates in the relevant promotion decisions and can give a qualitative assessment. That person can explain where the work remains short of the bar and help discuss what stronger work would look like. The desired input is specific feedback, not an assumption that proximity to a prestigious title automatically produces growth.

Source: 05:38–08:03 ↗

QWhat scope of work contributed to your own E9 promotion?

Philip Su

Su helped start Meta’s London engineering presence with twelve people and, over roughly four or five years, grow it to around four or five hundred. He describes managing the strategic and organizational transitions as the site expanded. A team of twelve could be run well by a capable engineering manager; several orders of magnitude of growth made problems more varied and answers less clear-cut.

One example was planning London internships and headcount based on anticipated visa constraints affecting future full-time arrivals in Menlo Park. He used data to recommend decisions roughly eighteen months before their consequences. Another was examining the site’s seniority distribution and whether engineers were developing at appropriate rates, rather than only checking each person’s nominal level.

The increased scope involved both breadth of people affected and the time horizon of judgment. He presents a collection of such decisions as the promotion story rather than naming one isolated code change or asserting that simply growing a site guarantees the same level.

Source: 08:04–10:36 ↗

DimensionWhat Su emphasizes

DepthSolve qualitative technical problems that adding less-senior engineers cannot reproduce.

Section 35 · lesson

Staff engineering begins with leadership beyond your own tasks

Peterman introduces staff engineering through scope, influence, and the individual-contributor career path.

A career branch, not an obligatory next promotion

Peterman describes a common progression from entry-level through mid-level to senior engineering. At many companies, senior can be a sustainable destination as well as a branching point: an engineer may continue on the individual-contributor ladder or move into management. He presents this as a broad framing, not a universal set of titles or a guarantee that every company organizes careers the same way.

Source: 00:00–00:41 ↗

Lead while remaining an individual contributor

In his framing, staff is the first individual-contributor level at which leadership is unavoidable. You can remain an engineer without becoming a people manager, but you must help other people and projects succeed. The promotion is difficult precisely because it is a change in scope and behavior, not merely recognition for writing more code.

Source: 00:43–01:31 ↗

Use engineering to extend your impact

He emphasizes the unusual scope of the engineering path: tools, systems, and methods can increase the effectiveness of both an individual and many other people. This creates a route to greater influence and compensation outside management. His comparison with other professions is an illustration of that idea, rather than a comprehensive claim about their career ladders.

Source: 01:33–02:14 ↗

Section 36 · interview

Adrien Friggeri: Negotiate Scope and Build Promotion Support

Selected passages on manager alignment, negotiating scope, team assembly, adoption, and opportunity-building relationships.

QWhat was the story behind your first senior-level promotion, at Instagram?

Adrien Friggeri

After the rumor work, Adrien met Instagram's co-founder and CTO. Facebook had acquired Instagram in September 2012, and the core team had about 30 people. Instagram had no personalization and no A/B testing. He started with the Explore tab, adding personalization, and needed a way to measure whether it worked. Product leaders said they had bigger priorities during Instagram's move from AWS to Facebook infrastructure.

He built the testing system anyway, with a product manager giving cover. He reused Facebook's system. Because Instagram ran on different infrastructure, he added a custom Facebook API endpoint, allowlisted to Instagram's app ID, to log exposures. He calls that hacky and probably expensive. He also added user hashing, connected the logs to the data warehouse, ran a server-side A/A test, and worked with mobile engineers on small experiments.

He says he did not know promotions existed. He was an IC4, and when his manager announced an IC5 promotion, he had to ask what the level meant. He then handed the A/B testing system to a newly created team that owned it.

Was reaching out to senior people and peers unusual early in your career?
Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says early Facebook was bottom-up: if you needed something you could not do alone, you found someone to help. In his first six months he joined about six hackathons, usually on Thursday evenings, working through the night on projects unrelated to his day job. He says that was the culture.

Source: 12:43–14:04 ↗
Source: 07:24–12:41 ↗

QWere there cultural differences between the early Instagram team and Facebook?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says he never officially joined the Instagram team. His data science group worked like consultants, embedding in other teams while his reporting line stayed the same, and he had two managers in his first few years. Instagram felt like a startup within a startup. Facebook had about 2,000 employees, and the core Instagram team of 30 to 40 people fit in one conference room, with a focus on design and craft over data.

What do you mean by your biggest career mistake, and where would your career be if you had joined Instagram?
Adrien Friggeri

He calls not joining Instagram one of his biggest career mistakes, but not a serious regret. His career might have grown faster, since colleagues who stayed reached senior levels sooner. He calls it a road not taken and says the counterfactual is hard to know.

Source: 15:43–16:33 ↗
Source: 14:05–15:42 ↗

QCan you tell the story behind your IC7, or senior staff, promotion?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien worked on projects that brought data to non-data teams. One project to count users of a Facebook product needed machine learning and inference, but the tools were poor. He built a library to run data pipelines inside the machine learning framework. He says a pipeline that took about 300 lines in a standard system could take about 20 with the library. That convinced him to build tools that help others move faster.

Half the company used Jupyter and half used RStudio, and setup depended on outdated wikis. He proposed that everyone have a Jupyter instance, pitched a two-to-three-month trial to his manager, and built the first version of Bento. At first it was only a setup script. The vision was to connect it to company tools, so a user could open a browser, type Bento, and get a notebook with internal libraries ready.

Bento on demand later let users request a temporary instance instead of a shared dev server. Adrien helped lead the work and built the team by hiring people who were already building tools on their own time. He became a tech lead manager and was promoted to TLM2, which he says is equivalent to senior manager and to senior staff engineer in the industry.

Source: 16:35–22:05 ↗

QWhat is the step-by-step process for getting internal tooling from an idea to something everyone uses?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says Bento did not try to win adoption within existing workflows. The team targeted bootcamp, the onboarding program for new hires, and told everyone who worked with data that this was the way to set up. The company was growing fast, so many newcomers did not know the legacy systems, and others followed their peers onto the new tool.

The team also maintained legacy setups that had gone unmaintained. Doing that built trust with users.

Was the approach an easy sell because the company was growing, and did leadership support matter too?
Adrien Friggeri

Adrien summarizes the approach in two steps. First, use network effects to get a group of users through an easy path. Second, give value to people on legacy systems. Once trust was built, the team offered Bento features in place of a 25-step manual recipe. The host notes that developer tools usually need people to leave something they already use, but new hires in a growing company choose on a fresh slate, so the product may have been an easy sell.

Adrien also went to the head of analytics and another leader, said teams had real pain, and offered help. One leader said it was a good first step, but there were about 20 other things to fix. They agreed to take it one step at a time. Adrien then moved into the developer infrastructure organization to build a team focused on data developer tools, since no team then built tools for data science and machine learning.

Source: 23:55–25:55 ↗
Source: 22:07–23:53 ↗

QYou took on a performance risk to build something that could flop. Is that harder today, and how should someone take risks for bigger rewards?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says the stakes for underperforming are higher now, but the approach is the same. Align with your manager first, because people are judged against expectations. He told his manager he would step away from assigned work and asked for two or three months to explore the idea. He called it a calculated risk that the team agreed to.

He thinks doing your own project in secret is riskier, since you can show up after three months with a result nobody knew about. His advice is to overcommunicate and be ready to hear no. Later, when he tried to build consensus for other ideas, he was sometimes told no.

Source: 25:58–28:10 ↗

QWhat was the thinking behind moving into a tech lead manager role?

Adrien Friggeri

The team was building a product that had to scale, and it needed more people. Adrien could hire a manager with a different vision or try management himself. The move was driven by a wish to lead the team he had assembled, not by a plan to become a manager. The team needed a manager, and he became that manager.

Source: 28:12–29:00 ↗

QWhat advice do you have for ramping up in a completely different domain?

Adrien Friggeri

He starts with a social network exploration: talk to people and ask who else to talk to. Do not fear basic questions, since everyone knows a newcomer is new. He also gets hands-on. Although he never officially worked on firmware, he read the code and made a few changes. He then picks a hard problem he roughly knows how to solve, because he learns by doing.

Source: 39:43–40:48 ↗

QWhat scope got you promoted to IC8, principal engineer?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien became responsible for all experiences on a device, across dozens of teams and about 35 product managers. Partner teams owned the operating system layer. His job was coordination, architecture, and hitting milestones. For a product such as Ray-Ban Meta, the experiences include on-device AI, music, photo capture, and the companion app.

IC5 surprised him. For IC6 he asked his manager to put him forward, and IC7 took a couple of review cycles. For IC8, his manager had never run that promotion, so they worked out the packet together, and Adrien wrote much of it. He built consensus with several vice presidents early, and asked a director for monthly check-ins on the gap to that level. Six months later, the director supported the promotion because he had been involved throughout.

Is identifying champions even more important for the highest-level promotions?
Adrien Friggeri

The host says champions matter most at the highest levels. Adrien agrees, but says the underlying impact still has to be there. Building consensus early keeps calibration from becoming a debate. His IC promotion took two cycles, and in the first, his manager socialized the idea without formally nominating him.

Source: 44:07–45:18 ↗
Source: 40:51–44:05 ↗

QWhen a role is limited to one person, such as the only tech lead for a program, how do you secure scope?

Adrien Friggeri

One engineer was the tech lead for the whole program. Adrien saw that much of the experience work could be handled by someone focused on it. He took it off the lead's plate so the lead could focus on the wider program, while the lead kept the systems work. The two built trust. After about a year, Adrien asked leadership to formally recognize the role, so he could describe it in one sentence.

He rejects the idea that taking scope is stealing. It is a problem only if you do not talk to the person. He asked the engineer first, who agreed, and he asked again later about a related area. Overcommunicating is the consistent theme.

Is giving up scope a win for the person who gives it away?
Adrien Friggeri

The host suggests that handing off scope can help a senior engineer grow into a bigger role. Adrien agrees, and says he has pushed junior engineers to take ownership, which helps them and lets him delegate more.

Source: 48:42–49:29 ↗
Source: 45:20–48:36 ↗

QYour career has been a series of bumping into the right people. Do you have tips for maximizing luck with people opportunities?

Adrien Friggeri

Adrien says none of his work happened in a vacuum. Early on he had rough edges and strong opinions that did not help him, and he learned that people succeed together. He says trust and respect mean people show up when you need them, but you should not help others in order to get something back.

He also says do not be afraid to ask. For career changes, he never applied through a job website. He reached out to people he knew and asked for small favors, with an easy way to say no. People are busy, so silence is not a verdict. On luck, he says taking more shots increases the odds.

Source: 51:41–54:34 ↗

QIf you could go back to yourself right after graduating college in France, what advice would you give?

Adrien Friggeri

He would say to be a good person, invest in things that are fun, and invest in relationships with co-workers. Credit matters less than it seems, since everyone gets credit for something. He was very credit-driven early on. He would also tell himself to be patient, since he sometimes pushed for promotions before he was ready, and to stay curious and enjoy the work.

Source: 54:36–55:23 ↗

Carey Nachenberg: Credit, Manager Trust, and Communicating Impact

Selected passages on claiming credit honestly, review records, communication to leaders, manager trust, and collaboration.

QCan you give the high-level story of your time at Symantec and how you grew to fellow?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg started in about 1992 as an intern at the Peter Norton Group, which Symantec later acquired. He thinks he was the first intern there and says the company had no desk for him, so he worked in the QA lab. By the time he left in 2016, he had gone from the most junior person to the most senior engineer at Symantec.

Did you set out to work in cyber security, or did it happen by chance?
Carey Nachenberg

By chance. Nachenberg first worked on a file-management utility, not security. In his third internship, Symantec bought an antivirus product and renamed it Norton Antivirus. The team that analyzed computer viruses needed an intern, and he was placed there with no experience.

Source: 02:43–03:21 ↗
Source: 01:27–02:42 ↗

QWhat did the career ladder look like at Symantec, and how did hiring work for someone as senior as you when you joined Google?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says the levels tracked those at Google and Meta from junior engineer up to staff. They differed at the top, with distinguished engineer and fellow at Symantec. Google told him it could not hire a fellow without knowing how he would perform there. He was effectively downgraded to principal engineer, level 8, from what he says would have been about a level 10 and a vice president role at Symantec.

Was your hiring process tailored to your seniority?
Carey Nachenberg

Yes. Nachenberg did not apply. A former Symantec chief operating officer had moved into Google X, where a stealth project was starting, and invited him to talk to the team. He had a meet and greet with the founders in Venice, then about eight interviews in a day. He had an offer letter roughly six weeks later.

Source: 04:16–05:09 ↗
Did that loop include LeetCode-style coding, or was it mostly behavioral?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg does not recall any coding problems and thinks there was one design problem. Most questions were leadership-style: how he solved a hard problem, how he handles conflict, and where the field is going. Some sessions were effectively sales pitches about where Google X thought the world was heading. He believes the team already thought he was a good fit, so the day was mostly about going through the motions and selling him on the role.

Source: 05:10–06:26 ↗
Source: 03:21–04:14 ↗

QWhat do promotions at the highest levels look like?

Carey Nachenberg

At Symantec, Nachenberg says, promotions up to senior technical director were handled within the organization, provided a vice president or senior vice president agreed. Distinguished engineer and fellow went to a core group of technologists led by the chief technology officer. The group met quarterly, reviewed applications, and had candidates present their work. The aim was a consistent bar across the whole company, not division by division.

Was your promotion to fellow a big moment, or something you expected?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg skipped that process. After Symantec merged with Veritas, which already had a fellow role, the company needed to set the level. He was nominated without his knowledge, his portfolio was passed to the evaluators, and he was told he was a fellow.

Source: 07:39–08:43 ↗
Source: 06:26–07:37 ↗

QWhat set you apart from other engineers on the way to fellow?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg credits impactful projects, not always the most technically difficult ones. He looked for gaps: things the company needed that no one was stepping up to do. Symantec in his early years was, in his words, the wild west, with no agile process and no engineers testing their own code. He was never handed a boxed-in project. Because he already knew the technology as an intern, he was told to work out what to do and do it, and he says he chose projects that landed, shipped and transferred into the product.

How did you train your project taste?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says he looks for large business impact and for gaps. His example was polymorphic viruses, which mutated themselves into huge numbers of variants. Teams hand-wrote assembly to catch each variant, a process that took six months because the product shipped twice a year. New variants appeared the next day. He saw a need to respond faster, noted that such threats could not be found by searching for a string, and picked the problem. It became his master's thesis and then a product feature.

Source: 10:54–12:25 ↗
Was your career a series of self-chosen side projects?
Carey Nachenberg

Partly. Nachenberg says that perhaps six or seven times he spotted a company need and spent from six weeks to five months on prototypes and talking to engineers. About 80 percent of his career was then incremental work on those systems, such as helping transfer the technology into products, fixing bugs and improving them.

Source: 12:39–13:13 ↗
Source: 08:44–10:52 ↗

QWhat kept you at Symantec for so long?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says, honestly, imposter syndrome. At Symantec he felt secure because he was well known there. He worried that his success came from having grown up in that company, and that he might not be good enough for Google or Meta. He stayed because it was comfortable and he complained a lot. Near the end he was unhappy, since senior roles bring more meetings and less building, which he describes as a lot of BS.

What helped you overcome it?
Carey Nachenberg

An outside pull. Someone at Google X said they wanted to interview him. Nachenberg was sure he would fail but went ahead. He says he needed that push to take the chance, and it worked out.

Source: 19:05–19:32 ↗
How do you avoid the BS at senior levels?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says some senior people stay hands-on, but as an individual-contributor vice president he found the strategy meetings inevitable. They bring many opinions, debate and power posturing. His best moments were picking his own projects and going two months with no one asking what he was doing. He gives one example: he wrote Symantec's technology strategy and the CEO agreed with it, but product teams then objected because of revenue targets. He calls those debates draining.

Source: 19:32–21:27 ↗
Source: 17:16–19:03 ↗

QWhat was Google X like, and were there cultural differences?

Carey Nachenberg

Fewer than expected, Nachenberg says. The main difference was the quality of the people, who were very smart, whereas Symantec lacked an engineering culture, at least until it began to form around 2016. What was the same was that many people lacked project taste. They were smart, but he doubted they picked projects that would land or were feasible. He says this is true of engineers at any company.

Why was one very bright colleague still at a low level?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg describes a colleague he judged astoundingly brilliant who was still at L4. He says the reasons were weak communication, work that interested the colleague but had little business impact, and apparently poor collaboration. He concludes that intelligence alone does not guarantee success.

Source: 22:57–23:20 ↗
If intelligence matters less, what matters more?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says a baseline is needed and that most Google engineers had it. He does not consider himself especially intelligent and says he learns slowly. Beyond that baseline he names communication and collaboration, including getting what you need from people without telling them they are wrong. He admits he has not mastered this and has failed at it. The big one, he says, is focusing on outcomes: engineers naturally focus on their own, such as making something 10 percent faster, but the company or another team has different outcomes. Identify those, the metrics behind them, and the few requirements that matter most, and he says that will take you much further than intelligence.

Source: 23:38–25:50 ↗
Is career growth in industry meritocratic?
Carey Nachenberg

By and large, yes, in Nachenberg's experience. He saw exceptions where a senior vice president pushed a promotion mainly to retain someone, which he says damages standards. The committees he sat on weighed the complexity and impact of work, communication and patents. He also found Google's discussions careful and fair. In his view senior levels required being well rounded, or at least very strong in some areas.

Source: 25:50–28:14 ↗
Source: 21:28–22:56 ↗

QWhy did you eventually leave Google?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg again cites imposter syndrome, plus a wish to work at a startup instead of a slower, more regulated environment. He says there were big problems he could have taken on, such as moving Chronicle's expensive storage design off heavyweight systems like Spanner. He lacked the confidence to try. Expectations at senior levels are high, and at Google he did not feel leadership would back him if a months-long attempt did not land. At Symantec his managers had known him for years and gave him rope. He was offered other roles, such as secure databases that compute on encrypted data. He wanted something new, and talks with Waymo people while at X had made him want to work on self-driving cars.

Did you consider asking for a demotion to reduce the pressure?
Carey Nachenberg

Not at Symantec, where he could do what he liked. He thought about it at Google but concluded it would not help. Even at lower levels, he says, there are expectations he might not meet if he went off for a couple of months to think, which is how he had been most successful. He calls himself a loosey-goosey prototyper who does not enjoy testing every edge case. Google expects that, so he would have had to do things he disliked to do the things he wanted.

Source: 36:29–37:42 ↗
Source: 34:24–36:27 ↗

QHow did you become a lecturer at UCLA, and how do you make your lectures engaging?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg taught programming at Learning Tree around 1990 to 1991, including to DeVry staff. He also ran evening whiteboard sessions at UCLA as an undergraduate. Years later, a colleague at Symantec who lectured part time at UCLA told him to apply. Nachenberg assumed his lack of a PhD ruled him out. After months of silence, UCLA called in a panic when a lecturer dropped out, and he had two weeks to plan an undergraduate course. That was about 25 years ago.

For lectures, he designs for roughly the 30th to 50th percentile of the class, and uses himself, a slow learner, as the model. He asks what he would want to know on first meeting a topic, and what students are likely to be fuzzy on. He says he spends days with ChatGPT o3 simplifying concepts, then checks with Gemini and compares differences, because he finds good online material scarce and textbooks poor. He also wants students to enjoy class, so he adds humor, color and surprise.

What tips do you have for public speaking?
Carey Nachenberg

Practice, says Nachenberg. He finds his own speaking declines within a year of not using it. He suggests giving a lunchroom talk about a project even when nothing requires it. People appreciate it, and you improve. He recalls giving his Stuxnet and malware talk privately inside X, after which colleagues said he was one of the smartest people they had met. He says people read good communication as intelligence, and it brings credit and opportunities.

Source: 51:31–53:22 ↗
Source: 46:53–51:29 ↗

QLooking back, is there anything you regret or would change?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says he should have left Symantec earlier. His rule is to stay while you are learning, building skills and feel free to fail occasionally. He lost that at Symantec, but stayed because he lacked confidence, not because the work interested him. He still values staying five or even ten years as long as you learn. Switching teams can keep a good reputation and institutional knowledge. Staying too long makes you stale and comfortable.

He also notes the cost of leaving. At Symantec he was widely known and appeared on TV and in major newspapers about Stuxnet. At Google nobody cared what he had done before, so he had to rebuild trust and reputation, which is stressful.

What about golden handcuffs, where you earn well but no longer learn?
Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg would never say to leave a good package. People need different amounts of money to feel safe, and people balance several things. Being comfortable and well paid for a while can be fine. But for someone who is solving for enjoyment and hard problems, he thinks too long in that state can become toxic.

Source: 1:06:36–1:07:13 ↗
Source: 1:03:39–1:06:36 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself on graduating from UCLA, what would you say?

Carey Nachenberg

Nachenberg says there is no single item. First, do not let fear of failure hold you back. You can probably do more than you think, and he says he might have had a richer career had he listened. Second, focus on outcomes: who will use the work, what they care about and how they measure success. Problems often need a small square piece, not a perfect round thing.

He says he once presented technology to senior leaders, who did not care how the algorithm worked. They wanted to know whether it was faster, by how much, and what it meant for revenue or headcount. Speak to their needs, not your own. Third, find a good manager who trusts you and gives you rope, since a manager can make or break your career and happiness. Fourth, learn to collaborate and not assume you are right and tell others they are wrong. He says he still struggles with this.

Source: 1:09:13–1:10:50 ↗
