Choose the staff role with its responsibilities in view

Ricky explains a fast Google promotion path built on ownership and measurable impact, while questioning whether faster advancement always improves daily life.

QWhat was the overall promotion and compensation timeline?

Ricky

Ricky joined Google as a new graduate in 2017 after an internship. He reports approximately $180,000 annual compensation plus a signing bonus, then promotion to L4 after a year and a half at about $250,000, L5 after another year and a half at roughly $350,000, and L6 three years later at roughly $500,000–$520,000. The amounts are retrospective figures from his own situation, including equity effects, rather than current compensation guarantees.

He credits a fortunate team match and considers reaching senior in three years faster than the typical path he observed. Staff took longer and involved a different kind of responsibility. The career story combines his deliberate work with opportunities he did not control.

Source: 00:43–02:30 ↗

QWhat happened in the junior-to-midlevel promotion process?

Ricky

In the review system Ricky describes, ratings arrived every six months. He first met expectations, then exceeded them, and received a still stronger rating alongside promotion. He believed his impact and independence matched the next level but worried that short tenure might count against him. His manager supported the attempt.

Who should initiate promotion discussions?
Ricky

He recommends employee initiative supported by an ongoing conversation with the manager. He regularly asked whether his current projects demonstrated the next level and aligned expectations about timing and scope. Managing upward made an accelerated path more deliberate; it was not a promotion that arrived without discussion.

Source: 03:12–04:30 ↗
Source: 02:22–03:56 ↗

QWhat behavior made the first promotion possible?

Ricky

Independence: finishing projects with less handholding and finding ways to unblock himself. This did not mean refusing to ask anyone for help. It meant learning enough to move the project without requiring the manager to solve every obstacle.

How did you become better at unblocking yourself?
Ricky

He deliberately asked questions despite fearing he would look incompetent. His alternative was worse: staying silent, learning nothing, and failing to deliver. Colleagues generally wanted him to succeed. Asking the knowledgeable engineer helped him learn to do the work himself.

They recommend a real attempt before asking, but not remaining motionless for half a day or longer. Repeatedly asking the same question or receiving the same code-review feedback without improvement is different from healthy learning. The desired pattern is increasing independence and fewer repeated mistakes over time.

Source: 04:49–07:05 ↗
Source: 04:19–04:49 ↗

QWhat changed when working toward senior?

Ricky

He became the owner and go-to person for a defined area, learning its code and delivering several impactful projects there. Ownership meant being able to answer questions and advance the area, not merely shipping more isolated changes.

Did you choose the area through an explicit promotion plan?
Ricky

At first he simply found a part of the advertising experience visually unappealing and interesting to improve. The improvements could also produce measurable impact. Repeated projects and exploration gradually made him the owner, rather than a manager initially assigning a complete senior-level charter.

Source: 07:34–08:46 ↗
Did you have to compete for that scope?
Ricky

His team allowed engineers to choose many of their own projects. He sought work with meaningful impact and enough challenge to extend his skills. He recognizes that managers may assign useful work too, but relying only on assignments would not necessarily supply the scope needed for his desired growth.

Source: 08:28–09:31 ↗
Source: 07:05–07:56 ↗

QHow did you recognize projects that were genuinely at the next level?

Ricky

He studied teammates’ successful senior promotions to understand the scope and complexity expected, generated comparable ideas, and asked his manager to calibrate them. Roughly a year before his promotion he proposed a roadmap and asked whether completing it would meet the bar.

This gave the manager something concrete to assess and made the growth plan explicit. The roadmap emerged after approximately six months of exploration following L4, rather than immediately on the day of that promotion.

When did you put that roadmap together?
Ricky

After the midlevel promotion he tried different projects and learned what interested him. He then wrote the one-year plan himself and sought managerial buy-in. Exploration preceded the more committed roadmap.

Source: 10:21–11:06 ↗
Source: 09:10–11:06 ↗

QWhat did you do when requested work did not advance that roadmap?

Ricky

He learned to say no to unrelated projects that consumed time without helping him grow. He distinguishes that from accountability: a bug he caused, or a bug within his owned area, still needed attention. A new request could also be worth accepting if its impact and scope were stronger than the existing plan.

How can someone say no without damaging the relationship?
Ricky

For an outside request he would bring the tradeoff to his manager and understand why it was assigned. For the manager’s own request he would ask whether it was required and explain the competing projects’ impact and growth value. This is a discussion of priorities, not a license to ignore obligations.

He believes managers should try to match important work with reports’ growth and interests. His own early record of finding and delivering projects earned trust, although the manager continued to guide which ideas were useful.

Ricky

First define what the organization values. In his advertising area, revenue was a central metric, alongside whether the work helped users, advertisers, and publishers. He found measurable results persuasive in arguments about project value. His emphatic statement that numbers settle the matter belongs to his experience in a revenue-measured area; it should not be treated as a claim that every engineering contribution is captured by one number.

Section 39 · interview

David Fowler: Initiative, Delegation, and Senior Promotion

Selected passages on initiative, mentoring, scaling through others, reorg/team evaluation, and senior promotion.

QHow does Microsoft's leveling system work, given that levels run upward from 59 with about two levels per title?

David Fowler

Fowler says he cannot explain why numbering starts at 59, and guesses the lower levels cover non-engineering roles. A college graduate typically starts at 59 or 60, depending on how many times they interned and how well they did. Fowler equates entry level with an SDE I at other companies.

A title maps to a band of about two levels, so a title does not reveal which level someone holds. Principal is the exception at three levels, and Fowler says that band is so broad that a new arrival from senior and a long-serving principal share a title. Above principal come the partner levels, which Fowler says have three bands, and then technical fellow.

Source: 00:37–03:14 ↗

QWhat did your performance review look like after NuGet, for someone who was not yet a senior engineer?

David Fowler

Fowler's first promotion came about eight months after joining, before NuGet. Because he had interned twice, he arrived with a lot of Microsoft experience. Beyond assigned work, he read forums for feedback on Microsoft's products, built features to answer it, and showed the results to product managers, architects and the team. Looking back, he says those people became sponsors and positioned him to build NuGet.

Fowler calls himself a code-first, ask-questions-later person and says code is currency: a working sample beats a PowerPoint or a document. A director once told him he would send people to talk to David because David has energy.

Did the lasting impact of something like NuGet carry over into later reviews?
David Fowler

Fowler says the bigger promotions felt like accumulated history plus current success. Impact is officially meant to be for the year, and crossing a band boundary, such as to senior or to principal, takes more than moving within a band. He is unsure whether Microsoft has an official deferred-impact rule, but says it clearly mattered at the higher principal levels, where the question was whether he had shown repeated impact over ten years.

QHow can others start projects like this within a large company, when the motivation comes entirely from them?

David Fowler

Fowler's one-sentence answer is that you can just do things, which people now call agency. He does not recommend spending every night and weekend on projects, but early on his goal was to get better at software engineering, and the way was to build everything possible: games, websites, many kinds of software.

The second habit was to find someone on the team whose career he wanted. Fowler attached himself to the architect David Ebbo, whose role spanned several areas and looked ahead, copied his behaviors, and for a while coded Ebbo's ideas, which turned into doing it independently. He then built prototypes and showed them to an advocate, the architect or the product manager, to ask whether they were useful. He says he would build a thousand things and maybe one would hit.

So agency at a big company came from energy, moonlighting and doing more than the assigned work?
David Fowler

Fowler agrees in part. Once an engineer builds a reputation for building things, more opportunities arrive and people ask for a take on new work. He cautions that this is not guaranteed, but in his case it was clearly true and continued after SignalR.

The host puts it that way, and the exchange adds that a stronger track record earns more room to be permissionless, because each success buys more latitude to fail. QWhat led to the promotion to principal?

David Fowler

Fowler recalls a boss who, when he reached senior, said promotions would slow. The jump to principal turned out to be large. Alongside SignalR, he built Kudu, an early Azure tool that let people push code and deploy an app instantly, as Heroku and AppHarbor did. A director then pulled him onto a new project that became the cross-platform .NET Core.

Fowler was senior, and he and another principal engineer were chosen as architects over about 30 engineers with free rein, which he calls amazing and terrifying. At first he tried to code review every change and was burnt out within a year, and had to learn to trust people and separate urgent from not urgent. He had his first child and was promoted to principal that same year.

How did you scale yourself out of necessity so you did not burn out as architect for so many engineers?
David Fowler

Fowler learned the first lessons on SignalR, a team of seven or eight including two new hires. Before that he never delegated to grow someone and assumed he could do the work faster himself. It flipped when he saw that investing in smart new hires would amplify impact even if early tasks took longer. He calls the senior-to-principal leap doing more through others than yourself, and the point where many engineers plateau because they prefer coding alone.

On .NET Core, where he says the team rebuilt the package manager, runtime and libraries from scratch, he stopped treating everything as equally urgent and let people fail. He says traits that get an engineer to senior, such as being a control freak or insisting on one way, hurt when scaling to a thousand engineers. The fix was to inspire others through one-on-ones and example, and to become outcome-focused.

QWhat does the architect role mean at Microsoft?

Fowler says it is a semi-official role open to the middle principal bands. When he joined, he saw a principal software architect and decided that was the role he wanted. He describes it as breadth over depth: overseeing the design of the whole system. Other archetypes at the top include a super coder who builds enormous amounts, deep specialists such as one of the leading garbage-collection experts working on the .NET collector, and people overseeing a hugely impactful product area.

As architect for ASP.NET Core, he oversaw the web framework, the web server and how packages shipped, vetting decisions that could last 20 years. He had not done this before and learned by shadowing mentors who had.

Fowler thinks so. A distinguished engineer is measured on organization-wide or company-wide impact, so part of the job is keeping the architecture sound, looking ahead, talking publicly, inspiring and mentoring. He gave four internal talks on using AI for software engineering, which began when someone asked after seeing him use it. Fowler calls it the craziest promotion he has experienced. Distinguished engineer is the last level within partner, and it comes through an official process, not an annual review: a set of technical leaders peer-reviews the candidate. Guido van Rossum, who created Python, is at the same level, and Fowler describes maximum imposter syndrome. He also thought he was young for the role, though that did not count against him.

Fowler says earlier work carried it, because the role requires a body of work and a track record, not one good year. The email promoting him from principal to partner cited .NET Core, by then about seven years old, and he had acted as architect helping many teams adopt the new .NET internally. QOne of your big-company tips is to ask when the last reorg was before changing roles. What is the thinking behind that?

David Fowler

Fowler calls big companies machines and recalls hearing, perhaps tongue in cheek, that executives show motion through reorgs. A reorg is always coming or has just happened, so learn about the last one: who the leaders are, what triggered it and where the org is heading. Because Microsoft is so big, he says, every new org is effectively a new company. The tweet likely followed a mentee who had been reorged several times in a row, or something that happened to him.

Is this about reading what a reorg means for your future?
David Fowler

Yes. Fowler also relays advice he heard recently: when changing jobs, think about what you hate, not what you love, because the things you love will be easy. Someone who hates open offices should not join a company with open-plan seating.

QWhat has kept you at Microsoft for so long, since your internships?

David Fowler

Fowler describes himself as part of a millennial generation that broke from the boomer-parent habit of staying in one place forever, and says many job-hopping friends were paid well for it. His closest call came when he was senior and a boss who had left for pre-IPO Twitter asked him to interview there. He interviewed at Twitter and GitHub, got both offers, and stayed after much deliberation. The morning Twitter went public, he adds, brought instant depression that lasted about a week.

Microsoft's counteroffer was fine but not the main reason. An executive vice president told him he would be a distinguished engineer in five years, which Fowler says oversold it. What mattered more was that he had built something impactful and permissionless and had gained autonomy, and leaving meant starting over. People overlook the network and track record they have built, and the people matter as much as pay: not just good engineers but good people to work with.

He also stayed because he got to work on something new about every two years, by design, which kept him from feeling the need to go elsewhere.

If a mentee at Microsoft had a pre-IPO offer from a company like OpenAI, would you say stay or go?
David Fowler

Fowler would tell them to go. He recalls a mentee with an offer from another company who was not in a place to do their best work, and told that mentee to leave despite any counteroffer. He says that, in the same situation himself, he might have gone.

You tweeted that once in a career you should stay on a project long enough to see the long-term impact of your decisions. What prompted that?
David Fowler

Fowler's career had been to work on something and move on, still helping those who took over. .NET Core, at about ten years, is the longest he has worked on anything. Seeing the effects of decisions made in the first two years, good or bad, gave him a new perspective. He jokes that on a ten-year project every small issue you postponed becomes a big one, because somebody will hit all of it.

He is unsure twenty years on one project is good for career growth, but says it teaches you the implications of your choices and what you would fix in the next version. The host wonders what a chain of ever-higher jumps does for judgment if each project declines after the person leaves. Fowler does not fault either path and has done both. He cannot name the ingredients of a successful project, but can tell when he is on one, like a fine-tuned internal model built over experience.

QDid you notice the culture shifting internally when Satya Nadella became CEO?

David Fowler

Fowler says the shift was huge, but it is hard to see the jump from Steve Ballmer's era because he lived through it and it happened gradually. A big one was that, historically, two teams could work toward the same end state and one would win. Under Nadella the focus moved to collaboration over being first. He saw teams building solutions before knowing the problem, though not on his own team.

He describes changes in meetings, email and remote friendliness. He remembers being surprised by someone raising a hand in a Teams meeting, having grown up in a culture where you wait for a pause and talk. Earlier meetings were often a highest-paid-person's-opinion affair, where a loud senior person could stop others from feeling safe to speak. Early in his career he saw people shouting and wondered whether he would have to shout too. Now leaders model behavior such as inviting quiet people to share their views.

Collaboration also became part of reviews: engineers who avoided other teams' work, or cloned it, were marked down. The host summarizes this as a change driven by performance incentives and top-down messaging, and Fowler adds the behaviors leaders modeled. The host recalls the XKCD comic that draws Microsoft as people pointing guns at each other. Fowler says the real shift went from guns to ambivalence, with teams staying out of each other's way, and then to rewarded collaboration.

Source: 1:17:16–1:23:01 ↗

QIf you could advise yourself when graduating college and entering the industry, what would you say?

David Fowler

Fowler's answer is to negotiate the salary. He did not know it was possible when he took his first job. A new graduate should get multiple offers and push the number up. Coming from Barbados and grateful for the most money he had seen, he was shocked to watch friends decline offers and say they would check Google or Facebook first. Having since sat on hiring committees for interns, he finds it impressive to watch a candidate bump up an offer well.

Section 40 · interview

Expand ownership without losing the engineer

Simon’s three-year rise to staff engineering shows how project ownership, mentorship, delegation, communication, and role fit interact.

QWhat work and team context supported your unusually fast growth?

Simon

Simon stayed with the same team and manager for about five and a half years. That continuity was unusual in his experience of Meta, but the team’s responsibilities changed substantially. It worked in ads payments, initially improving payment experiences and revenue, then supporting a large infrastructure migration, and later returning to product work.

The product context mattered. Revenue provided a relatively direct measure of impact, while local behavior created concrete problems to solve: in Thailand, for example, people bought through Messenger and exchanged bank slips as payment evidence. His career story therefore combines organizational continuity with changing technical and product scope, rather than repeating the same job for years.

Source: 00:55–02:32 ↗

QHow did you earn the IC3-to-IC4 promotion in your first half?

Simon

His earlier Meta internship reduced the learning curve for custom internal tools. He estimates that familiarity with tools such as Phabricator and the task system saved four to eight weeks. Before joining full time, he had also explored technologies through small projects, so bootcamp tasks were easier and he could help other new hires.

He joined as the second engineer on a new ads payments team. That gave him substantial access to a technical manager and impactful projects. Simon says the projects he delivered produced more than three times the team’s half-year revenue goal. The behavioral distinction was ownership of complete projects: finish the task, seek the next related opportunity, investigate disappointing results, and bring the work to a conclusion while asking for help where needed. In his account, promotion followed demonstrated next-level behavior rather than promising potential.

What preparation was actually useful before joining?

Small React projects and familiarity with what different technologies did were more useful than trying to memorize unavailable internal documentation. He describes engineers as pattern matchers: experience with TypeScript, for example, makes Meta’s Flow easier to learn even though the two are not identical. Exploration gave him enough vocabulary and examples to recognize new tools quickly.

Source: 04:10–05:32 ↗
Did an internship on another team still help?

Yes. The team was different, but internal tools and the workflow for landing code transferred. His internship did not remove the need to learn the product domain; it removed friction in getting started.

Source: 05:32–05:51 ↗
Source: 02:33–07:29 ↗

QWhy join a tiny product team, and where did the technical mentorship come from?

Simon

He originally expected to join an infrastructure team because C++ infrastructure was his interest and his internship background. During bootcamp, however, the first manager he met connected career growth with revenue impact and made a persuasive case for ads payments. The team also felt welcoming.

The manager had recently moved from IC6 engineering to management and could guide technical decisions as well as product experiments. Simon ran 20 experiments in his first half when the broader organization ran about 50. He attributes much of that velocity to direct, technically informed coaching.

Why were you already focused on impact as a new graduate?

He had set a personal goal of reaching IC5 within three years and explicitly asked prospective managers how they could support it. His eventual manager drew a possible path on a whiteboard and had followed a similarly rapid path himself. Simon credits that manager heavily; the opportunity was not simply the result of individual effort in isolation.

Source: 09:23–10:32 ↗
Source: 07:29–09:23 ↗

QWhat produced the first “redefines expectations” rating at IC4?

Simon

Simon says impact was the primary driver. His project exceeded an already ambitious team revenue target measured in many tens of millions of dollars. Recruiting and onboarding additional engineers also contributed, and he broadened his reviews across JavaScript, Hack, Android, and iOS as the team grew.

The revenue result was not obvious at the outset. A strong data scientist suspected opportunities, but several initial experiments were neutral. In one, a failed-payment notice did not help advertisers as expected; examining the result led to better targeting and design, after which the project contributed roughly a fifth of his impact that half. In another, a daily script changed advertiser settings but experimentation logging failed. He read the code, contacted the experimentation team, and worked with the data scientist to understand the failure. The important pattern was continuing to investigate rather than declaring the first neutral result final.

His code review also aimed to develop people. That required calibration: some feedback said his reviews were overbearing, while other feedback said they made colleagues better engineers. He does not present helpful review as having been effortless or perfectly balanced from the start.

Source: 10:32–17:48 ↗

QDid you expect those early ratings, and how did you interpret them?

Simon

He had little context for the rating scale. As a new arrival from Sweden, he had not understood that restricted stock would become a large part of compensation, and he was not predicting ratings closely. The first promotion was revealed through his manager’s routine of taking newly promoted reports to dinner.

He was happy with the later top rating, but receiving strong results so early made it hard to judge how unusual they were. His only prior comparison was a promotion with a “greatly exceeds” rating. He knew someone else with a top rating, which also made it seem less rare. His account cautions against treating a person’s early expectations as a reliable guide to the broader distribution.

Source: 17:48–19:59 ↗

QHow could the highest performance rating come without a promotion?

Simon

In Simon’s explanation, ratings largely recognized what he achieved, whereas promotion asked how he achieved it. IC4 work meant driving his own project. IC5 required broader responsibility for others and their projects. He was helping onboard people but was not yet accountable for their success, so very large individual project impact did not by itself demonstrate the IC5 role.

He and the host stress that ratings and promotion are correlated without mapping one to one. Repeating a great deal of current-level work can produce a strong rating while leaving the next-level behavioral gap unresolved.

Did you ask your manager about the missing promotion?

He remembers being sufficiently happy with the rating that he did not press the question. This was not an account of a promised promotion being denied.

QWhat happened during the COVID review pause and your eventual IC5 promotion?

Simon

The first COVID half used annotations rather than normal ratings and did not include promotions. Simon understood his annotation as indicating substantially above-expectation performance. He was disappointed because he felt on track; at that point a single half represented a large fraction of his career, although he now recognizes careers are much longer.

In the next half, he received another “redefines expectations” rating and the IC4-to-IC5 promotion. He qualifies that result: ratings were somewhat boosted to recognize work from the prior half, and his unadjusted result might have been near the boundary with “greatly exceeds.” He does not claim that all strong performers were automatically bumped to the top rating.

The substantive change was leading a pod of about four people through an unscoped product space from initial idea to completed projects. The product itself was not as successful as hoped, but handling the work, people, and director-level escalations showed broader ownership and communication. Promotion therefore reflected changed responsibilities even when the product outcome was imperfect.

Source: 21:35–25:13 ↗

QWhy did the team trust you to lead a pod while you were still IC4?

Simon

Simon sees two foundations: strong technical ability and an interest in people’s growth. He had studied computing from high school in Sweden and enjoyed solving difficult problems across platforms. He also cared about whether colleagues succeeded, had helped people improve, and had already done some sprint planning before taking full responsibility for a pod.

He distinguished prioritizing work from owning its outcome. Earlier he could help plan tasks without being responsible for the project’s or engineers’ success; the pod leadership assignment added that responsibility.

Did that leadership include career conversations?

With some people, yes. With others, he focused on whether they were happy and growing in a weak area rather than on a formal promotion plan. He remembers mentoring roughly four engineers around IC3 and IC4 while also managing one intern and serving as a peer for several others.

Source: 26:49–27:59 ↗
How did you help a struggling intern obtain a return offer?

The intern needed more time with fundamental React or Hack concepts and internal data modeling than anticipated. Simon invested enough time to get her over that early hump, after which progress improved. Helping her secure a return offer remains one of his proudest moments.

He calls generosity with time a potential way to create future capacity, because better-supported colleagues can contribute more independently. He also admits that some investments do not move the needle, that he may persist too long, and that helping this intern intruded on time with his wife. The story supports attentive coaching, not unlimited self-sacrifice as a universal rule.

Source: 27:59–29:53 ↗
Source: 25:13–26:49 ↗

QWhat changed between IC5 and IC6?

Simon

He earned the next promotion in two halves. First, one pod became two pods with roughly seven people, forcing him to delegate sprint planning and recruitment follow-through. He coached new pod leads and colleagues doing outreach, sometimes retaining the difficult initial recruiting conversation while letting others manage the candidate afterward. Those assignments also created growth opportunities for the people receiving them.

His initial delegation had a serious gap: he trusted that work would succeed without tracking it well enough, then discovered slippage near the end of the half. He later learned to zoom out, establish milestones and goals, notice stalled projects or struggling people earlier, and intervene in the specific gap rather than wait for a crisis.

His later scope included an eight-person team plus a separate project involving about 13 people. This tested whether he could combine roadmap and people leadership with deep technical contribution. Detailed reviews across clients and back ends helped him understand system interactions and catch incompatible implementations. Near a payment milestone, he also debugged a difficult path spanning Android or iOS, Instagram servers, Meta’s main backend, C++ payments infrastructure, and an external payments partner. He credits both broad coordination and the ability to go deeply into a hard technical problem.

What specifically fixed the accountability gap after delegation?

His manager’s principle was that delegation did not remove responsibility for the outcome. Simon began using regular progress conversations and two views of work: a project breakdown and a people breakdown. A project may look healthy because one person is compensating for another who has stopped progressing; the people view reveals a need for support.

He also had to avoid the opposite error. Earlier colleagues asked him to step back because he was interfering with their opportunities to implement and grow. His eventual approach was to trust colleagues with execution while checking progress and supporting them through the responsible lead, rather than personally controlling every detail.

QAfter reaching IC6, how did you decide whether to pursue management?

Simon

He remained ambitious, but management presented an identity concern: he valued being a capable engineer and worried that years away from technical work could leave him feeling less useful. The opportunity nevertheless came with his longtime manager’s support. Both had moved to London, and his manager was leading two teams with too many direct reports. Simon already led one of those teams technically.

He chose to try management because learning under a manager he admired seemed unusually favorable. He hoped to become a similar kind of manager, rather than viewing the move as the inevitable next promotion.

Source: 41:17–43:52 ↗

QWhat made that manager unusually helpful?

Simon

Simon emphasizes care for people, projects, and impact; familiarity with Meta’s processes; and firsthand understanding of rapid engineering growth. The manager was also strong at product direction, setting a clear roadmap and communicating upward and downward. That let engineers execute while learning how to reason about data, growth, and product choices.

Written communication was another major lesson. Simon believes people can do excellent work yet limit their careers by explaining only what they did, without explaining why it mattered, what was learned, or what the company gained. A clear internal post can reach thousands and remain available for future decisions.

Source: 43:52–46:38 ↗

QWhat makes a project update effective?

Simon

Assume a reader may spend only five or ten seconds on it. Simon recommends a genuinely short summary, visible before any “see more” expansion, with meaningful numbers when available. Readers should be able to recognize the result and its importance immediately.

He organizes the early portion around context, impact, and next steps, then offers technical details for specialists. Most of a large audience will not know the exact subsystem, but they can still care about outcomes and reasons. The host adds that engineers often lead with code-level investigation that only one or two collaborators understand; status, metric movement, and why the audience should care are more useful first.

Source: 46:38–49:24 ↗

QWhat did the management experiment teach you about technical work and role fit?

Simon

He managed for less than a year, too little time to know whether his technical abilities would truly decay. The more immediate problem was that he struggled to stop doing technical work. Reports asked him to step away; when he saw a gap, his old tech-lead instincts made him want to fill it. He acknowledges that he did not fully correct this before returning to individual contribution.

The circumstances were also unusually difficult. His immediate manager had an accident and was out for months, his skip-level manager was on parental leave, and the nearest available leader was a California-based director returning from prolonged sick leave. Simon was in London, so context and time-zone support were weak. He also had to leave London and was trying to support two engineers who wanted IC5-to-IC6 promotions on a small team. He believes he overpromised: one could take his former technical leadership role, but finding equivalent scope for both was hard.

Burnout and the loss of his support network contributed to switching back. When a director asked if he wanted to return to IC work, the answer felt immediately right. He remains open to management later. His conclusion is qualified: better circumstances might have kept him in management longer, although he suspects he might still have returned to engineering.

Why did returning to IC work fit better?

At IC6 he can combine hands-on work with mentoring and coaching while having more choice about whom and what to help. In management, developing and supporting every report becomes a central obligation and evaluation criterion. As an IC, those activities can add value without becoming his entire job. He is pleased with that flexibility, while recognizing that IC leadership still carries responsibilities.

Source: 53:13–54:45 ↗
Source: 49:24–54:17 ↗

QWhat was the discretionary or additional equity you received?

Simon

Simon describes additional equity as extra restricted stock units granted at a director’s discretion. He received it twice: around the IC5-to-IC6 promotion and about a year later as he moved into management. The first arrived through an unexpected 15-minute director meeting. He had seen compensation-group posts about such grants but recognizes that those posts skew toward unusually strong outcomes.

He speculates that retention and a low original new-graduate stock grant may have contributed to the first award; he does not know the decision makers’ full reasoning. He associates the second with successfully shipping a priority product in London faster than expected. Together, the awards materially increased his compensation. Market comparisons were hard at the time because Meta’s stock price had fallen.

What did you think when a director scheduled a meeting without an agenda?

He had no clear expectation and was nervous. The unexpected meeting turned out to announce good news. This is a personal anecdote, not a dependable signal for interpreting every short leadership meeting.

Source: 54:45–58:48 ↗

QFrom your experience as intern, intern manager, and intern director, what helps interns succeed?

Simon

He nearly failed to get his own return offer, later managed two interns with very different starting points, and served as an intern director overseeing roughly ten intern managers. That director role involved checking project plans and reviewing ramp-up at three weeks, midpoint progress, and the final evaluation.

He sees project completion and velocity as central, with safeguards for badly scoped assignments. A common problem is failing to ask enough early questions. During the first weeks, expectations are low and asking about basics is appropriate; delaying until week six makes the same gap much more consequential. He told interns and new graduates to ask him when a small question consumed more than roughly 30–60 minutes rather than lose repeated hours to an issue an experienced colleague could resolve quickly.

Peers matter as well as managers. A shared chat can distribute support when one person cannot answer everything. Peers also provide important evaluation evidence; knowing the intern’s project and behavior helps them give substantive feedback rather than forcing reviewers to reconstruct what happened.

Can an intern compensate by working extreme hours?

Reviewers try to distinguish sustainable performance from barely meeting expectations through round-the-clock effort. Repeated code submissions at both early morning and late night can be a warning, especially for someone near the pass threshold.

Simon also frames self-care as part of performance. He values exercise, journaling, and morning focus time. He has used a temporary 12–14-hour sprint for about a week and a half to solve a difficult bug, but noticed declining clarity while skipping workouts and drinking more coffee. Occasional intentional sprints and a permanent unsustainable schedule are different choices.

Source: 1:03:23–1:05:57 ↗
Source: 58:49–1:03:23 ↗

QWhat workload has felt sustainable, and how does motivation affect it?

Simon

He estimates an average around 50 hours a week, with variation for California meetings and his morning routine. He enjoys the work and people, but noticed that the same hours began to feel like a grind when his interest in the product area faded.

After reflection, he moved to an infrastructure team and regained enthusiasm and better-quality output. He and the host connect the felt burden of work to interest and motivation as well as hours. This is their experience, not a claim that enjoying work eliminates the need for limits.

Source: 1:05:57–1:08:11 ↗

QLooking back, what most explains your career growth?

Simon

Simon’s central theme is expanding ownership. Early on it means ensuring that a specific task succeeds; later it means owning a team’s success. Curiosity is integral: when another system blocks you, inspect its code and history, understand why a decision was made, and bring a researched question or proposal rather than simply wait.

He interprets Meta’s saying that nothing is someone else’s problem as permission to investigate, not as an excuse to ignore people. Cross-functional ownership requires empathy: learn a partner’s goals and incentives, including whether your proposed improvement damages the metric on which they are evaluated. Technical investigation and understanding people both help unblock the work.

Source: 1:08:11–1:11:13 ↗

QHow much of engineering career growth is technical skill versus other behavior?

Simon

He does not give a numerical split. He believes a solid technical baseline can support considerable success, including IC5, if an engineer can execute work to good quality, work with designers, use data, and collaborate effectively. Extraordinary ability to solve any technical problem is not his minimum requirement for that level.

He regards interpersonal skills as particularly important for gaining trust and opportunities to grow. He also qualifies this: exceptional technical talent can outweigh other weaknesses in some cases. His view is a description of a path he has seen at Meta rather than a universal rule for all roles.

Source: 1:11:13–1:12:34 ↗

QWhy have you stayed at Meta for your whole career so far?

Simon

People and flexibility have kept meeting his needs. His initial team grew from two engineers to around 16 before splitting, and because he helped recruit many of them, the young and supportive group felt close. He continues to value colleagues’ empathy and technical skill.

Internal mobility let him live and work in several locations, including California, London, and New York, and recently move into work that revived his interest. He did consider leaving when his motivation declined, then chose to give an internal move a chance. He acknowledges that some experiences cannot be found at Meta and that his preferences may change; he has simply not yet reached that point.

Source: 1:12:34–1:15:16 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself when joining as a new graduate?

Simon

Ask enough early questions to become productive, then keep investigating why systems work as they do. Be curious, take ownership, and avoid treating every existing constraint as permanent. In a large codebase, past decisions and abandoned experiments may no longer make sense; understanding their history can reveal useful cleanup or a way past a blocker.

He pairs that advice with time awareness. A new engineer still needs velocity and should not disappear indefinitely into investigation. Curiosity becomes more valuable once basic productivity is established.

Source: 1:15:17–1:16:57 ↗

Section 41 · interview

From Strong Output to Scalable Ownership on Instagram Web

An Instagram senior staff engineer traces three promotion projects, explains why collaboration can block a promotion, and shows how tooling and ownership multiply a specialist’s impact.

QWhy specialize in front-end engineering?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Marius describes a longstanding enthusiasm for the web, dating to school lessons in HTML and a CSS book he requested as a Christmas gift. He deliberately sought jobs where he could build web applications, including agency work while studying computer science.

The specialty was a positive choice about work he wanted to do, rather than merely the first technology assigned to him. That preference later helped him decide which opportunities and teams fit his career.

Source: 00:49–02:28 ↗

QWhy did strong performance ratings not immediately lead to promotion from IC4 to IC5?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

In his account, one behavioral gap held back the promotion: cross-functional collaboration. Strong conviction about his ideas sometimes came across as too insistent or intense. Advocating for a proposal was appropriate, but he needed to recognize when continued pressure became counterproductive.

He distinguishes a rating for delivered impact from promotion readiness. A person can deliver a great deal while still missing one behavior expected at the next level. His promotion also encountered a later company-wide pause during the early pandemic, after he had worked on the feedback. He describes these as separate causes, and his eventual promotion came at the end of 2020.

So a high rating and a specific performance concern can coexist?

Yes. A retrospective impact rating does not establish that every next-level behavior is present. Marius believes calibration wanted to see the collaboration issue addressed over another period before promoting him.

Source: 03:59–04:55 ↗
Source: 02:29–05:23 ↗

QHow did you handle the frustration of a delayed promotion?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

He acknowledges frustration, especially after peers reported a visible improvement and an external company decision still blocked the result. He reminded himself that careers are long and a half-year delay has limited meaning across that span.

He continued growing and taking work beyond his current title. With a lagging promotion system, refusing to demonstrate next-level behavior until the title arrives defeats the process itself. The work and learning could continue even while the paperwork lagged, and were eventually recognized.

Source: 05:25–08:04 ↗

QWhat work led to the redefined-expectations rating and IC5 promotion?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

As an IC4, he took a leading role in a large web project considered IC6 scope. More than ten engineers and several partner functions contributed. Delivering it on an ambitious pandemic-era timeline required much more than coding: interpreting product ambiguity, dividing workstreams, coordinating people, running meetings and communicating progress.

Operational excellence mattered too. A large launch that breaks systems does not become successful simply because many changes were submitted. The project landed without major issues, with attention to release hygiene.

Marius does not claim to know every detail of the calibration conversation. His interpretation is that work two levels beyond his assigned scope made the unusually strong rating easier to explain. Ratings need an articulated progression from expected work to additional contribution, rather than an unexplained assertion of excellence.

Source: 08:05–11:58 ↗

QHow did an IC4 get trusted with an IC6-sized project?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

The opportunity arose through a staffing domino effect. A senior engineer was on parental leave while a major priority changed the team’s work. Another engineer covered that gap, and Marius took a project that might otherwise have gone to someone more senior.

There was luck in the timing, but preparation shaped who was considered. He had established himself as a web specialist who wanted responsibility for that platform and had a record of strong delivery. A relevant opportunity was therefore a plausible match. He calls this increasing the surface area for luck, while recognizing that wanting the project did not guarantee receiving it.

Source: 11:58–13:59 ↗

QHave you always been ambitious about this work?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Yes. Understanding conditions and loops in JavaScript gave him an early sense of agency: he could make the machine do something of his own choosing. The web also appeals to him philosophically as connected documents making knowledge widely available.

His later ambition grows from that intrinsic interest, not solely from the promotion ladder. That distinction helps explain both his sustained effort and his preference for particular kinds of engineering.

Source: 14:25–15:28 ↗

QWhat led to the next redefined-expectations rating and IC6 promotion?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

He led another time-sensitive web project that enabled other pieces of a larger investment. Missing its hard deadline would block their impact. More time was unavailable, and other people were already assigned to important work, so he had to manage scope and quality with the team he had.

His preference was to reduce scope rather than casually sacrifice performance, reliability and design craft. A smaller well-built outcome was preferable to a broad but poor implementation. Some concessions can be necessary, but he wanted them made deliberately.

Product-management support was limited and important questions remained unresolved. He received credit for operating as a product-engineering hybrid: clarifying what needed to be built, aligning the decision with product and engineering leadership, defining success, sequencing work and then contributing heavily to implementation. He likens the early ambiguity to exploring a fog-covered map before the work becomes operational.

Source: 15:30–20:00 ↗

Source: 16:18–20:00 ↗

QWhy switch to Instagram web after things were going well?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

His previous organization’s priorities moved away from the work he wanted to pursue. He had learned that web engineering and product quality—performance, reliability and design craft—were especially satisfying. Staying successful on a less aligned direction was not necessarily the right long-term choice.

The Instagram web team had recently migrated its technology stack and needed quality work. The opening matched his experience and interests. He began with the notifications surface, which needed modernization and alignment with the native applications, then spent much of his time in product infrastructure.

That layer sits between visible product features and deeper infrastructure: code structure, safeguards, testing and architecture that help other engineers iterate confidently. It offered increasing leverage as the expectations for his own impact grew.

Source: 20:00–24:42 ↗

QWhat do you mean by engineering leverage?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Leverage means shaping defaults and tools so other well-intentioned engineers can succeed without personally consulting the specialist for every decision. The framework guides them toward a good outcome. Marius illustrates this with front-end reliability and React error boundaries, which contain a rendering failure to part of an interface.

Adding one missing boundary fixes one location. Auditing the whole site systematically solves a broader problem. Writing guidance that explains how to trigger failures and how to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary content lets other teams apply the approach themselves. Adding lint rules can make the editor warn about a known unsafe pattern before a change is submitted.

He uses that sequence to illustrate increasing levels of impact, while treating the level labels as his practical interpretation rather than an official formula. The more comprehensive solution continues helping after he moves on to performance or another problem. He cannot personally inspect every web product in the company, so direction and tooling extend his contribution.

Is the leverage that other people can prevent or fix these problems themselves?

Yes. Guidance and automated checks scale beyond the places he can directly work. The aim is to solve a class of problems sufficiently well that recurring intervention by the same expert is no longer necessary.

Source: 28:26–29:40 ↗
Source: 24:43–29:40 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 24:43–29:40 ↗

QHow did you begin working on Threads web?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

His manager offered an introduction to a small, initially secretive project. Marius discussed the needed web work with its hiring manager and became the only web engineer for roughly the first six to eight weeks. Scope was initially limited and later expanded.

He values that rare opportunity to help launch a new application from its beginning inside a large company. Other engineers subsequently joined, so being first is not the same as having built the entire eventual product alone.

Did you start a separate web application from scratch?

He first experimented inside Instagram web, hiding the existing interface to render something for the new product. He then decided a distinct surface needed separate components and organization to avoid unintended coupling. That separation was a reasoned architectural choice; it was not obvious at the first experiment.

Source: 33:11–34:05 ↗
Source: 29:41–33:09 ↗

QWhat made the Threads work a convincing IC7 promotion case?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

The work was intense, but its impact story was clear. Threads needed a web presence. Marius established its foundations, helped grow and organize the team, led delivery and wrote a substantial amount of code. The scope grew from logged-out viewing and sharing to a logged-in client with feeds, notifications, settings, search and posting.

The launch and reception made the outcome visible. He says this was an unusually easy self-review to write because the connection between business need, his responsibilities and delivered work was straightforward. That clarity does not mean the project was easy or that his teammates’ contributions were unimportant.

Attribution also required senior reviewers to understand that his involvement materially changed the result. Clear ownership and responsibility for the outcome supplied that connection more convincingly than a count of isolated tasks.

Source: 34:06–37:48 ↗

QWhat does owning a launch actually require?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Marius thinks through failure modes before launch and works backward to prevent them. A new domain raises DNS and infrastructure questions; the right experts should verify the setup rather than the team simply assume it works. Other predictable risks deserve the same treatment.

Not every problem can be anticipated. Operational readiness includes error reporting, QA, release hygiene and responsive feedback channels so an unexpected browser-specific problem can be diagnosed quickly. Ownership covers the outcome of that system of preparation, not only writing the feature.

Source: 37:48–39:33 ↗

QDoes being the directly responsible individual mean doing everything yourself?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

No. He divides the product into meaningful areas owned by other senior engineers. Those engineers are accountable for their areas, while he remains accountable for the overall launch. Delegating a portion does not allow the overall owner to blame that portion if the product fails.

The difficult skill is adjusting the amount of oversight. A lead should give people room to grow without disappearing from the work. His driving-instructor analogy places a hand near the emergency controls while someone is learning, then gradually increases freedom as trust and capability become established. The relationship should prevent avoidable failure without turning every decision into micromanagement.

Source: 39:35–42:02 ↗

QHow should a senior engineer distribute scope while preserving their own impact?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Marius favors reasonable ownership boundaries matched to people’s capabilities. A stretch assignment can develop someone; work far beyond their ability can set both the person and the project up to fail. Work far below their capability may also be a poor match.

He does not expect every change written by a senior staff engineer to contain extraordinary technical complexity. Sometimes the important contribution is quickly implementing many straightforward pieces that unblock a critical workstream. At other times the right role is coordinating work across teams or organizations.

The value is the necessary result and the role in achieving it. Hoarding work or judging every diff in isolation misses the context that makes the overall contribution important. He treats fast coding and broad coordination as different tools for different situations.

Source: 42:02–44:28 ↗

QWhat are you considering for the next part of your career?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

He has no fixed answer about IC8. At the time of the interview, he had moved from Threads web to an important Instagram server-side project, deliberately extending beyond his front-end comfort zone toward fuller-stack work. He finds that both exciting and a little intimidating.

Management is not his preferred direction because he enjoys deeply technical individual-contributor work. He wants his work to matter and offer learning, without assuming that the next title must be the immediate goal. He also offers the Tron: Legacy soundtrack as a personal recommendation for concentrated coding.

Source: 44:29–46:25 ↗

QWhen you reached IC6, did you immediately start aiming for IC7?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Not in the way he had immediately looked ahead after reaching IC5. A more senior promotion needs a business need that matches the level as well as successful execution. Threads web supplied a timely opportunity of that shape.

The opportunity was necessary but not sufficient: the work still had to land. Conversely, an engineer without such an opportunity may struggle to make a case despite ability. His story therefore combines delivery, fit and timing rather than treating ambition alone as the explanation.

Source: 46:26–47:30 ↗

QHave higher-level expectations ever frightened you?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Yes. As an IC4, he saw IC5 as the eventual expected destination under the policy he understood then, was apprehensive about IC6 and believed he never wanted IC7. His preferences changed as he grew. Even later, he was not actively pursuing IC8 because the role would need to fit and he would not want to lose too much work he enjoys.

The account is a reminder that a person’s view of the next level can change with experience. It does not prescribe indefinite promotion seeking, nor establish a current company policy for every role.

Source: 47:33–48:52 ↗

QWhat was your most unusually high coding output?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

He recalls just under two thousand diffs during the year Threads launched. The number suggests an intense implementation period, but he immediately cautions that diff counts are gameable and at best directionally interesting.

He sees no meaningful automatic distinction between, for example, three hundred and four hundred changes in a period: one person may simply split work into smaller commits. Output volume should be interpreted alongside the outcome and the context, not converted into a universal target.

Source: 48:52–49:48 ↗

QWhat advice would you give yourself when entering the industry?

Marius, Instagram senior staff engineer

Things are going to be fine; do not add unnecessary pressure. Early ambition led him to publish a blog post every week while balancing degrees, near-full-time agency work, friends and a demanding hobby. He sometimes wrote late at night merely to keep the commitment.

He enjoyed that work, learned a great deal and thinks his public writing helped a recruiter find him. He does not regret it. But he no longer considers that intensity a healthy default and would tell his younger self that the existing effort was already enough.

His practical web work also complemented university fundamentals. Theory gave him useful concepts, while years of building applications supplied expertise in the technologies he used daily. The lesson is a sustainable combination, rather than dismissing either kind of learning.

Would you have reached the same position without that early intensity?

He cannot know. The counterfactual is uncertain, and he does not rewrite his past as a regimen he hated. He valued it at the time while recognizing that he would choose a healthier balance now.

Source: 51:24–52:17 ↗
Source: 49:49–52:17 ↗
