Section 47 · interview

Philip Su: Senior Scope, Manager Credibility, and Communication

Selected passages on manager credibility, IC/management choices, senior scope, site culture, mentoring, and writing.

QWhat does Philip credit for the fast climb through Microsoft's ladder?

Philip Su

Philip names several causes. One was working with very good managers and teammates. The Microsoft tablet PC team had about 20 people, and three of them were distinguished engineers, which Philip calls very rare at Microsoft. Philip learned a great deal quickly from them.

Another cause was very long hours. In the first year Philip kept a sleeping bag in the office and often slept there. Philip set a 3 a.m. alarm to follow what Philip describes as Da Vinci's idea of sleeping in two four-hour blocks, coding between them.

Philip sums up fast growth as luck, talent and hard work. Luck means being in the right place at the right time, for example being at Stanford when Sergey and Larry were there. Talent matters because Philip rejects the idea that anyone can become anything: Philip will never be a great basketball player, and a weak public speaker can become passable but not a Cicero. Hard work matters because someone who outworks equally talented and equally lucky people will get further. Philip adds that Philip does not recommend this to everyone.

If the goal is growth at all costs, were those hours actually optimal?
Philip Su

Philip says the work week is often defended by pointing to Henry Ford's finding that each added hour is less productive. Philip agrees that output per hour falls as one stays up too long, but says that for many people the curve runs a long way before an added hour becomes negative. In Philip's view, working 50 or 60 hours probably gets more done in total, though each extra hour is less effective.

Philip adds a second consideration with a surgeon analogy. Philip heard from a surgeon that the quickest way to gain surgical experience is to log many surgery hours, so a long residency may pack six years of exposure into four. Nobody wants a surgeon in the 34th hour, Philip says, but a surgeon with wide experience is valuable. Philip would not recommend the crazy hours Philip worked early on, yet they gave Philip far more experience than a typical junior Microsoft hire. There are diminishing returns, but still returns, so a person who truly puts career above all, including relationships, should work more. Philip says Philip's own work life was out of balance for years.

QWhy did Philip become a manager, and why did the role keep changing?

Philip Su

Philip says the promotion to the Microsoft equivalent of E7 came as a manager, after which Philip also worked as an individual contributor at that level. Early on Philip was very ambitious and came from a culture, as an ethnically Chinese person, in which managers were more respected and advanced further. Philip now calls the belief that management was the next growth step somewhat misguided.

Over a career Philip has moved between managing and individual contribution at least six times. Philip loves being an individual contributor but is often asked to manage, for example as a temporary manager.

Did Philip step in on poorly managed teams, or did managers ask Philip for help?
Philip Su

Philip says both happened. Philip's order of preference is individual contributor first, then manager of a team that lacks a better manager, and left to their own devices Philip would rather not manage people. Philip would rather manage a team that is poorly managed than leave it that way.

Philip also says that four separate times a former manager of Philip's asked to report to Philip.

Source: 07:46–08:40 ↗
How does a manager come to report to someone they used to manage under?
Philip Su

Philip says each case differed. Sometimes the manager reported to Philip on the same team. Sometimes the manager asked, years later, to join Philip's team after both had moved on. In one same-team case the manager wanted to become an individual contributor while Philip, a strong individual contributor, wanted to manage, so it was almost a swap in place. In most cases Philip joined a team elsewhere and a former manager who liked working with Philip was happy to work for Philip there.

Philip suggests part of the reason is having learned from great managers. After chasing management early in the career, Philip stopped looking for management roles as actively as for individual contributor ones.

Source: 08:42–10:23 ↗
Source: 06:48–07:43 ↗

QHow should someone decide between staying an individual contributor and becoming a manager?

Philip Su

Philip is open to new experiences and generally advocates trying management if you think you might like it or be good at it, with a few caveats.

The first caveat is not to walk through a one-way door by accident. Philip has gone back to being an individual contributor roughly six times, but says many people cannot. They become managers of managers, drift far from the code, and are then unwilling to take a lower-level job or unable to meet an individual contributor's expectations at their old level. Philip kept the door open both ways by diving into code even while managing teams.

The second caveat is that people tend to think only about themselves when they want to manage. Philip's test is that you are ready to lead when your team would have elected you: "Would you want to work for you?" If the answer is not a solid yes, there is something to improve. Philip notes that nobody can truly make you lead, because teams can slow-roll or sandbag work, so people have to want to work for you. Philip expects that once those improvements are made, people will ask you to manage.

Source: 10:26–13:07 ↗

QDid Philip lose progress by switching between the two tracks?

Philip Su

Philip says yes, intentionally and willingly. When Philip moved from site director of Facebook London to an individual contributor on Oculus, Philip was eventually releveled from E9 to E7. Philip bought into that and says it was necessary, because the skills shown as a site director differed from those needed to be a good coder on Oculus.

Many people cannot accept such a step, Philip says, either for ego reasons or because lifestyles grow to fill whatever compensation people earn. Those who will not change their lifestyle paint themselves into a corner with fewer and fewer jobs they can take.

Philip also says timing matters. One or two years into a career, a lateral move such as junior software developer to junior product manager is easy, and many people will coach you. Around the senior E5 range, moving from E5 software developer to E5 product manager is very difficult, unless the engineering work already involved product management. At more senior levels the skills converge again, so the shape is a diamond. An effective E8 individual contributor, in Philip's description, has a technical vision, understands infrastructure weak points, plans staged migrations, coaches well and understands business strategy. Philip concludes that the middle of a career is where changing tracks is hardest.

Does the diamond come back for deep specialists, for example in AI?
Philip Su

Philip agrees that for some archetypes it does not come back. Someone who goes very deep, for instance on SQL query optimization, may not need to develop the other skills that go with leading teams, and may not transition well into management.

Source: 16:36–17:33 ↗
Source: 13:10–16:34 ↗

QHow did Philip handle the move down from E9 to E7?

Philip Su

Philip had worried about this when first promoted from E8 to E9 as London site director. Philip told the Facebook CTO of the day (captioned "Shrep") that, because Philip liked being an individual contributor, Philip doubted the performance level could be kept when moving back to coding. The CTO replied that they should worry when it happened and not withhold a promotion because of a possible future return to coding.

Back in code, Philip understood the E9 expectations were out of reach. Being moved back to E7, the level Philip joined at about eight years earlier, felt great. Philip says it is far better to perform well at a level than to barely tread water at one where you feel imposter syndrome and doubt you will stay qualified. Philip also did not want pay above what Philip deserved relative to teammates.

Philip says few people make so large a change, and it demands a particular ego. Philip went from running a site of perhaps 400 or 500 people to reporting to a manager who reported to a manager. Philip also had to avoid voicing opinions about running the site, and avoid using outsized influence from the past, so the new leaders could succeed.

Source: 17:35–20:05 ↗

QWhat do engineers at E7, E8 and E9 typically do?

Philip Su

Philip caveats that Philip's information is coarse and probably stale, since it comes from working at Meta starting about 15 years earlier. In general, levels reflect scope of influence: how big, long or valuable a project one can single-handedly guarantee. An intern might guarantee a small feature. A senior developer at E5 or E6 should deliver the work of about 10 to 15 people. At E7, Philip would expect regular influence over about 50 people, driving technical direction for a team that size, being consulted by product and engineering managers, and personally delivering about six months of work with no check-ins. A director might influence about a hundred people.

On the individual contributor side, Philip says large scope comes in different forms. Some people are narrow but deep in a way others cannot match, and four E6s cannot replace them. Others are broad generalists, especially valuable for new teams and startups, where three E6s cannot outperform one great generalist E8.

Philip stresses that the qualitative difference matters most and cannot be captured in an HR bullet list. People at those levels excel for different reasons, and someone more senior must judge them. When Philip was first promoted to E8, E9 did not exist. Philip says the company later had to invent such levels for individual contributors like John Carmack. Philip recalls, if memory serves, that when the first E9 promotions were discussed the company had several thousand people and was considering three engineers, each a different archetype. Philip compares this to becoming a professor, where there is no formula and it comes down to whether other E8s think you are an E8.

What if an excellent E7 has no E8s or E9s nearby to give qualitative input?
Philip Su

Philip says this happens often at small companies or on weak teams. When Philip worked at Microsoft it had about 140,000 people, and Philip believes it was about 240,000 before the layoffs. In a company that size there are always weak teams, where someone may feel awesome only because peers are weak. That leads to overleveling or to having nobody to learn from. Philip uses a real-estate analogy: you do not want to be the most expensive house on the block, with no room to grow, nor the worst, so find a block where you are the middle house.

At the highest levels, Philip says, good role models are hard to find and each excels differently, so a model may not match your strengths. More useful is a coach who has a say in promotions and can say you are qualitatively far from where you need to be. Then you can discuss what to do about it.

Source: 26:50–29:14 ↗
Source: 20:08–26:48 ↗

QWhat project or scope earned Philip the E9 promotion?

Philip Su

Philip brought 12 people to start the engineering portion of Meta's London office and, over roughly four or five years, grew it to about 400 or 500. A good level-six engineering manager could run 12 engineers, Philip says, but with each order of magnitude of growth the problems get harder and the solutions turn gray. The promotion rested on handling a wider variety of things and more strategic decisions.

One example: in one of Philip's last meetings as site lead, Philip argued to people in Menlo Park about how many interns to hire and how much headcount London should have that summer. The argument rested on math about expected H-1B volume 18 months ahead, for full-time offers moving to Menlo Park. Earlier, as an E8, Philip was the first of Meta's sites to look at the seniority pyramid and ask whether people were growing at a commensurate pace. Philip describes these as decisions that grow in scope, by breadth of people affected or by how far ahead one must think.

Source: 29:17–31:59 ↗

QWhat made the London site's engineering culture strong?

Philip Su

Philip names two helps. First, before London Philip had been the second person hired in Meta Seattle, the company's first office outside its Palo Alto headquarters, and saw it grow from four desks to 120, including mistakes in how it grew. Second, before starting London, Philip interviewed site directors from other companies. One was the former site director of Google London, David Singleton, whom Philip says later became Stripe's CTO.

Singleton told Philip that Google had experimented with landing teams, the group sent to bootstrap a site's culture, and concluded the team should commit for at least two years. Philip contrasts this with companies that send a team for three or six months and then leave the site on its own. Philip thinks that is a mistake, because culture is hard to hold while new people are about as numerous as those who have been around more than three months. The CTO wanted enough engineers for two full interview loops, about 10 to 12 people.

Philip interviewed nearly 50 volunteers from the company, plus some of their peers and their managers, to choose 12 who would carry the culture. Each was asked to bring a project to lead, and the group included exceptional individual contributors who were happy to do whatever the site needed. Philip says Philip was lucky in the choices and credits learning from people who had done it before.

Was the two-year commitment tied to pay or a contract?
Philip Su

Philip says no. Pay stayed what it had been and nobody signed anything. Philip had a serious conversation saying Philip wanted only people committed to at least two years, so those who could not commit opted out. One or two had to return sooner for understandable reasons, and Philip supported them.

Far more stayed longer than expected. Philip believes about four of the original team are still in London 15 years later. Philip says they did not join planning to settle there. They loved London and the office.

Source: 34:31–36:57 ↗
Source: 32:01–34:29 ↗

QDoes Philip have favorite stories from working with Zuck and Bos?

Philip Su

Philip's first manager at Facebook was Bos, who later became CTO, and during the London years Philip's manager was the then-CTO captioned as "Shrep." Both gave great advice and guidance. Philip spoke one-on-one with Zuck only a few times, so Philip's insight is limited, but Philip says Zuck felt genuine in how he led.

What impressed Philip most about both Zuck and Bos was their willingness and ability to grow. Philip joined at 33, when the company's median age was 27, and was the oldest person in the Seattle office for the first seven months, so most of the people Philip worked for were younger. People who had worked with either for years could say exactly how they had grown. Philip saw both as open to coaching, probably seeking it, and making a deliberate effort to improve.

Philip's small example is Zuck's AMAs. Within about two years of Philip joining, Philip says, they had improved a lot. Philip is pretty sure someone coached Zuck on how to hold his head, because early on his natural pose had the head tilted slightly upward, and over the years he deliberately corrected it to face the crowd straight on.

Source: 37:00–38:59 ↗

QWhy did Philip buy the whole company coffee for a day?

Philip Su

The host remembers it as a day of free coffee for everyone and puts the cost at over $23,000. Philip did not state a figure in this answer. Philip says the idea began several years into the Facebook years. After the company moved to its Menlo Park campus, a coffee shop opened in Hacker Square, and one Christmas Philip bought everyone a coffee for a day. Philip found the joy infectious, and the chief executive of the coffee chain wrote to say its staff had never seen anything like it.

When Philip left, Philip wanted to give something back. Philip stresses luck. People forget, Philip says, that when Philip joined, the talk was that Friendster might return, that Google+ would roll over Facebook, and that Facebook would never make money on mobile. Philip had left Microsoft after 12 years, in which Philip says the stock rose about 15 percent, and had low expectations. The Facebook outcome was, in Philip's words, "a brick of money" that came from luck, not design. Philip says Philip gave all IPO proceeds to charity because they felt undeserved, citing luck in being born when an interest in computer science pays and in emigrating to America. Philip then coordinated with coffee shops at the major Facebook sites, around five, by calling the owners, and says it was fun and rewarding.

Source: 41:42–45:51 ↗

QHow did OpenAI compare with Facebook?

Philip Su

Philip first notes that the stages differ: Facebook had about 500 engineers when Philip joined and OpenAI about 120. With that caveat, Philip calls OpenAI the highest talent density of any group of engineers Philip has worked with. Moving from Microsoft to Facebook was a big jump in the average quality of colleagues, and Philip felt OpenAI was a notch above that.

Was it technical ability that stood out, or something else?
Philip Su

Philip says the technical capabilities were exceptional. The difference Philip names is product focus. Facebook focused heavily on what the product is and why people use it, Philip says, because beyond a network effect and a product people loved it had little magic sauce. In the early ChatGPT days, with no viable competitors, a lousy product could still be used. Philip recalls that a year or two earlier a server error appeared in about every fourth conversation thread.

Philip expects OpenAI to get increasingly better at product. As competition heats up, Philip says, success will come from research shipped in compelling products, not from pure research.

Source: 53:56–55:40 ↗
Source: 53:02–53:53 ↗

QHow did Philip develop such strong writing?

Philip Su

Philip says Philip was a bad writer through college because Philip did not respect communication. Coming from a culture that prized getting A's, Philip viewed the hard sciences as real and history and English as a waste of time, with no right answers, and so did not invest in soft skills.

At Microsoft, in spare time, Philip reread classics hated in high school. Philip names Hemingway and The Great Gatsby, saw them differently as an older reader, and developed a love of language. Philip cites Virginia Woolf for the idea that to write well you need to read well, and names David Foster Wallace, Alice Munro's short stories and Pilgrim at Tinker Creek as writing that shows what language can do. Philip then came to see writing as a skill as valuable as a hard science skill, and started working at it.

Beyond reading well, Philip says, it takes a willingness to rewrite several times and to leave material on the cutting-room floor, and many of Philip's well-known posts were rewritten repeatedly. Philip also notes clever rhetorical moves in other people's Substacks and tries to remember them. Above all, Philip says, the change came from no longer disrespecting the skill and seeing it as essential even for scientists and technical people.

Was the non-chronological essay structure planned, and did an editor help?
Philip Su

Philip says the structure came from a moment of inspiration about how to tell that story compellingly. Philip says chronological order is usually the most compelling because it makes sense. Some stories work better out of order, Philip says, because a different, threaded arc in a person's life becomes visible, and Philip felt that way about this one.

Philip had no editor for those pieces. Philip did hire a professional editor, captioned Rebecca Ambrose, for a podcast miniseries, wanting the words well structured and expecting a professional to do better, and learned a great deal. Philip says nothing posted professionally was ever edited by another person, though Philip did receive feedback in the podcast case.

Source: 58:59–1:01:32 ↗
Source: 55:43–58:56 ↗

QHow did Philip win respect as a very young manager?

Philip Su

Philip says it was difficult, because Philip lacked humility and was overly ambitious. Philip says Philip would not have worked for Philip's own 24-year-old self. Philip became a manager because Philip was one of the team's strongest engineers, and the team figured it was better to keep a good engineer happy by letting Philip manage.

In that first year, at 24, Philip had to fire a 40-year-old. Philip calls it exceptionally difficult, made harder by awareness of how junior Philip was. Philip says the person deserved it for missing expectations but was two levels above Philip's own level, and Philip says Philip was too immature to know how to manage someone more experienced.

Philip says Philip was a pretty bad manager at first but obsessed with growth: Philip collected mentors, asked for feedback and read nonfiction about managing teams and hard conversations. Philip says Philip made huge mistakes even in the last year of managing. The biggest weakness Philip names is giving feedback. Philip pulls punches, hates confrontation and downplays how serious the feedback is, so people miss the point. Philip says Philip has gone from very bad to passable and does not expect to become excellent. A strength is motivating action, since Philip joins only teams Philip believes in, and Philip's passion and vision excite people.

Source: 1:07:03–1:10:20 ↗

Section 48 · interview

Rahul Pandey: Promotion Narratives, Mentors, and Relationships

Selected passages on manager calibration, promotion narratives, mentors, relationships, and the TLM transition.

QHow was Rahul leveled at Pinterest, and how did he choose a team?

Rahul Pandey

Pinterest had just created a leveling system, borrowed from Google and Facebook. Rahul came in at L3, the entry level (L4 is mid-level and L5 senior). He moved away from recommendation systems and data engineering into mobile, which he calls a career reset. It meant a longer ramp-up and, later, a rejected promotion.

Pinterest let new hires choose a team through "base camp," a two-to-three-week version of Facebook's boot camp. Rahul decided against backend work. He wanted to be close to the product and able to build things end to end, including side projects, and liked the idea of an app in the Android store that his Android-using family could try. His startup had no mobile team, so he saw Pinterest as a chance to learn Android professionally with strong people and benefit twice, at work and on the side.

Did Rahul learn what he wanted to learn on the Android team?
Rahul Pandey

Yes, though the first months were rough. A strong staff-level engineer joined a couple of months after Rahul, and the mentorship was a huge pivot. But Rahul says he had not yet learned how to learn. The Android app already had hundreds of thousands of lines of code. He read documentation and code but wrote little of his own, and he links that slow ramp-up to his first failed promotion.

What changed, he says, was being surrounded by good people, especially an L6 engineer from Facebook who started pair programming with him. Being accountable to a team that would judge his work was a fire under him. With mentorship and enough time in the role, it eventually clicked.

Source: 17:41–19:47 ↗
What matters most when picking a team?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul names two things. The first is the people, because what he learns is dominated by who he interacts with. The second is how important the team is to the company. In 2015 Pinterest's big initiative was international growth, and Android dominates outside the US, so he expected the company to put smart people and money behind it. His view is that working adjacent to an area of high growth means seeing some of that growth yourself.

Ryan relates this to the idea that a rising tide lifts all boats. Ryan has seen people go from new grad to director in five years by working on the company's most important problem and delivering, since career growth tends to track impact.

Source: 19:50–21:25 ↗
Source: 14:54–17:39 ↗

QHow did Rahul eventually get promoted after the failed promotion at Pinterest?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul calls it a difficult journey. The first rejection came about a year after he joined. He thinks the feedback was fair: he had done Android professionally for only about nine months and had not shipped much. He tried again six months later and was rejected again, which he found truly demoralizing. He had arrived through an acqui-hire expecting to be among the best engineers, and two rejections for the same promotion were a real setback.

Pinterest had an appeal process, and Rahul worked with his manager to use it. The appeal succeeded. The anonymous committee had read one project in his packet, described as 16 months of work, as a lack of urgency. Rahul says that was not true. His manager clarified and advocated for him. His lesson is to be clear about what a document says, because readers may interpret it differently, and to have promotion and one-on-one documents reviewed by experienced people.

Ryan notes that a long project can instead signal larger scope. Rahul agrees that context decides: align with the manager on the narrative and collect feedback from tech leads, because 16 months can look impressive, or count against you if it was a minor experiment others expect to take three months. His conclusion is not to assume how others will judge you. Software engineering is a social endeavor, so learn your evaluators' view of your growth areas before a review.

What helped Rahul build skills quickly from L3 to L4?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul credits a lesson from the mentor: be willing to work outside the main codebase. Building the Android app and deploying it to a phone sometimes took two to five minutes, so debugging was slow. The mentor showed Rahul how to create a small separate Android app, copy over themes, and iterate in that sandbox with a much faster loop.

Making a new app had seemed like a big, ambiguous task, but it was easy and raised his speed. It also removed his fear of breaking things and copy-pasting code, which helped with side projects. He calls this the biggest mindset shift behind the L3 to L4 promotion. Ryan agrees that a fast iteration loop matters when promotion rests on contributing more code.

Source: 25:30–27:50 ↗
Source: 21:28–25:28 ↗

QWhy did Rahul leave Pinterest for Meta in mid-2017?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul gives three reasons: Meta was a much bigger company with a stronger engineering brand, it paid more, and he did not see a clear path to rapid growth at Pinterest. He wanted to see whether he could get a meaningful bump in level or compensation.

He thinks job hopping works better early in a career than later. As people move up, he says, impact comes mostly through influence. A staff or principal engineer rarely writes enough code to justify the role; they build frameworks, tools and systems that make other developers productive, which takes years of relationships and trust. Early on, showing you can write high-quality production code may be enough to be hired higher.

Ryan's experience matches. Ryan's move from senior to staff was unusually quick because of long relationships on one team, while peers who switched companies quickly had fewer such ties.

Was another prestigious name on the resume the real reason?
Rahul Pandey

Partly, Rahul says. He admits some ego in wanting a brand everyone had heard of, since far more people knew Facebook than Pinterest. But he agrees it was not the main factor: he already had Facebook and other known names on his resume. The main reason was a sense that he could grow his career much faster at Facebook.

Source: 29:34–31:03 ↗
Source: 27:53–29:31 ↗

QWhat cultural and technical differences did Rahul notice between Pinterest and Meta?

Rahul Pandey

Culturally, Rahul found them similar, since Pinterest's culture was shaped by ex-Facebook and ex-Google people. He describes Facebook as the authentic version, "on steroids." At Pinterest, every change needed at least two reviewers, and Herald rules added blocking reviewers automatically. At Facebook one accept was usually enough to land code, which shocked him.

He also found people more direct at Facebook. At Pinterest, he says, a common criticism was that the company was too nice: people avoided hard feedback or prioritization, so projects and people who should not have stayed lingered. At Facebook people more readily said a project made no sense and should be cut, and he perceived a more aggressive performance-improvement-plan culture.

Was learning Meta's custom stack difficult?
Rahul Pandey

On paper the stacks were similar: Android with Java, and no Kotlin yet. Facebook's scale meant many workarounds and a custom build system, Buck, which Rahul found easy. The harder part was that he joined Portal, then called Building 8, a hardware team. Its software was a forked Android with about 30 custom Android apps on a custom operating system, so its build system and tooling differed even from the rest of Facebook. It took him roughly four or five months to understand it.

Ryan explains that Portal is a standalone video-calling device. Rahul adds that the team first used an Android tablet, later flashing custom hardware with their own OS. Building all 30 apps would take three or four hours, so each engineer built only their own app, in Rahul's case the calling app.

Source: 32:34–34:59 ↗
What did the debug tool Rahul built for Portal achieve?
Rahul Pandey

Because the Portal workflow was so unusual, Rahul came to understand how it differed from other engineers' and built a debug tool for people on Portal. He says hundreds of engineers in the Portal org or nearby orgs used it daily or weekly, and estimates it saved hundreds of hours of engineering time each month. Ryan says this sounds like IC6-level impact.

Source: 35:02–35:45 ↗
Source: 30:20–32:32 ↗

QWas Rahul hired at IC5, and did he have to do anything special for that jump?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul was hired at IC5 (senior), so the move from Pinterest was effectively a promotion. He did nothing special, he says; the level was Meta's proposal after interviews in which he felt he had solved nearly every problem.

He also came from a position of strength: a couple of pending offers, a Facebook internship, time at a respectable company, and a hot market for Android developers, all of which made Meta want to give him a compelling offer.

Source: 35:48–36:38 ↗

QWhat work led to the promotion from senior to staff (IC6)?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul worked on Portal. Facebook already had a mature cross-platform video-calling infrastructure inside Messenger. Portal's first step was to fork Messenger and go its own way as an experiment. Once Portal had hundreds of thousands of daily users, the team needed to return to the normal infrastructure, because the Messenger RTC team kept improving it. Rahul's main project was migrating Portal's core infrastructure back to Messenger's, keeping Portal's custom features and adopting the new capabilities RTC offered.

He calls it cross-functional work with a lot of bureaucracy, involving the Messenger team, Portal leadership and product managers. Some people can rely on one big project at staff level, he says, but a portfolio worked well for him. The second project was the debug tool, purely engineering-driven and built for himself and his teammates. Together, he says, the two made a clear promotion case.

Was Rahul intentional about reaching IC6?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul says how the promotion conversation is phrased matters. In his first year at Facebook the goal was to do well. Later, as a manager, he learned that a new hire who immediately asks for help getting promoted is a turn-off. He also felt imposter syndrome from joining at a fairly high level, so he focused on meeting or exceeding IC5 expectations first.

After about a year, with some trust built and good work landed, he had a clear conversation with his manager about growing on the IC ladder. Since he enjoyed talking to and mentoring people, they also discussed management. They agreed, and Rahul thinks it was the right call, that he should climb the IC ladder first and try management later.

Source: 38:14–40:29 ↗
Did Rahul create the scope for the shared-infrastructure project, or was it assigned?
Rahul Pandey

Neither, exactly. Rahul says it was obvious that someone had to do it, and both the RTC team and the Portal team wanted it. The open question was who would be point person. With long tenure, seniority and a relationship with the Messenger RTC team, he was a natural fit, and he says it was clear to everyone that he was one of the best people, perhaps the best, to take it on.

Source: 40:31–41:53 ↗
Source: 36:41–38:11 ↗

QWhy did Rahul move from IC6 to tech lead manager (TLM)?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says his current company is about helping people, and he sees good managers as people with a real desire to help others grow. As a byproduct, he says, they can have large impact, since managers are usually senior and respected. He also had context and relationships, so the move felt natural: a growing team needed someone to give feedback and keep people on high-impact work, and he had already expressed interest.

What concrete steps should someone take if they want to try management?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul starts with a question: do you enjoy helping and working with people? If you dread one-on-ones, he says, you will struggle, because management is mostly one-on-ones and reacting to pings, so a manager cannot guard their time. He suggests testing this by actually holding one-on-ones and leading meetings now.

His second point is having opinions: about the quality of the team's work, and about how the team and organization should change as priorities shift. He thinks the best managers have a strong point of view and bend the organization toward it. Ryan suggests tech-leadership and direction-setting work is a good simulation, and Rahul agrees: very senior ICs must also articulate and sell clear opinions about what the team should do over the next six months or year. Someone who would rather just execute and write code is not a good fit for management.

Source: 42:34–45:36 ↗
What surprised Rahul about management, and what did he learn about the TLM role?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul found the TLM role tougher and more taxing than expected. Straddling IC and management work meant that at the end of a day he asked what he had actually achieved, since his time went to meetings, one-on-ones and roadmapping.

He thinks TLM is fine as a transitional role while deciding between full-time management and full-time IC, but not sustainable long term. It is unclear whether you are judged on code or on people leadership. He switched teams afterward. Ryan, who also became a TLM, asked many TLMs beforehand and says every one advised against staying long term, because the role makes you a jack of all trades and master of none.

Source: 45:40–48:03 ↗
Source: 41:54–43:17 ↗

QIn which period did Rahul feel the most skill or career growth?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul names three. The first was meeting the mentor at Pinterest: pair programming, learning by osmosis, and discovering he was empowered to change his environment. The second was at Meta, leading the migration and building the debug tool, which was the first time in big tech he felt he created value, from an idea of his own that people chose to adopt. Before that he often felt like a worker bee carrying out work passed down from above. He says this helped give him the confidence to start a company.

The third, less relevant to a big-tech audience, was the two or three months of Y Combinator: weekly group check-ins brought intense pressure, since underperformers were effectively shamed, and he learned a lot.

Source: 57:05–59:12 ↗

QHow much of Rahul's career growth was luck?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul says he feels he has "failed my way into success" and that a lot of it was luck, in the opportunities and people he came across. He adds that luck can be manufactured by being curious about the people and opportunities around you. Finding his co-founder, the 2014 startup and the Facebook opportunities all came from keeping in touch: asking what someone is up to, what they like about a new job, or offering help on a project.

He says the debug tool came from talking to people about their workflows, and many job hops came from knowing what respected people were doing. He sees this as a repeatable process, not luck. He also describes posting on social media as deliberate: people who see helpful content think of you for opportunities.

Ryan notes that some people call this maximizing your luck surface area, and says internal writing and reaching out give the same visibility at a company. Ryan suggests that credibility from such sharing probably helped Rahul get the shared-infrastructure project that led to staff.

How can someone network without it feeling manufactured?
Rahul Pandey

Rahul hesitates to call what he does networking. He points to two ingredients: genuine curiosity about what the other person is doing, and thoughtfulness about what he shares. Rather than only asking questions or for mentorship, he says one of the best ways to build a relationship is to share something he has worked on that may interest the other person.

In his words, showcasing what you are up to creates gravity: people are drawn to you for your opinion, so it becomes a two-way street. If you always ask and it is never reciprocated, the other person may simply not be interested, or you may need to become more interesting.

Ryan recalls that networking felt artificial as a new grad, but side projects such as writing content and building a keyboard make conversations natural.

Source: 1:03:42–1:06:14 ↗
Source: 1:00:40–1:03:40 ↗

QWhat advice would Rahul give his college-graduate self?

Rahul Pandey

Rahul wishes he had realized much earlier that there are no gatekeepers: you need no permission to learn a technology or try something new. He did well in school by being methodical and studious, but not as creative or exploratory as he could have been. He admires Ryan's keyboard project as something nobody told Ryan to do. He cites his own recent projects, such as extensions for a Mac app launcher, as the kind of work he means.

In his view, feeling empowered to do something unique based on what you care about, rather than what peers, instructors or managers expect, is how you get an outlier outcome. He wishes he had cultivated creative interests earlier and set aside time for them deliberately.

Ryan observes that Rahul took more initiative later. Rahul agrees: YouTube tutorials, published Android apps and webinars with 800 people felt like a blindfold lifting. His advice is not to wait until you are ready to start a company, publish an app or teach, but to do it now. He was passive early on, waiting to get better and smarter, and wishes he had adopted that mindset in middle or high school.

Ryan frames this as main-character energy versus NPC energy. Rahul likes the framing but adds that you need not be the main character in every domain. It is enough to do so in the parts of life you care about or where you have a unique take.

Source: 1:06:17–1:09:55 ↗

Section 49 · interview

Build promotion support through initiative and delegation

Selected passages on manager support, explicit self-advocacy, delegation, mentorship, and behavioral evidence of scope.

QHow did you choose your first Meta team?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Meta’s boot camp let Evan try tasks for several hiring teams before making a mutual choice. He had expected to join cybersecurity after years of hacking, but the particular teams he met felt less welcoming than he wanted. Content integrity offered machine-learning problems, a mission he found meaningful, and colleagues he related to. He joined a terrorism-content team being established in Seattle, initially with a manager shared across teams and a part-time technical lead.

Ryan selected Instagram infrastructure with much less understanding of the long-term tradeoffs than he has now. He then associated product work with front-end work and infrastructure with technical depth, assumptions he now calls mistaken. Instagram felt exciting, and when the preferred manager lacked headcount, Ryan made an earnest case for joining until the manager found flexibility. Both see agency as a way to convert available opportunities into a better fit; good opportunities may require actively seeking them.

Where did boot camp happen, and did you deliberately choose a technical stack?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan split boot camp between two two-week stays in Menlo Park and time in Seattle. He gravitated toward backend work without an elaborate stack-selection strategy. Ryan thought more explicitly about product versus infrastructure and which product organization to join, although he stresses how incomplete his knowledge was as a new graduate.

Source: 17:27–20:24 ↗
Source: 15:34–21:59 ↗

QWhat was surprising about onboarding into content integrity?

Evan King

Evan’s early encounter with a colleague’s monitor displaying explicit content was jarring because it was plainly part of an ordinary working day. The team’s task required examining material that would be extraordinary in most offices; over time, colleagues became accustomed to that exposure. He remembers the team sitting out of the way in the Seattle office, and colleagues said that arrangement reduced accidental exposure to disturbing content. His story is about the unusual context of moderation engineering, including material more troubling than the initial anecdote.

Source: 22:01–24:05 ↗

QWas the first promotion something you negotiated with your manager?

Evan King

Evan’s first promotion arrived after roughly his first half year and was a surprise. He thought he was doing good work but had not discussed promotion or calibrated himself against colleagues. The manager’s praise, promotion announcement, and compensation change became a major confidence-building moment. He does not recommend relying on that kind of surprise.

An earlier Zillow internship had supplied another important boost. He completed the assigned work quickly, pursued interesting additional work, and received a return offer and unusually strong praise from a manager with substantial experience. That external confidence helped him enter Meta, although it did not instantly eliminate all insecurity.

Had you interned at Facebook first?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

No. Evan had interned at Zillow. His memories of that internship and the first Meta promotion illustrate how specific encouragement from experienced managers helped him believe he was capable.

Source: 26:19–27:40 ↗
Source: 25:38–28:03 ↗

QWhat did those managers see in you so early?

Evan King

Evan identifies curiosity and an unwillingness to treat the assigned task as the boundary of his job. At Zillow, after finishing his rental-team work, he turned posters about locking unattended computers into a playful internal security game. Colleagues could record an unattended machine, and leaderboards and graphs encouraged participation. Spending time with security colleagues eventually led to attending Defcon with them, despite security being outside his team’s charter.

He describes a similar pattern at Meta: completing the requested implementation created time to improve it and explore adjacent ideas. He frames this as pursuing useful, interesting work rather than merely doing extra work for its own sake.

Source: 27:42–29:02 ↗

QHow did you finish assigned engineering work fast enough to explore more?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan initially resists claiming a simple secret, because the reputation for speed feels more grand than his conscious process. Ryan describes deep familiarity with a code area, a practiced editing-and-review workflow, and enough repetitions to know exactly where a requested change belongs. At one coding-heavy period he remembers submitting about ten diffs a day. He also worked very long days and acknowledges that adding working time is one way to create an extra budget for growth.

Evan kept searchable notes whenever he solved a problem so he would not have to solve it from scratch twice. He also became comfortable investigating a blockage for roughly an hour, finding the person who knew the area, asking a focused question, writing down the answer, and continuing. Ryan emphasizes that a well-timed question can save days of blind searching, dwarfing small editor optimizations.

Both highlight code search as a lasting skill. In a large monorepo, someone has usually solved a similar problem already. Guessing likely function or variable names, finding the analogous implementation, and understanding the surrounding context accelerates junior execution and later work on ambiguous cross-system problems.

Does working extra only make sense if you enjoy it?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

They distinguish the experience of being absorbed in enjoyable work from forcing long hours on work one hates. Ryan enjoyed the novelty and growing fluency; Evan stresses that advice about extra hours becomes dangerous when detached from that motivation. The time-budget explanation describes their experience, not a claim that everyone should work those hours.

Source: 31:28–32:48 ↗
Source: 29:03–35:40 ↗

QWhat changed between the midlevel and senior promotions?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

As content integrity expanded, the initially tiny terrorism team acquired senior engineers and eventually split across terrorism, child-exploitation imagery, and graphic violence. Because Evan had arrived first, he held useful context and helped newer colleagues ramp up regardless of their formal level. His manager offered him responsibility for an underinvested graphic-violence area with a junior engineer and a research scientist.

He began setting weekly meetings, shaping the roadmap with management, and holding one-to-ones with teammates. The team improved its detection precision and recall, although he does not remember figures well enough to quote them. Guiding other people and improving a neglected area supplied the senior-level story; the informal tech-lead label mattered less than the responsibilities.

Ryan’s corresponding experience emerged when a cross-client/backend workstream grew around an area he understood deeply. He sometimes felt stretched while leading meetings but did the work anyway. An unusually capable intern showed him that entrusting execution to another person could free him for more scope. Evan similarly needed repeated managerial feedback before delegation clicked: doing everything quickly himself would eventually cap what the team could accomplish.

Why did the manager trust someone so early in their career?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan credits a strong manager who noticed potential, provided a larger challenge, and coached him through it. The preceding evidence was not just tenure: Evan was helpful in onboarding and willingly answered colleagues’ questions. His knowledge became useful to other people, which made expanded responsibility more plausible.

Source: 38:25–41:12 ↗
Did being the original owner create territorial feelings when senior engineers arrived?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Yes. Evan initially felt protective of his work when a technically strong senior engineer joined. He recognized that response, discussed it with his manager, and opened himself to the engineer’s feedback. Reviews and design discussions then became a major source of technical growth, and the colleague became a lasting friend.

Ryan recalls senior collaborators similarly improving his documents and projects. He did not know exactly how each person’s performance review divided the credit, but the collaboration produced better work and learning. They advise treating shared scope as an opportunity for growth rather than assuming someone else’s contribution diminishes one’s own.

Source: 41:44–44:41 ↗
Source: 35:40–48:21 ↗

QBy the senior promotion, were you openly discussing promotion goals?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

By then Evan and his supportive manager discussed target timing, requirements, and what still had to happen. Friends from his boot-camp cohort often lacked equally active advocacy. His advice is to state the desired next level and timing, ask whether the manager agrees with the plan, and surface gaps early—even if that feels vulnerable. Hearing bad news before review season is more useful than an unpleasant surprise afterward.

Ryan’s manager was supportive but did not proactively drive promotion dates, so Ryan repeatedly asked what the next level required and advocated for his growth. He sees strong performance and explicit discussion as mutually helpful: the manager has reason to invest in an engineer whose broader contribution helps the team. Evan later adopted more self-advocacy himself. They recognize luck in getting a capable, aligned manager and the engineer’s responsibility to make goals visible.

Source: 48:23–51:39 ↗

QWhy stay on the same team while many peers changed companies?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan enjoyed both the mission and the people. The organization grew so quickly that staying did not mean doing an unchanged job: terrorism work, child-safety work, graphic violence, managers, and colleagues all changed around him. He was not solely optimizing promotions, although the growth was rewarding. Ryan more deliberately evaluated how to grow fastest and repeatedly decided that another clear promotion opportunity, good colleagues, and enjoyable work made staying attractive.

Both acknowledge a possible trap in always pursuing a next milestone that feels close. It can postpone broader technical experience elsewhere. Nevertheless, they have little regret about staying through a fast staff promotion: that level improved compensation and made direction-setting and working through others possible, activities they found satisfying.

Do you wish you had changed environments sooner?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

At this point in the conversation Ryan defers the fuller discussion of his recent transition. They agree that a clear, enjoyable staff trajectory made staying reasonable, while recognizing that another environment might have produced broader technical learning. They present that as a tradeoff rather than a universal stay-or-leave rule.

Source: 54:14–57:08 ↗
Source: 52:10–57:08 ↗

QWhat was the anchor story behind the staff promotion?

Evan King

Evan’s progression took one half year for the first promotion, two halves for senior, and three for staff. During the last stage he led graphic-violence engineering when the Christchurch mosque attack was livestreamed and copies circulated. He describes an emergency response involving integrity leadership and policy colleagues, repeated overnight work, model training, and changes to detection and content-matching systems. He emphasizes the victims and families rather than treating the atrocity as a career opportunity.

The response exposed underinvestment in detecting catastrophic events on live video, which differed from screening existing photos and recordings. The company formed realtime integrity around Evan and a product manager and asked them to determine staffing, scope, and a roadmap. Early progress was slow because the events were rare: training on the handful of known cases risked overfitting, and waiting for another tragedy was an unacceptable way to assess the system.

His golden-set-recall project curated past examples and built an evaluation environment that replayed videos and comments through real production infrastructure while isolating them from users. It tested the complete path rather than only a model. Evan reports that the initial measured recall for the better-represented suicide examples was roughly nine percent.

Looking closely at misses revealed a neglected signal: viewers’ comments often showed they understood the danger before image and audio models did. Adding temporal comment signals raised recall to roughly fifty to fifty-five percent in his recollection, created more detected training examples, and enabled further improvements. He says recall eventually reached the mid-nineties by the time he left, but the staff promotion came earlier, when evaluation and substantial initial improvement had been established. These are his retrospective figures, with some uncertainty in the precise intermediate numbers.

How large did the new team become?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

At promotion time Evan remembers approximately four or five engineers. Realtime integrity later reached roughly twelve to fourteen before splitting into two teams of eight near his departure. Increased investment followed demonstrated progress and sustained attention from senior leadership; the original project was not assumed successful from day one.

Source: 1:03:51–1:05:14 ↗
Who decided to give you that scope?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

He does not know the exact decision maker. At the time he felt he had advocated strongly for the new team after the incident. Later he learned that his manager had done much more advocacy behind the scenes than he appreciated. His own initiative and leadership mattered, but he deliberately corrects a purely self-created-opportunity version of the story.

Source: 1:05:16–1:06:45 ↗
Source: 56:20–1:04:31 ↗

QWhich behavior mattered most in the staff story?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan points to trying the simple, obvious solution and keeping the whole problem in view. His multidisciplinary team crossed infrastructure and modeling boundaries, but technically sophisticated researchers could become absorbed in improving the model itself. With less investment in that particular expertise, he focused on what would move the actual detection number. Comments seemed obvious only after the team had been concentrating on pixels, audio, and complex temporal modeling.

Ryan describes a similar Instagram compute-efficiency project. He explored video-processing efficiency before pandemic usage made capacity critical. After brainstorming with strong engineers, the best improvement was a comparatively trivial removal of redundant work. He values the ratio of useful impact to time, complexity, and maintenance burden: a simple change with a large effect can beat an elaborate year-long project.

They praise the Meta culture they experienced for rewarding realized impact rather than merely implementation difficulty. The practical skill is to identify the important constraint, find what actually improves it, and drive the work even when the solution lacks technical glamour. Their descriptions of reward systems are personal observations of that context.

Source: 1:06:03–1:13:05 ↗

QWere you acting partly as a manager while still an individual contributor?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Yes. Evan’s role went beyond the usual technical-direction interpretation of tech lead. Engineers still had formal managers who owned promotion decisions, but he helped those managers understand performance, supported teammates’ growth, and participated in relevant discussions. An attempted invitation to calibration was ultimately rejected by a director; he does not know why.

He took people leadership seriously, observed his manager, and read a management book when given the graphic-violence team. He believes the arrangement worked because colleagues trusted that he was on their side. He qualifies that judgment rather than claiming to speak for them. Someone who feels competitive, aggressive, or inserted between an engineer and their manager could easily undermine the same arrangement.

Because levels were not public on his team, Evan could not rely on a displayed title as authority. He needed to earn credibility through useful technical judgment and supportive behavior. Ryan agrees that influence at staff comes from convincing people who do not report to you that the direction is sound and that they can trust you.

Source: 1:12:49–1:19:28 ↗

QDid you consider switching from the IC path into management?

Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Evan expected to reach staff and then become a manager, but a plausible IC7 path appeared while he had broad organizational context, senior-leadership visibility, and interesting cross-organization projects. Conversations with friends who had become managers also revealed the weight of directly owning people’s issues. He considered reaching IC7 first and perhaps later moving into a more senior management role.

Ryan faced a similar choice. His manager saw a clear continuation to IC7 but warned that management advancement depended more on organizational opportunity. Ryan nevertheless chose management to learn a different set of behaviors and preserve options for the longer term. He worried that a very senior IC career could become specialized to a handful of huge companies, with influence and compensation tied to internal credibility and equity.

Both describe these portability and compensation concerns as their reasoning, not a claim that senior IC skills have no value elsewhere. A fast internal progression may not transfer to an equivalent external title, and rebuilding trust takes time.

What is a tech-lead manager?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Ryan first moved into a role he describes approximately as seventy percent IC and thirty percent manager, with a small team focused on a narrow technical area. Contributions were still assessed primarily as IC work. He later moved toward conventional organizational leadership after deciding he wanted to grow further as a manager.

Source: 1:21:37–1:22:49 ↗
What has been the biggest learning from management?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Ryan’s manager had been right about the career dependence: advancement became more closely coupled to team and organizational growth. Moving during an efficiency-focused period reduced that opportunity. He also found the work shifted toward people problems and a solid block of daytime meetings. As an IC he could arrange fragmented meetings and complete technical work later; as a manager, much of the job requires other people being available. Review season adds substantial writing after those meetings.

Source: 1:23:52–1:27:05 ↗
Source: 1:19:28–1:24:38 ↗

QWhat is your biggest career regret?

Evan King

He wishes he had slowed down to understand why things worked. Iterating until a metric improved or a system functioned could produce immediate impact without building a durable explanation. The same shortcut appeared during early startup pressure: once something worked, he moved on.

As the company stabilized, he could finish required work with time left over and use that margin for reading engineering explanations and investigating underlying libraries and platforms. He sees a tension in an impact-oriented culture: it can reward shipping and moving on even when understanding the abstraction underneath would improve the engineer’s long-term foundation. He would keep the useful drive for impact while adding that inquiry.

Source: 1:48:55–1:52:06 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself when graduating?

Evan King

Invest in friendships, romantic relationships, and life outside work with some of the deliberateness given to career goals. Evan had roadmaps and frequent checks for professional growth but applied much less effort to broader life. Moving to Los Angeles and making more friends outside the technology bubble helped him value mutual investment and everyday support.

He now finds those relationships a major source of fulfillment alongside continuing work. This is not only an hours-allocation lesson: even when there was time, he had not recognized what deserved deliberate attention.

Would you accept slower promotion in exchange for stronger relationships?
Evan King and Ryan Peterman

Given a strict choice, yes: he would prioritize relationships. But he rejects the premise that he actually had to choose. He believes he had enough time to build both and simply did not invest enough in relationships or understand their importance yet.

Section 50 · interview

Steve Huynh: Promotion Processes, Performance, and Manager Support

Selected passages on promotion ownership, performance cuts, manager quality, interview impact stories, and role expectations.

QWhy is most interview prep advice poor?

Steve Huynh

Steve says most interview prep is not optimized. Candidates focus heavily on coding and, lately, on system design. Steve says prep turns the interview into a test. That view is partly right, since a candidate who cannot code or design a system is unlikely to be hired, but Steve says the focus is too narrow.

What would a better balance of interview prep look like?
Steve Huynh

Steve says an interview is more like a date than an SAT, because both sides are deciding whether they want to work together. Prep sources present it as a test because a test is easier to sell.

Steve suggests spending less time on coding and system design and more on behavioral work. A rough split Steve offers is 40 percent coding, 40 percent system design, and 20 percent behavioral. Steve treats the figures as an illustration, not a rule.

Source: 09:59–10:55 ↗
Source: 08:58–09:56 ↗

QHow much does the behavioral part of an interview count compared with coding and system design?

Steve Huynh

Steve says coding and system design work like the small and big blinds in poker. They are required to play, but they do not decide the hand. The behavioral round decides the hand. Steve was a bar raiser trainer and trained thousands of Amazon interviewers. Steve says the functional rounds are pass or no pass.

Steve says Amazon will say no to candidates with poor behavioral answers, even when coding and system design are strong. That does not mean the candidate lacks experience. Interviewers can often see early that a candidate will not fit the company. Once a candidate passes, the behavioral answers shape the level.

How can a candidate avoid being down-leveled because of weak behavioral answers?
Steve Huynh

Steve recommends packaging: presenting one's experience as a clear story about what one has done, how one operates, and what one is about. The story does not have to be entertaining, but it should be efficient and honest.

Steve says the core question of an interview is whether the interviewer wants to work with the candidate. Good behavioral answers help the interviewer answer that. Candidates should not misrepresent themselves, but should put their best foot forward.

Source: 12:55–14:24 ↗
What does a packaged answer sound like?
Steve Huynh

Steve gives an improvised example for a tell-me-about-yourself question: a focus on backend distributed systems, a love of customer-facing products, a sports interest, and experience building teams and improving engineering culture. Steve says many candidates rush through this question.

Steve says stories betray level. A story about an entry-level task sounds junior when the candidate is aiming for a senior role, and that mismatch can lead to being down-leveled.

Source: 14:25–16:13 ↗
Source: 10:59–12:52 ↗

QCan someone's level be judged in a short conversation?

Steve Huynh

The host suggests a blind test: talk to someone for five minutes and guess their level. Steve says Steve is fairly confident in judging level this way. A junior engineer usually shows it in how they carry themselves and what they talk about.

Steve says judging whether a strong senior engineer could pass as a principal would be harder. Steve believes Steve is well calibrated on level overall.

Source: 16:16–17:54 ↗

QHow can someone stand out before the interview, for example when seeking a referral?

Steve Huynh

Steve says a direct, genuine message to someone on a team with an opening can work. Steve suggests saying you noticed their team has openings, and asking what their day-to-day work is like. The message should not look like spam, an automated DM, or AI-written text.

Steve cites a poll Steve ran in a Discord community. About 90 percent of respondents said they would engage with a genuine message like that, and would refer the sender if asked. Steve presents this as informal, not as evidence.

Steve says real networking means making a connection and offering value. Newcomers who are willing to pick up a useful skill are also more attractive to big tech.

Source: 17:57–19:45 ↗

QHow did Steve move from support engineer to SDE1, SDE2, and SDE3?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the path from support engineer to SDE3 took about three and a half years. At SDE1, the focus is independence: understanding where one's work fits in the development life cycle and taking tasks all the way through, so that the team trusts the person without hand-holding.

Does independence mean never asking for help?
Steve Huynh

Steve says no. Self-contained is not the same as independent. Steve says the real skill is knowing how to unblock oneself, and being comfortable asking questions and raising issues when stuck.

Steve warns that hiding problems becomes a performance issue. A two-week task reported as on track until the Thursday before it is due is more serious than a task that is merely slow.

Source: 27:34–29:20 ↗
What changes at SDE2?
Steve Huynh

Steve says the key word at SDE2 is ownership. An SDE2 takes an active part in the development life cycle and acts as a steward of the team's codebase, cleaning up tech debt instead of leaving a mess. Steve likes the image of not littering, and sometimes picking up trash.

Steve says each step up is an argument for more scope. An SDE2 works at team level, understands the codebase's strengths and weaknesses, suggests where it should go, and takes on-call shifts. Steve calls this a meat-and-potatoes role, and says it is what a person needs to show to move from SDE2 to SDE3.

Source: 28:25–30:18 ↗
Source: 26:22–27:32 ↗

QCan an SDE2 stay at that level for a whole career, or is it a terminal level at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says this is debated at Amazon. Steve sees the SDE2 band as wide, and says many senior engineers at other companies would sit at the upper end of SDE2 at Amazon. Steve says SDE2 could be a terminal level, but Steve does not advise treating it as one.

Is there an up-or-out policy?
Steve Huynh

Steve says SDE1 is clearly up or out. Staying more than about two years brings progressively stronger guidance to move on, though it is not a fixed 24- or 36-month rule. Steve calls it a feel thing.

For SDE2, Steve says the answer depends on upper management and on the individual's manager. A manager who sees an SDE2 as overdue for promotion could make staying very hard. The conversation notes that many people worry Meta could become more like Amazon, which is known for intense performance management.

Source: 31:19–33:06 ↗
Source: 30:20–31:16 ↗

QHow many people is Amazon expected to cut each year?

Steve Huynh

Steve will not give an exact number. Steve uses five or six percent as an example. For an organization, that figure used to be a soft recommendation to manage out part of the team over a year. In the past couple of years, Steve says it has become much more of a mandate.

Steve says the pressure grew when backfills were paused. Until recently, Amazon did not backfill many roles, so people felt chased from behind, and Steve does not think that was healthy. As a self-described high performer, Steve says it is hard to speak to what it feels like to fear losing a job.

Is managing out the low end of the curve a relief or a problem?
Steve Huynh

Steve uses a group of 20 people as an example. In normal years, people on the low end of the curve are often not thriving in Amazon's culture. Steve says removing them can feel like a relief, a blessing in disguise, because it ends a poor fit.

Steve is uncomfortable when cuts reach people in the middle of the curve, who would be fine in other years. Repeated cuts of about six percent, with no backfill, push out people who are doing well.

Source: 34:54–37:45 ↗
Source: 33:09–34:52 ↗

QHow do senior engineers take part in the meetings where people are discussed for being managed out?

Steve Huynh

Steve says engineers are pulled into these discussions from senior engineer level, and definitely from L7 and above. The meetings can run three days, with people in a room discussing colleagues through measurable results and other people's feedback. Steve says some recent cuts of middle managers surprised Steve, since a 6 percent target makes little sense for a group of four or eight people.

Steve says the process is not linear. In a perfect world, each person would get equal time, but the discussion tends to focus on the edges, the strongest and the weakest. Steve sees this as a matter of the numbers, not a verdict on the decision makers, and says the process strips out some humanity. Steve says it is not a favorite time of year.

Source: 37:47–39:37 ↗

QIs Meta showing the same intensity as Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Meta appears to be on a hiring spree, and that a figure of about 5 percent of low performers has been floated around. Steve has a sense that people affected are not having a good time, but thinks most people at Meta are fine.

Steve says that with a large population, someone is always struggling. Meta's inflow of hires is far larger than its outflow, so Steve would not be too worried.

Source: 39:39–40:53 ↗

QWhat protects someone who is meeting expectations during a cut cycle?

Steve Huynh

Steve says solidly meeting expectations is the main protection. Steve does not think a 5 percent stack ranking should remove people who meet expectations, and Steve dislikes the label low performer. Steve describes it as a mismatch between a person and the culture around them, not a judgment of ability.

Steve says offers at Meta are hard to get, so the people in that process are not weak. Steve advises people labeled as low performers to find the specific dimension they are judged on, rather than trying to become high performers in general.

What should someone do first when judged to be below expectations?
Steve Huynh

Steve says to crawl before walking and running. Find out exactly what the judgment is about, then check with the manager whether expectations are being met. If they are not, propose a preemptive plan to get back to the median. Steve would avoid the phrase PIP, for performance improvement plan, when asking for one.

Source: 42:50–43:41 ↗
Should employees ask managers directly what the expectations are, and when should they report bad news?
Steve Huynh

Steve says most people never ask this. Steve estimates that about 25 percent of software developers have explicitly asked their manager about expectations. Steve recommends asking directly what the expectations are, then asking whether one is meeting them.

Steve credits a friend with the saying that early bad news is just news, while late bad news is terrible news. Steve advises surfacing problems early in the review cycle, not in the month before a review, so there is time to fix them.

Source: 43:44–46:34 ↗

QHow did Steve get principal-level scope at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says a reorg moved Steve into Prime Video after a team Steve cared about, the Amazon Tickets team, was spun down and its developers scattered. Steve chose a Prime Video team focused on delivering live sports, then saw a large catalog project that principal engineers knew needed doing. Steve decided to take it on and stay on the team.

Steve says the work fell in the gaps between principal areas, such as playback, clients, or catalog. It needed an end-to-end solution, and the other principals were busy with their own areas. The host adds that delivering such work gives principal engineers context to champion the candidate in a promotion packet.

Source: 46:37–49:25 ↗

QWhat usually blocks someone from going from senior to principal at Amazon?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Amazon effectively skips a level, and that a staff level could be inserted between senior and principal. Steve says the jump from senior to principal is two levels, so the criteria roughly double. Influencing multiple teams makes it hard to show that in one year.

Steve sees a common failure. People think they are ready, push for promotion, get rejected, and go back to their strengths. Closing the feedback takes a long time, and many give up. Steve knows people who left Amazon and now work at senior staff or principal levels elsewhere, but could not make the jump there.

How can someone get a low performance rating while doing principal-level work?
Steve Huynh

Steve says performance and promotion are decoupled. Reviews run yearly, with a smaller check every six months, and promotion can happen quarterly or every six months. Steve describes an anti-pattern: a senior engineer who stops doing senior work and focuses only on principal-level work.

Steve says senior engineers must code. Principals also code, but less, and they do cross-functional work such as sponsoring projects, acting as a backstop, or evangelizing an initiative across several dev teams. Steve recalls a promotion review that said Steve acted like a TPM, and Steve took offense.

Source: 52:23–54:32 ↗
What feedback did Steve get on coding, and why?
Steve Huynh

Steve says the review said to code more. Steve had checked in a lot of code, but in one six-month stretch Steve coded less, and the review looked only at the code delivered in that period. Steve says that gave no credit for time served.

Steve says on-call history was also raised, though Steve had been on call for years, including about four years in a row. Steve also says Steve reached senior in 2012 and principal in 2020, after the promotion process changed three times in four years.

Source: 54:35–56:15 ↗
Source: 49:25–52:21 ↗

QWhat did Steve learn from becoming an expert in the promotion process?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Steve did not get promoted through ability alone. Steve became an expert in the process of getting promoted, and thinks that skill is useful. Steve had not produced enough tangible evidence for the packet, and needed a manager's support. Steve says the process changed three times in four years.

Steve's first lesson is to start early. Many people wait until a big project lands, but the project landing is often not what a rejection is about. Steve advises submitting the packet early to get real feedback on the gaps.

Steve's second lesson concerns strengths. A packet gives some credit for strengths, but reviewers focus on the delta. Steve advises prioritizing weaknesses and gaps, and keeping strengths from regressing, the way a cook tends one pot of risotto while the other pans rest.

Source: 56:17–59:51 ↗

QWhat are Steve's favorite parts of Amazon's culture?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the biggest part is customer obsession. From interns to VPs, people were expected to put the customer first. Steve says working backward from the customer is the right North Star. Optimizing for short-term profit or for competitors can backfire, and Steve credits Jeff Bezos with the idea that long-term profit and customers are the same thing.

Steve calls the writing culture a superpower, and credits a writing background with making a six-page document easier to write. Meetings often begin with about 30 minutes of reading the document, followed by discussion. Steve says writing is learnable and need not be a focus before joining.

What does Steve dislike about the culture?
Steve Huynh

Steve says the inside joke among friends was frugality. Anything cheap or poor, such as the lack of free food or weak hardware, got the label. Steve says free food is a perk and its absence does not mean a company is bad, but frugality can go too far.

Steve recalls begging and pleading for a laptop with enough memory so the fan did not overheat while building code. Steve says a company hiring tens of thousands of developers should give them working computers, and recalls monitors being taken after intern season.

Source: 1:03:39–1:05:24 ↗
Source: 59:52–1:02:40 ↗

QWhat made a good manager stand out, given the many managers Steve had?

Steve Huynh

Steve says the count was more than 17, closer to the 20s. Steve says the best managers were personal, but Steve resonated with managers who reasoned from principles. Those managers treated the leadership principles as axioms, so decisions followed from them and had implications.

Steve says the best managers held firm on customer obsession and on thinking ahead. They would accept a short-term hack if it fit a future-facing choice. Steve found managers focused only on near-term delivery harder to work with. Steve also notes that some people who complain about micromanagers really need things broken down.

Who were the worst managers, and what made them bad?
Steve Huynh

Steve does not name names. Steve says the worst managers were a mix of style mismatch and a sense that the hiring and promotion processes should have filtered them out. A manager who is caring and engaged for one person may be a poor fit for another.

Steve says it was sometimes hard to see how some managers had reached their roles.

Source: 1:06:39–1:09:19 ↗
Source: 1:05:27–1:06:55 ↗

QWhy did Steve stay at Amazon for 18 years?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Amazon's size allowed many careers inside one company. Steve worked on the first Kindle, on a precursor to Prime Video, back on Prime Video, and in payments. Steve says it did not feel like one team for 18 years.

Did Steve consider leaving, and what is the advice on job hopping?
Steve Huynh

Steve says Steve considered leaving several times. Early in a career, job hopping makes sense to raise total pay, and Steve says that advice works until about the senior level.

Steve says distinguished, principal, and staff engineers at the top usually stayed on the same team, on the same problem, for at least three years and often about five. Steve's rule of thumb for a fast climb is to job hop every two years until about mid-level, then put down roots.

Source: 1:10:22–1:12:10 ↗
Why did Steve choose to put down roots?
Steve Huynh

Steve says staying made sense without a computer science background. There was a lot to learn in large amounts of code, wikis, and internal videos. Steve felt Steve could grow the way Steve wanted by staying.

Source: 1:12:13–1:13:00 ↗
Source: 1:09:20–1:10:19 ↗

QWhat would Steve tell a younger self who had just finished college?

Steve Huynh

Steve says Steve would warn against people pleasing. Steve describes a culture of tracks, such as school, then job, then marriage, and a sense of being ahead or behind. Steve also sought validation after each achievement, and doubts a younger self would have listened.

Steve says the person to please is oneself. Steve asks whether a person is doing what they want or what someone else expects, and whether they are climbing the ladder to reach the top or because it was put in front of them.
