Section 51 · interview

Zach Wilson: Job Hopping to Staff at Airbnb, Interviews, and Internal Brand

Zach Wilson recounts a rapid climb from junior data engineer to staff at Airbnb, arguing that interviews and impact stories outpaced promotions, and counts the cost of long hours.

Interviews and impact stories move a career faster than waiting for a promotion

Zach Wilson describes a path from junior data engineer at Facebook (called Meta by the host) to staff data engineer at Airbnb by age 26. Zach's central argument is that the interview is the highest-leverage part of a career. Two of the level jumps came from changing companies, and in each case the tool was a clear impact story, not hours worked. Zach also lists the costs: roughly 60-hour weeks, a staff-type role taken before the matching behaviors were in place, and a Netflix reorganization that ended in a mental health break. The host adds that companies hold back promotions when someone has impact but not yet the behaviors. Pay figures and company details are Zach's recollection and are not verified.

Source: 00:56–1:05:52 ↗

QHow did Zach get started in the industry?

Zach Wilson

Zach began at several startups as a data analyst. A plan to become a math professor faded because it meant a lot of school for modest pay. An early job at Think Big Analytics taught Hadoop when it was new, about ten years before the recording, and Zach credits that experience as the main reason Facebook later wanted to hire.

Zach held four jobs in two years. On graduating, Zach was unsure whether to be a mobile engineer, a math professor or a data scientist, and tried several roles before settling on data engineering. With a dual major in computer science and applied math and only math tutoring on the resume, Zach still got four or five interviews and calls this luck.

How did the Facebook offer come about, and why did Zach turn down a counter-offer?
Zach Wilson

After a year in Utah, Zach moved to Washington, DC, to try something new. Six or seven months later a Facebook recruiter reached out on LinkedIn, a site Zach says has been critical since the Think Big job in 2015. Zach had been rejected twice by Google for mobile roles, so the approach felt almost as if Facebook were applying to Zach.

The DC employer countered. Zach recalls about 180 from Facebook against about 200 from the DC company, with units not stated. Zach declined because a request for a 20 percent raise two months earlier had been refused for lack of budget. Money that appears only when someone is leaving, Zach reasoned, signals that growth there would be painful.

Source: 03:02–05:11 ↗
Source: 00:56–03:00 ↗

QWhat was boot camp like, and how did Zach choose a team?

Zach Wilson

Moving to Silicon Valley also put Zach closer to family in Utah, which had felt distant from DC. Zach says the first month of boot camp felt like Disneyland more than a job. The onboarding sold the company's values, such as moving fast and being bold, and felt like college because no deadlines applied yet.

Zach interviewed for three teams: ads, growth and community support. Ads pitched making Facebook millions through data, community support pitched preventing bad content, and growth pitched having fun. Zach joined core growth and notifications, partly on that pitch and partly because of an entrepreneurial manager who is still a close friend.

Source: 05:14–07:28 ↗

QDid Zach understand the career ladder on joining?

Zach Wilson

No. Zach did not know what L3, L4 and L5 meant and did not realize the hire was at L3. Zach had two years of big-data pipeline work at startups, yet new Stanford graduates with no experience were paid the same, and Zach found that unfair. Zach concluded the hire was at the wrong level and worked hard to reach the next level, which took about seven months.

Zach says this taught that how someone interviews is the highest-leverage part of a career, more important than the impact made in the role.

What did Zach do to earn the L3 to L4 promotion?
Zach Wilson

Zach could tell early that things were going well: work was clearly tasked out, energy was high and a lot of code shipped. Notifications had a waterfall framework for tracking conversion, click and delivery rates, and Zach found it poor. Fixing it meant XHP and React work, not SQL and Python, so Zach learned both. Zach says the manager took this as proof of someone who solves problems outside the job description, and nobody had asked for it.

Doing only the assigned tasks, Zach says, earns a meets-all rating at L3, so Zach looked for where the impact was.

Source: 09:11–10:32 ↗
Was the promotion expected?
Zach Wilson

It came as a surprise. The half lasted five months for Zach because the start date was late July. Zach thinks the company recognized the mis-leveling and skipped the usual steps. The host adds that a promotion within one half usually signals a hiring miss that the company fixes quickly.

Zach contrasts this with Utah, where promotion follows tenure, not impact. In Utah, Zach had thought a software engineer would top out near 200k at about age 35. Facebook offered about that figure at the start, with a route toward a million, and Zach says companies reward business impact because the value created exceeds the pay.

Source: 10:34–12:52 ↗
Source: 07:30–09:08 ↗

QHow many hours did Zach work at Facebook?

Zach Wilson

After boot camp, Zach ramped up to roughly 50 to 60 hours a week, usually arriving around 9:30 and leaving near 8 pm, because breakfast, lunch and dinner were all provided. Zach jokes that free meals left a basic life skill, cooking, unlearned.

Source: 12:54–14:13 ↗

QAfter L4, why did the next promotion, to L5, not happen?

Zach Wilson

Zach wanted L5 within a year and felt confident while the first manager was in place. That manager left the next summer. The team reported to the director for a while and then to a new manager from Netflix, so Zach had three managers in one year. None had the full context, and Zach had to restate past work again and again. Zach says this disrupted the plan, and that trust takes time to build. Zach says good managers extend trust by default, while others demand proof first.

Zach earned a greatly-exceeds rating in the first half as an L4 and again in the next. The feedback was that Zach was not yet operating as a senior engineer. Zach was taking on too much work, and leadership doubted that delivery at L5 level was sustainable.

The host says a promotion must be sustainable, and a leader may wonder whether someone working long hours can keep it up. Did that match what Zach learned?
Zach Wilson

Zach says it did, and calls it one of the most important lessons from Facebook. Hours worked do not necessarily drive promotion. Extra hours can cover a skill gap, but they do not give leadership confidence that someone is ready for the next level.

The host agrees that promotion committees look for behaviors, meaning the ability to take on more leadership, and not simply extra hours. The host notes this can leave a hard worker bitter.

Source: 16:28–17:24 ↗

QWhat did Zach do once the promotion stalled?

Zach Wilson

Promotions at Facebook usually landed around March, and after learning there would be none, Zach decided it was time to take the story to market. Facebook had rated Zach as greatly exceeding expectations, which made it a strong story.

Zach points out that an interviewer does not see hours worked, only what was done, and gets a different vantage point on impact without much of the negative data from the current job. After the notification machine-learning optimizations and other technical work, Zach was sure a senior role was available at any big tech company by describing that work in detail.

How did Zach sell a senior (IC5-level) profile at Netflix while still mid-level with few years of experience?
Zach Wilson

Zach credits luck: the Netflix hiring manager was the former Facebook manager, who had already seen the work and trusted it. Zach says this is why building a network matters.

Zach separates personal brand, such as LinkedIn posts or videos, from internal brand, meaning how colleagues know a person. Zach says a strong internal brand was what worked here, built by working hard with that manager.

What else, besides the stalled promotion, pushed Zach to leave Facebook? (editorial prompt for Zach's unprompted continuation)
Zach Wilson

Zach also wanted to stop being a data engineer. On a team of about 15 data engineers, Zach says they wrote roughly 90 percent of the team's JavaScript. Zach also says data engineers sit off the engineering track and receive 30 to 40 percent less equity, a claim not verified here. Zach asked to switch to software engineering and was told it would mean a down-level to L3, which Zach rejected as absurd given what had already shipped. Zach says the title counted for more than the work, and that a manager who listens to career goals matters a great deal.

Zach adds that down-leveling when moving from data to software engineering was standard practice, but not the reverse. Zach also wanted bigger-data work, not just SQL, and says the role held at Facebook would be called analytics engineering today.

QHow did the Netflix hire work, and how much did the old manager's backing count?

Zach Wilson

The former manager said he could not hire Zach as a senior software engineer, given thin software experience, but could hire Zach as a senior data engineer and move Zach into software engineering within six to twelve months. After about six months Zach became a senior software engineer.

Zach recalls that in 2018 Netflix hired only seniors, with levels added about two years before the recording and no staff level. Managers controlled hiring, in line with the freedom-and-responsibility culture, and were also pressed to fire people. Zach contrasts this with Meta's standardized interviews, where a referral counts for less. Zach adds that this part of the culture has downsides.

The host reads this as an internal brand story: the manager had seen Zach deliver as a junior and wanted Zach on the team regardless of level. Zach agrees it matters more than people think, and says not to burn bridges and to find people you click with, since you may work with them again.

What did the move do to pay?
Zach Wilson

Zach says compensation roughly doubled to about 385 to 390, all of it cash. The captions garble the starting figure and give no units, so the numbers are approximate.

QWhat was Zach's plan at Netflix, and how did promotions and reviews work there?

Zach Wilson

At 24, Zach pictured becoming a principal engineer (L7 or L8) by 30, doing deep technical work, and judged that data engineering would not get there. The Netflix work was real-time security threat detection, which Zach calls cutting-edge and hard.

Netflix had no promotions in the Meta sense. Managers gave a quarterly color: green meant fine, yellow meant pick it up, and red meant imminent firing. Once a year came a pay discussion based on what other companies would offer, not on past work, and a manager could adjust pay at any time.

Zach did not mind the lack of levels. Zach expected high pay and still had much to learn from the manager. Zach says to think about the story of impact at every company and to tell it in an exciting way.

Source: 27:40–29:51 ↗

QWhat does Zach mean by a story, and how does it support job hopping?

Zach Wilson

Zach tends to leave jobs about every two years, so Zach has to be satisfied with the story first. At Airbnb, Zach felt an urge to quit early but realized there was no good story yet and stayed six more months. A story is a fully delivered package of impact that can be sold: if hired, here is what will be delivered in two years.

What was the Facebook story that Zach sold to Netflix?
Zach Wilson

Zach names three items. The first was a reachability metric for notifications, a counterweight to spam that tracked who was turning off settings and proved more complex than expected. The second was the first growth dashboard that covered WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger and Facebook in one chart. The third was the pipeline behind Facebook's notification-selection machine-learning algorithm, which Zach made 90 percent cheaper, or ten times more efficient, using sorted merge bucket joins.

Zach Wilson

Zach says short tenure invites the thought that the person does not play well with others or is a disloyal job hopper. Zach says this must be defeated early in the interview, by showing ambition, hard problems solved and a path toward solving more. Zach has seen interviewers start skeptical and then warm up after a conversation.

QWhat made Zach leave Netflix?

Zach says the first manager believed in Zach too much. Zach was on security threat detection when a separate team's asset-inventory role opened after a ten-year engineer left. Zach went from working with one team to interfacing with 11, was not ready for the volume of conversations, kept answering everyone and overworked. Netflix rewarded the move with a raise from the upper 300s to 550 the next year, by Zach's account.

In 2019 Netflix decided data engineering was no longer a necessary organization and folded it into data science. Zach says the VP, the director and the first manager were fired, and everyone began reporting to data science leaders.

How did Zach respond to the reorganization?
Zach Wilson

It caused so much stress that Zach took a month-long mental health break. Zach did not want to sit in a data science organization, having disliked that at Facebook, and wanted an engineering organization. Zach asked to transfer to the cyber security team, where the asset-inventory work belonged, and was told to stay in the current role.

Zach quit with nothing lined up, planning to travel the world in 2020. The last day was March 6, 2020, and COVID ended the plan. Zach says Netflix would pay a lot but give nothing else Zach wanted.

Zach agrees that the Netflix case shows the problem the delay is meant to prevent. Zach lists better work boundaries, planning ahead (a lesson Zach is relearning as an entrepreneur), and selling a technical vision. Zach says content creation has helped with the last one, which means presenting an idea so others will back it.

At earlier levels an engineer simply delivers the assigned work and solves the hard problem. At staff level, Zach says, the new behavior is deciding which problem to solve, which Zach found overwhelming at Netflix.

QHow did Zach go from leaving Netflix to interviewing at Airbnb?

Zach Wilson

By December 2020, Zach had played a lot of video games and felt unfulfilled and depressed. Zach's girlfriend at the time asked what Zach was doing with life, and they broke up. With no job, no partner and a dog to support, Zach decided to take another swing at interviewing.

Zach also started making content on LinkedIn that month, having told Netflix colleagues in March that they would see Zach again as a famous person. Zach regrets not starting during the pandemic, when growth was easier. Zach interviewed at Meta, Google and Airbnb, for software engineering at the first two and data engineering at Airbnb, and received offers from all three.

How did the offers compare?
Zach Wilson

Google and Facebook both offered senior roles. Zach recalls about 400 to 415 from Facebook and a lower Google figure that the captions cut off, similar to what Netflix had paid years earlier. Airbnb offered, by Zach's account, more than $100,000 above that, which made the choice easy even though the offers were not really competing.

Zach also liked how Airbnb does data engineering. The work was about 95 percent Scala and 5 percent Python, with no SQL, and the pipelines had to match online pricing and availability systems. Zach says this blend of pipelines, integrations and optimization was what Zach had wanted at Netflix.

Immediate, blunt feedback feels harsh at first, but Zach learned that colleagues wanted growth, and says Airbnb interviewers were impressed by that.

Did Zach push for staff?

Yes. The recruiter said up front that the result would be senior or staff, which annoyed Zach, who would not take a senior-only offer. Airbnb then leaned toward an interview-based middle path. Google and Facebook said they would offer senior only.

The host says the interview shows its value here: Zach landed the level with less than six months of work, while colleagues went through hoops for years. The host adds an analogy to pre-revenue startups, which get generous offers because the outcome is open, and says a track record builds inertia: an employer that hired someone at one level resists moving them up. In the host's view the interview has more variance, so it gives a step change while promotion inside a company gives only a gradual one. This is the host's analysis, not Zach's.

QIf Zach started again as an IC3, what would Zach change?

Zach Wilson

Zach would be more open to other perspectives. In the first years Zach focused on becoming the most technical person, and now thinks that matters mostly up to senior engineer. After that, technical skill helps only marginally and other skills are needed.

Zach did not start building soft skills until Netflix, when things were on fire and the skills were urgently needed. Developing them earlier at Facebook, in lower-risk situations where failure felt smaller, would have given better balance and probably faster growth.

Zach also says not to eat dinner at work. Zach calls it a scam: in Zach's view, Facebook and Google offer it to keep people at the office longer. Zach would have used those hours for the gym, since fitness started only in 2018, and for other parts of life.

Given the fast growth, does Zach wish for less work, and was it worth it?
Zach Wilson

Zach says the growth was worth it, and Zach now aims for balance and tranquility. Zach would not repeat the work from age 22 to 25, but does not regret it, because it was what Zach needed to feel powerful and grow. Zach adds that health matters: earning $20 million while stressed and dying at 50 is not a good life, and health, wealth and happiness each matter differently at different times.

Zach also says working hard gave a young person a sense of purpose by making them useful. Zach then asks whether that purpose could have come without so many sleepless nights, nights of feeling out of depth, and a couple of panic attacks. Zach says such costs are rarely discussed.

Source: 1:03:38–1:05:06 ↗
The host sums up the advice to an IC3-level Zach. What does Zach add?
Zach Wilson

The host sums up the advice as: stop being one-dimensional, keep working hard, look after health and enjoy the ride. Zach agrees on enjoying the ride more and not becoming fixated on getting promoted, and says things come in time for those who put in the hours daily. Zach believes the universe gives people what they want if they are willing to pay the price.

Section 52 · interview

Lead through managers and compare the scope behind titles

Selected passages on managing managers, trust, organizational growth, leadership relationships, and comparing actual role scope.

QHow did the director opportunity at Square arise?

He corrects the host’s premise: he joined Square with a director offer rather than receiving an internal promotion from frontline manager. The team grew from approximately twenty-five to more than fifty people in about a year. Building machine-learning and data infrastructure teams exposed him to a new job: directing through managers rather than directly managing engineers.

Source: 03:23–05:07 ↗

QWhat was the biggest skill gap in moving from manager to director?

At Facebook he had become a manager after being an IC, so knowing the team’s technical details gave him authority. At a new company, his reports had longer tenure and knew more than he did. He could no longer justify the extra leadership layer by being the most informed person in the room.

He thinks he performed poorly during roughly the first half-year. Reflection led him toward strategic direction, cross-department resource coordination, and the organization’s hardest problems. The job was to guide an organization toward a better future, rather than reproduce the frontline managers’ work.

Another turning point was understanding what each manager wanted from him. He tried to identify missing capabilities and help them grow toward the next level. That reframed him as someone adding value to their careers.

How did you handle managers who hoped to receive the role you were hired into?

He recognized the natural disappointment and tried to demonstrate that his arrival could help their prospects rather than block them. Building trust came first, followed by concrete help with growth and obstacles they could not remove alone. He credits The Five Dysfunctions of a Team with emphasizing trust as the foundation beneath other team behavior.

Source: 09:16–11:29 ↗
Source: 05:09–09:16 ↗

QIs changing companies the best way to move up management levels?

He does not think so; former Facebook colleagues reached very senior roles by staying. His own moves followed a different goal: eventually becoming CTO of an AI company. The intended outcome revealed gaps in infrastructure, frontend work, products, and how an industry business operates.

At Snapchat he could lead data or camera. He deliberately chose camera despite a data and machine-learning background, learning iOS and Android work and spending about two months on iOS study. The product role forced collaboration with product managers and designers that he might not have gained by staying in a familiar backend specialty.

He recalls those first two years as especially happy because he was expanding his knowledge every day. The lesson is to choose an opportunity for the capability it supplies, rather than infer that any external title increase is a sound strategy.

Source: 11:31–15:31 ↗

QHow much must an engineering leader know the team’s details?

Facebook’s bootcamp impressed him: even a newly hired VP fixed bugs and submitted code alongside other hires. He adopted the belief that engineering leadership should remain technical. He still writes and reviews code, mentioning several pull requests a week, and wants enough detail to make sound strategic judgments rather than speak without understanding.

How do you balance technical depth with higher-leverage leadership work?

At the start of a week, he identifies the three most important outcomes and concentrates there. Sometimes learning implementation detail is one of those outcomes; other weeks it is not. Recalibrating priorities toward his broader goal matters more than repeating the same activity or simply adding hours. Time is finite, so the key is allocation.

Source: 17:03–18:52 ↗
Source: 15:31–17:03 ↗

QWhat drove your organization’s growth to about 250 engineers?

He relates the team’s growth to Snapchat’s overall expansion from approximately one hundred employees to three thousand in two years, while crediting recruiting and interviewer effort. Rapid growth was also painful: a culture that works for one hundred people differs from one for three thousand. He likens each doubling to building a new company. Leaders need to adapt instead of insisting that an earlier organizational answer remain right indefinitely.

Source: 20:54–22:42 ↗

QWhat did you learn from working with Evan Spiegel?

He recalls an unusually high product-quality bar, down to pixel-level issues in demos. His team learned to bring a genuinely polished demonstration, and he compares that attention with the familiar image of Steve Jobs.

He also describes a leader who valued personal relationships and kept promises. One story is Spiegel telling another leader not to fire the first fifteen engineers because of their founding contribution. Another is returning to the small house associated with Snapchat’s beginnings for board meetings. These are the guest’s accounts of leadership and loyalty, not a recommended universal employment rule.

Source: 22:43–24:58 ↗

QHow were you recruited into later leadership roles?

He says opportunities came inbound through recruiters or personal connections rather than an active search. He preferred people he knew because companies inevitably face both good and difficult periods. He wanted partners he could trust and think with through downturns. Building a professional network early made those later opportunities possible, though his personal inbound experience should not be assumed for every candidate.

Source: 24:59–27:23 ↗

QHow do you compare leadership offers when company size and titles differ?

He does not primarily rank valuation or reporting headcount. In fact, he says he would welcome fewer direct reports. The central test is whether the work brings him closer to the product-building outcome he wants.

Titles belong to a company’s structure and can lose significance when someone leaves. He would rather be known for making a useful product than for holding a senior label. He imagines a very small team building an extremely valuable company, but presents that as an aspiration and prediction rather than an established requirement.

When hiring for his startup, he wants candidates both to believe a large outcome is possible and understand that its probability may be very low. The small probability is a candid framing of startup risk, not a measured forecast.

Why tell candidates that the chance of success is low?

He wants people to choose the challenge consciously so normal difficulties do not immediately overturn their expectations. Transparency helps identify the subset of engineers who want the journey, rather than persuade everyone. His battlefield analogy emphasizes preparation for uncertainty and shared commitment.

Source: 31:26–32:15 ↗
Source: 27:23–31:26 ↗

QHow much management growth is situational rather than controllable?

Management roles are constrained by the organization’s needs and structure, which depend on company strategy. He increasingly accepts that he cannot control much of the timing. Doing excellent work in the current role is within his control; promotion is a later signal shaped by other conditions.

He criticizes treating the next level’s bullet points as a contract guaranteeing promotion once checked. That makes happiness dependent on an outcome the person cannot fully command. His alternative is impact now and movement toward work one wants over the long term, while remaining open to later opportunities or founding a company.

Source: 36:00–38:30 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself just after your PhD?

Conventional wisdom need not decide a unique person’s path. He recalls choosing Carnegie Mellon over more broadly prestigious alternatives because of computer science, and leaving research for a small Facebook when few research peers would have done so. An unfamiliar route is less comfortable, but he believes independent thinking can reveal opportunities others miss. The advice follows from his goals rather than asserting that every unconventional choice wins.

Source: 38:30–39:58 ↗

Jay Jo: Recognition, Mentoring, and Team Growth

Selected passages on promotion/recognition mismatch, domain ownership, mentoring, and maintaining culture as teams grow.

QDid growth at Robinhood match what Jay expected?

Jay Jo

Jay says Jay joined a bit too late for the fast growth earlier hires got, and by then the company was already moving toward a more conventional big-company path. Jay missed the first review because of a late start, and went through the process at nine months, after long hours that sometimes ran until 2 a.m.

Jay also describes a painful on-call rotation, centered on an overnight batch process that ran after market close and sometimes went until 4 or 5 a.m., close to a business problem.

Did that leave Jay jaded about big tech?
Jay Jo

Jay says the time put in did not match the reward. Jay considered becoming more checked out and going through the motions, a pattern Jay saw in many colleagues. That made Jay jaded about the big-tech environment and convinced Jay there was something bigger to work toward.

Source: 13:17–13:57 ↗
Source: 10:11–11:52 ↗

QWas Jay promoted while doing only the minimum?

Jay Jo

Jay says Jay was promoted in the second performance cycle and was technically up for another promotion before leaving. By then Jay was putting in the bare minimum to stay close to average and spending time elsewhere.

Jay says that at a company that grew about tenfold, being a competent engineer made Jay the only person who knew many systems. That turned Jay into a domain expert and an engineering lead for several systems.

In a fast-growing company, does competence alone make someone load-bearing?
Jay Jo

Jay agrees that when both the team and the workload grow, competence is rewarded almost automatically. Jay also mentored three people, the first about a year and a half into the job, which Jay says is much less common at larger companies.

Source: 17:38–18:17 ↗
Source: 16:04–17:36 ↗

QHow has the company's team grown since it started?

Jay Jo

Jay says the company started in 2022 with five to seven people and now has around 60 full-time staff across its entities. Jay calls that lean growth relative to places like Robinhood and says it was the right decision, because slow growth keeps the culture intact and avoids bureaucracy and confusion about what to do.

Section 54 · interview

Review with trust and constructive judgment

Selected passages on trust-based review, coaching/autonomy, separating risk from personal preferences, and constructive acceptance.

QHow do you decide how deeply to review a code change?

Guest

The guest allocates review effort according to risk. Live production code and the core architecture receive close examination. A gated, noncritical leaf component may receive only a high-level review, including a check for serious problems such as security risks, because the blast radius and cost of rewriting it are smaller.

His trust in a known teammate is part of the calculation. This is not a philosophy he applies automatically to a new colleague, nor one he claims all Meta engineers share. He separates correctness and architectural risk from forcing every implementation to match his personal style.

Do colleagues push back on quick approvals?

Yes. His team knows it can explicitly request a deep review in the description or test plan, or return an approved change to review. The author may know that a superficially small component has a subtle performance or design issue. That signal changes the reviewer’s time allocation even if the component is still peripheral.

Source: 02:34–03:48 ↗
Source: 00:03–02:46 ↗

QWhy ask how to accept a change instead of how to reject it?

Guest

He wants to identify what truly prevents safe progress: major architectural problems and critical bugs. He is less interested in making another engineer write the code exactly as he would. Greater experience can make reviewers more comfortable with several valid approaches.

He takes conditional approval unusually far. If he spots a bug that would break production, he may leave a clear warning and approve while explicitly requiring the author to fix it first. He says trusted colleagues have not landed such a known defect in his experience. For someone new, or a fix he doubts they can make correctly, he asks to be contacted again before landing.

The title and opening excerpt can obscure that condition. He is not claiming that deliberately shipping a known production-breaking bug is acceptable; he is relying on the author to resolve it before shipping. His reported track record does not prove that this convention is safe in every workflow.

Source: 04:07–06:12 ↗

Section 55 · interview

David Malan: Mentoring, Clear Explanations, and Collaboration

Selected passages on mentoring, explaining difficult ideas, cross-institution collaboration, pride, and contribution beyond authored code.

Make explanations memorable

David J. Malan

Malan’s team creates memorable demonstrations tied to the ideas being taught. The aim is a memory anchor: an overwhelmed beginner may forget terminology but remember a concrete scene and reconstruct the idea from it. Malan wants at least one such moment in a class, for remote and in-person students alike.

Source: 10:35–13:39 ↗

QWhy not share the strongest teaching materials across institutions instead of duplicating every course?

David J. Malan

Malan sees substantial duplication in preparing lectures, assignments and grading systems. Sharing that work could free educators for the more personal parts of education: mentoring, supporting and interacting with students. His aim is not to eliminate educators but to make their effort more valuable.

He describes collaborations with Yale and Oxford as exceptions rather than the normal structure of higher education. During pandemic teaching, he hoped institutions would let students take one another’s courses more freely, but found little appetite for it.

He does not propose one monopoly introductory course. Healthy competition and different modes of instruction remain useful. He imagines a smaller collection of strong shared resources that other teachers can adopt and adapt as an educational buffet, instead of repeatedly recreating all the same material.

Source: 16:56–20:46 ↗

QWhat prevents a college from using another institution’s better resources?

David J. Malan

He suspects a combination of institutional pride and fear of making one’s own work seem unnecessary, while acknowledging that others could explain their motivations better. He encountered a desire for Harvard to offer only what Harvard itself created, even when nearby institutions had richer catalogs in some areas.

Research collaboration across campuses is normal; educational collaboration can feel more personal or threatening. Malan would rather let institutions specialize, share resources and provide different local support experiences. In that model, borrowing a strong course is a way to improve service, not an admission of failure.

Source: 20:48–22:36 ↗

QHow do you help someone understand a difficult concept?

David J. Malan

Use a familiar metaphor or a memorable physical example. A phone book, a contacts application or doors with hidden numbers can make search behavior visible. The learner may discover that an apparently arcane algorithm resembles something they already do.

Source: 47:31–49:14 ↗

QWhat is your biggest career regret?

David J. Malan

Professionally, he wishes he had spent more time in industry before remaining in academia. A later semester as a professor in residence at GitHub let him observe team meetings, issues, feature requests and design conversations. He found it rewarding to experience the working environment his teaching discussed. The regret is about missed exploration, alongside appreciation for the career he did have.

Did you ship code during the GitHub residency?

He does not think he contributed production code. His role was an educational voice, supplying issues, bug reports and feature requests and explaining what teachers and students needed from the products. Contribution can take that form even when it does not appear as an authored code change.

Source: 57:48–58:27 ↗
Source: 55:12–57:47 ↗

Section 56 · interview

Earn adoption, listen to feedback, and own the outcome

Selected passages on iC influence, handling pushback, manager feedback, owning failure, role fit, and clear stakeholder communication.

QWhy was adoption difficult?

Core products such as feed had obvious performance gains, but the remaining teams sometimes saw little benefit compared with their other priorities. Some iOS engineers also strongly preferred built-in Apple frameworks. Ernst had to repeatedly explain the particular limits at Facebook’s scale rather than assume everyone valued replacement for its own sake.

Source: 06:46–07:56 ↗

QHow can an IC influence other engineers without formal authority?

Speak in person or over video when possible; nuance and tone can be easier to convey than in writing. Begin sympathetically: he too would prefer standard Apple frameworks if they solved the problem. Then provide concrete evidence of why they do not.

The team investigated Core Data’s otherwise opaque implementation, including disassembly, to explain initialization costs. Research gave the argument more substance than a preference for a new framework.

He also often performed migration work himself. Asking someone to approve a completed improvement is easier than asking them to spend their own time adopting scaffolding. He qualifies the tactic: Meta’s later codebase became too large for one person to finish such migrations, making broader alignment more necessary.

Source: 07:57–10:18 ↗

QWhy spend so much time reviewing code?

Code review supplies a concrete opening for influencing engineering habits. Ernst can discuss an actual design rather than issue an abstract company-wide message. He tries to explain concerns flexibly, allowing a reasonable differing choice or helping the author make a necessary change. Authors who understand the reasoning may carry it into their future work and their own reviews, spreading the influence organically.

What makes a good review comment?

Explain why a change matters instead of merely ordering X to become Y. Admit that context may be missing and ask whether it would change the recommendation. If it does, encourage including that context in the diff summary so others can review the decision on its merits. Flexibility does not mean abandoning concerns; it means making them intelligible and revisable.

Source: 11:43–12:53 ↗
Source: 10:18–11:42 ↗

QHow did you convince engineers to adopt an unfamiliar declarative model?

Examples showed much less code; performance demonstrations showed work moving off the main thread. Some engineers remained unconvinced, so more senior engineers helped mediate. React’s established reputation internally also helped. Ernst acknowledged awkwardness in the Objective-C++ approach rather than deny its costs, and repeatedly explained the benefits for this application.

Source: 15:33–17:03 ↗

QWhat general lessons did the disagreements teach?

Allies could persuade in ways his own style could not. Compromise also mattered: another team’s Panels framework was meant to be the next UI direction, and the overlap was painful. Incorporating part of its data-source technology into ComponentKit created a shared win. He recommends bringing people into the solution rather than insist on every detail being his own.

Source: 17:03–18:25 ↗

QDid strong pushback make you doubt ComponentKit?

He remained convinced for news feed, while rejecting it as the only acceptable UI architecture. A mostly static scrolling list with complicated nested content suited declarative rendering. A highly dynamic drag-and-drop interface might feel much less natural. Conviction about the intended application coexisted with awareness of paradigm tradeoffs.

Source: 18:26–19:34 ↗

QWhy publish such a candid retrospective?

Writing it was cathartic, answered repeated questions about the project, and explained the failure once without continually reliving the conversation. He hoped others would recognize the same traps before repeating them. He does not clearly remember whether someone also encouraged him to write it.

Source: 25:53–26:39 ↗

QHow did the failure affect performance reviews?

A “meets most” rating helped him realize that the project needed to stop. He thinks a new manager’s fresh view was useful and that the performance process did its job.

He then helped every dependent team move to native code, React Native, or another chosen option, and deleted the framework completely. He did not leave a permanent remnant for someone else to maintain. He believes taking responsibility and publishing lessons gained goodwill afterward.

His advice is qualified: responsibly winding down a failed project can be better received than indefinitely dragging it out. This is his experience, not a guarantee about another organization’s evaluation.

Were there signs you could have acted on earlier?

For the last year he sensed that the project was going badly and sometimes lost sleep over it. His habitual response was to write more code and migrate more features. In retrospect, that treated an adoption and strategy problem as a coding shortage. He wishes he had accepted the signal earlier and found another useful problem.

Source: 28:28–29:02 ↗
Source: 26:39–28:28 ↗

QHow did you know management was wrong for you?

He strongly prefers writing code and thinks he is better at communication tied to a concrete technical problem than at broader direction, documents, or organizational alignment. Managing would distance him from the part of the work he enjoys most. He describes himself as an extreme example and says the choice depends on the individual.

Source: 29:04–30:07 ↗

QHow do you make sure your coding meets IC9 expectations?

He stopped trying to judge each piece of code by its level. Instead, he regularly checks with his manager that he is solving important organizational problems and does work he enjoys. ComponentScript is his reminder that he can become attached to a direction that no longer matters; feedback should then cause him to listen and adjust. He does not advocate ignoring business relevance or management input.

Source: 33:33–34:56 ↗

QWhat makes other senior engineers exceptional?

Ernst admires several different strengths rather than one archetype: high-volume implementation, diagnosing unexplained metrics deep in unfamiliar systems, repeatedly starting complete useful projects, clear writing, and cross-team or cross-company alignment.

One colleague’s project-starting ability included not just code but deployment, documentation, naming, and multiple platforms. Other colleagues made complicated messages clear enough to become examples for engineers improving communication. He particularly respects a collaborator who manages the difficult Apple relationship—work Ernst lacks patience for himself.

The examples make complementarity explicit. A senior engineer who writes little code may still contribute through coordination that a productive implementer cannot supply. Several names are unclear in the captions, so the summary preserves their roles and contributions without inventing identities.

Source: 34:56–37:37 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself just after graduation?

He would avoid changing a path that worked well for him. He nearly applied to Facebook in 2010 but discarded its puzzle-style process; joining later meant arriving at the native rewrite instead. He cannot know whether joining earlier would have been better. His broader advice is to find work one enjoys that intersects with industry needs, while recognizing the luck involved. Enjoying problem-solving does not mean every moment of debugging is pleasant; it supplies motivation for difficult work.

Source: 37:40–39:41 ↗

Mike Stonebraker: Evaluate Accomplishment and Real Understanding

QHow do you identify extraordinary engineers?

Section 58 · interview

Boris Cherny: Cross-Team Influence, Sponsorship, and Trust

Selected passages on cross-org culture, executive communication, manager sponsorship, disagreement, delegation, and rebuilding credibility.

QWhat work led to your senior-engineer promotion at Meta?

Boris Cherny

Cherny recalls a project connecting Messenger chats with Facebook groups, after several earlier attempts to bring the products closer. The product hypothesis was that interaction was moving from public social spaces toward more casual, real-time conversation. He picked up a PM’s idea, built an early version, then recruited a few engineers and design and data-science support as it showed promise.

The small team did work beyond coding. Without dedicated user research, they showed features to cafeteria workers and watched whether they could accomplish tasks without much prompting. He taught teammates the same method. The rough early experience still helped test whether the core idea worked.

He values that generalist approach at Anthropic too: engineers with product sense, design interest, and willingness to speak with users, plus other functions willing to code. His own background in small companies taught him to own the whole outcome. He says the initial half brought his promotion and the next half brought promotions for the rest of the early engineering team.

Source: 01:00–05:39 ↗

QHow do you work across organizations with very different cultures?

Boris Cherny

His Facebook product team prioritized rapid releases and engagement, while Messenger prioritized reliability and performance. The clash was built into goals, incentives, and organizational design, not just personalities. Messenger engineers had reason to fear changes that would damage the metrics they were responsible for.

He believes a version of the project failed partly because the benefit was much clearer for Facebook than for Messenger. Find a goal, hypothesis, or interest that both groups can genuinely share; simply expecting collaboration despite divergent rewards is weak.

What would you change if you could revisit that project?

He would seek an organizational arrangement with a closer common manager and better-aligned incentives, potentially bringing Messenger into the Facebook organization for the effort. He is describing a hindsight proposal, not a reorganization he carried out then.

Source: 09:08–09:42 ↗
Source: 07:06–09:08 ↗

QWhy do you think entering Meta underleveled was fortunate?

Boris Cherny

Lower expectations gave him space to explore and build things without immediately satisfying a larger set of project and people requirements. The host suggests that exceeding an initially lower bar can also create momentum and a strong first impression; Cherny agrees. He sees a downside to seeking a higher title at every move if it raises pressure before the person understands the new organization. This is his personal benefit from one circumstance, not a universal recommendation to accept lower compensation or responsibility.

Source: 17:05–18:56 ↗

QWhat work led to the staff-engineer promotion?

Boris Cherny

He wanted a better JavaScript-based web experience for Facebook groups, which still relied heavily on PHP with fragmented interactive state. Leadership initially resisted because supporting infrastructure was not ready. When the broader Facebook desktop rewrite, Comet, began, he offered groups as an early customer and helped argue that participating would let the team get ahead of required migration work.

The effort grew from an initial group of roughly a dozen engineers into a substantially larger migration. By helping build the platform rather than merely consume it, his product team could shape abstractions other teams would later use.

One example involved optimistic button updates and server responses arriving out of order. He built queuing around mutations to preserve consistent state. He recalls choosing a consistency tradeoff suited to the problem, and the shared work built relationships with the infrastructure team. His broader lesson is that product engineers can go a layer deeper into infrastructure and infrastructure engineers can talk to users.

What additional opportunities came from being early?

Besides shared infrastructure, the team helped define what product quality should mean on the new platform. Cherny wrote notes and gave talks about lessons others could reuse. Getting ahead of the migration gave the team a chance to set standards rather than only comply with them.

Source: 22:53–24:04 ↗
Source: 18:56–22:52 ↗

QWhy did you joke that VPs usually pick the middle of three options?

Boris Cherny

It was deliberately tongue-in-cheek. He thinks a distant decision maker wants evidence that the team explored options and tradeoffs, while also wanting to contribute a decision. A middle option can provide that. He qualifies the observation: some leaders investigate for themselves, and leaders differ in how much they trust teams. The “80%” framing is a joke from his story rather than a reliable statistic or a reason to manipulate every review.

Source: 25:20–26:39 ↗

QHow did reporting to a very senior manager affect your opportunities?

Boris Cherny

Cherny treats this as company-dependent. At Meta, access to leaders could help an engineer find scope and navigate an impact-focused review system. At Anthropic, he sees highly senior people reporting to line managers, so reporting level says less about authority or capability.

He also likes common titles because they make it easier to do useful work outside a narrow role. He describes Meta engineering titles and Anthropic’s broader member-of-technical-staff convention as supporting that culture.

Do common titles make it harder for another team to know how seriously to take you?

Yes, but he thinks the upside is stronger: people must earn trust rather than assume a prior title gives them authority in a new setting. Everyone deserves respect, yet authority over a particular decision still requires evidence and relationships. He recognizes the lost shorthand and considers it an acceptable tradeoff.

Source: 28:58–29:38 ↗
Source: 26:39–28:58 ↗

QHow did you scope work for hundreds of engineers?

Boris Cherny

Cherny recalls a large investment in Facebook groups as a community platform, leaving leaders to determine what newly allocated engineers would do. He produced many rough scoping documents with options and staffing estimates. In hindsight, he would have added people more gradually as specific products found fit: solving users’ problems is not made easier simply by distributing a huge allocation all at once.

A difficult groups-and-pages data-model problem stalled despite senior involvement. He brought technical leads into a short architecture exercise, split them into two groups, and gave both the same requirements. After a few hours, the designs overlapped substantially. Agreement showed where execution could begin; differences exposed risks to investigate with small technical spikes.

This let the team stop treating the whole problem as unknowable. The exercise created a concrete comparison without requiring one person to understand every detail in advance.

Did people accept the unusual design competition?

He scheduled it and made it appealing as an engineering problem. He thinks a leader sometimes needs to act to create a process through which consensus can form, while at other times acting without consensus would be wrong. Here the uncertain path made convening people useful.

Source: 33:29–34:19 ↗
Source: 29:39–33:28 ↗

QWhat helps a technical lead produce a quick scope?

Boris Cherny

Start at a high level and time-box the initial pass rather than disappear into unlimited detail. Cherny suggests roughly half an hour for a very rough view, or a few hours when code investigation is needed. Identify experts and show them a strawman instead of only asking open-ended questions; a concrete proposal makes feedback easier. He now sees coding agents as another way to explore relevant systems, but that is a tool-assisted extension of the same need to expose a reviewable first plan.

Source: 34:20–35:49 ↗

QWhat made the public-groups project a senior-staff-level challenge?

Boris Cherny

The visible change sounded simple: allow people to read, and in some cases comment in, public groups without first becoming approved members. The downstream changes were much harder. Following without reciprocal approval raised questions about how to represent membership, what admins needed, and how to handle more spam.

A senior engineer argued for separate data-model representations, and the team undertook a lengthy migration. Cherny also used a simple simulation of comment quality and spam to make moderation risk concrete, helping bring an integrity team into comment ranking. The work involved many experienced engineers whom he initially felt awkward directing because they shared his nominal level.

After auditing many call sites, he concluded the migration had mostly added branching without changing substantive logic. The old member field could support the needed behaviors. He pushed to reverse the migration, asking the senior engineer with the most context to help undo it. That engineer accepted the evidence and later supported Cherny’s leadership. The reversal was costly but reduced confusion for future developers.

His eventual judgment is that level does not reliably determine who has the best result. The achievement was not simply leading a large migration; it included recognizing when its premise was wrong and earning the trust to correct it.

Source: 35:49–41:10 ↗

QHow can a strong technical disagreement improve rather than damage a relationship?

Boris Cherny

Earn trust first. Cherny initially disagreed but committed to implementing the senior engineer’s decision, then developed evidence and showed technical judgment. A relationship in which both people know you will execute honestly makes later pushback easier to hear. His recommendation is to invest in that trust before assuming a correct argument alone will carry the disagreement.

Source: 41:13–42:02 ↗

QHow did you deal with imposter syndrome while leading strong peers?

Boris Cherny

He says not to assume that others at any level have everything figured out. His confidence did not arrive in one dramatic moment; it grew with experience. He regards some discomfort as a possible sign of stretching into unfamiliar work. This is encouragement grounded in his trajectory, not a complete technique that instantly removes anxiety.

Source: 42:03–42:42 ↗

QWhen should an engineer fill a product-management gap versus ask for more PM support?

Boris Cherny

Understand the decision maker’s tradeoffs before arguing for a preferred answer. A project may be hard to hire for, PMs may be needed on something more important, or an organization may have spare PM capacity that could sensibly be reassigned.

The same request therefore means different things in different settings. Think about what leadership values, what work your request displaces, and whether the proposed allocation helps them succeed. He does not give a universal rule that engineers should always absorb another function’s work.

Source: 42:43–45:04 ↗

QHow do you find useful engineering opportunities and give them to others?

Boris Cherny

He looks for repeated friction in his own coding and asks how to eliminate it. During review he kept a list of recurring comments with examples; once the same issue appeared repeatedly, he wrote a lint rule rather than continue to police it manually. Automation freed his own time and could improve work for many engineers.

He did basic validation on ideas, then connected engineers who wanted those opportunities. He thinks understanding their goals is better than simply ordering them to do a project. At Meta, better-engineering work helped an evaluation dimension many people struggled to demonstrate, so a useful project could meet both a system need and an engineer’s growth goal.

He also warns that prolonged distance from code weakens a technical leader’s intuition. Hands-on experience anchored the opportunities in actual constraints. His very large approximate count of people involved in side projects is a recollection, not a precise audit of his personal influence.

Source: 45:04–48:38 ↗

QWhat is a concrete way to source repeated, high-value side projects?

Boris Cherny

He gives large-data testing as an example. Ordinary tests did not cover a group with millions of members, a highly followed profile, or a very large event, so scale failures appeared only in production. Seeing the same pattern across products, he proposed infrastructure for creating and testing large objects; another engineer took it on and recruited help. The pattern is to notice recurring pain, check whether others share it, and build an abstraction that prevents a whole class of incidents.

Source: 48:39–50:44 ↗

QHow did you rebuild credibility in a new organization from far away?

Boris Cherny

Leaders and colleagues helped him connect with people working on code quality and technical debt, but he still had to earn trust. He spent early weeks meeting people, mapping goals and the organization, and writing code to understand the codebase.

The severe time-zone gap made meetings difficult, but unexpectedly restored time for coding after years of documents and conversations had left him unhappy. He says he still avoids standing one-on-ones. That made it possible to do work others wanted done but could not fit around their obligations.

He explored migrating parts of Instagram’s Python environment toward Hack and Meta’s infrastructure. He considered the original simple choice sensible at small scale but less suitable after years of product growth and a much larger engineering group. This is his contextual assessment; his praise of the alternative serving stack is not a universal language ranking.

He began with the people most likely to disagree, building personal trust before debating the migration. Supporters who had been reluctant to speak then joined the discussion. In a product-led organization, creating space for an engineering-led investment required those relationships as well as technical scope.

Source: 54:20–1:00:15 ↗

QWhen did you delegate the large migration, and how did you decide to trust another lead?

Boris Cherny

Cherny saw a colleague closer to the relevant organization as an excellent owner. He recommends delegating something you understand and care about so you can judge progress, rather than treating delegation as a way to dump disliked work. He cites High Output Management as an influence. Check more at first and less as evidence of reliability grows; with a proactive and technically strong lead, he needed little intervention. The handoff matched the project’s needs rather than preserving personal ownership for its own sake.

Source: 1:00:15–1:01:55 ↗

QWhat happened around the principal-engineer promotion?

Boris Cherny

His manager proposed putting him up for IC8, and he agreed. He had not been campaigning for it. He credits the manager’s willingness to notice readiness and advocate for people, with large modernization projects providing the context. He does not offer a detailed promotion packet or claim that a simple conversation alone caused the result.

Source: 1:01:55–1:02:28 ↗

QDid levels guide how you sought more impact and leverage?

Boris Cherny

Cherny sees levels as company tools for communicating expectations, comparing people in reviews, and planning costs. His own motivation was interesting problems, useful products, and making people’s experience better, rather than the next level itself.

He pitched ideas from his earliest weeks as IC4; several were rejected and one appeared in another form later. The point is a willingness to seek useful work without waiting for a higher title. His career happened to reward that approach, while he does not claim every company will do so automatically.

Source: 1:02:11–1:04:27 ↗

QWhat felt different about Anthropic’s engineering culture?

Boris Cherny

He values a startup’s shorter distance between decisions and consequences: useful changes can seem obvious enough that less effort goes into persuading multiple layers. Mission is also personally powerful. He had felt it in Facebook groups’ community work, felt less of it in Instagram, and felt it strongly again at Anthropic. He acknowledges that geography or his own experience could have influenced the difference. He is describing what motivates him, not a ranking of how meaningful every employee’s work is.

Source: 1:08:47–1:10:14 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the start of your career?

Boris Cherny

Use and develop common sense. Organizational history and misaligned incentives can pull people away from what users and a business actually need. In startups as well as large companies, he would trust practical judgment, examine assumptions, and build toward the real market or user problem. The advice ties his generalist work, side projects, migrations, and product choices back to the same habit.

Source: 1:22:57–1:23:50 ↗

Section 59 · interview

Choose valuable problems and support the people doing the work

Selected passages on selecting higher-value problems, delegation, approachable leadership, management support, and senior promotion.

QWhich experiences changed your idea of how an individual contributor creates value?

Dwayne Reeves

The first was a broader PHP-to-Hack migration. He spent much of a half talking to engineers, identifying useful work, and helping people contribute, while writing less code himself. At first he thought this was his worst period. His manager initially suggested he find more time to code, then revised that advice to focus on the outcome.

Adoption grew from roughly 20–30% to 60–70% of the codebase in his recollection, and Hack became a default choice. He received his highest review so far and a promotion to IC5. The result challenged his assumption that personal code volume defined his contribution: the job was to identify and solve problems, sometimes through clarity and coordination.

The second came after he joined the Hack team as technical lead. With much of the previous team gone, he was learning what that role meant. He designed changes to the collection system, secured runtime-team agreement, and saw implementation begin. He wanted to finish the project himself as a route to IC6.

His manager asked him to hand it off. The analogy was a staged rocket: Reeves had done the work of getting the effort moving; another person could carry the next stage. He reluctantly delegated and moved to another problem, then learned he had already been promoted. In both cases, his mental model of the next level lagged the work the organization actually valued.

A good manager relationship is a through-line he sees in his career. Connection and clarity helped him do his best work; disconnects were associated with frustration. The lesson combines choosing the right direction with being willing to release direct control of every implementation step.

Source: 16:09–23:46 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 16:29–23:46 ↗

QWhy did you try management?

Dwayne Reeves

It was not his original plan. As the team grew, his manager suggested he become a manager; he initially declined. A technical-lead-manager role sounded like a way to retain technical involvement while experimenting with management.

His manager first warned that it could mean two jobs, then supported trying it. Reeves had noticed that several useful career changes came from doing something outside his comfort zone, so he accepted the chance to learn.

Did combining technical leadership and management work?

Initially it did. His reporting group grew from a few people to roughly a dozen, and he began supporting other managers while still giving technical direction.

As the organization expanded, the best use of his technical leadership for a group of around 35–40 people could differ from what his six or seven direct reports needed from a manager. He was doing strong technical leadership and adequate management, but was not optimizing those individuals’ development as a focused manager might.

The conflict was therefore about responsibilities and organizational health as much as workload. He could replace himself as technical lead and focus on management, or return to the IC path and focus on broad technical needs. Finding a manager for the smaller reporting group seemed easier than replacing the broader technical role, so he returned to being an IC.

Source: 25:26–28:55 ↗
Source: 23:46–25:26 ↗

QWhat differs between supporting an IC and supporting an engineering manager?

Dwayne Reeves

The center of attention shifts from technical problems toward people and organizational problems. Both coaching relationships have a longer feedback loop than coding: advice might not visibly help for six or nine months. The manager-of-managers loop can be even less immediate.

He admits that he remained focused on whether the organization was operating adequately so he could continue technical work. A more intentional organizational leader would also examine the structure, how managers coach their teams, what opportunities they should create, and whether the role is still right for each person.

He enjoyed one-on-one coaching, particularly helping people with their technical challenges. But switching from a day dominated by technical direction to a smaller portion focused on organizational design did not come naturally. His reflection is about where his attention and strengths were, rather than a claim that managing managers is merely more delegation.

Source: 28:57–32:52 ↗

QWhat led to the senior staff-equivalent promotion?

Dwayne Reeves

The uncanny-valley argument became a shared technical vision. As the organization executed it and results accumulated, the effect became attributable to his direction. This time he discussed the path more actively with his manager; they needed to see enough progress against that vision.

He was still a manager when promoted and returned to the IC path afterward. He believes the promotion reflected technical contribution more than organizational leadership.

The scale was substantial. When he joined in 2015, there was a mixture of PHP and Hack, and only a small fraction of Hack files used strict mode. By the later period he describes, the relevant codebase was more or less strict Hack, alongside runtime and language improvements. The adoption and strict-mode percentages refer to the codebase and times he discusses, not all programming at Meta.

Source: 32:54–35:40 ↗

QWhich colleagues helped you develop?

Dwayne Reeves

He credits a colleague who brought the product developer’s perspective to changes Reeves saw from the language side. That perspective helped the team plan migrations around what engineers actually needed to build.

Another colleague was a patient sounding board for language and compiler questions. Reeves had little prior compiler experience when he joined Hack and remembers not knowing what a lexer was. The ability to ask basic questions safely was crucial.

He also describes learning from Andrew Kennedy, whose foundational type-theory work initially made Reeves feel junior by comparison. Kennedy’s humility and willingness to consider a practical viewpoint helped Reeves recognize that different strengths can each contribute. He could offer useful insight without possessing the same background.

Did that experience make accomplished engineers feel more approachable?

Yes, and he wants to pass that experience on. He does not want newer engineers to see his years on Hack as a reason to withhold their ideas. Past accomplishments do not make him always right, and he wants to keep learning. Senior colleagues who explained concepts patiently set the example he thinks others should follow.

Source: 39:16–40:32 ↗
Source: 35:42–39:16 ↗

QWhy have you stayed at Meta for so long?

Dwayne Reeves

He has considered leaving and interviewed elsewhere. Before accepting a move, he asks whether it would solve the fundamental issue or merely react to a temporary period of discomfort.

He values the influence he has earned, opportunities to help bring in diverse talent, an unusual chance to work on a programming language, and a strong team. In several cases, the temporary issue improved without leaving.

He does not treat staying as an unconditional rule. Feeling fundamentally unvalued, no longer believing in the mission, or being in a toxic management environment would be different. Those were not his circumstances. He emphasizes the good fortune of his experience and the difference between solvable frustration and a persistent mismatch.

Source: 40:33–44:38 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at graduation?

Dwayne Reeves

When asked to write some code, first ask how the requester knows that it is the right code to write. Aim to participate in deciding what should be done. He wanted his earlier self to see the value of his ideas and judgment beyond keyboard output, especially when impostor feelings made that value harder to recognize.

Source: 44:38–45:26 ↗
