Section 60 · interview

James Cowling: Leadership Credibility and Clear Accountability

Selected passages on promotion incentives, mission-based teams, management credibility, explicit accountability, and senior mentoring.

QEngineers I know have had promotions rejected because their work was not complex enough. What do you make of incentives that reward complexity?

James Cowling

Cowling says it nearly angers him and is partly why he started his own company. His ideal is to be appreciated for solving the problem. He uses a farming analogy: there was no incentive to make milking a cow complicated, because the reward was milk. A startup works the same way. At a large company, with many layers, people build alternative incentives such as green checks on an OKR plan, and he finds it maddening when people chase artificial goals. He accepts some people have no choice, but says working where you are appreciated for problem solving makes you a much better engineer.

From interviewing, he says some engineers at big companies, with Google as his example, describe building a system but cannot say why or how it is used, only that a VP asked. He calls this a caricature, and says it allows competent engineering but the best engineering comes from a deep understanding of why. At Convex everything exists for a reason; you should not build a fancy load balancer unless needed, though he notes the team now does need one.

To cynical juniors he says to fight the system a little. His happiest times were spent dedicating himself to a cause and trusting that promotion would follow, or he would go elsewhere. He suggests finding a team that wants to do good work, which he calls being true to yourself, not selling out.

Source: 44:31–49:20 ↗

QYour writing on system bias argues for orienting teams around missions, not systems. How do you do that?

James Cowling

Cowling says one of his least fun but most impactful jobs at Dropbox was shutting down projects, such as one with 60 people working for two years that did not seem to make sense. In private the team often doubted it too, but inertia and fear of trouble kept them going. He tells a story about the storage team. While building the system it was called the Magic Pocket team, after a silly code name. As soon as it shipped, he renamed it the storage team, which took real work across emails, channels and repositories.

His argument was that the storage team's job is to meet the organisation's storage needs, not to advocate for Magic Pocket. If moving back to S3 were better, the storage team should be the one to say so. A team named for the system would find that threatening to its identity and career, but a storage team would see a new product. He says it sounds like a silly management philosophy, but a team's identity should be built around solving a problem, not defending a system.

If inertia is so strong, how did you fight it and close those projects?
James Cowling

Cowling credits some luck. He was there early and worked 16-hour days, which he does not recommend, and people saw that he cared. That gave him what he calls confidence capital. He was afraid for wrong decisions, not for his career.

When staff-plus engineers he mentored complained about an inefficiency, he asked whether it should be solved right now, and if so what lower priority work should stop. Often nothing was lower priority, and then, he says, you accept it. He sums it up as you break it, you bought it. Shutting a product meant redirecting it, not causing problems, and he credits his success to ownership: instead of complaining he wanted to fix things. When infra had seven to nine people, a new hire from Google would say someone must build a logging framework, and he would ask who, since it was only them. Complaining that an idea is dumb does not work, he says, but offering another idea and owning it is a recipe for success.

Source: 53:14–57:09 ↗
You asked people whether a project would still be the best use of time. How does that help a tech lead?
James Cowling

Cowling says almost nothing is a yes or no question; it is a question of prioritisation. Redesigning the database may be fine in principle, but if it is not the most important thing now, you do not do it. When people say a VP will not let them do something, he notes the VP probably has different priorities, not that the VP is dumb.

He applies the same view to the career ladder. He disputes that becoming senior means getting better at programming, and says his own peaked around level four. What grew was the scope he cared about. A first-year engineer should not try to redirect company strategy for lack of wisdom, but IC6, 7 and 8 engineers are not necessarily the best programmers; they have broader perspective.

Source: 57:11–59:26 ↗
Source: 49:23–53:12 ↗

QWould you choose doing the wrong thing and getting promoted, or doing the right thing and not being promoted?

James Cowling

Cowling picks the second without hesitation. He calls his argument tacky: above a certain level of skill and seniority, he says, pay is high enough that money stops mattering, so junior engineers over-optimise for promotion and salary when they should invest in themselves. He notes it is easy for an older person to say this.

He says that for a long time Dropbox had no proper level system, and he believes that as tech lead he earned the least on his team, which he knew as a technical manager. It worked out. He would take working with the best people over 20 percent more money. There is no shame in a regular job, he says, but anyone maximising career growth should maximise skills, and he believes talent correlates with pay and growth. His advice to early-career engineers is to land at the best company, with the best people, on the most important problems.

Many people face the same incentives and conclude differently. What motivates you to do the right thing when the system does not reward it?
James Cowling

Cowling says the system does reward it, but not visibly at first. People who job-hop less grow the most, he argues: if you do not stay around three years, you do not see whether your decisions were good, and you cannot become a very talented senior engineer without owning their consequences. He compares leaving early to leaving a basketball game before the end. If the job is bad, he says, leave it.

He left academia because he disliked inventing a problem and a solution and then writing a paper to persuade others; he wanted to build and ship and see whether it worked. Readers living paycheck to paycheck may reasonably ignore his advice, he adds. For others, enjoying work every day matters more to quality of life than a fancier car, and he says he loves cars. He and his co-founder can only do work they care about, which he calls a bigger luxury than a first-class flight, and which takes very active effort.

Source: 1:04:02–1:08:11 ↗
Source: 1:00:15–1:04:00 ↗

QYour profile calls you an occasional manager. How did you decide to dip into management?

James Cowling

Cowling says most people should not want to be managers and he sees too much desire for it as a bit of a red flag. Each time he did it, a team needed a manager. He enjoys accountability and having weight on his shoulders, but returned to engineering whenever someone else could take over.

He calls management educational, because you see that companies and engineers are more complicated than you thought. But he cautions strongly against going in too early, as well-meaning people push it as career advancement. In his view people should generally not manage in their first three years, and ideally should reach staff engineer first, because management before becoming an excellent technician limits later influence on strategy.

How does that play out for someone who goes into management too early?
James Cowling

Cowling says they become people managers who see the job as keeping a team happy, coordinating it or handling day-to-day issues, but are not organisational leaders pushing the team toward excellence or shaping technical strategy. He says the best companies have managers who are very technical, since a non-technical manager cannot evaluate the team's work. The host adds that this may feed complaints that a manager does not understand the team, and Cowling suggests a manager may not, if they have not spent enough time developing technical skills.

Source: 1:10:24–1:11:35 ↗
Source: 1:08:13–1:10:23 ↗

QTech workers can be anti-authoritarian. How does a tech lead keep credibility?

James Cowling

Cowling says command-and-control companies, where a manager just tells people what to do, are typically not excellent. To get engineers who feel personally responsible for good decisions, they must believe in what the team is doing. As founder and CTO of Convex he cannot just tell someone to do something; they might because they like him, but they would ask why. He spends time explaining where the market is trending and where the product has gaps.

He describes a hierarchy of values, then why, then what, then how. Engineers often debate the how, but he says most organisational conflict comes from well-meaning people who disagree on why: one team thinks the priority is more features to grow, another thinks it is reliability. He wants everyone to have 100 percent alignment on why, and then trusts the team.

At Dropbox one of his jobs was resolving cases where one team called another an idiot. In his telling the other team was not, and once he learned their motivations they chose to do the project, not out of fear. A tech lead has little authority, he says, and leading by authority produces a culture where people do as they are told and good ideas do not arise.

Meta technically has no titles. Is Convex run the same way?
James Cowling

Cowling says Convex is very flat but has tech lead roles. He does not fully buy that everyone is just a software engineer; at a company where everyone is a member of technical staff, people still notice when the most senior person comes to their desk. What matters is a culture where no one acts only because a senior person said so. Reputation counts, and an experienced person's explanation probably holds wisdom, but even the most senior should win hearts and minds. A principal engineer who orders a database deleted without saying why is not empowering, he says; one who offers to talk through where the product is trending is.

Source: 1:15:19–1:17:19 ↗
Your article is titled “don't lead by example.” Why not?
James Cowling

Cowling says leading by example is passive, and engineers are passive people at the best of times. When he first became a leader he tried to model on-call ownership: first to answer pages, writing the reports, jumping on bugs. The team just saw the lead doing many jobs, and might think it was his job, that he knew how and they did not, or that he liked it. He says he was actually just figuring it out. Leadership, he concludes, means understanding human psychology: act with integrity, but also explain what you expect.

He describes a common path for high-achieving tech leads. They care so much that they review every line and join every decision, become the bottleneck, are told to let go, take their hands off the wheel, and the team falls apart. His alternative is a slider between oversight and accountability. With newcomers you check the work. Over time you dial down oversight and dial up accountability by asking about plans, dates and how they will know it is correct, and saying it is theirs. He has found most people like accountability, so long as the lead still shares responsibility. A tech lead should be developing team members so they can take the lead's job.

Source: 1:17:20–1:21:53 ↗
Source: 1:11:36–1:15:18 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 1:19:56–1:21:53 ↗

QWhat if you give someone accountability and they blow it?

James Cowling

Cowling says that is part of growth and it does not always work. He recalls writing about paper cuts: low-stakes decisions where a mistake costs about a week. These are good candidates for giving accountability. If the decision fails, the person feels it, which he says is good as long as they are not demoralised, and they learn from it. What he would not allow is for someone to lose an arm, such as a junior person designing a core replication system. He says one of the arts of being a CTO or tech lead is judging how far to trust someone with ownership, and putting safeguards in place.

Source: 1:21:55–1:23:22 ↗

QHow do you mentor someone who is already a senior staff or principal engineer?

James Cowling

Cowling says there are two parts. Many senior engineers still share common problems, such as delivering harsh feedback. And at that level there is no single archetype, so each person has to find their own brand. He describes himself as a strategic engineer of collaboration, simplicity and abstraction whose coding fell off a cliff, and others as deep science-and-problem-solving engineers. His mentoring helps people become more spiky in the area that makes them special, and works on the personal side: understanding people and the why.

One thing he tells senior engineers is that you cannot change someone's mind in a meeting. Changing a mind takes processes that do not happen live in front of ten people, and forced agreement only bruises the ego. Meetings are generally not for decisions, he says. State the disagreement and reasons, give enough information, let the person reflect, and return a week later.

He compares the alternative to a capitalist attitude toward interpersonal behaviour, where good intentions do not count if you did not convince anyone. You can be the smartest person in the world, he says, but if you cannot change minds you are kind of useless. At that level, effectiveness includes interpersonal dynamics, because hard problems usually need ten or twenty people working together.

Source: 1:23:23–1:27:28 ↗

Section 61 · interview

Ryan Olsen: Small Teams, Promotion, and Executive Tension

Selected passages on small-team leadership, strong collaboration, mentor visibility, promotion calibration, and executive turf tension.

QDylan Field of Figma and Devon Finzer, a later OpenSea founder, were both interns. Did Olsen notice traits that foreshadowed their success?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says both were plainly determined to start companies, unlike his university classmates, whose highest aspiration was a job at big tech. There was a lot of talk about ideas.

On Figma's early days, he says the founders had one real insight: WebGL was a new technology that would enable new things on the web, and Dylan's co-founder was a skilled early WebGL engineer. They went through iterations not aimed at designers, including, as Dylan once described it, a meme generator app for about a week. Olsen's view is that it took time to find the use case and customer, but they stuck to the belief that the technology would change things.

Source: 08:08–10:05 ↗

QWhat was the Instagram iOS team like when Olsen joined, and what did he do first?

Ryan Olsen

About ten iOS engineers worked on Instagram when Olsen arrived. As the story was told to him, the team had been about twenty before an internal war over the codebase. The manager, Scott Goodson, had built Async Display Kit for Facebook's Paper app; some engineers backed it, others wanted vanilla iOS. Olsen says the factions fought until nobody won and many left, so few engineers had been there more than six months to a year, and there was low-hanging fruit.

His first move was profiling cold start with Xcode's time profiler. The startup path did work for the profile tab that most people never open, and deferring it cut cold start by about 20 percent. Next, AFNetworking was built with assertions on and so crashed the app on benign failures such as a network error. A one-line change to block assertions cut the crash rate by 80 percent, he says.

That earned him the axe, a weekly award for outsized impact open to any function, in the form of a large physical axe carried around for a week.

Where did the axe tradition come from?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen's account is that a men's magazine asked the founders for a holiday gift guide, they listed a bespoke axe, and an investor read it and sent them a huge one. Facebook security disliked a weapon in the office, so it was mounted on a plaque.

Later in his time there the tradition was ended deliberately, apparently because people felt excluded by a weapon being passed around. Olsen was sad, since the founders were gone and it felt like early Instagram culture being swept under the rug.

Source: 20:48–21:59 ↗
Source: 16:37–20:46 ↗

QThe host notes that Olsen credited finding an amazing designer. How did he find one, and what makes a designer great?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says he has tried to be the engineer that top designers want to work with. At companies like this, designers' work can flow through you, and a product engineer's impact is multiplied by building a good working relationship with a strong designer.

Why a designer rather than a very senior engineer?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen distinguishes roles. For product engineers building user-facing features, the best pairing is a designer. In an infrastructure role the analogy is a super-senior engineer with great ideas, and being the engineer they want to work with.

Source: 33:11–34:07 ↗
Source: 32:29–33:10 ↗

QWhite Out was in 2016, the same year Olsen helped build Stories. What is the story of building Stories?

Ryan Olsen

After the redesign, Olsen's team moved to New York and he declined to relocate, so he joined Search and Explore. Within weeks a friend who led the creation team and the project that became Stories quit, and his manager said it was an important effort and a good opportunity. Olsen believed in it because Instagram felt, in some ways, like it was dying: everyday sharing among normal people was evaporating, replaced by creators and influencers, with some going to Snapchat's ephemeral format. The task was to make normal people comfortable sharing on Instagram again.

One of his first moves as iOS lead was to cut the team substantially. The project had churned through directions that did not feel good, and there was too little real work for the people on it. The core was Olsen and one other iOS engineer, plus help from other iOS engineers, two Android engineers, and only half the time of someone from infrastructure. Full ownership meant no stepping on toes and faster decisions. His summary: to go fast, go small.

They built it in two to three months. Olsen says he worked 16 to 18 hour days, seven days a week, driving home to San Francisco at 1 or 2 a.m. rather than sleeping in the office, which he now calls silly. It was intense but fun, the team bonded, and the product manager is now his co-founder. They felt like the underdog against Snapchat.

What did the Instagram version do better than Snapchat?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says Instagram had an unfair advantage: people already had their friends there but lacked the right outlet to share with them. Once that existed, the outflow of everyday sharing to Snapchat stopped. He gives Snapchat full credit for the container, a 24-hour, full-screen, immersive format, but says Instagram added touches such as tapping left to go back.

He also built hold-to-pause after using an early autoplaying build that moved too fast and instinctively pressing his thumb to stop it. His advice to engineers he mentors is that product engineers can build their own ideas, so they should build and put them in front of people.

Source: 39:51–42:07 ↗
The host asks about the 16 to 18 hour days. Did he ever feel a person could not survive that?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says it probably was not 16 to 18 every day, but it was a lot, and he sacrificed other parts of life. A serious rock climber who had competed in World Cups on the US team, he effectively gave that up. It was a unique chance to build something going to hundreds of millions of people, and he loved seeing someone on the Caltrain using a feature he had built a week earlier. He calls the pace unsustainable but says it can make sense in stints.

Olsen thinks Stories was better executed than the efforts at Facebook and Messenger, partly from the team's care. He feared it would crash and burn and was surprised when people called it polished. Delivering on a tight timeline with that craft, he says, helped him get onto the most interesting projects afterward.

Source: 42:09–45:19 ↗
Source: 34:08–39:49 ↗

QOlsen went from IC4 to IC6 in two consecutive halves. What happened?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the promotion cycle was in July while Stories shipped in early August, so calibrations took place mid-crunch. He believes managers were cautious, and he felt fairly confident he had been underleveled when hired, having not known much about levels. His Android counterpart, Will Bailey, who he says was tech lead for Stories and an IC8, got him into meetings with Mike and Kevin and set an example of a successful product engineer. Seeing IC4 beside IC8 on similar roles opened his eyes to leveling.

He told his manager, Eddie, a director to whom he reported directly because of the project, that he had been misleveled and should go from four to six that cycle. Olsen credits him with not brushing it off: he checked with HR, who said it had been done twice in company history and both people left quickly. Olsen says he mainly wanted to seed the idea that his correct level was higher. He got IC5 for White Out and infrastructure work, then IC6 for Stories.

His broader point is that levels and promotions are an incentive system. He thinks there is a real effort to make them fair, but promotions can be delayed so two do not come in quick succession, because it is a carrot dangled in front of people.

The host asks how strong performance gave Olsen the freedom to choose projects.
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says it showed that if he is put on a project he will do well, so when a new effort starts the company picks people who did well on earlier ones. He calls himself lucky, with good execution setting him up for later chances. When the host notes that Threads reused this model of pulling proven people into a small team, Olsen agrees it is a fun environment.

Source: 48:51–50:08 ↗
Source: 45:21–48:48 ↗

QThe next promotion, to IC7, came through IGTV. What was that project?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says IGTV began with Kevin, the CEO, and a designer, Ian, who unveiled a vision for longer-form, mobile-native vertical video at an end-of-year all-hands. Olsen wanted to work on it. He says recent antitrust litigation against Facebook shows tensions between the two companies then; his team was told for a while not to work on it, and he sees it as roughly the end of the founders' time.

The team was small: Olsen, Will Bailey and Thomas Dimson as iOS, Android and server leads, each with one or two others per platform. The product no longer exists and did not do well. Olsen thinks it held part of the future, since vertical video is now central, but it tried to put YouTube-style long-form content in a vertical format and people were not producing high-quality long-form vertical video.

The team tried AI techniques to reformat landscape video for vertical, on which Olsen holds a patent, but creators were horrified. Pushing creators to make original vertical long-form never produced the inventory, and Olsen sees some hubris in assuming Instagram could change what creators make. He believes it informed what shipped as Reels.

Source: 50:09–53:26 ↗

QThe host asks what the antitrust angle is that Olsen mentioned.

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says internal communications made public through the antitrust suit, in which he understands the Justice Department is trying to unwind the Instagram acquisition, made some confusing events less confusing. His reading is that Instagram, small when acquired, grew into a peer of Facebook and the new popular kid. Stories was received better than Facebook's Stories, creating tension between the leaderships and concern that Instagram would cannibalize Facebook, which he says guided some strategy decisions.

The host recalls confusion at the time about cross-sharing from Facebook to Instagram being turned off and says Mark Zuckerberg's internal memo explains it. Olsen says he read the same material.

How might Mark Zuckerberg view it today?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen wonders, since the communications suggest an understandable emotional attachment to Facebook, which Zuckerberg created, while Instagram was less his own thing. Olsen's own view is that the best outcome for a company owning both is to let them compete and improve each other, since stifling competition makes it likelier an outsider builds something better. He adds that he is armchair CEOing about someone running a multi-trillion-dollar company.

Source: 56:03–57:27 ↗
Source: 53:42–56:01 ↗

Editorial note

The antitrust and Facebook-Instagram tensions in these two rounds are Olsen's and the host's readings of public litigation material and their own recollections. Olsen hedges (he thinks the Justice Department is the plaintiff), and this section does not verify them.

Source: 53:42–57:27 ↗

QWhat is the story behind IG Labs, and how did it lead to the IC8 promotion?

Ryan Olsen

After IGTV, Olsen says he spent time in what Thomas Dimson calls the impact desert and was close to leaving. Reels was the new effort, and although his manager worked on it, he was fairly sure he did not want to work on passive video consumption.

Culture was changing too: the founders had left, new leadership came from Facebook, and old Instagram culture felt pushed out. Olsen pitched the new head of engineering on bringing back small teams, attention to craft and a wider scope, arguing the brand could support things beyond the existing app, such as location, maps and places ideas.

He started the group with a designer, Vivian Wong, at first just the two of them, as a Delta Force-style small, high-talent-density team for initiatives that did not fit cleanly into the org. By his account Instagram had grown so large that projects outside its structure were underinvested. The group tried many things, and much of it never shipped. He points to collaborative posts, with multiple authors on one post, as a lasting result and another of his patents. The group could also be pulled onto a major new initiative, which he says ended up being Threads.

Source: 57:37–1:01:45 ↗

QOlsen tried the rare tech lead director role. What was his thinking, and how did it go?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the role was rare at Facebook. It happened mostly because he had started the group, and it made more sense for him to manage the people than for his manager over Reels, who was less connected to their work. He was already representing them in calibrations, so the role was a formal recognition.

He says Facebook keeps individual contributors and management separate, and he disagrees. He cites Tesla as more flexible, with ICs often having reports and managers expected to be competent technical contributors. He holds what he calls a controversial opinion that senior engineers should code, citing Nassim Taleb's skin in the game: a senior IC who codes will not hand off an architecture as someone else's problem, and a manager close to day-to-day work operates better.

He also found an upside to a visible title. Facebook levels are private, which he likes for engineering debates because nobody can pull rank. In cross-functional work, such as shipping collaborative posts across many teams' PMs, a higher title gave a better baseline of credibility, since in a huge company you keep re-establishing reputation. He supported at least a public senior designation.

The host says people warn that doing two jobs means you drown and neither career flourishes. What does Olsen say?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says the criticism is probably correct. He was not optimizing for career and never intended to stay long: on Facebook's sentiment survey asking how long you plan to stay, he never put more than one year. He had no aspiration to reach IC9, which freed him to do what suited the team, and he knew he would not be fired for performance.

He also saw the cost firsthand: he believes his ratings were lower than they would have been as an IC, since he was exceeding as an IC but only meeting as a manager.

Source: 1:06:32–1:08:18 ↗
Source: 1:01:47–1:06:49 ↗

QWould the company be better off if half the people were laid off?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen says yes. His team used to discuss a Thanos-style thought experiment in which half the company vanishes at random, and they often felt things would go better. He acknowledges that at Instagram's scale a 0.1 percent improvement can be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, but thinks the cost of each added person is underappreciated.

He cites organizational overhead of stakeholders, meetings and coordination, and the weight of more code. Just before leaving, a tool showed him spending more than four hours a day waiting for the app to build, because tooling had not kept up with how fast people wrote code. With a thousand engineers that slows everyone, though it is not noticeable per added person. When the team was ten and the app small, things were far easier, and he says White Out would be a massive project at Instagram today.

The host raises Twitter's post-layoff experience as a case study. How does Olsen see it?
Ryan Olsen

Olsen says projections were that Twitter would fall over entirely after the cuts. His experience of it is somewhat buggy, but it keeps running, and he says he saw that its economics improved and it is now profitable, whereas it lost money through most of its history. Editorial note: these are Olsen's impressions, not verified figures.

Source: 1:24:20–1:25:08 ↗
Source: 1:21:32–1:24:19 ↗

QWhat stories show what made the founders and other colleagues exceptional?

Ryan Olsen

Olsen calls Mike Krieger something of a hero and says much of his thinking about engineering leadership came from him, including a simple-thing-first approach and attention to detail and craft. He describes a lead-from-the-front style in which Krieger never put himself above the team and jumped in wherever help was needed. At the end of Stories, a friend Olsen had borrowed from another Facebook team to build the drawing tools was pulled back partway through. Krieger said he would finish it, coded the neon brush, worked the same insane hours, and was up at 2 a.m. reviewing Olsen's diffs. Olsen says that informs how he leads teams.

Of Will Bailey, Olsen describes a strong product vision. During the dark days when Stories was spinning in circles, Bailey wrote a document outlining how the product should work, which Olsen later saw as essentially the five-year roadmap. He was an example of how a product-focused engineer can succeed and influence product direction, which Olsen says was valued more at Instagram than at Facebook, where he recalls bootcamp talk that juniors go to product teams and seniors to infrastructure.

He calls Thomas Dimson probably the smartest person he has met, and not in a savant way, since Dimson has social skills and understands people. Dimson started ranking at Instagram, with infrastructure skill but a product mindset. Olsen says he is interested in technology only as a means to create things for people, and sees Bailey and Dimson as similarly human-oriented, thinking about psychology and how products make people feel.

Source: 1:25:10–1:31:28 ↗

Section 62 · interview

Principal work begins by defining the problem

Ilya Grigorik describes senior technical agency, versatility across execution styles, and the resilience of a broad skill portfolio.

QWhat distinguishes principal and distinguished engineering?

Grigorik resists a fixed checklist for principal engineers. At that level, defining useful work is part of the job. He expects someone entering an unfamiliar organization to understand its landscape, locate problems, form relationships with directors and other partners, and determine where their skills can help. His seven-day reconnaissance analogy emphasizes agency rather than a literal universal deadline.

Distinguished work adds evidence of dynamic range. Technically, someone must be able to reconstruct constraints from low-level implementation while also understanding business requirements and translating them into useful changes. Equally important is choosing an execution style that matches the problem.

At a frontier, rapid experiments reveal what is unknown: act, observe, adjust, and repeat. A platform API with consequences for a partner ecosystem years later needs slower, more deliberate analysis. Even there, divergent exploration must converge into an actionable recommendation. He compares distinguished expectations to a VP’s responsibility for difficult, irregular problems that lower layers could not resolve.

His broader career philosophy is to become the only person able to combine a useful portfolio of skills, rather than always compete to be the best at one specialty. He respects specialists, but thinks broad combinations can be more resilient when a field, company, or market changes.

Source: 00:00–09:57 ↗

QDoes “be the only” mean combining multiple skills to handle ambiguous situations?

Yes. He illustrates it with his own ability to combine modest design, sales, support, hosting, security, and engineering skills to create something useful without assembling a large team. When a true specialist joins, he can hand over that component and redirect his attention.

Learning enough of another domain to understand its language can make cross-functional work possible. He recalls reading many marketing books to converse with marketing colleagues, while writing experience helped with PR. His estimates about acquiring a high fraction of competence quickly express a heuristic rather than a measured universal learning curve.

The senior person need not be the most knowledgeable. Grigorik’s role can be to understand platform fundamentals and business needs, identify the people who know the implementation details, and help them navigate the decision. Pattern recognition, knowing where to find answers, and facilitating the right expertise are different from memorizing every API.

Management experience provides another usable skill: an IC can temporarily coach or give feedback with an understanding of managers’ concerns. The portfolio matters because it lets someone change how they contribute as the problem changes.

Should ICs try management, and can they return?

He encourages a team-lead role as a way to learn, and management itself if it suits the person. He rejects treating the transition as one-way or viewing a return to IC work as a demotion. Managers sometimes remember being happiest before taking the next role, even while valuing what management taught them. Organizations should let people carry those skills across roles without penalty.

Source: 11:29–13:12 ↗
Source: 09:57–11:27 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Different uncertainty requires a different execution style
SituationUseful mode
New product or frontier with unknown constraintsRun quick experiments, observe results, and redirect.
Platform decision with lasting ecosystem effectsExplore consequences deliberately, then converge on a recommendation.
Source: 02:23–04:55 ↗

Section 63 · interview

Scope quickly enough to learn, and concretely enough to get feedback

Boris Cherny recalls planning a rapidly expanding organization and using parallel designs to expose risk.

QHow can one person scope projects for hundreds of engineers?

Boris Cherny

Cherny describes a period when Facebook Groups grew from roughly 150–200 people to roughly 600–800 as leadership invested in a communities strategy. Executive support created resources quickly, and technical leads then had to decide what those engineers would actually build. He repeatedly produced rough scoping documents that compared several technical options and matched an approximate team size to the selected approach.

In hindsight, he would have added fewer people at first. He thinks the important work was solving people’s problems and finding product fit, then gradually increasing investment. Headcount could not create that learning all at once. The distinction is between an executive’s capacity to fund a priority and the product team’s need to discover a good direction.

For a particularly large migration merging group and page data models, the problem spanned product, integrity, advertising, and data layers. Rather than wait indefinitely for a decision, Cherny gathered technical leads, divided them into two teams, and gave both the same requirements and roughly three hours to design a solution. The independently produced designs were about 80 percent alike. Their shared core offered a direction for execution; the differences made the uncertainty visible and suggested targeted technical spikes.

Source: 00:00–03:42 ↗

QHow did people react to the internal design competition?

Boris Cherny

Cherny says it was an unusual idea and he largely acted by scheduling the session. The unclear path required action, but because he did not already know the answer, it also required gathering people to build agreement. He treats leadership as balancing those two modes: sometimes a leader must create the conditions for a decision instead of first obtaining consensus on every part of the process.

Source: 03:44–04:34 ↗

QWhat advice would you give a technical lead who needs to scope work quickly?

Boris Cherny

His main warning is spending too long in details. Start at a high level and time-box a rough plan—he suggests about 30 minutes for an initial pass, or a couple of hours when the code needs investigation. Scoping cannot eliminate every detail before work begins.

Find the experts and present a straw-man design rather than only asking an open-ended question. A concrete proposal gives them something to correct. He also says the AI tools available in his interview context could help explore a codebase and identify systems involved, a task that previously demanded more manual investigation. That tool example is part of his account, not a requirement to adopt a particular product.

Source: 04:34–05:44 ↗
Editorial synthesis
Source: 01:39–05:44 ↗

Section 64 · interview

Brendan Burns: Earn Leadership Buy-In and Build Coalitions

Selected passages on prototypes for leadership buy-in, persuasion, governance, coalition-building, and independent community leadership.

QWhat would Burns have told Google's leadership about the impact of building Kubernetes for the industry?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the hardest early task was persuading people inside Google, though the team was clear on the goal. Burns gave three arguments. The first drew on MapReduce and the big data wave. Google had written the original white paper, but Hadoop re-implemented the ideas as an open source project, and Google got no credit.

The second argument was about containers. Burns says reliable software needs systems that act like autopilots for applications. The third was open source, which Burns calls the most interesting part. People accepted that the system should be built, then asked why it should not stay on Google's own platform.

Why would it not work to keep Kubernetes only on Google's platform?
Brendan Burns

Burns says many people were on other clouds or on premises, and an exclusive product would shut them out. They would build an alternative. Burns compares this with Linux, which won because it could run anywhere. Most people were not on the leading platform, and Google Cloud was not the leader.

Burns's answer is to build for everyone, and make the system strongest on Google's platform. Burns also says that if nearly everything else was open, a closed project would need to be so differentiated that people wanted it anyway.

Source: 03:47–05:24 ↗
Was the idea to take market share from AWS, so developers would migrate to GCP?
Brendan Burns

Burns describes AWS as dominant and first, and GCP as up and coming. Burns agrees the aim was attention, but adds that copying an existing model, such as virtual machines, is hard to sell. Creating a new field where Google was the thought leader gave it a voice, even among people who did not use its platform.

Burns says the strategy did not fully work, because GCP was still third. Burns would not call it a failure. Kubernetes consolidated across the cloud market and is now a utility everywhere.

Source: 05:26–07:09 ↗
Did leadership understand the visibility benefits when they agreed to the project?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the team explicitly wanted to be front and center in thought leadership. That value is hard to quantify. The effort was cheap, with about eight or nine engineers.

Burns calls the separate Kubernetes brand a blessing and a curse. It gave the team freedom to fail without damaging Google Cloud's reputation. Moving to the Linux Foundation let companies such as Red Hat, Azure, and AWS bet on it with confidence. Burns calls the structure an insurance policy, and says it made the team more agile than startups such as Docker.

Source: 07:12–09:24 ↗
Source: 00:37–03:46 ↗

QMany engineers think they cannot build something like this beside their existing responsibilities. What advice would you give?

Brendan Burns

Burns gives two answers. The first is advice Burns has given everyone who worked for Burns: hide about 10 percent of your effort from management. Everyone has slack, and as an organization grows, that 10 percent can do more. Burns says many influential ideas came from it. The aim is to let people make local decisions without asking permission up the chain.

Burns warns that some ideas will fail, and the failures waste time. Still, one success may separate exceeding expectations from meeting them. A person has to accept betting on several ideas. Burns says this is not everyone's path.

Burns's second answer is that the time has to come from somewhere. Burns asks what people give up, since most have 10 to 20 hours a week outside work, spent on games, streaming, or YouTube. Burns says the returns were exponential: two times the time for a year could bring 20 times the impact.

Burns also found the work addictive. Once users filed issues on GitHub, Burns wanted to keep closing them, and kept going until falling asleep at the laptop. Burns was not thinking about a career payoff.

Source: 11:43–16:12 ↗

QIt seems it took a while to get leadership buy-in. How did that happen?

Brendan Burns

Burns says it took a solid six months to go from a very hacky prototype to something a team could use. Many early hires had built similar systems, so the project felt like a clean-room chance to rebuild with better ideas. Burns says that is rare for an engineer.

There were no users yet, so the team did not have to fix bugs for a paying customer. The people involved had long thought about what the system could look like, and could now build it.

Source: 16:13–17:30 ↗

QWhat does hiding 10 percent of effort from management look like in practice?

Brendan Burns

Burns says a person should always have a side project that nobody assigned but that matters. The host compares this to Google's 20 percent time, and Burns agrees the idea is similar.

Burns says hide is meant literally: do not ask permission at first. A project may need a couple of months before it can be shown. Burns says a running system is far more persuasive than a document or slide deck. The manager then decides whether the built idea is good, not whether to spend time on it.

What if nobody cares when you launch, or it is not as good as you hoped?
Brendan Burns

Burns says that is the flip side. Some time will be wasted, possibly including a promotion that did not come because the work was not the breakthrough the person expected. Burns says this is a risk, like a startup. A person should enter thinking the idea is good, worth trying, and acceptable to fail.

Source: 19:51–21:18 ↗
Do senior engineers need to take that kind of risk to be promoted?
Brendan Burns

The host says senior engineers who ask how to get promoted are often told to find the project, since the work has become too ambiguous to hand over. Burns agrees this becomes a necessity at higher levels, where people must come up with good ideas, not only execute them.

Burns says the project helped Burns's own career. Credit for an idea you create entirely is obvious, while credit for a bigger project or someone else's idea is harder to attribute. Burns calls it a roll of the dice, and says timing matters too.

Source: 21:20–23:25 ↗
Source: 17:33–19:49 ↗

QBorg looked like a competitive advantage for Google. How did you convince people it was acceptable to share part of it?

Brendan Burns

Burns says people who leave Google are not wiped like the characters in Men in Black. The team also talked to Facebook, Twitter, and other scale-out companies building similar systems, so the technology was not really a secret. Mesos was similar, so an open source option was coming.

Burns says the team reframed the choice. The question was not whether an open source version would exist, but whether Google wanted to influence it or see someone else control it. A proprietary option was not viable.

Source: 23:33–25:27 ↗

QHow did you get companies such as Red Hat, with OpenShift, to bet on Kubernetes?

Brendan Burns

Burns says many early partners were building a platform or a reliable web service anyway. For them, building the same layer together beat building it alone, because their value was not in that layer.

Burns says partners had to be equals. Taking a dependency also means depending on someone's roadmap, so the team offered a seat at the design table. Later, networking and storage providers joined, because their users were moving to Kubernetes.

Source: 38:47–41:05 ↗

QHow did you keep Google from dominating the roadmap, when Google started and largely funded the project?

Brendan Burns

Burns says independence was critical to adoption. The first step was a foundation. About a year in, the team donated all of Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, because partners cannot easily collaborate when one company holds the trademarks.

The second step came later. The project had no written governance for its first few years, which Burns calls a mistake. In 2016 the team wrote rules so that no single company could take control, with a distributed, democratic model rather than a benevolent dictator. The host says contributors would not join without good governance, and Burns agrees.

Do you mean a constitution? Did you write it yourselves, or did lawyers?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the team wrote it. About seven or eight people met in a couple of intense sessions, looked at other communities, and codified loose arrangements that already existed informally. They also created a steering committee, which had never existed before.

Burns says the group was called the bootstrap committee. Its members were respected leaders who did not fight with each other. Burns credits Sarah Novotny, the community leader at the time, with bringing them together.

Source: 44:02–46:06 ↗
Source: 41:06–44:00 ↗

QWhat share of contributions comes from the community, and what share from the main companies?

Brendan Burns

Burns does not have Kubernetes numbers. From general open source experience, core contributors make up roughly 80 to 90 percent of the work, and less than 10 percent comes from other people. Companies such as Microsoft commit to upstream teams, but for many users, technology is a means to an end.

Burns says it is hard to justify putting 10 percent of staff into upstream work at a bank or retailer, especially when leaders did not grow up in open source. Legal teams also block some contributions, because they fear liability for bugs. Burns says that worry does not hold water, and the Linux Foundation can supply case law, but it can still be enough to stop a contribution.

Would someone actually be sued for adding a bug?
Brendan Burns

Burns says the chain of logic is easy to imagine, such as an open source JPEG library in a smoke detector causing a fire. Burns does not think it holds, since many open source licenses include indemnification language. Burns says a developer in a non-tech company may not be able to argue with legal, so the contribution fades away.

Source: 48:17–50:00 ↗
Source: 46:07–48:15 ↗

QIs there a book that most affected your career?

Brendan Burns

Burns says the biggest early influence was the Gang of Four book on design patterns, from the late 1990s or mid-1990s. The host names it as Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, and Burns agrees. Later, Leadership on the Line mattered as Burns became a large organization leader, and The Five Dysfunctions of Teams is good for how teams operate, though Burns is unsure of that title.

So engineers should read the first book, and managers the other two?
Brendan Burns

The host sums it up that way, and Burns says that is about right, though a career evolves and a person may read both.

Source: 1:05:07–1:05:29 ↗
Source: 1:04:16–1:05:04 ↗

Section 65 · interview

Lead across teams while earning trust and adoption

Selected passages on cross-team scope, approachable leadership, earning adoption, autonomy, and protecting time to lead.

QWhat was your path from joining Meta to principal engineer?

Bolam joined at IC6 in Facebook Groups during early pandemic remote onboarding. With election work limiting teammates’ availability, he had a slow start. His manager helped represent that context in reviews. He later moved to Instagram Web, closer to the UI and React work he had intended to do, and could contribute immediately.

Was your performance at risk during the slow onboarding?

He remembers a satisfactory rather than exceptional rating and thinks his manager’s explanation of the slow onboarding mattered. He does not claim that every slow ramp is automatically protected.

Source: 01:50–02:20 ↗
What was your background before Meta?

He began with frontend work but repeatedly moved into frontend and then backend infrastructure. He hoped a large company would let him specialize in product UI; the same pattern recurred. Experience made infrastructure easier for him to influence, and the larger server platform offered a greater impact surface.

Source: 02:50–04:45 ↗
Source: 00:48–02:50 ↗

QWhy did your managers offer you leadership across several teams?

He had already told them he wanted career growth and had led several teams before Meta. The organization needed coordination during a stack migration, and a strong first month demonstrated readiness. He was offered an opportunity to stretch from one team to multiple teams; he still had to deliver the project rather than treat the assignment itself as a promotion.

Source: 04:45–06:30 ↗

QWhat do IC7 and IC8 scope mean in your kind of work?

In his lens, IC6 often leads one team and IC7 works across teams or a broader area; IC8 extends the reach further. The significance of the problem also matters. Framework work affecting thousands of engineers can have substantial scope even without a corresponding reporting structure. He explicitly recognizes another path through deep specialists whose small code changes produce very large savings. These are examples, not fixed team-size rules.

Source: 06:30–08:40 ↗

QDid you deliberately choose a leadership archetype?

Not especially. He tries to do what the project needs while leaning on strengths in communication, coordination, and creating a team people enjoy working with. He wants others to succeed and thinks that can compound across a long project. He does not usually think in the host’s “force multiplier” label.

Why not management?

He has tried short management stints but wants the option to write a large amount of code when needed. He also prefers having managers who can check his occasional careless remarks. His preference combines the technical work he enjoys with awareness of interpersonal responsibilities.

Source: 09:50–10:18 ↗
Source: 08:42–09:50 ↗

QWhy remain available to colleagues despite senior responsibilities?

Accessibility reveals ideas and problems that might otherwise remain invisible and helps people move forward. He may have to defer a meeting when overloaded, but tries to find a route to help.

How do you decide whom to give time?

He tries to ignore levels, including for interns. Genuine questions and acting on advice encourage further investment. When he lacks time, he may defer or connect someone to a better-informed colleague. This is an attempt to balance access with limited capacity.

Source: 11:22–13:00 ↗
What makes a good question?

Be sincere about what you want to understand rather than script an impressive interaction. A real question makes it easier to identify the right person, including someone else with more time or expertise.

Source: 13:00–13:49 ↗
Source: 10:18–11:38 ↗

QWhat work drove the IC7 and IC8 promotions?

For IC7, a migration originally thought to take roughly two years achieved most of its work in about six months. That freed most resources for other work, including ads on Instagram Web. He credits the team rather than claim individual ownership of the speedup.

For IC8, leadership trusted him with the much harder move of Instagram’s backend into the main Meta stack. Many engineers initially saw no reason to leave a familiar, effective environment. Instead of beginning with a demanded migration, the team improved developer experience between the stacks, then added missing Instagram capabilities to the destination.

Over several years, crossing the boundary became easier, more surfaces moved for their own benefit, and demand shifted toward completing the migration. Major surface and traffic milestones demonstrated scope before the entire program was finished. He describes approximately one hundred fifty involved teams and meaningful performance or development improvements, while leaving exact credit and promotion decisions to their broader context.

How did a two-year migration become a six-month effort?

They cut scope, changed the strategy, and developed team momentum. Moving pages in larger batches rather than one at a time created difficult initial integration work but then allowed compounding progress. The team played to individual strengths and became convinced it could move sooner.

Source: 14:37–15:37 ↗
How did you make the team excited?

He cannot fully explain an organic process or take all the credit. He brought energy, colleagues reinforced one another, and people enjoyed shared progress. Finishing earlier benefited the whole team and enabled valuable subsequent work.

Source: 15:37–16:37 ↗
Source: 13:49–20:55 ↗

QHow did you keep developers satisfied during the infrastructure change?

A server-champions group connected representatives from across the organization, with product engineers making up most of the participants. That kept infrastructure grounded in everyday development. A continuing feedback channel often revealed trouble within hours, earlier than broad complaint groups where issues had to become severe before someone posted. Metrics complemented, rather than replaced, those relationships.

Source: 20:55–22:44 ↗

QHow did your work hours change as responsibility increased?

Hours fluctuate with excitement and the project: he sometimes works sixty or seventy hours, then deliberately returns toward forty or less during another period. He wants a life beyond work and attributes recent balance to systems developed across his career. The pattern is personal, not an assertion that a particular average guarantees principal-level impact.

Which systems protect that time?

He reserves roughly half the week for focus, avoids morning meetings because mornings suit him, aims for no meetings on Wednesdays and Fridays, and groups one-on-ones on Monday afternoons. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons can then hold project discussions. Exceptions occur; the value is a protected default, not rigid adherence.

Source: 23:54–24:55 ↗
What changes during a concentrated coding period?

He cancels many meetings for a few weeks once work has momentum and people know the plan. His projects may have necessary workstream meetings without layers of central recurring syncs. Lead coordination happens when needed through direct conversations or broader forums, and he remains reachable for urgent questions.

Source: 24:55–27:17 ↗
Do you also review code during those periods?

Yes. He checks pending reviews before his own coding and revisits them frequently because waiting for approval can block another engineer. Review is part of moving the project forward, rather than an interruption to personal output.

Source: 27:17–28:16 ↗
Source: 22:44–23:54 ↗

QHow do you decide the depth of a code review?

He scales effort to risk. Core architecture, live production changes, and system-wide decisions receive thorough attention. A gated, isolated leaf component can receive a much lighter review because its failure or rewrite is contained. He still looks for conspicuous hazards. He calls this controversial and acknowledges that it differs from many colleagues’ expectations.

What if someone actually wants a deeper review?

Authors can flag that in the summary or return an approved change for more scrutiny. Their signal can correct his assessment of risk or indicate a desired design discussion. The approach also depends on team trust; new colleagues do not immediately receive the same assumptions.

Source: 30:42–32:10 ↗
Why ask how to accept rather than how to reject?

He wants to identify real blockers rather than require code to match his personal style. Experienced engineers can recognize multiple workable forms. His unusual extension is to approve with a clear warning even when a fix is mandatory, trusting known colleagues to correct it before landing. He says that has not caused the feared production failure in his experience, while asking unfamiliar authors to return when ready. This is an attributed team practice, not a recommendation to treat known defects as safe.

Source: 32:10–33:50 ↗
Source: 28:18–30:42 ↗

QHow do you judge whether you are moving too quickly?

He uses production feedback and metrics to adjust. If a rollout is healthy and brings little negative signal, he may increase exposure faster than conventional increments; if problems appear, he pulls back. The host and Bolam agree that some risk accompanies speed, while daily breakage suggests too much. The transcript does not establish that absence of complaints proves absence of harm; it records the signal-based judgment he describes.

Source: 33:50–35:33 ↗

QWhat is a tech lead responsible for?

The project’s success, in his view. Usually the most useful action is aligning people and ensuring they contribute in the right direction, but the lead may need to write code or debug a problem no one else can resolve. He gives an example of spending weeks tracing an elusive bug. The role is flexible contribution to the outcome rather than a single activity.

What mistake do new technical leaders make?

They can become absorbed in daily operations and lose sight of the goal, especially when the surrounding direction changes. The lead must notice and redirect the team rather than continue executing an obsolete plan.

Source: 36:57–37:46 ↗
Source: 36:14–36:57 ↗

QHow do you balance coding with wider leadership?

He usually writes some code weekly to stay in the complete toolchain, often taking a task he can finish far faster than someone else. Focus blocks help. But he may stop coding for weeks when reviews, resource planning, or another activity offers greater value. The aim is useful allocation, not preserving a coding quota.

How do you learn what is worth your time?

Experience helps. An earlier heuristic was to seek work he believed important that nobody else would do. He now recognizes that neglected work can also be neglected because it is unwise, so the judgment still needs scrutiny. He also reserves time for useful contributions that may not appear in performance-review credit, including helping colleagues and maintaining technical contact.

Source: 39:10–42:12 ↗
Source: 37:46–39:10 ↗

QWhat is your note-taking system?

A separate VS Code window contains plain-text files in one large folder, named for people, projects, and priorities. He navigates by fast filename search, adds dates and times through shortcuts, and writes frequent notes because memory is unreliable. He avoids elaborate filing. Links between files provide connections; a graph view is interesting but not central. The archive includes work and personal thoughts accumulated for years.

Do you maintain an achievement diary for reviews?

Not consistently. He did so for one year but usually reconstructs achievements later, acknowledging the cost of spending a day on that reconstruction. His existing notes serve current thinking more than daily credit accounting. The host suggests launch posts as another record because they already need to be written, and Bolam likes that idea.

Source: 44:40–45:55 ↗
Source: 42:12–47:00 ↗

QWhat advice would you give a new graduate version of yourself?

Go where your strengths are valued. Someone good at frontend, debugging, or frameworks can be ineffective in a role whose leaders need a different contribution. A poor review does not automatically mean those strengths are worthless; recognizing the mismatch and moving can change both performance and enjoyment. He also advises being kind, simple, and able to enjoy work as oneself.

What is the cost of bringing an informal personality to work?

He sometimes says something unwise. He tries to acknowledge it and apologize promptly, while relying on an established reputation for good intent. He does not treat authenticity as permission for extreme or harmful remarks.

Source: 49:21–50:02 ↗
Source: 47:00–49:21 ↗

Section 66 · interview

James Everingham: Relationships, Role Clarity, and Right-Sized Teams

Selected passages on useful networking, leadership role boundaries, right-sized teams, relationships, and avoiding overcontrol.

QWhat does useful networking look like for an engineer?

Ask questions, show curiosity about others’ work, offer help, and participate in discussions. He credits a colleague’s advice to seek mentorship by being useful rather than opening with a request to be mentored. Avoid burning bridges: the people beside you may occupy very different roles twenty years later. He views lasting working relationships as the foundation, rather than networking as a schedule of transactional coffee meetings.

Source: 10:49–13:10 ↗

QHow did you become Instagram’s head of engineering?

He spent six and a half years on Luminate, a product he likens to shopping functionality for publishers, without finding the desired success. A sale to Yahoo, a board relationship, and a prior Instagram acquisition conversation later connected him to Instagram. Although he had verbally accepted another opportunity, meeting the team clarified his enthusiasm: he actually used and cared about Instagram. He credits network, timing, and relevant image-product experience, including lessons from a company that had not become a breakout success.

Can founding a startup let someone return to big tech at a much higher level?

It can, but a company still needs evidence that the person can do the job. His own move from a small startup into a much larger Yahoo organization relied on previous experience leading substantial teams at Netscape and Tellme. Founding alone did not substitute for demonstrated leadership capability.

Source: 27:54–29:14 ↗
Source: 25:38–27:54 ↗

QWhy reduce the initial Instagram Stories team?

A competitive threat does not always call for more people. He wanted a small group of highly capable, proactive engineers with clear ownership and few dependencies. With the founders closely involved, the team could get a product working quickly, then integrate and scale it. Larger teams can create federated components and dependencies that slow the same work. He connects the roughly three-month effort to Instagram’s principle of doing the simplest thing first to test a thesis before committing the whole company.

Source: 29:15–32:55 ↗

QHow did the CTO and head-of-engineering roles differ?

Mike Krieger wanted to focus on technology and coding, while Everingham took responsibility for people and execution as engineering approached one hundred employees. They published job descriptions and decision-routing examples to prevent conflicting expectations. Technology experiments and roadmap questions went to the CTO; headcount, hiring, structure, and reviews went to the engineering head. He often finds companies asking for a CTO when the actual difficulties concern engineering management.

Source: 32:55–35:32 ↗

QWhat else did Instagram teach you?

He initially expected familiar communication failures around one hundred engineers but found the team functioning well longer than expected. Problems appeared later, around one hundred fifty to two hundred. He attributes the delay to talented people maintaining a great deal of shared context. He also values builders being power users of their product; an intern’s quick hackathon project became a highly engaging feature. These examples explain his appreciation of the team rather than define universal organization-size thresholds.

Source: 35:32–37:17 ↗

QWhat do you think of management that stays deeply in every detail?

Different environments call for different tools. His normal style is to support capable people, focus them on outcomes, remove obstacles, ask questions, and let them create the solution. He has temporarily intervened more closely with failing teams, then stepped back. He worries that permanent micromanagement drives talented people away, but does not claim enough knowledge to judge every public leader’s circumstances. Management detail is one intervention rather than his only mode.

Source: 51:11–54:45 ↗

QWhat regrets or lessons would you share?

He recommends going where capable people and mentors are, which helped him almost by accident. He also wishes he had appreciated that time eventually becomes the scarce resource: years of unproductive struggle are costly, and doing work one loves matters.

Source: 54:45–56:27 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning?

Speak up even when afraid of appearing uninformed, ask more questions, and build relationships. He also wishes he had deliberately moved earlier to a place offering the opportunities and resources relevant to his field. Being recruited to California changed his career; he compares waiting in Pennsylvania to an actor not considering Hollywood. This is his own geographic experience rather than a claim that everyone must make the same move.

Source: 56:27–57:41 ↗

Section 67 · lesson

Recognize bottlenecks and keep work moving through interruptions

Selected passages on recognizing an individual bottleneck and keeping work moving through interruptions.

The founder was the bottleneck

He personally researched guests, reviewed all the footage, and handled production. Despite working more than before, he struggled to maintain one episode per week. If he stopped, production stopped: his personal effort had become the bottleneck.

Source: 00:57–01:57 ↗

Create room for interruptions

Illness made the fragility concrete. A nearly finished episode allowed him to publish during a week when he could not work. The experience pushed him to build a backlog and make recording more efficient so he could produce two episodes a week when needed.

Source: 01:59–03:03 ↗

Section 68 · interview

Bjarne Stroustrup: Consensus and Diplomacy Across Teams

Selected passages on consensus-building, committee stakeholder constraints, and shuttle diplomacy between disagreeing specialists.

QWhat would you change if you had sole control instead of a standards committee?

He rejects the premise that he once had unrestricted control: users create obligations of stability. Standardization became necessary when major vendors said they could not rely on an unstandardized language owned by a potential competitor, however much they trusted him personally. He initially resisted because experimentation continued, then accepted that the computing community needed a vendor-neutral foundation.

His annotated reference manual documented both language definitions and rationale, supplying the basis for standards work. The governance compromise enabled wider use while making unilateral changes harder.

What if you had refused?

He suspects C++ would have remained a small academic language and faded from mainstream use. This is a counterfactual opinion. He regards independence from one corporation and a published standard as major adoption strengths.

Source: 53:21–54:35 ↗
How did adoption happen with so little marketing?

He recalls a tiny marketing budget and contrasts it with Java’s corporate promotion. Standards work still suffers from limited funding for experimentation and implementation. He points to a large committee that seeks broad consensus to avoid dialects. He does not need the host’s unsupported claim of a precise adoption ranking to make that point.

Source: 54:35–56:44 ↗
Does consensus mean unanimity?

No. He prefers a very large majority, but there is no fixed numerical threshold that settles every case. A ninety-five-percent vote against all major implementers could still fail to represent usable consensus. The convenor consults national representatives, implementers, and other essential participants when disagreement matters. Judgment can be wrong, yet he sees it as necessary because votes alone do not encode feasibility or informed commitment.

Source: 56:45–1:00:33 ↗
Source: 49:26–53:21 ↗

QWhat was the shuttle diplomacy between hardware representatives?

Different machine models and cache-coordination requirements collided with large bodies of existing code. Rewriting one side’s low-level assumptions was impractical, including code whose original authors had left. Stroustrup walked between two groups, asking for the actual constraint and translating it to the other side. Agreement entered C++11; later, both sides adopted combinations of the approaches. The outcome was cross-pollination rather than one winner.

Why not gather everyone in one conversation?

They had already tried that without progress. He could ask questions and translate despite not being the deepest expert in either hardware model. The useful contribution was communication across expertise and constraints.

Source: 1:08:45–1:09:56 ↗
Source: 1:05:11–1:08:44 ↗

Section 69 · interview

David Patterson: Disagree with Courage and Care

Selected passages on constructive disagreement with company leaders, courage, and avoiding needless personal conflict.

QWhy do you consider courage important in a career?

He traces some personal confidence to wrestling as a smaller young student. Professionally, he believes safety does not eliminate failure, while a meaningful chance can make success possible. Courage also includes challenging arguments he believes are wrong.

He feels an intellectual responsibility to object when weak reasoning drives decisions, even from a company leader. Debate can improve ideas if participants share the goal of finding the best answer. He tempers this with an older colleague’s warning that enemies can endure longer than friendships: stand up when it matters, while being careful about unnecessary personal conflict.

Do you mean confronting technical errors?

Yes, along with weak political or organizational arguments. He wants a marketplace of ideas in which criticism strengthens the result. He extends the principle to public life, where he has written about issues he believes require correction. The point is a shared purpose and stronger ideas, rather than confrontation for its own sake.

Source: 52:29–54:01 ↗
Source: 50:02–52:27 ↗
