Section 70 · interview

Michael Bolin: Influence, Promotion, and Clear Writing

Selected passages on aligning impact with employer needs, influence/conflict that delayed promotion, and effective writing.

QWhat drew Bolin to Google and to Google Calendar, and what was the culture like?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he got online in the 1990s, when finding anything meant trying five search engines. A roommate pointed him to a newer search engine in March 2000, which struck him as better. He contrasts Yahoo's cluttered pages with Google's sparse, principled design, and he noticed that good people were taking jobs there.

In Bolin's account, Google understood the web better than Microsoft did at the time, since Microsoft had dismantled the Internet Explorer project while Google was web-forward. With the engineering quality and impact, it was the place he most wanted to go coming out of school.

What was the culture like, in terms of product versus infrastructure?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says founders keep a soft spot for whatever the company was first good at, which at Google meant information retrieval and infrastructure. Products such as Gmail were what drew him in, but they did not carry the same standing inside the company as search.

Calendar, he says, was mostly consumer-facing and was also sold to enterprises, though his team was not the one making the money. He compares the team to a call center.

Source: 04:05–05:02 ↗
Source: 02:45–04:05 ↗

QWhy did Bolin leave Google after four years, given that the departure read as bittersweet?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says the financial picture changed once the four-year mark passed. The deeper problem, he says, was a bad habit of working hard on things that mattered to him but not to Google. He lists Calendar, which was important, Google Tasks, a small feature with two to three orders of magnitude fewer users, and the JavaScript infrastructure and Closure toolset. He wrote the book on Closure out of motivation.

He is proud of that work, but says it was not the best career move, since others were being recognized while he was working hard on the wrong things. He calls it the harder-not-smarter mistake, and decided to look for a place where what excited him matched what the company cared about.

Source: 05:04–06:45 ↗

QHow did he influence people at a new company where he had no credibility?

Michael Bolin
Michael Bolin

Bolin says one prolific senior Android engineer, also ex-Google, advised him to do it fast before anyone cancelled the work, and promised support if it succeeded. That engineer welcomed a faster development cycle and was among the first to praise it.

Bolin also admits a mistake. Coming from Google, he thought of Facebook as a bunch of college kids and several times argued that Google did things a certain way. People told him they did not care, and he says they were mostly right: what worked at Google would not necessarily work there.

Source: 13:23–14:49 ↗

Earn credibility and make the case for an initiative

Michael Bolin

Bolin saw a developer-tools problem with real business value and scoped his proposed editor narrowly rather than trying to serve every platform at once. Another team already had users, but leadership supported his approach. He attributes that decision partly to his argument about how the tool should fit the company’s needs and partly to the credibility he had earned with Buck.

Source: 16:35–21:12 ↗
Source: 21:12–22:22 ↗

QHow did Bolin react to the promotion to E8, described by the host as principal level in the industry?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he was very excited. Having felt out of step with his employer at Google, he saw the promotion as validation that he was growing in more than technical skill: he was learning what it means to do work that is in line with the employer. That was as satisfying to him as the promotion itself.

Source: 22:22–23:06 ↗

QAfter the promotion, what did Bolin do next, and what is the "hero quest"?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he got a little over his skis by trying to help with web speed. Load time on facebook.com was poor and the architecture stale, and many colleagues had worked on web for a long time while he had been in mobile and dev tools. He and another engineer compiled V8 from source to see whether generating JavaScript differently would help. None of it panned out.

He concluded that different people suit different projects. He is better when a project involves writing a lot of code from the beginning, whereas this effort was about looking at data and talking to many people, which is not his strength.

What does hero quest mean?
Michael Bolin

Bolin calls it embarrassing, because it involves ego. Engineers say that if only someone would come in and cut this Gordian knot, and he assumed that since he knew JavaScript, he could be that person. He says he did not succeed, and that he has had to relearn the lesson at least once since.

He can do many things, but a smaller subset is what he genuinely enjoys, and he will be much more successful staying within that subset while trying to expand it over time. In his words, people do not all have to be the best at everything, and should accept and embrace that.

Source: 27:42–28:36 ↗
Source: 26:01–27:40 ↗

QWhat did Bolin learn about influence and conflict that delayed a promotion?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says most people at the E8 level and above do not write code. They spend their time on influence, writing the large document and getting teams on board. For a senior engineer who writes code, he says, reaching the expected impact means spending at least some time influencing others.

His problem was that he was so confident in his insights that he came down too hard. When Microsoft acquired GitHub, the editor he had built relied on GitHub technology, and he feared it would be replaced because VS Code would not let it stay a project. He says that turned out to be true. But he was anxious, pushed people, and did not account for people being happy with what they were doing and not wanting their cheese moved. He received a talking-to, and his promotion waited.

From the coaching that followed, Bolin says, he became more aware of what triggers him, including technical decisions, and tries to notice that and not act in the moment. If he is not in the best place to have the conversation, he might talk to the person's manager rather than charge in like a bull in a china shop.

He was right about the editor in hindsight but told to calm down. How does he feel about that?
Michael Bolin

Bolin says that about a year later he had conversations in which he asked to balance the ledger a little, and they worked it out. He agrees with the host that the learning was about how he went about it, not what he was right about.

Source: 39:00–39:52 ↗
Source: 35:53–38:58 ↗

QHow does Bolin think about the very high expectations at senior-staff levels and above, and is it stressful?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says it was never not stressful. He sat in calibrations, discussing others' levels and impact and wanting to be fair, and he imagined someone doing the same for him. At E8, one is compared to a director who may have over a hundred people, and it is hard to match that impact.

Many senior engineers, he says, do it through a different form of people management, writing the right document and aligning people. They remain individual contributors because technical credibility makes their words land differently than a director's. Influencing 50 to 100 people that way is, in his words, director-level impact.

For those who mostly code, project choice matters, and it cannot be one that is merely fun. Bolin often decided not to write a fun feature himself and let someone else do it. On Codex he asks which code he personally should write to maximize impact, and if someone else could do it about 80 percent as well, he lets them. He looks for force multipliers such as the virtual file system, which he knew would unlock things later.

He also says senior managers do not get enough recognition for pairing the right senior engineer with the right project. Some senior engineers are excellent fixers and coders but not idea generators, and a manager can see that a hard project needs a person who would never have chosen it.

Source: 1:06:54–1:11:25 ↗

QA former colleague praised Bolin's ability to start projects. What advice does he have for engineers who want to build something from scratch?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says good projects often come from being a bit dissatisfied with something. He admits he often charged ahead without thinking about the best way to build it. His example is weather icons in Google Calendar: he mostly knew JavaScript, cobbled together the backend, and stored the weather data as a blob of XML. His tech lead asked why he had not discussed protocol buffers and binary formats. He had been so set on the feature that he never asked anyone whether there was a better way.

The host notes many people simply wait on a slow build. What gave Bolin the confidence he could make it better?
Michael Bolin

Bolin credits his time at Google. He never worked on the Blaze team or touched its code, but he knew a tool with that shape existed and was much better, which he calls an existence proof. Whether he could build it was still to be seen. He says prior art gives him confidence, and that he thinks of himself as a coding machine who can build a prototype and test the basic hypothesis that a way forward should exist. If you are determined, he says, you find a way. The host adds that people who see world-class infrastructure at big companies often go elsewhere and rebuild it.

Source: 1:13:09–1:14:39 ↗
Source: 1:11:27–1:12:54 ↗

QWhat advice does Bolin have for engineers who want to write better, given how clear his technical writing is?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says reading good writing is a start, since patterns get picked up consciously or not. He then stresses thinking at a high level about what he is trying to convey and what readers would really want to know, and outlining a lot up front. He asks whether the points follow linearly, and whether any jump from one point to the next is too big, such as something a reader could reasonably miss. He feels he has a reasonable sense of where such gaps arise, and says that for technical writing, anticipating them and adding the example the reader needs to make the jump matters a great deal.

Source: 1:14:41–1:16:03 ↗

QCan Bolin explain the three-step plan for impact from his career note?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says step one is figuring out what you really like to do. It is good to broaden that, but also to be honest with yourself, and he ties this to his hero quest, which failed because he was working on things he did not truly love. Step two is working out what is really valuable to your employer, and he says that at Google he did not do this well. He did work he was excited about, but it was not AdWords for Google. Step three is finding the intersection and leaning into it.

He says the more you can do that, the more successful you will be, but the intersection is not always there. If it is not, you may have to find somewhere else to make it happen.

Source: 1:16:03–1:17:05 ↗

QKnowing everything he knows now, what advice would Bolin give himself at the start of his career?

Michael Bolin

Bolin says he should have been open to learning more things sooner and been gentler with himself, as many beginners should. He observes that people have a soft spot for their first programming language, since it first let them do something, and that this is also a hazard. Having finally become productive, a person is tempted to hold on, not knowing how long the next foothold will take.

In his case he thinks he went too deep on JavaScript, and it took a long time before he wrote C++. Being more curious and flexible about project types and what he was willing to learn would have been the biggest shift. The host points out that Bolin's later stories, such as Objective-C and C++ for Miles, show deliberate effort to learn rather than openness, and suggests that Codex may lower the hurdle, for example by asking it to write something in Rust from JavaScript knowledge. Bolin agrees that it opens many doors.

Source: 1:17:06–1:19:04 ↗

Section 71 · interview

Bryan Cantrill: Recognition, Team Trust, and Leadership Responsibility

Selected passages on stack ranking, recognition, team trust, role boundaries, leadership accountability, and interpersonal regrets.

QYour goodbye post said you did not particularly want to work for Sun. What changed your mind?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says the people he met in other Sun groups were fine but not energizing. He was used to being the youngest person in a group, but he wanted colleagues who shared his passion. Meeting Kevin Clark and Jeff Bonwick was, in his words, a bolt of lightning. Both were energized and saw the same potential for operating systems to be innovative. Both wanted to rip out broken code and replace it with beautiful code.

He remembers coming back from that trip certain that he would take an offer from Sun.

Source: 06:42–08:14 ↗

QWhat was the career ladder at Sun like?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill describes the ladder as member of technical staff, staff engineer, senior staff engineer and distinguished engineer. He thinks Sun may have originated these titles, though Xerox PARC is another possibility. He is not sure.

He tells a story about business cards. Early on he did not know his rank and assumed that an engineer on staff was a staff engineer. Colleagues soon told him that would be like claiming tenure. He was an MTS3. Most college hires started at MTS2, but he says he was an unusual hire. He had done kernel development at a company in Canada for two summers. After school in the Northeast and work in Canada, he wanted to come out to Silicon Valley.

Source: 08:15–10:09 ↗

QWhat stands out in your growth from MTS3 to distinguished engineer?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says he never focused on grade, rank or promotion. He would rather be underpromoted than overpromoted, and he did not want to do work performatively. He did what he judged most important: solving customers' problems and making the operating system what he believed it could be. Sun, he says, was accommodating of headstrong engineers. In 1996 he thought Sun was the only company still invested in its own operating system, and work on the Solaris kernel was energizing. Promotions simply happened along the way.

He also reports a plain finding about formal reviews: they never made him perform better. In his view a review measures performance, while it should be about feedback that helps everyone be the best they can. He found the annual cadence broken. His reviews looked like his own self-review with grammatical errors added. The highlights of his career were never promotions. They were a significant body of work, a hard bug, or working with someone on something they thought impossible.

He describes Sun's rating tiers as superlative, excellent and good, with a rough split he recalls as about 70, 20 and 10 percent. A superlative rating forced a promotion, and Sun did not want promotions faster than every 18 months. So managers gave apologetic reviews that rated clearly better work as merely excellent. Cantrill says he did not care. He was promoted to staff engineer, by his estimate around 2001, just as the dot-com crash hit. The company bonus, which depended on company performance, was zero from then on.

Cantrill calls the process for becoming a distinguished engineer regrettable and stupid, though he is not describing his own promotion. He says there were two routes. One was a vote by existing distinguished engineers, which he calls a political process and a country club, and a bad place for democracy. The other was an acqui-hire in which the acquired company's CTO arrived with the title. He says people could tell the homegrown ones from the acqui-hired ones.

His own case, as he understands it second-hand, was presented by Sun's CTO, Greg Papadopoulos, who had chartered the Fishworks group that built a storage product. Papadopoulos reportedly said he expected no one to vote against it, and the vote was unanimous. Cantrill says he is grateful and did not want to deal with the politics. He sees ranks as corrosive, and Oxide has none.

Source: 10:11–19:33 ↗

QIf an ambitious new graduate wants to become a distinguished engineer, should they focus on the work or ask their manager what the next level needs?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill would steer them to a third path. He would ask why they want the title, since reaching it does not give meaning, and he calls it a recipe for a midlife crisis. He would try to find what drives meaning for that person and what fuels them. His aim is to stop them depending on external validation. He would introduce them to miserable distinguished engineers, and to miserable wealthy people, to show that the title or the money cannot be the answer. In his view, once the person finds the real driver, the work and the promotions follow.

What if the mentee says they want financial independence?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill first asks what that means in such a well-paid field. He points out that anyone in San Francisco can buy an excellent six-dollar coffee. If it means never needing to work for money again, he asks, what then? If the meaningful thing does not pay, he says to balance it with a career. He thinks it is a mistake to plan to reach independence first and pursue meaning afterwards.

He draws on the dot-com boom and bust. Most people around him made money on paper and lost it. He argues the bust helped, because people who had come for the money left and the rest had to remember why they came. He knew people who made fortunes in the boom, were not much interested in tech, and struggled in the next decade, wondering what to do. One bought several houses and found them a pain. He says too many people work in the industry only to leave it. His advice is to go and do the thing you would do after leaving. His example was quitting a job at Meta to become a podcaster, and the host answers that they did just that.

Source: 21:24–25:38 ↗
Does that match the posts from people who say they reached financial independence and do not know what to do now?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says the same problem appears in engineering even when the goal has meaning. He calls it postpartum engineering. When a team is focused on shipping something, shipping becomes the lens for everything. He feared this after Oxide shipped its first rack, when people who had pulled hard for a long time might ask what comes next. He adds that some people respond to the emptiness by chasing even more money. He names Larry Ellison as an example of a result people should not aspire to.

Source: 25:40–27:08 ↗
What about someone who is genuinely happy doing nothing?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill jokes that anyone with a billion dollars would simply do that every day. He then tells a story about one of the earliest Yahoo employees he knew. This person was hired as a web surfer to help curate Yahoo's directory of links, in the era before search engines. The person received an equity grant on joining, never got another, and made a fortune. Cantrill says the person was never promoted, complained that the job was awful, and by the end owned only one topic, snowboarding in Northern California. He concludes that whatever this person found meaningful, it was not the work.

Source: 27:09–29:39 ↗
Source: 19:36–21:21 ↗

QSun's ratings had no bad tier. Why not, and what do you think of stack ranking?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Sun did not use performance improvement plans or the rank-and-yank approach Intel was known for, which is stack ranking. He calls stack ranking organizational cancer, especially when a bottom percentage is terminated. In his view it rewards managers for keeping dead weight on their teams, so that someone always ranks last.

He says this happened at Sun anyway. Someone once took him aside and said that a weak colleague was in his interest, because that person always received a good rating, which left room for others to receive excellent or superlative ones. Cantrill calls this a set of perverse incentives. His main objection is that stack ranking teaches people their teammates are adversaries. He believes teams do extraordinary things, that everyone should want to serve the team, and that stack ranking works against that.

Sun's stock fell 98 percent. Was there no push for mass layoffs?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says the stock traded below the company's cash at one point. Sun resisted layoffs for a while, and Scott McNealy famously did not want to lay people off. Cantrill calls that a mistake and says McNealy waited too long. Once layoffs began, Cantrill recalls counting about 35 rounds over roughly eight years. Some were small, some large.

Employees could pull the staff directory programmatically from the internal organization tool. They ran a daily script they called the obits, which showed who had left. Some days it showed 1,500 or 3,000 people.

Source: 31:36–32:59 ↗
Was the company aware that you had that data?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says Sun's strength and weakness was that no one was truly in charge, so it would not have surprised him if people knew. He thinks Sun was a transparent company and that using the organization tool broke no policy. It was a way of knowing what was happening.

He adds that the whole industry was in the same position. He dates the dot-com collapse to the end of 2000, says September 11 made it worse, and says tech was basically dead for about five years. He places the founding of Y Combinator around 2006 and suggests it reflected a capital deficit, though he defers to Paul Graham on that. He calls the period bleak.

Source: 33:01–34:48 ↗
Source: 29:34–31:35 ↗

QWere top engineers confiding in one another that they had to leave Sun?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says it was less like confiding and more like running from a burning building. Before the deal closed, some employees were not going to become Oracle employees and would be laid off with rich severance. He describes a line of people wanting to be on the list. He says he was not one of them. He says some people still resent colleagues who left that way. He was at the Fishworks group in San Francisco and was somewhat optimistic that the best of both companies could be combined. He quit after about 45 days because he could not work there in good conscience.

What did you see that made you leave so quickly?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says it was clear this was a very different company. After he decided to leave, he says, Oracle gave him several more reasons. The one he stresses is customer trust. Sun, for all its faults, had its customers' trust. They rooted for Sun to prevail because Sun was straight with them even when that did not serve its own interest. He says Oracle does not have that trust.

He realized he could not work for a company with such profound distrust. It eroded his sense of meaning. He felt ashamed to work at Oracle. At Sun he had sometimes felt embarrassed, but never ashamed.

Source: 42:08–43:33 ↗
How do you get yourself laid off?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says there is no web form. You tell your manager to put you on the list, or you whisper around to learn what is going on. He says it was not about underperformance. It was about saying that Oracle had no interest in your work. Then, he jokes, if Oracle shows interest in what you do, you are upset.

Source: 43:34–44:14 ↗
Source: 40:23–41:57 ↗

QWhat is the difference between VP of engineering and CTO?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill gave a talk at Joyent on this contrast, but he is not sure how much he buys the difference now. In both roles you are an engineering leader. He says a CTO is more outward-looking, spending a lot of time on the road with customers, and jokes that the title could stand for chief travel officer. A VP of engineering tends to focus more on the mechanics of an engineering organization.

He joined Joyent as VP of engineering because the company already had a CTO, and he says he did not particularly care about titles, as at Sun. When the founding CTO left, he did care that the company not hire externally for the role. He later became CTO.

Why not hire externally?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill says an outside CTO was not what the company needed at that point. The company had removed its CEO and needed a terrific CEO, which he says it later got.

Source: 49:34–49:53 ↗
Source: 48:03–49:32 ↗

QIn 1996, as a new graduate, you replied to a long technical post by David S. Miller with a personal jibe. What was the context, and what do you think now?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill puts it firmly in the regret column. He says he has few regrets in his career. He was about 22 and had no idea the post would last 30 years. He explains that the jibe referred to an obscure Saturday Night Live sketch in which William Shatner, at a Star Trek convention, tells fans to get a life. He says that does not make it better, and he is not defending it. It was a mistake.

Miller had plenty to say in reply. Cantrill says he wrote a longer post taking Miller's points apart one by one. He has never met or talked to Miller, whom he calls a very talented person. He recalls reading in a book about Linux that Miller said a Sun engineer had put him back in his place. If that is Miller's account, Cantrill says it is generous to him. He hopes both of them regret it a little, as young and excitable people. He calls it a life lesson.

Source: 1:02:38–1:06:55 ↗

QIn 2022 you tweeted that failure at a startup is almost always bad leadership, not the team. Does that apply to Sun, which ultimately failed?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill does not remember writing the tweet, though he likes it and cannot recall what he was responding to. On Sun, he rejects the premise. Sun was founded in 1983 and was acquired around 2008 to 2009, by his dating. It was a public company in the Fortune 200. Many children went to college because their parents worked there. He says it did not succeed to the scope of its own ambition, but he regards Sun as a success, not a failure.

Could different leadership have changed how Sun ended?
Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill thinks so. He lists several reasons Sun did not survive as an independent company. It had become strung out on the high margins of the dot-com boom and never fully got off them. It embraced x86 too late. The company became fractured, and the layoffs did not help. He thought Fishworks could have been an exemplar of the products an independent Sun might develop, but that would have required leadership strongly interested in that change, and Sun did not have it.

In hindsight, he says, it was probably time for a change. He compares it to a forest fire in a healthy forest, which is part of the life cycle and allows rebirth. He concludes that Sun had succeeded, had run its course, and had its time.

Source: 1:08:26–1:09:52 ↗
Source: 1:07:05–1:08:25 ↗

QIf you could go back to the start of your career, what advice would you give yourself?

Bryan Cantrill

Cantrill's answer is essentially not to mess anything up. He says he has been very lucky, in the right place at the right time many times, and that he trusted his gut when that was controversial. He would be scared to give his younger self advice, since he might tamper with a lucky career in which he worked with extraordinary colleagues. He says those colleagues have been essential to everything he has done.

He admits he made mistakes. He says the mistakes became load-bearing and important, and he would not want to remove them.

Source: 1:19:21–1:20:40 ↗

Section 72 · interview

Neetcode: Recognize Team Culture and Role Expectations

Selected passages on recognizing cutthroat versus supportive teams, manager signals, realistic agency expectations, and exit caution.

QWhat happened after the first full-time job offer at Amazon, and why did Neetcode leave so quickly?

Neetcode

The Amazon role came soon after college, around age 22. Neetcode had expected a hard environment but found the culture a shock. The team had about five new grads who joined in the same month, and several burnt-out mid-level and senior engineers. Neetcode says the team was unfriendly and that most people left within about a year.

Neetcode says the decision to quit after a couple of months was a poor one, made without a backup plan or savings, though it worked out. Neetcode would not recommend it to most people.

What did you see at Amazon that made you want to quit so quickly?
Neetcode

Neetcode separates intense high-performing teams, where people compete and still root for each other, from cutthroat teams where people do not. The Amazon team felt like the second kind. Icebreakers were cold, and nobody seemed to be rooting for anyone else.

Neetcode stresses the limit of that judgment. Neetcode was there for only a short time and cannot say whether people tried to harm each other.

Source: 01:54–03:17 ↗
What gave you the confidence to quit so quickly?
Neetcode

Neetcode calls the decision uncharacteristic. Shortly before starting at Amazon, Neetcode had been broke and felt on top of the world. Within the first day, the manager signalled that the team was burnt out, and the situation seemed to get worse steadily.

Source: 03:19–04:04 ↗
Source: 00:37–01:54 ↗

Role expectations and honest self-presentation

Neetcode

The leadership-principles interview was the harder filter. Neetcode admits giving answers that matched the company’s picture of a high-agency, risk-taking employee, although Neetcode is naturally risk-averse and careful about mistakes.

The real work at Amazon asked for much higher initiative than expected, and adjusting to that took time.

Source: 04:08–05:14 ↗

Section 73 · interview

Navigate client incentives and explain your work clearly

Selected passages on consultant/client incentives, navigating a new company’s culture, mentorship, and clear explanations of work.

QWhat does software engineering consulting actually involve?

Asian Dad Energy

A consulting firm supplies skills such as content-management systems, ecommerce, backend integration, or digital transformation. Teams enter a client’s environment to build systems, working alongside the client’s technical staff and often other vendors.

The environment can be dynamic and chaotic. A consultant has to find a place among several actors, learn quickly, build as well as possible, and then move to another project. He enjoyed the pace and the need to adapt.

Who maintains the software after the initial build?

There are different arrangements. A retainer can support a relationship lasting years, with continued maintenance, enhancement, and accumulated knowledge of the system. He preferred that continuity, especially when the firm had built the platform from the beginning.

A short build-and-exit engagement can have different incentives: the agency needs a pipeline to keep consultants employed. Across multiple vendors, the client can accumulate redundant and incompatible systems. A later integration project then has to stitch together the resulting patchwork. He has encountered both models, with their different technical challenges and anxieties.

Source: 13:01–15:58 ↗
Source: 11:36–13:01 ↗

QWhat is it like to be dropped into another company’s culture?

Asian Dad Energy

It depends on the client. He has seen rigid hierarchies, cooperative environments, and internal startups. Technical skill alone is insufficient: a consultant must understand how client teams relate to one another and to outside vendors.

As seniority grows, navigating that environment and opening space for the firm’s next engagement can become part of the job. His own work gradually shifted from hands-on system design toward selling a vision to executives. The earlier learning and adaptation were enjoyable; the later shift eventually burned him out.

What caused the burnout?

The gap between the smooth vision sold to executives and the implementation reality. Diagrams promised a clean path from customer insight to decisions and revenue, while the underlying work involved incompatible systems, unmaintained code, broken integrations, and teams struggling to communicate. As the technical director responsible for making those worlds meet, he found the gap exhausting.

Source: 18:14–19:24 ↗
Source: 15:58–18:12 ↗

QDoes a consultancy still get paid when the implementation is poor?

Asian Dad Energy

He frames the answer around the early digital-transformation period he experienced. Executives could see visible improvements, such as replacing an analog workflow with a mobile experience and delivery notifications, while having little visibility into the workarounds beneath the surface.

Moving from no digital workflow to a working one could produce substantial value even with an imperfect implementation. That did not mean the architecture or operational quality was good; it meant a visible business result could be enough to make the engagement look successful initially.

Source: 19:24–21:32 ↗

QWhat prevents a consultant from overstating the quality of the work?

Asian Dad Energy

The guest emphasizes engineering integrity: tell the client the truth about quality, even when a large investment has produced a poor result. Personal boundaries and pride in the work matter when the client cannot fully judge the implementation.

Peterman raises reputation and incentives. A firm that repeatedly delivers bad work can lose future customers. He also contrasts the client’s limited technical visibility with an engineering organization where technically informed leaders assess operational quality and reward it.

The guest agrees that poor work can be hidden temporarily, but describes a strong culture of care among the mentors, colleagues, and leaders he knew. His answer relies on both a human commitment to craft and the longer-term consequences for the firm, rather than claiming that the incentive problem disappears.

Source: 21:34–27:09 ↗

QWhy do some employees react negatively to consultants?

Asian Dad Energy

He thinks some of that reaction comes from management consulting associated with organizational cuts, rather than technical consulting itself. A study of people and processes can lead to redundancy decisions and layoffs, making a consulting team’s arrival feel threatening.

In his own technical engagements, most relationships became positive once people knew one another. He distinguishes the fear created by the situation from a belief that the individuals involved are necessarily unhelpful.

Source: 27:09–29:20 ↗

QWhich period of your career produced the most growth?

Asian Dad Energy

The progression from senior software engineer to senior enterprise architect was the period he valued most. It expanded his work from coding into design, integration, and understanding multiple applications. Strong mentors guided that growth. After director-level work became more about helping leads and selling to executives, he found less enjoyment and less personal growth.

Source: 38:18–39:34 ↗

QWhat lesson from a mentor stayed with you?

Asian Dad Energy

Stay flexible. Adapt to the technology stack, delivery pipeline, client teams, and changing conditions in front of you. In consulting, that ability was a survival skill as well as a way to keep learning.

When did keeping up start to feel harder?

For him, learning new frameworks became slower after about forty. He explicitly recognizes that others have different experiences, including people learning quickly in their fifties. This is his personal account of frustration and adaptation, rather than a general claim about the abilities of older engineers.

Source: 40:23–42:12 ↗
Source: 39:35–40:23 ↗

QHow can an engineer explain their work more clearly?

Asian Dad Energy

Relax the connection between your identity and the topic. He remembers a technically brilliant engineer whose intense attachment to a cache-optimization project made it difficult to explain to a less technical audience.

Take a step back and choose the level of explanation the listener can use. Speaking in the same detail as your own technical thinking can obscure the point. A simpler explanation should help the audience understand what matters and the decision or support you need.

Source: 46:43–49:07 ↗

QWhat would you tell yourself at the beginning?

Asian Dad Energy

Work hard, keep learning, and stay flexible. Those habits connect the earlier consulting career with an uncertain next chapter.

Source: 49:09–49:26 ↗
